8 November 1986_1.Title: Health chiefs to face MPs on complaints by bereaved (423)
8 November 1986_1.Author: MARTIN FLETCHER
8 November 1986_1.chunks: Two district health authorties are to be questioned by a Commons select committee today about their failure 'to give caring and sensitive attention' to the relatives of people who arrived dead at hospitals.The latest findings of the Health Service Commissioner, who described one of the cases as 'a sorry tale of ineptitude with few redeeming features', have shocked MPs on the select committee, which oversees the work of the Ombudsman, and officials from health authorities in Dudley, West Midlands, and Wandsworth, south London, will face tough questioning.The Dudley case concerned a woman whose husband collapsed at home. She mentioned in passing that her husband had previously had hepatitis (two years earlier).It was not made clear that the man had died of heart failure, not hepatitis, and her remark set off 'a series of panic reactions which were to cause great but needless further distress to his family'.First the hospital made two calls to the family in the small hours of the morning seeking details of his medical history.His clothes were incinerated, while his wallet, money, personal papers and photographs 'disappeared without a trace'.The undertakers, warned of a hepatitis risk, stuck vivid yellow tape across the coffin instructing 'danger of infection' and 'burn without opening'.Her request to view her husband's body and have it returned home before the cremation was denied, and, soon after the funeral, environmental health authorities visited her home to burn the settee on which her husband had died as well as his bed, bedding and clothes.When the widow remonstrated, they agreed to fumigate the home, killing all her house plants.The Wandsworeth case concerned a woman who was asked to go to hospital to identify her husband, killed on a motor cycle accident. She was taken into the refrigeration room of the mortuary where the charge nurse 'began to open boxes in the wall and she realized that he was expecting her to identify her husband's body there'.The change nurse, irritated at having to do the work because the porters were on tea break, allegedly complained 'Oh God, have I got to do it properly? ', when police pointed out the widow's distress.The commissioner found the charge nurse guilty of 'uncaring and unsympathetic remarks', while his demeanour 'betrayed a lack of consideration for her feelings'. But the commissioner also upheld her complaint that during her whole time at the hospital, the widow was not once offered 'a cup of tea, a telephone call, a glass of water or any vestige of human sympathy by the nursing staff at the hospital. 'The staff were guilty of 'an unacceptable lack of sympathy'.

December 18, 1986_1.Title: Research funding crucial to quest for Aids vaccine (447)
December 18, 1986_1.Author: PEARCE WRIGHT
December 18, 1986_1.chunks: An increase in government spending, through the Medical Research Council, on research into Aids will intensify the search for a vaccine.The main effect will be to bring together the efforts of experts in viruses working on cancer research with those trying to conquer HIV, the human immunodefiency virus responsible for Aids.More than 20 special research projects, costing just over pounds 2 million, are supported by the Medical Research Council.They include an investigation of the risk of heterosexual spread of the disease via prostitution, scrutiny of the methods for screening blood donations for signs of HIV contamination and a detailed study of every molecule of the Aids virus from which a vaccine could be formulated.The details of possible new directions of research will be explained today by Sir James Gowans, secretary of the Medical Research Council, to a parliamentary select committee.Scientists believe the most likely method of producing a vaccine might be from the blood serum of infected individuals, similar to that pioneered recently for hepatitis-B.The compound contains a fragment of the virus which has nothing to do with the genetic material or potency of the organism, but it is sufficient to stimulate the defence system of the body.The only reason for reluctance by the Department of Health and Social Services to permit more than a limited use of the vaccine is its cost of pounds 70 a treatment.Even if an Aids version was more expensive, the cost would be set against the estimate that care of an Aids patient from onset of illness to death is nearly pounds 20,000.Professor Avrion Mitchison, of University College, London, has appealed for measures to avoid any possible delays for the testing in humans of potential vaccines.But the British Medical Association cautioned yesterday against ill-judged haste in trying experimental vaccines before they have been tested to the proper satisfaction of the Committee on Safety of Medicines.The BMA said there was a confusion sometimes because people believed a vaccine would benefit people already infected, whereas it would only protect others against infection.Nevertheless, the Department of Health gave assurances that no administrative delay would hamper vaccine work.The only treatment is with the Burroughs Wellcome drug AZT, presently under trials and with only sufficient to sustain a course of therapy for 6,000 patients in Europe and the United States.A newer potential treatment is being explored at Cambridge. It involves separating pure extracts of the protective antibodies from the blood serum of people who were HIV-positive but who had not developed the disease.The extract would then be infused into other patients with the illness to help restore their immune system. March 2, 1985_1.Title: Timmins, Nicholas_ More than third of tested homosexuals 'showed evidence of Aids virus'
March 2, 1985_1.Author: No author
March 2, 1985_1.chunks:
More than third of tested homosexuals 'showed evidence of Aids virus'

By Nicholas Timmins; Social Services Correspondent

Over a third of a group of homosexuals attending sexually transmitted disease clinics in London and almost 40 per cent of haemophiliacs tested by the Central Public Health Laboratory have evidence of infection with the Aids virus.

The results suggest that while many individuals with evidence of exposure to Aids virus remain symptom free 'there may soon be a considerable increase in Aids and related disease in Britain', doctors from the Virus Reference Laboratory at the Central Public Health Laboratory in Colindale report in today's British Medical Journal.

Aids infection has become prevalent in homosexuals throughout the country, the team led by Dr Marguerite Pereira, director of the Virus Reference Laboratory, says, and urgent action is needed to limit its spread among both homosexuals and haemophiliacs.

The survey involved testing for antibody to Aids virus in the blood of 282 homosexuals whose blood had been sent for hepatitis B testing.

Thirty-four per cent proved positive, as did tests on five per cent of 955 homosexuals outside London.

Among 81 haemophiliacs whose blood was tested last year, 38 per cent proved positive.

The results, Dr Pereira and her colleagues say, show that since 1980 infection with the Aids virus 'has become well established among British homosexuals attending sexually transmitted disease clinics'.

Among haemophiliacs, while the infection has taken longer to appear, it is more prevalent than in sexually active homosexuals. Among those who have been regularly treated with imported Factor VIII, the clotting agent, about 50 per cent now have antibody to the Aids virus.

About three-quarters of the Factor VIII used in Britain is imported from the United States, where Aids is more common. Because Factor VIII is made up from pools of many thousands of blood donations, a single infected donation can probably contaminate a whole batch, the doctors say.

Dr Pereira and her colleagues said that to limit the spread of the infection, those haemophiliacs without evidence of exposure to Aids virus must be identified and treated with heat-treated Factor VIII.

New resources must also be provided to limit the spread of the infection among homosexuals and drug abusers. While it is impossible to predict how many Aids cases there will be, the trend, which has produced 140 cases; and 61 deaths; is constantly upward, the say, 'with no signs of a plateau'.

Babies may become infected with Aids through breast feeding if their mothers have been exposed to the disease, a group of doctors has claimed (Our Science Correspondent writes).

A baby in Sydney, Australia, probably became infected through breast milk after his mother received a transfusion of blood from a male homosexual, the doctors say in the latest issue of The Lancet.

The man who donated the blood developed Aids 13 months later. The mother was given the transfusion after the delivery of the baby by caesarean section, and breast fed the child for six weeks.

The number of British homosexual men infected with the virus responsible for Aids is at least five-times higher than in 1982, medical researchers reported yesterday at an international conference on the disease (Reuters, AFP report from Atlanta).

The results, reached by a team of nine scientists, indicate that at least 2,600 men in London have been affected.More than third of tested homosexuals 'showed evidence of Aids virus'. By Nicholas Timmins, Social Services Correspondent. The Times (London, England), Friday, Apr 19, 1985; pg. 3; Issue 62116. October 14, 1985_1.Author: No author
October 14, 1985_1.chunks:
BMA guide on Aids safety
Advice on how to avoid Aids (acquired immune deficiency syndrome) and recognize symp-toms of the disease is published in a booklet by the British Medical Association today.
The booklet warns readers against having sexual relations with multiple partners and sharing syringes, razors or other skin cutting instruments.
The disease is spread, like hepatitis B and syphilis, by sexual contact, blood transfusion, syringe needles or other sharp instruments contaminated with infected blood, the booklet says.
Symptoms which may mean a person is suffering from Aids include reduced energy, fever, swollen lymph glands, loss of resistance to infections, and some cancers.
Dr Tony Smith, medical editor of the BMA's Family Doctor Publications, said better understanding would help re-duce anxiety and some mis-taken ideas about Aids.

October 14, 1985_1.Author: SIAN GRIFFITHS
October 14, 1985_1.chunks: MEDICAL staff throughout Wales were alerted this weekend to a serious outbreak of hepatitis among young people. It is believed to have started from the use of dirty syringes stolen from bins at the East Glamorgan general hospital in Pontypridd.More than 50 people, most of them teenagers, have been diagnosed as suffering from the disease in recent weeks and doctors believe that many more cases can be expected. Most have been found on council estates just 200 yards from the 450-bed hospital.The hepatitis is of the 'B' type, which can be highly infectious between people who have close contact or share needles. Health officials admit that the source was almost certainly discarded syringes.Syringes used in the treatment of hospital patients can carry a number of dangerous diseases and there are strict rules governing their disposal. John Hill-Tout, the hospital's administrator, said yesterday that procedures for storing syringes prior to burning had now been tightened up. 'This is a very big hospital with 15 wards and two or three of these bins in every ward,' he said. 'If there are people determined enough, they will be able to steal such things, but we are doing everything possible to prevent this happening. 'Mid Glamorgan health authority yesterday faced calls for an immediate inquiry into how the syringes fell into hands of young people, who used them to inject drugs.Allan Rogers, Labour MP for Rhondda, said yesterday that the availability of syringes would worsen the local drugs problem and that the hospital's failures were a disgrace. 'One would have thought that needles would have been properly disposed of,' he said. 'I shall be calling for a full investigation.' (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 1985

October 14, 1985_1.chunks:
Blood banks may spread Aids illness By Pearce Wright Science Editor

A report of three cases of Aids (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) in haemophiliacs suggests that the incurable infection could have spread from the United States to Europe via blood banks.

The fears have been raised by a letter in the latest issue of The Lancet. It describes the contraction of Aids by three haemophiliacs who were treated with blood which included concentrates from commercial sources of plasma containing Factor VIII, which is the product vital for the stimulation of clotting.

The haemophiliacs who are in hospital in Seville are the first reported cases of Aids in Spain.

A report in the Mail on Sunday that two haemophiliacs, one in London and one in Cardiff, had also contracted the disease through blood transfusions could not be confirmed yesterday by the Department of Health.

Nor have those cases been reported to the Centre for Communicable Diseases, at Colindale, north London, which has established a special Aids monitoring unit.

An appeal to doctors to notify the centre when a case of Aids came under their care was made in the last issue of the British Medical Journal where preliminary findings of 14 patients suffering from the infection in England and Wales were described.

There were no haemophiliac sufferers among those patients, but 11 cases of Aids among haemophiliacs who had all received Factor VIII concentrates have been reported to the United States Centre for Disease Control.

The link with transfusions of Factor VIII concentrates indicates that Aids may be transmitted by a blood-borne virus. Medical staff are being advised to use the same rigorous procedures to avoid infection from handling blood or other human materials of a suspect as they do when treating infectious hepatitis and similar virulent conditions.

The first cases of Aids appeared in the United States almost simultaneously in 1981 among the homosexual populations of New York, San Francisco and Los Angeles.Blood banks may spread Aids illness.
By Pearce Wright Science Editor.

October 14, 1985_1.Author: IOLA SMITH
October 14, 1985_1.chunks: HAEMOPHILIACS who fear catching Aids or hepatitis from using a clotting agent derived from human plasma will be glad to know that an animal alternative is now available.Developed by Speywood Laboratories, a Welsh biotechnology company, and marketed as Hyate C, it is a purified form of porcine Factor 8. October 14, 1985_1.Title: Private health insurer to ban drug abuse and alcoholism patients / Provisi ons of Private Patients Plan provident association (544)
October 14, 1985_1.Author: NICHOLAS TIMMINS
October 14, 1985_1.chunks: Tough new exclusions to private health cover affecting more than 750,000 people insured with Private Patients Plan, Britain's second biggest private halth insurer, are to be announced today.Under the provident association's ravamped personal insurance plan, PPP will no longer pay for long-term kidney dialysis, for any form of investigation of treatment of infertility, or for the treatment of drug abuse or alcoholism. Conditions arising from drug abuse and alcoholism, or associated with them, will also be excluded.The latter exclusions seem to imply that people developing conditions such as cirrhosis of the liver, anaemia, epilepsy, hepatitis, septicaemia, vein inflammations or other conditions that can be associated with drug of alcohol abuse may find themselves or their medical advisers questioned about the cause of the illness.Subscribers wishing to be covered for psychiatric treatment, pregnancy complications, or consultations and diagnostic procedures which are not part of in-patient treatment or out-patient and day case surgery, will have to pay extra 15 per cent in premiums.PPP is trying to control steeply rising costs and claims. As a result increases in subscriptions have been running well ahead of inflation.Mr Roy Forman, managing director of PPP, said the decision to exclude drug abuse and alcoholism was taken after detailed market research showed that people would prefer lower premiums with such conditions excluded.The decision to end long-term kidney dialysis for chronic kidney failure was made because PPP's aim was 'to give insurance for the treatment of illnesses which can be cured, not sustaining people for long periods of treatment for chronic illnesses'. Dialysis for those awaiting transplants, however, would still be covered.The proposals have already brought an angry reaction from parts of the private sector. Mr Peter Marno, administrator of the Hampstead Clinic of Charter Medical, which specializes in drug and alcohol addiction, said: 'PPP is unilaterally taking away cover for any form of private treatment for addiction. Patients are being given no option even to take out extra cover, yet addiction treatment can be very effective.Under PPPs new plan there will be no limit to the amount that can be paid out for treatment which is covered, whereas under the main plan, being replaced there was a limit of pounds 45,000 or 180 days treatment.The British United Provident Association, PPP's main rival, changed its rules to exclude long-term kidney dialysis earlier this year, but it still provides specialist treatment for drug and alcohol abuse up to 180 days or the plan's financial limit.Mr Frank Dobson, Labour's health spokesman, said: 'These exclusions will mean that the NHS will have to provide these often expensive treatments while the private sector continues to crow about its expansion and how it is doing the job when it is not doing anything like all of the job. Private health insurance already excludes many people who are expensive to treat.Subscribers to the British United Provident Association, Britain's biggest private health insurer, face increases in premiums averaging about 11 per cent to 12 per cent from January; double the rate of inflation.Bupa said yesterday that 'medical inflation', the combined effect of private hospital charges, doctors fees, and more high technology medicine, was running at about 15 per cent this year. Bupa provides cover for about 3.2 million people. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 1985

Infection with this blood-borne virus occurs primarily during transfusions.Some 5 per cent of patients receiving blood in the US are said to come into contact with it. Half of them develop chronic hepatitis and a further fifth, cirrhosis of the liver.Biocine's discovery opens the way to a screening test and a vaccine for acute and chronic forms of related liver inflammation.The company has started the scale-up process for biotechnological manufacture of the proteins, permitting the development of immuno-diagnostic agents to screen donor blood and blood products, as well as vaccines to prevent infection. Since this will be a synthetic vaccine, there will be no risk of infection during its manufacture or administration.The next step will be to try to isolate the whole virus to establish its causative role in hepatitis non-A, non-B.An estimated 90 to 95 per cent of all cases of hepatitis arising after blood transfusions are attributed to the non-A, non-B virus, adding up to 150,000 cases annually in the US alone.

Transplant hope as TV host Harty slips into coma
by Jeff Postlewaite and Alan Massam

TV STAR Russell Harty was fighting for his life today suffering from hepatitis and acute liver failure. Doctors expressed grave concern for the 53 year-old BBC presenter and that show host, who is unconscious and in a critical condition. He is being treated in the intensive care unit of St James's University Hospital, Leeds.

Harty spent two weeks last month in Airedeale General Hospital, near his North Yorkshire home, being treated for viral jaundice. A hospital spokesman could not say which strain of hepatitis he is suffering from.

Bachelor Harty, who to TV viewers last saw on BBC's Grand Tour of Europe, could have a liver transplant even though he is so ill a leading specialist said today. Dr Roger Williams, director of the liver unit at King's College Hospital, London, said: 'I imagine that may be being considered.'

'We do a lot of transplants for liver failure at King's and our unit has about a 60-70 per cent survival rate. We do transplants for acute liver failure.' Dr Williams said acute viral hepatitis could be very severe and cause liver failure. About 200 people died as a result each year in Britain.

Hepatitis is an acute inflammation of the liver, which initially causes flu-like symptoms and later progresses to fever, acute fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and loss of appetite.

There are three types: Type A enters the body through water or food; Type B enters via blood transfusions or injections with contaminated syringes; and Type Non-A, Non-B, which again enters through transfusions. The last two types, by far the most dangerous, are highly infectious, and need to be treated by 'barrier nursing' in hospital. Hepatitis B can also be transmitted by sex practices common among homosexuals.

Harty has never made any secret of his unconventional sex life. But friends say he would rather go to bed with a good book than with a lover.

A BBC spokesman said: 'We are all very distressed to hear of Russell's illness. Our thoughts are with him.'

With his camp mannerisms and downright rudeness, Russell Harty's television interviews at their best contain an element of danger that single him out from Parkinson's chat or Wogan's charm. He is best known for his run in with seagurds Grace Jones. The TV host decided that the statuesque pop singer wasn't worth talking to, so she thought she would get her own back by clouting hapless Harty on the head. The drama was wonderful publicity for both entertain-ers and confirmed Russell Harty's status as a household name.

'I'm like a soldier who sometimes injects a tiny bit of poison into the fly,' he said.

And Harty hasn't melted with age. His recent Harty's Grand Tour of Europe series was the subject of a vituperative attack by The Observer's TV critic John Naughton who was amazed that more people hadn't answered Harty's questions with a punch.

Infection with this blood-borne virus occurs primarily during transfusions. Some 5 per cent of patients receiving blood in the US are said to come into contact with it. Half of them develop chronic hepatitis and a further fifth cirrhosis of the liver.Biocine's discovery opens the way to a screening test and a vaccine for acute and chronic forms of related liver inflammation. The company has started the scale-up process for biotechnological manufacture of the proteins, permitting the development of immuno-diagnostic agents to screen donor blood and blood products, as well as vaccines to prevent infection. Since this will be a synthetic vaccine, there will be no risk of infection during its manufacture or administration. The next step will be to try to isolate the whole virus to establish its causative role in hepatitis non-A non-B.An estimated 90 to 95 per cent of all cases of hepatitis arising after blood transfusions are attributed to the non-A non-B virus, adding up to 150,000 cases annually in the US alone. 7 March 1988_1.Title: Obituary of Dr Hans Popper (273)
7 March 1988_1.Author: No author in byline
7 March 1988_1.chunks: Dr Hans Popper, the Viennese-born doyen of liver pathologists the world over, died in New York on May 6 at the age of 84.For 40 years he worked on all aspects of the subject raising it to a major clinicial and scientific speciality. He made important contributions to the fields of auto-immune drug-induced and alcoholic liver disease.In recent years Popper was particularly interested in viral hepatitis, liver transfers and the mefchanisms underlying the development of cirrhosis. He contributeed work until a few weeks before his death.Amongst his research Poper showed that the liver was the only organ in the human body which does not deteriorate with age. This bad major ramifications for liver transplants.Popper, who went to work in the United States because of the Navis, was a frequent visitor and lecturer at the University of London, chiefly at the Royal Free Hospital.He was renowned as a teacher and trained many as today's leading international figures in his field.Popper's scientific eminence went with a powerful personality and a strong Viennese accent, which showed no trace of the time he had spent at Oxford as a postgraduate many years before.Audiences often had to struggle to follow his words but he delighted to point out even German-speaking audiences experienced the same problem with his native German.Popper had founded the American Association for the Study of Liver Disease in 1949 and the International Assoication for the Study of Liver Disease in 1949 and the International Association nine years later.He is survived by his wife, Lina, and two sons. 7 March 1988_1.Title: Cash boost for new vaccines (351)
7 March 1988_1.Author: Our Service Editor
7 March 1988_1.chunks: British scientists who pioneered a method of designing vaccines to protect against viral infection have been awarded research grants of Pounds 225,000 to develop vaccines of Aids and infectious hepatitis.Research groups working with Professor Jeffrey Almond, of the department of microbiology, Reading University, and Dr Philip Minor, of the Institute for Biological Standards and Control, Hertfordshire, are also seeking to develop innoculations against the common cold, the recently-recognized post-viral fatigue syndrome, known as ME, the chlamydia organism, which causes blindness, and other viruses.They are seeking to devise an antidote to the Aids virus for the Medical Research Council and against infectious hepatitis for the World Health Organization.Professor Almond said yesterday there should be enough information in four to six months to know whether the method could produce effective, commercial vaccines.The desinger vaccines will be based on a method perfected in the laboratory for altering the established vaccine against poliomyelitis infection.Dr Minor said they worked with the poliomyelitis vaccine because it is so effective in endowing protecton. Another advantage of using it for Aids is that it should produce protective antibodies in the linings of the vagina and anus, as well as in blood.This offers a possible first line of defence and night lessen the chances of infection from already infected sexual partners.In practice, the polio vaccine consists of a combination of the three inert strains of the virus.The scientists have found that with genetic engineering they can transfer characteristics important for making vaccine between the three polio viruses, thereby creating a single new antidote against infection.The principle they have evoluved, published in the journal, Nature, is the basis on which the research grants were awarded to continue the work.The goal of the new research is to redesign the polio vaccine by changing just 60 of its 7,500 molecules. However, the alteration to a tiny part of the envelop, or coating, of the polio virus would imitate one of the structures found on the coating of the Aids virus.

14 August 1988_1.Title: Epidemics threaten cholera-hit Delhi;India
14 August 1988_1.Author: No author in byline
14 August 1988_1.chunks: Delhi (Reuter) - Typhoid and hepatitis are threatening to follow the cholera epidemic raging in Delhi.Doctors gave this warning yesterday as city officials accused each other of criminal negligence in allowing the health crisis to arise.By yesterday, in the month since monsoon rains brought cholera to the slums of east Delhi, city officials said 215 people had died. Hospitals are littered with victims. The rains sent sewage seeping into the water supply, pumped up by slum residents from government-installed handpumps.``Cholera is the water-borne disease that takes hold first, but typhoid and hepatitis thrive in the same filthy conditions,'' a doctor at the World Health Organization said. ``There is a very real danger that they will surface in east Delhi on the same scale cholera has done. ''In the worst-hit area, where sewage raked from open drains lies in stinking heaps by the road, typhoid and hepatitis are already on the rise. Mr K. Agarwal, head of a hospital surrounded by slums, said: ``My doctors tell me there has been an increase in both diseases, but we have yet to determine the scale of it. ''Political heads have rolled since the Prime Minister, Mr Rajiv Gandhi, visited east Delhi on July 22 and said he was appalled by the squalor.Health, development and administrative bodies have accused each other of criminal negligence in allowing a third of the capital's people to live in desperately unhealthy conditions. On Friday the Lieutenant-Governor of Delhi, the city's chief executive, resigned; health officials have also been replaced.The opposition has accused the Government of sinking dangerously shallow pumps, which now spew out contaminated water, just before the 1984 general election.CALCUTTA: Adulterated cooking oil has paralysed more than 400 people below the waist, made thousands ill, and spread panic throughout this city of 10 million people (Reuter reports). The first victims were diagnosed a fortnight ago, and new cases are being reported every day. The oil, contaminated with insecticide, was distributed through the government-controlled food stores in the capital of West Bengal. ``Somebody has been doing this deliberately,'' the Information Minister, Mr Bhuddadev Bhattacharya, said. Eleven people have been arrested.

Blood test for rare hepatitis considered

By Our Health Services Correspondent

THE Department of Health is considering 'screening blood supplies for a new form of hepatitis to ensure the greater safety of blood transfusions, it was disclosed yesterday.

A test for the virus responsible for Hepatitis C has been developed in California and is being evaluated in Britain by scientists at the National Blood Transfusion Service.

A Department of Health spokeswoman said Hepatitis C was an extremely rare disease suffered by 0.7 per cent of the population, but the American study had shown the virus responsible was carried by 10 per cent of the population.

She said: "We have not been able to screen blood for this condition until now because no test was available that would identify it. Now that a test has become available, we are considering using it to screen blood supplies to make transfusions even safer than they are at present."

April 21, 1989_1.Author: No author found
April 21, 1989_1.chunks: Hepatitis blood test may hit transfusions By Celia Hall Medical Editor Leaders of European blood transfusion services and leading haematologists will meet next month to assess a new test that detects the liver disease Hepatitis C. Transfusion services stand to lose thousands of pints of donated blood if the screening is taken up internationally. However, the test, developed in the United States and available here for less than two months, has raised as many questions as it appeared to answer. It is hoped that an assessment of thousands of screened blood donations and patients with liver problems will provide more information. Using the method, Hepatitis C was found in 1 in 150 of 9,000 British blood samples, and the West Germans have had similar results with 5,000 tests, said Dr Harold Gunson, national director of the UK Blood Transfusion Service. This could mean that 15,000 donations a year, or 0.75 per cent of donated British blood, would no longer be acceptable. However, Dr Gunson said the test was not necessarily specific to Hepatitis C, which can cause a range of problems from mild illness to cirrhosis of the liver. This may result in an unknown number of false positive results, denying the service donors and alarming some with the knowledge they may have Hepatitis C. "What this means is that all of these people may not necessarily carry the disease, be ill, or transmit it in their blood," Dr Gunson said. "We need confirmatory tests to tell us if the screening is really picking up anti-bodies."

The Guardian (London)

August 24, 1989

Dilemma on virus blood test

BYLINE: By AILEEN BALLANTYNE, Medical Correspondent

LENGTH: 736 words

 
 EVERY pint of blood donated in Britain may have to be screened for a newly-isolated form of hepatitis for which a test has just been developed.
 Random tests on the national blood supply over the last month have shown that up to 6,000 people last year may have received blood transfusions contaminated with hepatitis C.
 The pilot study, carried out by the National Blood Transfusion Service, which came to light as a result of inquiries by the Guardian, revealed that up to one in 100 blood donors was carrying the virus. There is no known treatment.
 The virus is transmitted through blood and is thought to be one of the main causes of unexplained cases of viral hepatitis which have in the past developed after blood transfusions. 
 Although hepatitis C (HPC) often has no symptoms, about 10 per cent of those infected can develop cirrhosis of the liver, which is likely to prove fatal within 10 years.
 Health ministers will have to decide whether to introduce screening, which could seriously deplete the already falling number of blood donors.
 The alternative is to continue to risk the safety of the national blood supply.
 Officials from the Department of Health yesterday met representatives of Ortho Diagnostics Systems, an American company based in High Wycombe, which has developed a test for HPC.
 Government health advisers on blood transfusion, virology and liver disease are to meet the chief medical officer, Sir Donald Acheson, in October. He will advise ministers whether to go ahead with the testing programme.
 Ministers will also have to decide on the need to check supplies of stored blood plasma for hepatitis C now that a test is available.
 Supplies are already kept 'in quarantine' for several months before use in case a patient who has given blood develops hepatitis B, for which donated blood is already screened.
 A 10 per cent fall in blood donations over the last four years has meant that while there is enough blood for emergencies, operations such as hip replacements, knee joint replacements, or liver transplants often have to be delayed because of shortages.
 Professor Harold Gunson, national director of the Blood Transfusion Service, said: 'We don't know how infectious HPC is when it is passed on through blood. But the technology for testing for many infections in blood is now advancing rapidly.
 'We are looking very carefully at the option of introducing the test for all blood donated. At present we are discussing with the manufacturers the results of the tests.
 'We want to do everything we can from the patients' point of view to ensure the maximum protection of the blood supply.'
 Experts believe HPC may be transmitted sexually as well as through blood. If so, it is thought to be far less easy to transmit through sexual intercourse than HIV, the virus that leads to Aids.
 Random screening of more than 5,000 pints of blood donated throughout the country in the last month is understood to have been carried out with the donors' consent.
 They were simply asked to consent to checks being made on their blood for 'markers' of non-A and non-B hepatitis.
 This is the name scientists used for post-blood transfusion cases of hepatitis before the HPC virus was isolated using genetic engineering techniques.
 It is not clear whether or not the people found to have antibodies to HPC will be contacted by doctors. 'People who have been giving blood freely for many years are now going to be told 'you may be carrying a virus which could kill you in 10 years time',' a leading blood transfusion expert said yesterday.
 Professor Howard Thomson, a liver expert at St Mary's Hospital in London, and the main UK expert on hepatitis C, said yesterday that its presence in the general population was likely to be up to 5 per cent.
 The HPC test will add an estimated Pounds 2 to the cost of each of the three million pints of blood collected every year in Britain. At present the cost of producing each pint of blood is about Pounds 25.
 The pilot study showed that up to 1 per cent of blood donors have antibodies for HPC. This means about 30,000 pints of the three million donated in Britain each year may be contaminated with the virus.
 Each transfusion takes around five pints of blood, so up to 6,000 people are likely to have received blood from donors carrying HPC this year.

April 21, 1989_1.chunks: Hepatitis: Dangers Minimized A blood expert has moved quickly to correct an impression that people receiving transfusions face a big risk of developing the liver disease hepatitis. Dr. Harold Gunson, director of the National Blood Transfusion Service, was responding to a report in The Guardian suggesting that 6,000 people in the last year could have received blood contaminated with the hepatitis C virus. He said that the blood transfusion service had tested 9,000 samples and found that less than one percent was positive for hepatitis C. Moreover, the infection was "one of the milder forms of the disease, more commonly known as Non-A and Non-B hepatitis." The true number of contaminated samples was thought to be even lower because the test only registers antibodies to the virus rather than the virus itself. "If I needed a blood transfusion tomorrow, I would have one," said Dr. Gunson. "The chances of a complication are very small." Dr. Gunson said that the test for hepatitis C had only become available within the past few years and was currently being evaluated in Britain.

April 21, 1989_1.Title: Appeal for action on blood checks
April 21, 1989_1.Author: AILEEN BALLANTYNE
April 21, 1989_1.chunks: THE Government was urged yesterday to carry out an immediate review of international evidence on the newly-developed test for the hepatitis C virus to ensure the national blood supply is protected. The recommendation came from the British Medical Association, which represents Britain's doctors. It follows disclosure by the Guardian that the Government is considering screening every pint of blood donated in the UK for the virus, which can in some cases lead to the disease hepatitis C and fatal liver failure. Dr Vivienne Nathanson, assistant secretary of the BMA's science and ethics division, said that blood donors should also be given 'clear, well defined advice' from the Government on the exact meaning of a positive test for the recently isolated hepatitis C virus, so as to allay anxiety. If the test proved reliable. this would allow those found to be carrying the virus to receive expert treatment and counselling 'at the earliest possible opportunity'. But Dr Marcela Contreras, director of the North London Blood Transfusion Centre, who carried out a pilot study of the test on more than 5,000 blood donors, writes in a letter in today's issue of the Lancet that 'precipitate action' in using the test to screen donors should be avoided. She warns of the 'enormous and costly undertaking' involved in contacting up to 25,000 of the 2.5 million donors who give blood every year. The pilot study using the new test found that up to one in every 100 blood donors is the tested positive for the hepatitis C virus (HPC). Dr Contreras was commenting on a leading article in the Lancet earlier this month, which concluded that results from the new tests in Germany, Spain and Holland showed that the test was 'sensitive and specific'. The Lancet suggested that the results 'underline the urgency of making the system available for donor blood screening.' Dr Harold Gunson, national director of the Blood Transfusion Service, said yesterday that availability of the test for the hepatitis C virus could make the blood supply the UK even safer, provided that it proves to be a suitable test. A spokesman for the Department of Health said the UK's blood supply was considered one of the safest in the world. 'We are continuing to investigate ways of making it safer still.' Along with other countries, the National Blood Transfusion Service was 'examining all available data' before making a decision on extending testing to all donated blood. Dr Nathanson added that those found to be carrying the hepatitis C virus after their blood was screened might consider liver function tests. The Guardian (London)

August 24, 1989

Hepatitis A is common in developing countries

LENGTH: 247 words

 
 HEPATITIS A is common in developing countries and areas where there is poor hygiene.
 It can be transmitted orally or through faeces but is usually picked up from contaminated water. Symptoms include flu and mild jaundice. It can cause liver failure but this is much less common than in hepatitis B or hepatitis C.
 Hepatitis B is transmitted almost exclusively through sexual intercourse and through blood. It is thought to lead to fatal liver failure in about one in 500 cases.
 It is transmitted far more easily than HIV, the virus that leads to Aids. Most sufferers make a complete recovery within three to four months but about 5 per cent will become carriers of the disease. Its symptoms include nausea, anorexia and vomiting which eventually culminate in jaundice.
 Hepatitis C used to be known as non-A, non-B hepatitis because the virus which caused it had not been isolated. Those infected with the virus often have no symptoms, but when it leads to acute viral hepatitis it can cause liver failure and death. These immediate, acute consequences of infection are rarer than with hepatitis B.
 The most worrying aspects of hepatitis C are its long term consequences. In an estimated 10 per cent of cases, those infected with the virus can go on to develop fatal liver failure within 10 to 20 years. Experts do not yet know how easily hepatitis C can be transmitted through blood - or whether or not it can be transmitted through sexual intercourse.

April 21, 1989_1.Title: Leading Article: Trouble in the blood stream
April 21, 1989_1.Author: No author in byline
April 21, 1989_1.chunks: THE EIGHTIES are proving a troubled decade for the blood transfusion service. So the discovery, first reported on our front page yesterday, of a new form of hepatitis virus which could infect one in every hundred blood donors confronts it with a dilemma it could well do without. Pressures have already mounted in the blood donation world from every direction. Scientific and technical staff, dismayed at low pay and poor prospects, have left the service in droves. The often chaotic regional fragmentation of the system in England and Wales (Scotland has a nationwide system) produced delays and shortages affecting vital operations which moved the Government last year to reorganise it centrally, a move which under the guidance of Dr Harold Gunson now seems to be getting results. Above all, there has been Aids, which has necessitated a reorganisation of screening procedures and which, most alarmingly of all, has led to a sharp drop in blood donation, especially among poorer people. All of which had already forced the service to start a rethink of its public relations needs. The problem of the newly isolated hepatitis C virus adds a further disturbing element to this catalogue. If the random tests carried out by the National Blood Transfusion Service are correct, then as many as 25,000 of the 2.5 million registered blood donors in this country could be carrying the blood-transmitted virus which, in turn, can eventually kill up to 10 per cent of those infected. As a result of these findings, it is now estimated that 6,000 people last year alone may have been given contaminated blood transfusions. That in itself is serious enough, but the real headache for the authorities is that, in order to find out which donors are actually affected, it must decide whether to screen all future blood donations, as well as existing stocks, for the HPC virus. That would be time consuming for staff and would add approximately Pounds 2 per pint to the existing Pounds 25 per pint production cost, producing a total extra cost of approximately Pounds 6 million. Obviously, it would also eventually mean the loss of the infected donors to the service. Additionally, the episode might risk creating a more general deterrent to other existing or potential donors at a difficult time. Donations have fallen by an alarming 10 per cent in the past four years. With the Department of Health increasingly recognising the seriousness of the blood shortage problem - it is playing havoc with some transplant timetables - there must inevitably be some temptation, both on cost and public relations grounds, to decide to turn a blind eye to the case for screening. That would, though, be an unacceptable conclusion for the Department of Health to adopt when it meets to draw up its response in October. Blood donations are already tested for three other serious infections: syphilis, hepatitis B and HIV. There is now no technical reason why HPC should not be added to the screening list. To do so would remove the risk of infection which, on the basis of last year's figures, may ultimately cause 600 critical liver failures every year. It would also, no less importantly, help to bolster public confidence in the blood transfusion service. That confidence is not lost yet - the public rightly has high levels of faith in the service - but it is already more vulnerable than it was a decade ago, and the HPC threat will weaken it significantly, as HIV has already done, if it is not now dealt with effectively. April 21, 1989_1.Title: Hepatitis test 'may deter blood donors'
April 21, 1989_1.Author: AILEEN BALLANTYNE
April 21, 1989_1.chunks: UP TO one in 100 blood donors may learn that they are carrying a virus that could kill them within 10 years if the Government decides to screen all donated blood for the newly isolated hepatitis C. The alternative to identifying and turning away those infected is to risk passing an untreatable disease to transfusion recipients. Blood transfusion experts fear that screening will discourage the already rapidly diminishing number of donors from coming forward. Although doctors believe hepatitis C (HPC) is likely to be transmitted through blood and by sexual intercourse, they do not know the extent of the risk. As yet there is no hard evidence that HPC is sexually transmitted. The most immediate concern facing the Department of Health is how to set up a mechanism and find the staff to tell donors carrying antibodies to hepatitis C what it will mean for them. 'The resource implications are enormous,' said Dr Marcela Contreras, who carried out a random screening study for the virus for the National Blood Transfusion Service. About three million pints of blood are collected from donors every year in the UK. The average transfusion requires about five pints of blood. The random tests in centres including London, the North-west and South-west, found between one in 200 and one in 100 people are likely to be carrying antibodies to the HPC virus. Unlike the HIV test, there is still no second confirmatory test for HPC, but Dr Contreras said the presence of antibodies meant it was 'very likely' that the individual was carrying the virus. HPC has been isolated as a result of genetic engineering techniques. The virus is thought to be responsible for a large number of unexplained cases of hepatitis following blood transfusions. Before the virus was isolated it was known simply as 'non-A, non-B hepatitis'. Dr Brian McClelland, director of the South-east Scotland blood transfusion service, said doctors had simply relied on diagnostic techniques to classify the disease as non-A, non-B hepatitis. Even now that HPC has been isolated, there might still be other types of the hepatitis virus. The blood supply in the UK is still regarded as one of the safest in the world. One of the main reasons is that there are no payments, free meals or lottery tickets for blood donors so there is no financial motivation for them not to declare they are, for example, drug addicts and therefore more likely to be at risk of a virus which can be transmitted through blood such as hepatitis or HIV, the virus that leads to Aids. Dr McClelland points out that since 1970 in the US, when payments were stopped for all 'whole blood' used in direct transfusions, the incidence of hepatitis B in recipients went down significantly. Payment is now only offered in the US for blood that will be used to make plasma to make Factor 8 for haemophiliacs, for example. Since 1947 all blood donated in the UK has been screened for syphilis. Screening for hepatitis B was introduced in 1970 and screening for HIV in 1985. Donors in the UK are asked not to give blood if, among other things, they have had homosexual intercourse, sex with a prostitute or if they inject drugs. The self-selection process appears to be successfully excluding HIV. Doctors are now picking up only about one HIV positive result a month from tests given to all blood donors. But the real dilemma facing the Government and the leading virologists now advising health ministers is in balancing the safety of the national blood supply with the fear that by rejecting one in 100 donors, the shortage could create a crisis of its own. 'It is amazing how many people simply say to me at parties, 'Oh no, I'm not a blood donor',' said Dr Contreras. 'I say to them - what do you think would happen if you were run over by a bus?. Why should other people give blood for you if you wouldn't give it for them?' April 21, 1989_1.Title: Aids study supports fears of deadly nature of virus
April 21, 1989_1.Author: Pearce Wright
April 21, 1989_1.chunks: Fears that all people infected with the Aids virus will eventually develop the disease are strengthened by the latest results from the longest study in monitoring the virus.The conclusions presented yesterday by Dr George Rutherford, of the San Francisco department of public health, to the Fifth International Conference on Aids, meeting in Montreal, Canada, were based on data showing that 10 years after their initial infection with the human immuno-deficiency virus, HIV, 54per cent of a group of nearly 6,700 homosexual and bisexual men had developed full-blown Aids.Although Aids was not recognized as a disease until 1981, the San Francisco health department started collecting blood samples from a large group of local men in 1978 as part of a study of hepatitis.The blood samples are the earliest available evidence of the presence of HIV in the United States, where there are nearly 95,000 cases of the disease and an estimated 1.5 million carriers of HIV.The study has shown that the risk of an infected individual developing the full-blown disease is ``quite low'' in the first years after infection, but increases with time. One year after infection, the risk of disease was zero. After four years it was 10per cent, and after nine it was 43per cent.Dr Rutherford said that treatment with AZT, the only drug available to reduce the spread of the virus after infection, and other therapies ``may significantly alter'' the onset of the disease. Health experts at the conference, however, are divided about the best way to halt its apparently relentless spread. Several million people are infected with HIV worldwide.Dr Rutherford said a few men in the study who were infected at least eight years ago have remained totally free of symptoms. Scientists would continue to monitor the group to see whether any escaped.Some hopeful news came from teams in London, Amsterdam and Tacoma, Washington State, who reported on the success of needle and syringe exchange programmes for intravenous drug users, now regarded as being most at risk of contracting and spreading the infection through needle sharing.An evaluation of the busiest exchange scheme in London, given by Dr Graham Hart, of Middlesex Hospital, showed that there were an average of 257 participants who made about 762 visits each month.The programme dispensed 8,950 needles and syringes, of which 6,918, were exchanged.On entry, seven of 121 addicts, or 6per cent, were HIV-infected and they reported sharing equipment with twice as many intravenous drug users as those who were not HIV-infected. Intravenous drug users account for a growing proportion of Aids cases in the US and Europe.Nevertheless, the experts have clashed this week over possible measures to stop the epidemic. A serious disagreement flared after Dr Stephen Joseph, the health commissioner for the city of New York, proposed an end to anonymous testing for HIV. He recommended that all people found infected should be confidentially reported to the health authorities.A team of health workers would then trace any other people with whom the carriers had had sexual relations or shared needles.Dr James Mason, the US assistant secretary of health, came out against mandatory efforts to trace the partners of Aids-infected people. He was opposed to removing anonymous Aids testing. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 1989

29 June 1989_1.Title: Protest fear leads to silence over Aids ward;Scotland
29 June 1989_1.Author: Mark Whittet
29 June 1989_1.chunks: SCOTLAND'S biggest health board is withholding the opening date of a ward for patients suffering from full-blown Aids and HIV-related diseases for fear of protest demonstrations, writes Mark Whittet.The ward is set to open sometime during August at Ruchill Hospital in Glasgow, but the city's health board has declined to name the day because of concerns over public safety.When the board started a needle exchange at the hospital last year for syringes used by drug addicts, there were public demonstrations.Greater Glasgow Health Board said that the protests proved so damaging that for a year few people used the facility.As a result, it has refused to publicise the opening of the Ruchill ward, but Dr Campbell Love, a consultant in the hopsital's communicable diseases unit, last week confirmed that the purpose-built ward will start ``sometime'' in August.Funded by the Scottish Home and Health Department at a cost of Pounds 500,000, the 15-bed ward will be the first of its kind in the west of Scotland, following a similar 15-bed facility in Edinburgh's City Hospital and another 10-bed unit in Dundee.Love stressed that the Ruchill ward had not been designed specifically for Aids patients.He said: ``There has been a lot of speculation and some misconception about this unit.``Our instructions from the Scottish Home and Health Department were that 15 beds should be made available in Glasgow to cope with the expected increase in west central Scotland in HIV related diseases over the next few years.``This ward is our response to that request. But we are not intending to segregate Aids patients. The unit will also accommodate patients suffering from a number of infectious diseases, including those who are HIV-positive or have hepatitis. ''Love added that the aim of the specialised ward was to promote a better and more efficient service for sufferers, but said that although the statistics were escalating in the Edinburgh area, the increase in Strathclyde had been lower than predicted.Scottish Office figures published last month showed 102 Aids cases in Scotland, which resulted in the deaths of exactly half. A total of 1,668 Scots were reported to be HIV positive.Earlier this year, residents in Edinburgh's Niddrie housing estate protested after Princess Diana opened a Pounds 130,000 centre for Aids sufferers. Householders have since tried to leave the area for fear of catching the virus from resident drug-addicts.Last month, as reported in The Sunday Times, the Scottish Office authorised screening of a public information film at Edinburgh's Saughton prison to combat widespread myths about how the disease is spread, the first such move in the UK.

29 June 1989_1.Title: Patients heal own incisions;Innovation
29 June 1989_1.Author: Anne Moffat
29 June 1989_1.chunks: SURGICAL glue made from a patient's own blood is being used to close wounds too delicate for ordinary sutures. The adhesive is made from two natural blood clotting chemicals, fibrinogen, which is taken from the patient's blood, and bovine thrombin, which is taking from cow blood and is used routinely to promote clotting during surgery.In the operating theatre, the two are combined to make a rubbery, white clot. The glue is eventually reabsorbed by healing tissue. The adhesive is especially useful in microsurgery where a suture or staple would damage delicate tissue, says Dr Leslie Silberstein of the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia. Such procedures include, for example, middle ear surgery, corneal transplants and skin grafts.The idea for a human glue was inspired by Austrian research, which produced an adhesive derived from a large pool of donated blood. ``Our glue is unique because it is the first blood-based adhesive developed from the patients' own blood,'' says Silberstein. This system, he claims, avoids the threat of transmitting hepatitis and the Aids virus via donated blood.Production begins when patients give a few small phials of blood to the hospital's blood bank. The plasma, the blood's clear fluid that contains the clotting factors, is separated out. The all-important fibrinogen is removed from this fraction and stored at sub-zero temperatures.When the fibrinogen is needed for surgery, it is thawed and, in the operating theatre, is activated by adding thrombin. A mucilaginous, fast-holding glue is formed.The Pennsylvania glue was first used experimentally to bind together tiny structures in the ears of chinchillas, the squirrel-like South American animals whose ears are structurally similar to those of humans.A first round of human clinical trials, where the glue was used to repair ear damage, has been successfully completed. 19 November 1989_1.Title: NHS LABORATORY STAFF TO BALLOT ON PAY OFFER OF 6.5%.
19 November 1989_1.Author: No author in byline
19 November 1989_1.chunks: The National Health Service faces the prospect of further disruption with 18,000 medical laboratory staff being balloted on industrial action over the same 6.5 per cent pay offer rejected by ambulance crews.These skilled workers in hospital laboratories, blood transfusion centres and public health laboratories, provide diagnostic information for medical staff. They analyse blood and urine samples for diseases such as AIDS and hepatitis, conduct cervical cancer screening, and carry out post mortems and immunology tests.MSF, the general technical union which represents 13,000 of the laboratory staff, is balloting its members on the suspension of non-emergency weekend working and on daily one-hour strikes. It has recommended acceptance of the action. The ballot result should be known on November 8.The three other unions involved - the Nalgo and Nupe public service unions and the Cohse health service union - are balloting their members on the daily one-hour strikes. If the action is approved, the impact on patients across the country 'would be considerable,' John Chowcat, MSF national officer, said yesterday.The proposed action would not stop the pathology service, but would mean an increasingly slow turn-round. The NHS laboratory staff had fallen far behind their opposite numbers in the scientific civil service and even further behind staff in the private sector.It was getting increasingly hard to attract young people with good science 'O' and 'A' levels with trainee rates starting at 4,600. Top grade medical laboratory scientific officers (15,000 of the 18,000 staff involved) are paid between 7,500 and 9,000. The other groups are medical laboratory assistants, cytology screeners and mortuary pathology technicians. (c) The Financial Times Limited 1989.

19 November 1989_1.Title:
, Thursday

A to E of hepatitis; Medical Briefing
19 November 1989_1.Author: No author found
19 November 1989_1.chunks:
The Times (London)

November 30 1989, Thursday

A to E of hepatitis; Medical Briefing

BYLINE: Dr THOMAS STUTTAFORD

SECTION: Issue 63565.

LENGTH: 634 words

 
 The bewitching smile with which the toddler Linda Prime rewarded the staff at Addenbrookes Hospital, Cambridge, as she left after her successful liver transplant, as well as the tragic failure of the battle to save the life of Mrs Aisling Barnett, has highlighted liver disease in general and transplants in particular.
 Mrs Barnett's case was comparatively unusual; she suffered acute liver failure after taking a very properly prescribed drug. Most drugs are detoxified in the liver; unfortunately, in occasional cases the liver tissue is unusually sensitive to them and liver damage, and even necrosis, occurs.
 The great majority of people, excluding those who suffer from alcoholic cirrhosis, who reach the progressive end stage of liver failure the point at which the physician can offer no more help, and only transplant surgery gives a chance of survival are not suffering from an idiosyncratic response to medical treatment, but from the late effects of viral hepatitis or auto-immune chronic liver disease. 
 Three national liver units are funded by central government. They are able to perform about 250 transplant operations a year. Last year the Royal Free Hospital in London, which has had an international reputation for the treatment of liver disease for nearly 40 years, allocated cash from its own resources to help deal with the thousands of patients in this country who are in severe liver failure, and whose only chance of survival depends on a transplant. A team led by Mr Keith Rolles undertook 23 operations 17 patients survived. Of the 23, 21 were suffering from late viral hepatitis or auto-immune disease.
 Transplants can help a few individuals, but the major impact on the death rate from liver failure can only be achieved when heavy drinkers monitor their intake, and when medical science finds ways to limit the spread of hepatitis.
 Until the late 1940s all cases of viral hepatitis were lumped together as catarrhal jaundice, but by the 1950s it was realized that there were at least two separate diseases, infectious hepatitis and serum hepatitis. Doctors now distinguish the many different types of viral hepatitis by assigning them a letter: we already have hepatitis A, B, C, D and E.
 The original infectious hepatitis is hepatitis A, and blood tests have shown 50 per cent of British people have at some time been infected with it, even though many will not have noticed an attack of jaundice. Hepatitis A is caused by a virus related to the polio virus. It is spread by infected sewage, contaminated water and unwashed hands in the kitchen. Hepatitis B is a totally different virus, only related to various animal viruses. It is a serious disease spread by blood and other body fluids including semen; it is endemic in the Third World, where it is transmitted from mother to child soon after birth. In Britain it is commonly found in health care workers, homosexuals and prostitutes. Ten per cent fail to make a full recovery, and may eventually develop cirrhosis or cancer of the liver.
 Hepatitis D is a virus which can exist only in conjunction with an established hepatitis B infection; it enhances the ill effects of the hepatitis B, and may, if the disease has become quiescent, cause a relapse.
 Hepatitis C has recently been isolated; it is usually spread by blood transfusion, probably occasionally by sexual intercourse. When the attack is severe enough to cause jaundice, it will in 50 per cent of cases give rise to chronic hepatitis, progressive liver failure and later, in an alarmingly high proportion, cancer of the liver.
 The hepatitis E virus is related to the yellow fever virus, but is not insect borne but spread by faulty sewage disposal. Outbreaks have occurred recently in Mexico, Delhi and parts of China.

23 November 1989_1.Title: Tests reveal liver disease treatment.
23 November 1989_1.Author: By Celia Hall, Medical Editor
23 November 1989_1.chunks: Scientists in the United States have discovered a treatment for the liver disease believed to be responsible for 90 per cent of cases of hepatitis that follow blood transfusions. Half of the patients responded to treatment with interferon, some to low doses. Mild flu-like side effects disappeared quite quickly.

February 26, 1991_1.Title: International Company News: Abbott Laboratories climbs 10%
February 26, 1991_1.Author: By KAREN ZAGOR
February 26, 1991_1.chunks: ABBOTT Laboratories, the Chicago-based pharmaceuticals and healthcare company, yesterday turned a 10.6 per cent rise in fourth-quarter net income to Dollars 279.6m from Dollars 253m in 1989. Sales jumped 17.1 per cent to Dollars 1.71bn from Dollars 1.45bn a year ago. The company had fewer shares outstanding in the latest quarter, and earnings per share grew 14 per cent to 65 cents from 57 cents. For the whole of 1990, Abbott's net profits improved 12.3 per cent to Dollars 965.8m from Dollars 859.8m. Earnings per share rose to Dollars 2.22 from Dollars 1.93. Sales in 1990 advanced to Dollars 6.16bn from Dollars 5.38bn. Mr Duane Burnham, chairman and chief executive, attributed the improved performance to higher unit sales worldwide from each of Abbott's main businesses, significant new product introductions and results from the company's continuing emphasis on improving productivity. During the year, the rate of return on shareholders' investment was 34.7 per cent, against 33.1 per cent in 1989. Sales of pharmaceutical and nutritional products rose 13.5 per cent in 1990 to Dollars 3.16bn. In the US, sales increased 10.2 per cent to Dollars 3.84bn, while sales in international markets, including direct exports from the US, surged 22.4 per cent to Dollars 2.32bn. Abbott is benefiting from a growing stable of new medications. During 1990, the company received approval from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to market its blood screening test to detect hepatitis C. The hepatitis C virus is said to be the most prevalent transfusion-related disease in the developed world.

February 26, 1991_1.Title: Victims to sue in new infected blood scandal.
February 26, 1991_1.Author: by Caroline Lees and Margarette Driscoll
February 26, 1991_1.chunks: Health service patients infected with a new and potentially fatal virus through NHS blood are to sue the government for compensation. Solicitors are preparing claims on behalf of at least 10 people who have contracted hepatitis C, and many more are expected to come forward. The virus causes liver cancer and kills 700 people in Britain every year. A high incidence of infection has been found in kidney patients, who regularly receive blood transfusions, and haemophiliacs. Those given emergency transfusions after accidents or during operations are also at risk. The new claims come after a hard-fought victory by Aids-infected haemophiliacs, who won a #42m out-of-court settlement from the government last year after contracting the fatal disease through NHS blood products. Payments are expected to begin in June. Health ministers have now ordered that all blood donors should be screened for hepatitis C, and have advised the National Blood Transfusion Service to give the virus the same priority as HIV, the Aids virus. Testing of donors has been routine in America, West Germany, Sweden and France for more than a year. Hepatitis C, identified in 1989, is believed to be carried by one in 200 donors. Every year, 750,000 people in Britain receive 22m pints of blood. Research by Dr Iain Murray-Lyon, a consultant physician at Charing Cross hospital, London, showed that 11% of patients in the hospital's chronic renal unit had the virus. "All the patients had received multiple blood transfusions and although we cannot say where the virus came from, we suspect it was transfusions," he said. Almost all of Britain's 5,000 haemophiliacs, who receive long-term treatment with blood-related products, have become infected with hepatitis C, and are in the forefront of the new legal action. They claim that the government was aware of the existence of hepatitis in the blood supply but failed to do enough to tackle the problem. "They have had a long time to get the blood supply in this country right but nobody has bothered," said Peter Mossman, a retired coach-driver from Manchester, who intends to pursue a claim against Central Manchester Health Authority and the Department of Health. Mossman, diagnosed as a haemophiliac in 1976, was told 18 months ago that he was suffering from chronic hepatitis C, likely to end in fatal liver disease. He is angry and perplexed that he must bear the burden of a second debilitating condition on top of haemophilia. "Even before I was told I had the virus I knew that something was wrong," he said. "I began to get terrible bouts of exhaustion, headaches and horrible abdominal pain." Those such as Mossman, 47, who intend to put their cases before the courts, may have a long struggle to prove negligence against their health authorities. Hepatitis, previously identified in two strains, A and B, has long been recognised as a risk in treating patients with blood and related products. Doctors judged that the benefits of using such treatment on patients with chronic diseases outweighed the risk. In late 1984 heat treatment of blood products, which eliminates 80% of viruses, was introduced. Patients treated with blood products who can prove that they became infected after that date will have the strongest cases, as will those transfusion patients infected within the past year, when the screening process for whole blood, due to be introduced in Britain in September, became available. Doctors and lawyers are divided as to the ultimate success of the new legal claims if, unlike the Aids-infected haemophilia cases, they have to be pursued through the courts. One doctor dismissed the case as a "dodo" because it would be so difficult to prove. The Department of Health refused to comment on the threatened legal action. The new screening test places an added strain on an already stretched transfusion service and will add #2.50 to the cost of a pint of blood, making British blood among the most expensive in the world. The government will not fund the new testing programme, which will cost #10m a year. Transfusion centre directors are concerned about the possible effects on the service and fear they may be forced to buy more blood from overseas.

February 26, 1991_1.Title: New blood test adds 10m to transfusions
February 26, 1991_1.Author: ALAN MASSAM
February 26, 1991_1.chunks: THE cost of supplying blood to National Health Service patients is to soar by another Pounds 10 million next year because the Government has decided that every donation should be screened for the Hepatitis C virus. The check will be introduced in September, providing evaluation of the procedure proves that it will work as well here as it does in the US. The test will cost Pounds 2.50 per donation. A spokesman for the North London Blood Transfusion Centre, Edwgware, said: `We collect about 200,000 donations a year so clearly this is going to represent a financial bombshell. `The cost will be passed on to users of the blood as the Government has declined to make special funds available.' Government determination to make British blood ultra safe follows a Pounds 42 million out-of-court settlement for haemophiliacs who contracted Aids from contaminated blood.

"They have had a long time to get the blood supply in this country right but nobody has bothered," said Peter Mossman, a retired coach-driver from Manchester, who intends to pursue a claim against Central Manchester Health Authority and the Department of Health. Mossman, diagnosed as a haemophiliac in 1976, was told 18 months ago that he was suffering from chronic hepatitis C, likely to end in fatal liver disease. He is angry and perplexed that he must bear the burden of a second debilitating condition on top of haemophilia. "Even before I was told I had the virus I knew that something was wrong," he said. "I began to get terrible bouts of exhaustion, headaches and horrible abdominal pain." Those such as Mossman, 47, who intend to put their cases before the courts, may have a long struggle to prove negligence against their health authorities. Hepatitis, previously identified in two strains, A and B, has long been recognised as a risk in treating patients with blood and related products. Doctors judged that the benefits of using such treatment on patients with chronic diseases outweighed the risk. In late 1984 heat treatment of blood products, which eliminates 80% of viruses, was introduced. Patients treated with blood products who can prove that they became infected after that date will have the strongest cases, as will those transfusion patients infected within the past year, when the screening process for whole blood, due to be introduced in Britain in September, became available. Doctors and lawyers are divided as to the ultimate success of the new legal claims if, unlike the Aids-infected haemophilia cases, they have to be pursued through the courts. One doctor dismissed the case as a "dodo" because it would be so difficult to prove. The Department of Health refused to comment on the threatened legal action. The new screening test places an added strain on an already stretched transfusion service and will add #2.50 to the cost of a pint of blood, making British blood among the most expensive in the world. The government will not fund the new testing programme, which will cost #10m a year. Transfusion centre directors are concerned about the possible effects on the service and fear they may be forced to buy more blood from overseas.

1 Sept 1991_1.chunks: Did the cost of screening allow a virus to spread? The Blood Transfusion Service has begun mass screening for hepatitis C, a rare blood-borne virus which can cause chronic liver damage and, ultimately, death. Up to 12 sufferers plan to sue the Department of Health because, they believe, screening should have begun nearly two years ago, when a test was first available. They claim cost was a major factor in postponing the screening. The C virus has recently paid out 8 million to 1,200 haemophiliacs infected with HIV from contaminated supplies of Factor VIII. But it could win the proposed action if lawyers can prove that sometimes the health needs of the many outweigh those of the individual. There are two or three cases of post-transfusion hepatitis annually. The obvious symptom is jaundice. Death can result and, 30 years ago, it was a major concern. The virus was hepatitis B, which was not identified until 1965. It took another five years to create a crude laboratory test to identify some of the blood donations which carried the virus and another 15 to give transfusion laboratories the full battery of diagnostics to detect all stages of the disease's progress. Only then could all donations be confidently shown to be clear. Even then, some post-transfusion hepatitis still occurred. Since it was not due to hepatitis B, nor to hepatitis A, which is not blood-borne, it was described as Non-A Non-B hepatitis (NANBH). Transfusion specialists, anxious to determine the incidence of NANBH, examined the medical records of patients with liver disease, but found no obvious correlation except the well-known link with heavy drinking. It took another decade before the nature of NANBH was discovered, after a Californian biotechnology company, Chiron, finally devised a new kind of test. Dr Marcela Contreras, director of the North London Blood Transfusion Service (BTS), and Dr John Barbara, a microbiologist, used the test and found that in 400 blood samples, only two showed raised liver enzyme activities consistent with NANBH. And just one was associated with the virus now called hepatitis C a prevalence of 0-25 per cent. But the new test was prone to cross-reactivity with other antibodies.

1 Sept 1991_1.Author: No author in byline
1 Sept 1991_1.chunks: The government yesterday moved to stifle a serious scandal of public medical negligence, by setting up a multi-billion-franc fund to compensate Aids victims infected through transfusions of blood known to be contaminated.The fund may eventually total between FFr10bn and FFr14bn, according to preliminary estimates. It is expected to be financed mainly through a new tax imposed on French damage insurance policies, though it may be supplemented through a special charge on incomes. The scandal dates back to 1985, when the French National Blood Transfusion Centre (CNTS) continued for several months to release blood for transfusions even though it may have known it to be contaminated with Aids, hepatitis and other viruses.Some 7,000 people are thought to have been contaminated with the infected blood, including around 1,200 haemophiliacs. The scandal has been made worse by the fact that the French authorities at the time deliberately delayed introducing a newly-developed American blood test for Aids, because a rival French test being developed had not been perfected. Three doctors, including the then director of the CNTS, have been charged in court with responsibility for the contaminations.They in turn have attempted to implicate government ministers of the day, including Mr Laurent Fabius, then prime minister, Mr Pierre Beregovoy, finance minister, and Ms Georgina Dufoix, for social affairs minister. The amount of compensation, which is likely to vary widely according to the circumstances of the victims, could range from FFr1m to FFr2m per person, according to some estimates.The French Insurance Companies Federation has protested against the 'profound inequity' of funding the compensation through a special tax on damage insurance policies. It points out that such a tax would penalise those who had taken out insurance policies. However, Dr Iain Murray-Lyon and a team from Charing Cross hospital, in London, have conducted a randomised trial to evaluate the effects of alcohol on recovery from hepatitis. Heavy drinkers, teetotallers, those with pre-existing disease and chronic hepatitis B carriers were all excluded.
