21 February 1994_1.Title: THOUSANDS OF IRISH MOTHERS IN CONTAMINATED BLOOD SCARE.
21 February 1994_1.Author:
Joe Joyce in Dublin.
 The Guardian
21 February 1994_1.chunks: THOUSANDS of Irish women sought advice about screening for hepatitis C yesterday after the revelation that they may have been infected by a contaminated blood product in the 1970s. Health authorities are providing telephone helplines and free tests for up to 100,000 women who have given birth in the past 20 years. Those at risk are rhesus-negative women who received Irish anti-D immunoglobulin to protect their rhesus-positive foetuses. Incompatibility between the mother's and foetus's blood can lead to anaemia, brain damage or stillbirth. Evidence has emerged that one or more batches of the anti-D produced in 1977 may have been contaminated with hepatitis C, which was unknown until 1989. The alarm was raised by the Irish blood transfusion service after it found, among its donors tested last month, nine rhesus-negative women who had given birth in 1977, and who have hepatitis C antibodies. Their cases were linked to six reports of unexplained jaundice in the same year. Yesterday the health authorities reassured women that the numbers infected were likely to be small. Hepatitis C can remain dormant for years, and may lead eventually to chronic inflammation of the liver. The helplines were inundated with calls, and there was criticism of the apparent unavailability of detailed hospital records from the 1970s. Estimates of the numbers who need screening are based on the fact that 10-15 per cent of the population is rhesus-negative. Brendan Howlin, the health minister, tried to play down the front-page controversy when questioned in parliament yesterday. He said he was determined to identify every woman at risk, and plans were being made to trace women given anti-D in 1977. About 4,300 of the 6,000 had been contacted. 'I would like to reassure the public there is no need for alarm,' he said, but admitted there was no certainty that the problem was confined to anti-D used in 1977. The virus is not readily transmitted through blood transfusions, he said. Details of screening centres were listed in Irish newspapers yesterday. The transfusion service's chief medical officer, Terry Walsh, said: "It is important to say that there is no panic, but there is a need for concern, otherwise we would not be carrying out the screening." Nora Owen, the deputy opposition leader, demanded that every woman who may have been affected should be tested, including women who had had miscarriages, as they had also received anti-D. Irish hospitals have stopped using locally-produced anti-D, which came from a pool of male rhesus-negative donors, since last weekend, and are using Canadian imports.

21 February 1994_1.Title: HIV BLOOD SCARE GRIPS EUROPE
21 February 1994_1.Author: IAN TRAYNOR
21 February 1994_1.chunks: GERMANY'S contaminated blood scandal sent ripples of panic across western Europe yesterday as it emerged that the company at the centre of the HIV controversy had sold its suspect blood products in several other countries. Governments moved to withdraw the potentially contaminated products and to calm the public. But hospitals, health authorities and Aids helplines have been inundated with anxious calls from former patients. A senior health official in Italy sparked a furore by stating that more than 500 people had died from contaminated plasma, and 16 medicines in circulation had been branded as dangerous. UB Plasma, the Koblenz-based firm, has sold widely in Austria, Italy, Switzerland, Sweden, Greece and France, as well as Germany. The Department of Health said two products marketed in Britain which originated with UB Plasma were being withdrawn as a precautionary measure. A spokeswoman said there had been no risk to the British public, as the products were heat-treated and fractionated (broken into constituent parts) in this country to kill HIV. Last night, the Government's chief medical officer, Dr Kenneth Calman, said the potentially tainted imported blood products had been cleared. He said those being recalled from British hospitals were from Immuno, an Austrian drugs firm which is supplied by UB Plasma. They had been tested and found free of HIV contamination. Immuno is withdrawing eight batches of albumin and immunoglobulin, used to boost the immune system, which had come from UB Plasma. The Department of Health spokeswoman said: "We are being ultra, ultra cautious. It is a precautionary measure. There is no evidence that anyone in this country is at risk." Members of the armed forces and their families serving in Germany are supplied with blood by the army's tranfusion service at Aldershot, which is tested to NHS standards. The Austrian, Swiss and Swedish governments have also recalled for testing all products originating with UB Plasma. A Vienna health official expected "tens of thousands" of products to be withdrawn pending testing, and doctors are being asked to advise patients treated with the suspect medicines to have HIV tests. But the Austrian health minister said there was "no risk of infection". The panic in Austria intensified after a Vienna tabloid claimed vaccines routinely used to combat insect-borne diseases could be tainted. "I've got weeping mothers calling up asking about their children," Dr Wolfgang Maurer of Austria's state serum-testing institute said. "The phones haven't stopped for two days," a volunteer at a Vienna Aids helpline said. The Aids scandal erupted last month when the German government admitted officials had hushed up hundreds of cases of HIV-contaminated blood in the 1980s. UB Plasma was closed down last week and four of its employees have been arrested on suspicion of cutting corners on the company's blood-screening methods to save money. Four cases of HIV infection originating with UB Plasma products have been established in Germany, the latest affecting a Bosnian child treated in Frankfurt for cancer. It emerged yesterday that blood donations in Germany have fallen by a tenth since the scandal broke. Meanwhile, Germany's Red Cross president, Prince Botho zu Sayn-Wittgenstein, disclosed that since 1985 - when compulsory HIV tests on blood donations were introduced - less than 20 blood transfusions had caused HIV infections. He said in 25 million donated samples since May 1985, only 382 had tested HIV-positive. But Ulrich Mobius, a Berlin physician who helped expose the scandal, said at least 400 haemophiliacs had died through infected blood and more than 1,000 other patients may have been infected. The German government found UB Plasma had screened for HIV only around one-third of blood donations received in the past year. The British and Austrian governments said that similar negligence in their countries was unlikely since it was illegal, and state monitoring bodies also checked blood products. But HIV screening of blood is also required by German law. The president of Italy's Blood Transfusion Dependents' Association, Angelo Magrini, claimed in an interview with La Stampa newspaper that 508 people had died from blood banks which had not been screened for HIV. He said that when he first protested to the authorities four years ago, 39 per cent of the 8,000 blood tranfusion dependents on his books were HIV-positive. Since then, he said, 508 people had died of either Aids or Hepatitis C. The association claims a 1992 law, which requires all blood to be drawn from tested blood banks only and screened for HIV, is not being observed. The Italian scandal centres on Duilio Poggiolini, who is already under investigation for accepting bribes to grant pharmaceutical licences. He is charged with allowing companies to sell dangerous medicines. 16 November 1994_1.chunks: _F By Nicholas Timmins and Martin Whitfield. Health ministers yesterday resisted cross-party calls for compensation for haemophiliacs who have contracted hepatitis C from contaminated blood products, amid controversy over how many people may be infected by the virus. Estimates of the number of people carrying the virus ranged from 9,000 to more than 500,000. A pioneering study of current intravenous drug users found that 60 per cent had been affected. The Independent revealed yesterday that 12 British men with haemophilia had died from hepatitis C within the past year. More than 2,000 are believed to have contracted the virus and the figure could be as high as 90 per cent of the 3,122 of haemophiliacs who received the anti-clotting agent Factor VIII before 1986. Alf Morris, the former Labour Minister for the Disabled, said the principle was exactly the same as that which led to a #42m pay-out in 1990 to 1,200 haemophiliacs who became infected with HIV, the Aids virus, after being given contaminated Factor VIII. But Gerry Malone, the Minister for Health, said: "It would be wrong to embark on a system of compensation unless negligence has been proved by those who have been treated in some way or another. That is a principle by which we will stand." Those infected by HIV had been a special case, suffering social as well as clinical problems. "Some people were deprived of their employment, they were not able to obtain mortgages, insurance, things like that." A further 3,000 non-haemophiliac patients could have received infection through blood transfusions before a screening test was introduced by the National Blood Authority in 1991. "The treatment for hepatitis C is not particularly successful and we must have the funds urgently to develop proper treatment regimes," Alison Rogers, the society's director, said. 16 November 1994_1.Author: By David Brindle, Social Services Correspondent.
16 November 1994_1.chunks: HOSPITAL records are to be trawled to try to trace 3,000 people feared to have contracted hepatitis C through transfusions of contaminated blood, the Department of Health announced yesterday. More than 6,000 people are estimated to have been infected by transfusions before September 1991, when routine screening of blood donations for the hepatitis C virus was begun. At least one in two is assumed to have died since. The department is stressing that people who had a blood transfusion before autumn 1991 run a risk of only one in 2,000 of having contracted hepatitis C - and that very few even of those infected will need treatment. Jeremy Metters, deputy chief medical officer for England, said the department was concerned in case family doctors were besieged by worried patients. "There is no need for those who received blood transfusions to take any immediate action." Ministers have decided to authorise a "look-back exercise" involving transfusion records following concern over hepatitis C infection via transfusions and disclosure that 12 men with haemophilia died from the liver disease in 1993. Previously, the department has argued that it would be technically too difficult to mount such a tracing operation and that no treatment for the disease was available. The policy change has been prompted by the success of a pilot exercise, showing it may be possible to trace many of those infected, and by the licensing of a drug - Interferon Alpha 2a - for use in the treatment of hepatitis C.  The tracing exercise will start by identifying former blood donors discovered since 1991 to have been carriers of the disease. Transfusion centres will then check records and inform hospitals which were sent consignments of blood taken from the donors. The hospitals will seek to establish from their records which patients, if any, received the possibly infected blood and will contact them direct or inform their GPs. Tom Sackville, junior health minister, said: "We shall do all we can to care for patients who have become infected in this way through counselling, and where appropriate, treatment." Health officials estimate that 3,000 people infected before 1991 are still alive. Hepatitis C infection is usually mild in the initial stages. About one in five cases leads to cirrhosis of the liver after 20 years and a few cases lead to liver cancer. A Haemophilia Society spokesman said the society was not seeking compensation across the board. 16 November 1994_1.Title: THE HAEMOPHILIA CONTROVERSY - MEDICAL EXPERTS DIVIDED OVER EXTENT OF PROBLEM.
16 November 1994_1.Author: No author in byline
16 November 1994_1.chunks: _F By Martin Whitfield. Survey identifies new group at risk as legal dispute jeopardises checks. Medical experts are sharply divided on the extent of infection of hepatatis C among the general population. Estimates vary from as few as 9,000 to more than 500,000. Intravenous drug users and people who received blood transfusions before 1986 are most at risk. However, considerable numbers of people carrying the virus have no known risk factors. The British Liver Trust, the only patient organisation for people with hepatitis C, believes that as many as 1 per cent of the population may be infected. Most would have no idea that they were carrying the virus as the symptoms of liver disease can take up to 20 years to develop. Virtually no research has been carried out to discover the scale of hepatatis-C infection although the first studies among drug users have found a high incidence. The trust is urging the Government to fund a detailed national survey. Professor Peter Scheuer - medical adviser to the trust and a former leading pathologist at the Royal Free Hospital, north-west London, until his retirement in 1992 - said the rate of infection was a serious medical problem. He supported the trust's prediction that up to 500,000 people could be involved. "A common history is someone who may have taken drugs once or twice when they were young," he said. "They may be in their 40s or 50s before they find they are in serious trouble." But Professor Roger Williams, head of the liver unit at King's College Hospital, London, said he believed that estimates of half a million infected people were "much too high". He said latest blood transfusion figures showed that 0.016 per cent of new donors had the viral infection, not 1 in 100. "It is very unlikely that throughout the general population of the UK the figure is more than 0.01 per cent." The National Blood Authority believes that around 3,000 patients may have been infected as a result of transfusions from infected blood donated before 1991. Professor Williams, who is a member of the board of governors of the British Liver Trust, maintained that the level of hepatitis-C infection was lower than in most other countries. The incidence of infection is known to vary considerably between states although there is a world-wide estimate of 300 million people carrying the virus. A large study in Italy found that 1.7 per cent of the population had the virus, while even higher levels are found in Egypt and in the Far East where large-scale "shared-needle" immunisation programmes have been carried out. Professor Williams and Professor Scheuer agreed that blood-to-blood contact is the most likely form of transmission, but there remains a low risk of the virus spreading through sexual intercourse and exchange of body fluids. All blood donations have been screened for hepatitis C since 1991, and about one in 2,000 new donors has been found to be a carrier. Far more people are likely to be infected in the general population as blood donors are a self-selecting group, with most of the high-risk groups explicitly prevented from giving blood. Another unknown factor about the virus - only identified positively in 1989 - is the percentage of carriers who later suffer from liver disease. It is believed that up to 20 per cent could develop cirrhosis, with half of these going on to suffer from liver failure. Heavy drinking, often associated with the onset of cirrhosis, and the added presence of HIV have accelerated liver problems among haemophiliacs. Dr Christine Lee, director of the haemophilia unit at the Royal Free Hospital, said 255 patients attending the unit had hepatitis C, and it was known that virtually all of the 3,122 haemophiliacs who received blood products between 1965 and 1986 would be infected. "There is a probability of some form of sexual transmission but the amount is small. Very few of the sexual partners of haemophiliacs have been affected," she said.

16 November 1994_1.Title: EDITORIAL - JUSTICE FOR THOSE THE NHS INFECTS.
16 November 1994_1.Author: No author in byline
16 November 1994_1.chunks: _F Yesterday's front-page report about haemophiliacs infected with hepatitis C after treatment with contaminated blood has produced a surprising reaction from the Haemophilia Society. To lay observers, there seems to be a strong analogy between this episode involving about 2,000 people, and the earlier case of 1,200 haemophiliacs infected with HIV in the course of treatment. In 1990, the Government agreed to pay them #42m in compensation. In both instances, those requiring treatment with a blood product picked up a dangerous infection. But yesterday the Haemophilia Society said it had "no plans to seek compensation". Not enough was known, said the society, about how the disease progresses. This cautious approach has a certain medical logic, since the two infections have very different consequences. Compared with HIV, hepatitis C's advance is far less inexorable. Of those infected, 20 per cent recover quickly, while the rest develop persistent infection lasting many years. About half the larger group will develop a chronic form resulting in inflammation of the liver. Only one in five of those - making 8 per cent of the initial total - will develop cirrhosis of the liver, which is not necessarily fatal. Whereas HIV tends to develop into Aids within 10 years, symptoms of liver disease can take 10 to 40 years to develop. That helps to explain why the Haemophilia Society is playing down the latest scourge to afflict its members. Most of those infected, it pointed out, have had the condition for several decades, and remain well. None the less, 12 men - only males suffer from haemophilia - are understood to have died from hepatitis C as a result of treatment before 1991; four have had liver transplants; and the society concedes that a "small proportion" of others have had severe problems. Their number is likely to increase as the infection takes its course. Furthermore, not only haemophilia sufferers are affected. An additional 3,000 adults and children who received transfusions before 1991 may also be at risk. Hepatitis C is never likely to be as acute a threat for those who have used blood products as HIV has been, and it will not reach its peak for years. Yet when people fall seriously ill as a direct result of NHS treatment, natural justice dictates that some provision should be made to compensate them. That should apply to haemophiliacs and non-haemophiliacs alike. For the Government to rule out all compensation at this stage, as it did yesterday, is both insensitive and unfair.

The Times

November 19, 1994, Saturday

Need for research into hepatitis C

SECTION: Features

LENGTH: 305 words

From Professor Roger Williams
Sir, Recent publicity about the likely means of infection of up to 3,000 haemophiliac patients with hepatitis C (report, November 17) highlights the need for continuing research into this serious disease.
 Clinical illness may not arise until after 20 to 30 years of infection which should give some reassurance to those who have acquired the infection by whatever route. Nevertheless, the hepatitis C virus (HCV) is highly infectious; it leads to much morbidity and mortality in the world, with some estimated 300 million persons affected.
 The virus is transmitted by blood-to-blood contact, mainly via transfusions and injections; but there are still many cases where doctors simply do not know how hepatitis C has been acquired.
 The Times has recently drawn attention to the case of Chiron v Murex, where a biotechnology company is seeking to limit competitors carrying out research into hepatitis C by claiming that it, effectively, ''owns'' the virus (''Blood feud in the High Court'', Mind and Matter, October 31). Already one HCV research project has been dropped because the Chiron patent is so broad that no resulting vaccine could ever be commercialised.
 As a society we cannot afford to be restrictive about scientific knowledge in so vital a field. A vaccine which would protect, say, health workers and those exposed to intravenous infection would be an extremely important advance, and research to achieve this end should not be restricted.
 It is hoped that the current storm, while it may stir up undue alarm, emphasises the fact that excessively broad patents which are used to discourage commercial endeavour must be against the public interest.
Yours sincerely,
ROGER WILLIAMS (Director),
Institute of Liver Studies,
Bessemer Road, SE5.
November 17.

16 November 1994_1.Title: 3,000 HAD HEPATITIS INFECTED BLOOD.
16 November 1994_1.Author: By Jeremy Laurance.
16 November 1994_1.chunks: ABOUT 3,000 people who may have been infected with hepatitis C after receiving contaminated blood transfusions are to be traced and offered counselling and treatment, Tom Sackville, the Health Minister, announced yesterday. The hepatitis C virus, which was identified in 1989, causes liver inflammation but may not produce symptoms for 20 years. About one in five of those infected develop cirrhosis, which can lead to liver failure. A small proportion develop liver cancer, which is nearly always fatal. Mr Sackville said that all donated blood had been screened for the virus since 1991, when a test became available. "Prior to that some recipients of blood transfusions may have been infected but the chances of this are extremely small," he said. The Health Department ruled out compensation. One in 2,000 donors carries the virus. Blood transfusion centres are to check their records to see whether donors identified as positive for hepatitis C have given blood in the past. A further 3,000 people with haemophilia are estimated to have been infected with hepatitis C through blood products received before 1985, when procedures were introduced to destroy viruses such as HIV and the then unknown hepatitis C. The same procedures could not be used on fresh blood. A helpline has been set up on 0800 716197. The immune systems of people infected by HIV, far from being weakened by the virus, work overtime to defeat it, scientists claim. Findings published in Nature suggest that healthy cells almost succeed in overcoming the condition and slow its progress.

16 November 1994_1.Title: THE HAEMOPHILIA CONTROVERSY - HEPATITIS C VIRUS SPREADS AMONG DRUG ABUSERS.
16 November 1994_1.Author: No author in byline
16 November 1994_1.chunks: _F By Jason Bennetto. Survey identifies new group at risk as legal dispute jeopardises checks. An estimated 400,000 people who have injected drugs are infected with hepatitis C, according to an unpublished study. A survey of more than 2,000 intravenous drug users in the United Kingdom found that 60 per cent were hepatitis anti-body positive. Several injectors are believed to have died from the disease, which can destroy the liver. Others are believed to have been infected after just a few injections, which took place as far back as the Sixties. International studies have shown that most people who are anti-body positive are infected, although in many cases the hepatitis C virus may be dormant or non-infectious. Hepatitis C is easily spread by sharing needles contaminated by blood containing the virus. The new two-year study - the first national survey of injecting drug users - was carried out by the West Suffolk Drug Advisory Service. They obtained test results from 2,081 injecting drug users. The authors of the report, Dr Tom Waller and Roger Holmes, say that, at a conservative estimate, there are about 400,000 people infected via injecting. This assumes there are about 150,000 to 200,000 people currently injecting drugs. However, symptons of liver diseases can take 30 years to appear and therefore tens of thousands of former injectors will have been exposed to the virus. Nearly half the 131 respondents who carried out the tests reported difficulty in getting clients tested, or in following up a positive test with further tests or treatment. The new report, which is expected to be published in the next few months, is being presented to the independent Government advisory body, the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs, later today. Studies have shown that the longer someone injects, the more likely he or she is to contract the disease. In an Australian study, 95 per cent of drug users were positive if they had been injecting for more than 10 years. The type of drug affects the degree of risk, as some substances are injected more often. Cocaine addicts who can inject 15 times a day are more likely to be infected than heroin users, who need the drug far less often. Mr Holmes, co-author of the study, said: "Shared needles are the main way the virus is spread, but sharing razors or contaminated tattoo equipment might also be involved." He added that his department knew of a small number of "deaths related to the effects of hepatitis C". The proportion of people who are expected to die after being contaminated is unknown. Mr Holmes said: "Although about 60 per cent of the drug injectors may develop some form of chronic disease, we are not sure how many are life-threatening. There's a possibility that some of the people who are believed to have died from Aids could have been victims of hepatitis C." Because the viral infection was only identified in 1989, many of the people currently infected are likely to have been contaminated by dirty needles from the 60s and 70s. Christopher Tibbs, a specialist at the liver unit at King's College Hospital in London, said earlier this month: "About 10 per cent of the cases referred to me are City yuppies who have had it detected when they had a standard Bupa-type insurance medical. "These people have no idea how they caught it or how long they had it. Most likely it was in their university days in the Sixties. They might have had a wild party and had one or two shots in the arm. "These are middle-aged people whose past history has suddenly been thrown back in their faces."

The Times

November 17, 1994, Thursday

Late cirrhosis

BYLINE: Dr Thomas Stuttaford

SECTION: Features

LENGTH: 245 words

 THERE is no reason to doubt reports that 5,000 people have caught hepatitis C from contaminated blood given during transfusion before 1991, and that 12 patients last year died from cirrhosis, which is in some cases a late complication of the infection. Once the virus had been isolated, it was accepted that many people must have been infected before the causative agent had been found, and blood for transfusion could be checked for it. 
 Professor Arie Zuckerman, dean of the Royal Free Hospital, London, says: ''It may well be that hepatitis C represents a bigger public health problem than does hepatitis B.''
 The viruses responsible for hepatitis A and B were recognised many years ago, and at that time it was also known that other cases of hepatitis were the result of infection by other causative agents which had not yet been isolated.
 The initial illness caused by hepatitis C is mild, but given this, there is a surprisingly large number of patients who later develop a persistent, mild, often symptom-free low-grade hepatitis. Of these, 20 per cent may, years later, sometimes up to 30 years later, develop cirrhosis. Professor Zuckerman said that response to treatment at this stage had been rather disappointing. In carefully selected patients who had been treated with Interferon combined with other anti-viral agents, early evidence suggested that not more than 40 per cent would have a good response, and that the virus would be cleared.

16 November 1994_1.Title: MINISTER BLOCKS HEPATITIS PAYOUTS.
16 November 1994_1.Author:
Tim Radford.
 The Guardian
16 November 1994_1.chunks: The health minister, Gerry Malone, said yesterday that the Government would not pay compensation to sufferers who contracted hepatitis C from contaminated blood or blood products unless negligence could be proved. "I think it would be a significant and unwelcome step if the Health Service were to move forward to a position of `no fault' liability and we don't intend to do that," he said. The minister's announcement came despite the Department of Health's decision in 1991 to pay out #42 million to 1,200 haemophiliacs who contracted the Aids virus by the same route. However, the Haemophilia Society confirmed last night that it had no plans as yet to seek compensation. The hepatitis C virus was isolated only in 1989. It can lead to a chronic liver condition which may take many years to develop. At least 2,000 haemophiliacs could have been infected, and 12 who received blood products have died from the infection. The blood product usually given to haemophiliacs is a blood-clotting agent known as Factor VIII - although some of these patients also needed transfusions of blood or its components. Around 3,000 who are not haemophiliacs but who received blood transfusions before a new screening process was adopted in 1991 may also be infected. The Haemophilia Society said it had no plans "as yet" to press for compensation. "Our priority is to ensure help and support for people who are unwell as a result of hepatitis C," said a spokesman. There are many types of hepatitis transmitted by viruses: which are little more than a slip of genetic material which hijacks the body's machinery and often lies latent. Healthy humans may be host to numbers of them. The National Blood Transfusion Service already conducts four or five screening tests on up to 10,000 samples a day. Nevertheless the detection remains a challenge. "Hepatitis C, before it was identified, only left its footprint in the form of its disease. It's like: does the yeti exist? Can you simply tell from the footprints?" said John Barbara, head of microbiology at the North London Blood Transfusion Service.

16 November 1994_1.Title: HEPATITIS C  STILL PASSED IN SURGERY.
16 November 1994_1.Author: No author in byline
16 November 1994_1.chunks: _F By CELIA HALL, Medical Editor. Up to 150 patients a year could be infected with the hepatitis C virus as a result of receiving contaminated blood plasma during surgery, a consultant physician said yesterday. He said patients risked infection because the "safest" product available was not being used. Dr Jonathan Freeman a transplant anaesthetist and intensive care specialist who has himself been involved in the transfusion of more than 20,000 units of blood and blood products, says other countries use treated plasma. He said: "Some countries in Europe such as Belgium and Norway have already switched to the sole use of this specially treated plasma in place of untreated frozen plasma and this is a growing practice." Dr Freeman said that in Germany there is a law which deems it medically negligent if a patient becomes infected after the prescription of a product known to be inferior and to have identifiable risks when a safer product is available. "Are the residual risks acceptable and are we doing enough to reduce them even further in the UK? Infection with hepatitis C is not to be taken lightly," he said. He said that by 2000 the commonest reason for liver transplant could be liver failure caused by hepatitis C.  He has based his estimates on data published in the British Medical Journal in August. It described the risk of being infected with hepatitis C as "less than 1 in 13,000". He says that 2.5 million units of blood are used in England and Wales every year so "anything up to 150 units could possibly be infected with hepatitis C virus [HCV]". Dr Freeman, who works at the prestigious liver unit at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Birmingham, stressed that he was making a personal statement. "I am concerned for my patients. I want to be assured I am giving them the best possible product." Last week, the Independent revealed that 12 patients with haemophilia had died from liver failure caused by hepatitis C. They were infected by contaminated Factor VIII, a blood product. A total of 2,000 haemophiliacs have hepatitis C.  Another 3,000 patients who are not haemophiliacs are estimated to have been infected through blood transfusion. The risk to both groups has diminished since Factor VIII is now treated and donors are screened. But it is accepted that there is a small risk of HCV getting into the blood supply because tests may not detect it in a donor who has been newly infected and has not created measurable anti-bodies. Dr Angela Robinson, medical director of the National Blood Authority which supervises the transfusion service, said: "The screening is 90 per cent effective. We put the risk at 1 in 100,000." She said the authority was "treating the matter urgently", and was considering two courses of action. "Quarantine" of the frozen plasma, would mean that before it was used the donor would have to be recalled for another blood test for HCV 6 to 12 months after the orginal screen. "We are also trialling the treated product, which is not currently licensed for use in this country. We are treatiang this matter urgently," she said. She said that the treated plasma would cost twice as much as the #30 a unit for the untreated product.

16 November 1994_1.Title: CONTAMINATED BLOOD KILLS 12.
16 November 1994_1.Author: No author in byline
16 November 1994_1.chunks: _F By CELIA HALL Medical Editor. Doctors believe 5,000 people have caught liver disease from transfusions and clotting agents  Twelve British men with haemophilia have died from the liver disease hepatitis C after they were given contaminated concentrates of blood. All 12 men died last year. At least 2,000 more people are infected, and four have had liver transplants as a result. Another 3,000 adults and children, who are not haemophiliacs but did receive fresh blood transfusions before 1991, may also have been infected, according to the Blood Transfusion Service, but are unaware of their condition. The emergence of these previously unreported deaths echoes the case of hundreds of haemophiliacs who caught the Aids virus from contaminated blood. Haemophilia is an inherited disease whose major symptom is the failure of the blood-clotting mechanism. Haemophiliacs, who are always male, often have to be given blood-clotting agents - called "factors" - which are produced from donated blood. Doctors say 90 to 95 per cent of haemophiliacs who used factors regularly before May 1985 have contracted hepatitis C.  Now the Haemophilia Society is considering seeking redress from the Department of Health. The society is organising meetings to inform haemophiliacs and is in contact with the department. The National Blood Authority is also considering what action to take. Dr Fereydoun Ala, chairman of the Standing Advisory Committee on Transfusion Transmitted Infections, said: "Those working in the field believe we have a duty of care of patients and that we should be open about this. We are deciding how we can best proceed." At the same time, the consultants who head the regional haemophilia centres around the country have their own working party on haemophilia and hepatitis. The hepatitis C virus (HCV) was only identified in 1989. Before that, it was recognised as non-A, non-B hepatitis. It is a slow, chronic condition leading to cirrhosis of the liver in 20 per cent of cases. Ten per cent of these go on to liver failure in five years. Symptoms of liver disease can take 10 to 30 years to develop. Doctors admit they still do not know enough about the progress of the disease. Hepatitis C is transmitted by blood-to-blood contact, mostly via transfusions and injections. In 1985, blood products, including the clotting agent Factor VIII, were subjected to anti-viral heat treatment designed to eradicate HIV. Haemophilic boys up to the age of 10 who use factors are not, therefore, at risk. No cases of hepatitis C in this group have come to light for the past nine years. However, fresh whole blood or fresh parts of blood cannot be treated in the same way. In June 1991, the Department of Health paid out a total of #42m to 1,200 haemophiliacs who caught HIV from factors made from infected blood. In September 1991, on advice from the Department of Health, the Blood Transfusion Service began to screen donors for hepatitis C to protect the blood supply. Simon Taylor, vice-chairman of the Haemophilia Society, said: "At this stage, because the information about hepatitis C is so slight we are not sure which way we should proceed. The difficulty is the vast majority of haemophiliacs have no hepatitis symptoms because the disease could take 30 years to show itself. There is no medical consensus on diagnosis, treatment or prognosis. One thing we are considering is seeking compensation when people become ill."  Haemophilia experts say the true number of patients infected with hepatitis C is not known but 2,000 is a reasonable estimate. There are 10,000 men and boys with haemophilia in the UK. Of these, 2,500 - including 500 boys aged under 10 - need factors regularly, the rest intermittently. Mr Taylor said most of the 2,000 adults had contracted hepatitis C.  The infection rate is very high because between 20,000 and 30,000 donations are pooled to produce the factors. Dr Ala, who is also director of the West Midlands Blood Transfusion Centre, said they were able to arrive at the estimate of the 3,000 transfusion patients with hepatitis C by checking the records of blood donors who were subsequently found to have hepatitis C.  "What we now have to consider is whether we identify the recipients and contact them. These people may have no symptoms at all. These are very difficult issues," said Dr Ala.  A spokesman for the Department of Health said: "We have the greatest sympathy for these people. "There are no plans to extend the settlement scheme for haemophilia patients who are HIV-positive to patients who have been infected with hepatitis C. The Government does not have a policy of no-fault compensation. Patients received the best available treatment in the light of medical knowledge at the time."

16 November 1994_1.Title: THE HAEMOPHILIA CONTROVERSY - PATENT ROW THREATENS BLOOD TESTS.
16 November 1994_1.Author: No author in byline
16 November 1994_1.chunks: _F By Steve Connor, Science Correspondent. Survey identifies new group at risk as legal dispute jeopardises checks. A legal dispute over who "owns" the hepatitis C virus could lead to a third of the blood tests for the disease being banned in Britain by the end of the year. A High Court judge is soon to rule whether to grant an injunction against a company whose blood test for the virus (HCV) accounts for 34 per cent of sales in Britain, including more than one-third of HCV tests used by the national blood transfusion service. The company, Murex, is involved in a patent dispute with Chiron, a biotechnology company based in California, which identified HCV in 1987 and subsequently applied for patents on the virus's entire genetic sequence. Chiron won a legal challenge claiming that Murex has infringed its UK patent, and it wants the High Court to impose a ban on its competitor's blood test. Murex has appealed against the patent-infringement decision and wants to continue selling its blood test until its appeal is heard in about a year's time. Leading liver doctors and transfusion scientists have condemned Chiron's use of its patent to create what they claim is a monopoly. Professor Roger Williams, director of liver studies at King's College, London, said: "It is very dangerous to have any area of research restricted to one company. It's against the public interest because the testing for hepatitis C is many times more expensive than for HIV, which is a similar sort of test, because of the patent. The cost could be greatly reduced if you had free competition." Professor Williams said it would be better for Murex to be allowed to continue selling its HCV test kit and so have the incentive to continue research on the virus. "For a doctor, the most important aspect is that unless you have several groups checking their own ideas and doing the research, you don't get any progress," he said. A transfusion scientist, who wished to remain anonymous, said that competition "has improved the nature of the product", and the broad range of the Chiron patent will eliminate this competition. He said that the cost of the HCV test kit ranges between #1.50 and #2.50, compared with 35p to 50p for the HIV test. "When you get a monopoly situation, there is no way you'll get the prices coming down." About 3 million HCV test kits are used each year in Britain and the National Blood Authority said that about 1 in every 2,000 new blood donors are confirmed as testing positive for the virus. Bob Blackburn, chief patent counsel for Chiron, said the patent on HCV covers the entire genetic sequence of the virus, but insisted that this was normal for viral blood tests. He said the patent dispute did not prevent Murex or any other company from doing research on HCV. "We're not trying to monopolise the virus," he said.

16 November 1994_1.chunks:
No cash payout for bad blood victims

BY VERA ORRICE

HAEMOPHILIACS who contracted Hepatitis C through contaminated blood will not receive compensation, the Government announced yesterday.

The decision follows disclosures that 133 patients died from the disease last year.

83 of them were haemophiliacs and 50 patients below the age of 40 contracted the virus while they were children when they were not screened, according to government figures released today.

Treatment

In 1981 the Government set up a special fund of £30m to treat haemophiliacs and their families for the effects of Hepatitis C, but the blood donor charity Medcare added yesterday that this fund is being depleted rapidly.

A spokesman said a haemophiliac who has been diagnosed with Hepatitis C could be given a lump sum of £15,000 to cover treatment costs.

But family will press for £50,000

The family of one of the 133 haemophiliacs who died of the virus have launched a high profile campaign calling for compensation.

They have based a claim that the Government is not doing enough to prevent the disease and should pay £50,000 for the loss of each victim.

The claim is being heard by the Scottish courts.

Last week some after being given the blood infected with Hepatitis C have been offered compensation by the charity Medcare.

16 November 1994_1.chunks: A High Court ruling yesterday confirmed that a common virus is effectively owned by a California biotechnology company. Twelve haemophiliacs died last year as a result. Four have had liver transplants. Since 1985 Factor VIII has been given anti-viral heat treatment. Another group of 3,000 people was also infected from fresh or frozen blood or blood products used routinely in hospitals. This blood cannot be heat treated, so instead since 1991 all blood donors have been screened for hepatitis C. Ms Page said: "Anyone who had a fresh or frozen blood product before 1991 is at risk. There are a lot of people involved here. I don't know at this stage what we will do, but I want people to contact me. "Many need support and to be able to talk about this. We may go for compensation; we may have an educational role. It will be up to the group." Ms Page, 42, a health visitor, is married and has a 12-year-old daughter. She stresses that hepatitis C is not passed on in normal contact, that the infection route is blood to blood, classically by injection and transfusion. "There is no risk to others in the normal course of events," she said. It is still something of a medical enigma. The heptitis C virus was identified in 1989. Six strains have been indentified and it can take 10 to 30 years to produce symptoms of liver damage. It can be hard to detect in the blood or in the liver. Progress of the disease varies from one patient to another. Liver damage can take the form of cirrhosis which can lead to liver failure and the risk of liver cancer is increased. Ms Page's story must mirror the experience of many. "For 18 months to two years I was feeling increasingly tired. I am a very energetic person but I was feeling exhausted all the time. I was getting breathless at the gym. "My GP surgery is very good but they said I was really doing too much; I was getting older." Ms Page also had a longstanding gall bladder problem which caused her pain. In the summer the surgeon she was referred to decided to remove her gall bladder but he was not convinced that her symtpoms related to it alone. So, during surgery, he performed a liver biopsy. "It was all a bit of a puzzle. He suggested that I had a test for hepatitis C," Ms Page said. "To be honest I knew that there was something wrong so when he told me it was not a complete surprise." Ms Page is now being investigated for her suitability for treatment with interferon, the anti-viral drug used to treat heptitis C which has proved successful in 25 per cent of cases. "We have made some small adjustments to family life. When I feel tired I have a sleep and I do not feel guilty about it. I pace myself. I refuse to become a failing Victorian lady lying about swooning on a chaise-longue. "The message is that we can get out on the other side of this," she said. - Send SAE to Gabrielle Page, 112 Hunter Avenue, Shenfield, Essex, CM15 8PG.

Haemophiliac victims will not receive compensation

HAEMOPHILIACS who contracted hepatitis C through contaminated blood will receive no compensation, the Government said yesterday.

Mr Gerald Malone, the Health Minister, said that the Government would not compensate people infected by contaminated clotting agent before 1986, when sterlisation was introduced.

Responding to a report that 12 haemophiliacs had died from the virus, he said that everything possible had been done by the standards of the time.

"I think it would be a significant and unwelcome step if the National Health Service were to move forward to a position of 'no fault' liability and we don't intend to do that," Mr Malone said.

In 1991 the Government paid £42 million compensation to 1,200 haemophiliacs who had contracted the Aids virus HIV through contaminated blood.

Dr Christine Lee, director of the haemophilia centre at the Royal Free Hospital in London, said last night that 3,122 haemophiliacs were infected with hepatitis C before 1986. About 20 per cent of those infected develop symptoms, but the number of deaths is unknown and the total of 12 appears to be speculation.

Dr Lee said she was sure that most of those who died would also have had HIV.

The National Blood Authority said that some people who had been administered clotting factor had died from liver trouble, but the number was unknown.

Dr Lee said there was not a strong case for compensating haemophiliacs. The Government should instead make available genetically engineered clotting factor which, although more expensive than that made from natural sources, was guaranteed free of infection.

The Haemophilia Society said it did not intend to press for cash payments. "Our priority is to ensure help and support for people who are unwell as a result of hepatitis C," said a spokesman. The situation would be kept under constant review.

The British Liver Trust said it was "lamentable" that there had been no national study of the scale of the problem.

Hepatitis C was identified only in 1989. The chronic liver condition can take up to 30 years to develop.

16 November 1994_1.Title: IMPROVING THE NATION'S BLOOD SUPPLY.
16 November 1994_1.Author: No author in byline
16 November 1994_1.chunks: _F After recent scares, Simon Hadlington reports on the quest for safer products  The revelation that an estimated 3,000 people who received blood transfusions before 1991 have been contaminated with the hepatitis C virus has focused attention on the purity of the nation's blood supply. First reports appeared in the Independent last week, describing the spread of hepatitis C through blood or blood products, affecting those who had received fresh blood and another group, haemophiliacs, who received the blood-clotting agent Factor VIII before heat treatment began in 1985. Despite the fact that infections from hepatitis C through contaminated blood have been extremely rare since screening of donors began in 1991, viral contamination of donated blood and its products is a big concern among professionals involved in blood transfusion medicine. The problem is an international one. Earlier this year, Dr Harvey Klein, chief of the Department of Transfusion Medicine at the National Institutes of Health in the US, said, "The risk of infection from hepatitis and HIV, as well as from future unknown viruses, remains a major concern among medical and scientific communities." Dr William Murphy, a senior lecturer in medicine at Edinburgh University and honorary consultant to the Scottish Blood Transfusion Service, says that most people in the medical profession are confident that the blood supply is safe. "You get very little expression of unhappiness and I think that confidence is probably not misplaced. Most of the deaths associated with transfusion are due to things other than viral transmission. Nevertheless, we are constantly on our toes just in case new infective agents appear. There is no room for complacency." In the UK, donated blood is screened routinely for HIV, hepatitis B and C and syphilis, and, in certain situations, for another virus, cytomegalovirus. Procedures for eliminating the risk of HIV infection through contaminated blood appear to have been largely effective. "There is a theoretical possibility of transmission if a donation is made within two to three weeks of the donor having become infected, when sufficient antibodies have not been produced to be detected by the test. So there is a gap in the security," Dr Murphy says. He points out that since 1985 in the UK there has been only one known instance of HIV transmission through blood products. The other big issue is ensuring a regular, consistent supply of blood. Reliance on the goodwill of donors, coupled with the short shelf-life of blood products, can cause shortages. Red cells can survive for between five and six weeks; platelets, which are vital for the clotting process, expire after only five days. The manufacture of artificial blood products could go some way to improving both the purity of supplies and their availability. Researchers have not been slow to recognise the potential of the market. But natural blood is a hard act to follow. One candidate undergoing clinical trials at centres around the world is a group of synthetic organic chemicals called perfluorocarbons, which are capable of carrying oxygen. Their attraction is that being synthetic they are potentially cheap to produce. However, while the perfluorocarbons were initially thought to be largely chemically inert, there have been concerns about what happens to them in the body. If their safety is guaranteed, however, perfluorocarbons would be used principally for providing oxygen to tissues in emergencies, such as at the scene of an accident, rather than for more chronic conditions. A number of companies in the United States are extracting and purifying haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying component of blood, from red cells. The chief problem here is that in the body such "naked" haemoglobin, which is no longer protected within the blood cell, is broken down into its constituent sub-units. These are called alpha-beta dimers, and they can interfere with the function of the kidneys. Furthermore, such "recycled" haemoglobin does not release oxygen as freely as its native counterpart. Work is under way to stabilise the haemoglobin sub-units in the body. Meanwhile, trials of a genetically engineered haemoglobin are being undertaken in surgical patients at the University of Utah in the US. This "recombinant" haemoglobin is being produced in the bacterium Escherichia coli by Somatogen, a Colorado-based biopharmaceutical company, which has signed a marketing agreement with Eli Lilly, the drugs giant. According to Somatogen, its product is comparable to human red cells in its efficacy of oxygen delivery and safety. Also, the company says, it is active for a sufficiently long period to permit its use in surgery. The company further claims that the product has a low risk of being attacked by the body's immune system; it requires no tissue typing or cross-matching, and may release oxygen into the tissues more effectively than transfused red blood cells. Yet another American firm, Delta Biotechnology, is gearing up for human clinical trials of genetically engineered human albumin, which is an important component of blood plasma. The trials are due to begin next year, and will examine the safety and effectiveness of the product as a means of "expanding" blood, to help eke out supplies. Some professionals involved in the field, however, are concerned that it will be difficult to make genetically engineered products sufficiently pure; that they will remain contaminated by tiny quantities of foreign proteins emanating from the organisms which were used to produce them. The fear is that these proteins will trigger the body's defence mechanisms against the blood products. One of the most interesting projects is the development of a "bone marrow bioreactor" by Dr David Wu at the University of Rochester in New York. Bone marrow is the "factory" for the production of all red blood cells and platelets and most white blood cells. "Our overall goal is to develop an artificial bone marrow to support the maintenance of stem cells and their differentiation into mature blood cells," Dr Wu says. Stem cells are blood cells that have been newly produced by the bone marrow and that have not yet been modified (differentiated) to perform specialist functions. The reactor comprises a culture chamber filled with tiny, highly porous spheres that are inoculated with marrow cells. This porous matrix is overlaid with a liquid culture medium containing a cocktail of the nutrients necessary for the cells to grow. "The various physiological parameters, such as nutrient and oxygen levels, can be closely controlled," Dr Wu says. He says the bioreactor can support both human and mouse blood cells, and that a wide range of cell types can be harvested from the system at various stages of their development. "It is different from the traditional flask culture in that it produces almost all the blood cell types and thus resembles much better the marrow tissue in the body. With further study we hope to produce mature blood cells for transfusion."

The Times

October 31, 1994, Monday

Blood feud in the High Court

BYLINE: Nigel Hawkes

SECTION: Features

LENGTH: 682 words

 A legal battle is raging over the 'ownership' of the hepatitis C virus
Abattle over whether anybody can ''own'' a virus will next month get a hearing in the High Court. Squaring up are two biotechnology companies which have already gone several rounds in courts both in Britain and abroad.  So far Chiron, the California-based company which successfully patented part of the hepatitis-C virus, is well ahead on points.
 But its opponent, Murex, claims that the patent is so wide that it amounts to an abuse of the system. Allowing Chiron control over diagnostic tests for hepatitis C and over potential vaccines to treat the disease will discourage further research, Murex claims. 
 The Chiron test is used by the NHS to ensure that blood products are free of hepatitis C, a virus that causes chronic liver disease. In a proportion of patients, fatal cirrhosis of the liver may follow, usually about 20 years after infection.
 Peter Silveston, of Murex, argues that Britain is already paying a high price for granting such a broad patent to Chiron. The NHS carries out about 3.5 million hepatitis C tests a year, costing Pounds 2 each. Tests marketed by other companies against hepatitis B cost only 30p a time, and against the Aids virus, HIV, just 70p.
 Chiron's stranglehold on hepatitis C dates from 1987, when its scientists were the first to identify part of the hepatitis C virus. What they produced was a sequence of 859 amino acids that make up about a third of the entire virus in the strain they were studying.
 They then applied for patents to cover this sequence and any other that matched it by 40 per cent. This is a very broad claim, Murex argues, which leaves Chiron in effective control of every strain of the hepatitis C virus.  In an extreme case, there might be only a 13 per cent match between a particular strain and the sequence patented by Chiron, but the patent would still be valid.
 Mr Silveston questions whether the patent should ever have been granted.  ''For a start, was it really an invention? This is a naturally occurring life form, so there is an argument that it shouldn't even be patentable.''
 Chiron has defended its patent vigorously. Murex has already lost twice in the High Court, which upheld the patent in October last year, but refused to enforce it because Chiron had signed a deal with a licensee, Ortho Diagnostics, which contained invalid provisions. This left Murex able to continue marketing its own tests. In a second action, Chiron's patent was again found to be valid and infringed by Murex.
 Murex has now appealed over the upholding of the patent, and in the High Court on November 7 it will argue that Chiron should not be granted an injunction against it at least until the Court of Appeal has ruled, on the grounds that it would be against the public interest.
 Dr Stephen Locarnini, of Melbourne Fairfield Hospital, claims that the Chiron test was ''incredibly expensive'' when first introduced, and that only the intervention of Murex had brought down the price.
 He believes that the present tests need improvement, but doubts that anybody will now put money into the field, as they would face the inevitable prospect of paying fees to Chiron.
 Chiron has denied that it owns the hepatitis C virus, or that its patent prevents others from continuing research. ''Without the reward offered by the patent system, it is doubtful whether companies such as Chiron would make the substantial investments needed to solve biotechnology problems,'' says Larry Kurtz, vice-president of Chiron. He estimates that since the introduction of the tests, more than a million cases of hepatitis C in blood recipients have been prevented around the world.
 Chiron's position is strong because it is not a matter of choice whether blood is tested: by law it must be.
 ''We could simply roll over and accept it,'' says Dave Tholen, president and chief executive of International Murex Technology Corporation, ''but if any company is allowed to get away with this, the effects on healthcare costs could be scary.''

The Times

December 9, 1994, Friday

Hepatitis C patent

SECTION: Features

LENGTH: 288 words

From Mr Larry Kurtz
Sir, On behalf of the Chiron Corporation, which in 1987 discovered the hepatitis C virus (HCV), I would like to allay the fears of Professor Roger Williams (letter, November 19) that upholding Chiron's HCV patent rights, as the High Court has just done (report, November 30), may limit research.
 Since Chiron's patent application was published (in May 1989) research in the hepatitis C field has burgeoned. In fact, since Chiron's patent was granted in January 1992, more than 4,500 scientific papers related to HCV have been published and more than 350 patent applications related to HCV have been filed (only 20 by Chiron) by at least 25 commercial and research organizations. This puts into context the one project that Professor Williams says has been dropped as a result of our patent.
 Chiron does not ''own'' the hepatitis C virus. The company's patents generally cover reagents based on the HCV genetic sequence and the application of the reagents to diagnostics. Since the invention of those reagents, Chiron has entered into a number of licensing arrangements with international diagnostic companies, three of them in the UK, to supply HCV tests.
 A commitment to research must go hand-in-hand with a commitment to protection of intellectual property rights. Without the reward offered by the patent system, it is doubtful whether companies such as Chiron would make the substantial investments needed to address problems such as HCV. Safeguarding these rewards is vital if future advances in healthcare are to be achieved.
Yours etc,

16 November 1994_1.Title: SHADOW OF THE `OTHER' HEPATITIS.
16 November 1994_1.Author: No author in byline
16 November 1994_1.chunks: _F Janet Morgan on a liver disease that even some doctors have never heard of  Each day, a little bit more of Jamie Clarke's body is slowly destroyed. Though it causes him little, if any, pain, he still knows the disease is attacking his liver. He is infected with hepatitis C, a recently identified virus which can be more insidious than its better known relatives, hepatitis A and B. A and B both produce flu-like symptoms, ranging from mild to serious. In some cases, B can lead to liver failure and is linked to cancer of the liver. People who have had hepatitis B can also become carriers. Hepatitis C is a life-long chronic condition. It progresses slowly with few symptoms: people can have it for years before a random blood test picks up signs of infection. Jamie estimates he had been infected for between 10 and 15 years before he received advice from the National Blood Service last year that he could no longer give blood because a routine test had detected hepatitis C antibodies. The service began screening for hepatitis C in 1991, two years after the virus was first identified. A study carried out by the service estimates that about 0.3 per cent of donors have hepatitis C antibodies. Dr Christopher Tibbs, a specialist at the liver unit at King's College Hospital in London, says no one knows how many thousands of donors and non-donors in the UK have contracted the virus and are still unaware they are carriers. "A study we carried out in Camberwell, London, showed the prevalence to be about 1 per cent of the population," he says, admitting that residents of one inner-city area could not be seen as a representative sample. Dr Tibbs sees five new patients each week - about 200-300 new cases every year. Intravenous drug users are the largest group of carriers, but the virus is evident in people with a great variety of lifestyles. "About 10 per cent of the cases referred to me are City yuppies who have had it detected when they had a standard BUPA-type insurance medical," he says. "These people have no idea how they caught it or how long they have had it. "Most likely it was in their university days in the Sixties. They might have had a wild party and had one or two shots in the arm. These are middle-aged people whose past history has suddenly been thrown back in their faces." Others may never be able to identify how they picked it up. Clear risk factors for infection can be detected in most patients, says Dr Tibbs. The route of transmission is sometimes more difficult to establish. Jamie, a 35-year-old journalist with a young son and newborn daughter, has never injected drugs and has no clue of the source of infection. Hepatitis C attacks the liver. It enters the liver cells and multiplies, forcing the body's immune system to destroy the infected liver cells. In 40 or 50 years it can destroy the liver. Cirrhosis develops in 20-40 per cent of carriers, some others may develop liver cancer. Jamie is still in the early stages of the disease: his liver function tests reveal near normal liver levels. In an attempt to rid his blood and liver cells of the virus, Jamie is on a nine-month course of the anti-viral drug interferon. The treatment is experimental. Results from earlier interferon trials show a 50 per cent response rate among those at a more advanced stage of the disease. However, half these people relapsed when they stopped taking the drug. Nine months of interferon injections three times a week is difficult, says Dr Tibbs, particularly for those who feel perfectly healthy - or at worst mildly lethargic. "The side-effects of interferon might well make them feel worse. In the early phases, the treatment will make people feel as though they have bad flu. Each injection will bring on fever, shakes and chills." These effects reduce with time and after a while the person will merely feel lethargic and possibly depressed. Occasionally the interferon can interfere with the thyroid function or cause hair loss. The treatment is not ideal, admits Dr Tibbs, but it is the only drug available. Testing of other drugs used in combination with interferon or even Aids drugs is likely. Advanced cases of hepatitis C can only be given supportive treatment for the complications as they arise, says Dr Tibbs. If liver failure develops, a transplant is possible. Removing the diseased liver will not, however, eliminate the virus, which is present in blood cells, but will give the patient more time - another 20 or 30 years - while the disease begins its course all over again. Following his diagnosis, Jamie has given up alcohol and tries to maintain a healthy diet and to get adequate sleep. But the disease also interferes with his family life. He and his partner, Mary, have to be particularly careful around the house with their two children. "If the kids cut themselves, Jamie can't really help them, and I can't even help Jamie if he cuts himself," Mary explains. The fear of transmitting or contracting the disease can also put pressure on the relationship. Between 1 and 5 per cent of people whose partners have hepatitis C contract the virus. But Dr Tibbs points out that it is unclear whether this increased risk is caused by sexual intercourse or from some other lifestyle factor common to two people living together. There is a similar increased risk of contracting hepatitis C when sharing house with a carrier in a non-sexual relationship. "It is the sort of rate that may be caused by toothbrush sharing or the like," explains Dr Tibbs. "There is no evidence of greater transmission with differing sexual practices." There is a high level of ignorance about hepatitis C. When Jamie first contacted his GP about the letter from the National Blood Service, she admitted she had never heard of hepatitis C.  "It was only when I was finally referred to King's and saw Dr Tibbs that I found out how serious it was," Jamie explains. "I was in shock." He still thinks about the disease slowly destroying his liver, and occasionally feels pain around the organ (although he says this may be psychosomatic). But Jamie is optimistic, and there is reason to hope. "The positive news for those with hepatitis C is that it progresses very slowly, so those who have failed to respond to current treatment have time to wait for a new and better treatment to come," says Dr Tibbs. - Jamie is not his real name.

16 November 1994_1.chunks: _F A firm's monopoly on a vital blood test has been upheld in court. Steve Connor explains On Tuesday, a High Court judge granted a company that "owns" the hepatitis C virus an injunction to prevent rival firms from selling blood tests for the potentially lethal infection. Mr Justice Aldous decided, in effect, to enforce a legal monopoly in a vital area of medicine - the protection of the nation's blood supply. "When you get a monopoly situation, there is no way you'll get the prices coming down," he said. Such arguments appear to make a powerful case against Chiron on the grounds that its patent is against the public interest, yet Mr Justice Aldous has already ruled - last May - that the patent must stand and that public interest is not threatened. He has now decided to enforce the patent by granting a permanent injunction preventing competitors, notably Murex Diagnostics Ltd, from manufacturing or selling their own test kits for hepatitis C. Murex has appealed against the earlier patent-infringement ruling, but as this is unlikely to be heard for another year, Chiron and its patent licensees insisted on the Murex test kits being taken off the market immediately.

16 November 1994_1.chunks: Hidden perils of blood transfusion Could it be that the Jehovah's Witnesses are right in refusing blood transfusions? This radical thought is prompted partly by the latest scare: blood contaminated by Hepatitis C. An earlier alert concerned blood donors who were HIV positive. The life-saving blood transfusion is one of the most potent medical images, but infection is only one of a number of dangers that have been described in professional journals. However, studies such as the one that estimated the chances of an adverse reaction to a transfusion as high as 20 per cent are little known to the public. Equally unfamiliar are the studies that have found that having a transfusion is the best predictor of making a poor recovery after abdominal or colon operations. "If blood was a new drug it wouldn't receive a product licence," said Tom Lennard, consultant surgeon at the Royal Victoria Infirmary, Newcastle upon Tyne. "There have never been proper trials to show when it is useful and when not. If blood was a new drug it would not receive a licence, say experts. Transfusion can save lives, but it can also have dangerous side-effects and these are all too often ignored." Even more vehement is Lynne McTaggart, editor of the newsletter What Doctors Don't Tell You. "The latent 'window' period during which no blood tests can detect the presence of HIV in an infected individual can be eight years," she says. She claims that transfusions are dangerous and often given unnecessarily. "One study by the US Office of Technology Assessment Task Force estimated that as much as 25 per cent of the red blood cells and 95 per cent of fresh-frozen plasma transfused into people were not needed." Jehovah's Witnesses maintain that the Bible prohibits transfusions. Media interest concentrates on life-threatening cases where the refusal of a transfusion technically condemns a Jehovah's Witness to death. But in America, researchers found that out of 1,404 operations on Jehovah's Witnesses, a lack of blood was only involved in 20 deaths or 1-4 per cent of them. What is more, survivors had no more post-operative problems than similar patients who did have transfusions. "I think blood should be regarded as a powerful drug," says Mr Lennard. "At the moment most surgeons are far too cavalier with it. I think that is changing, if only through pressures to keep costs down." The Times

January 14, 1995, Saturday

Worry of the week

BYLINE: Nigel Hawkes

SECTION: Features

BYLINE: Chris Mihill

SECTION: THE GUARDIAN HOME PAGE; Pg. 2

LENGTH: 185 words

 
 HEPATITIS is an inflammation of the liver caused mostly by viruses, although drugs - including paracetamol - excess alcohol and immune-system disturbances can also cause it.
 Until recently, scientists had identified only two viruses, hepatitis A and B.  Hepatitis C, D and E have now been discovered. They all cause a similar "short, sharp" illness, but there are differences in the long-term effects and the way the viruses are spread.
 The most obvious sign of acute hepatitis is jaundice. In many cases there is a flu-like illness with nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite and pain in the joints. In some cases a chronic condition follows, with liver damage.
 Most sufferers have no symptoms and the virus usually clears from the body. But 5 to 10 per cent become carriers, with an increased risk of liver disease and potential to pass on the virus.
 Hepatitis B can be caught by contact with the body fluids of a carrier. It can passed from mother to baby.
 Hepatitis A arises mostly from food and drink contaminated because of poor hygiene. It does not cause chronic liver damage.

16 November 1994_1.Title: HEPATITIS LINKED TO RECORD NUMBER OF DRUG DEATHS.
16 November 1994_1.Author: No author in byline
16 November 1994_1.chunks: _F By JOHN ARLIDGE. Researchers investigating the record number of drugs deaths in Glasgow this year are examining new evidence that a hepatitis epidemic among addicts is the cause. Almost 100 intravenous drug users have died from overdoses in Strathclyde since January. The latest two victims were David Aitken, 26, and Max Smith, 21, who were found dead in a working men's hostel in Cheapside on 17 December. Police said yesterday their deaths may be linked to a particularly pure batch of heroin. Most researchers and drugs welfare workers point to the popularity of high-strength drug "cocktails" - mainly mixtures of heroin, sleeping tablets and pain killers - to explain the rising death toll. But pathologists now have evidence of a hepatitis C epidemic among addicts which, they say, could be the major cause of death. Recent post-mortem examinations have revealed that up to 80 per cent of Glasgow's 10,000 injecting addicts have contracted hepatitis C - more than double the proportion among drug users in other British cities. The blood-borne virus, which was formally identified only five years ago, weakens the liver, reducing the body's ability to break down drugs and increasing the risk of overdose. Dr Marie Cassidy, a consultant forensic pathologist at Glasgow University, said: "If an addict has hepatitis C, his body may well be unable to `digest' and excrete drugs properly. That means that every time he takes, for example, heroin, small amounts ofthe drug will remain in his bloodstream after the `high' has worn off. "Over time, this heroin residue will get larger and stronger, increasing the risk that one day his usual `hit' will combine with remnants of previous hits to create a lethal overdose. Because the physical effects of hepatitis are rarely felt, the addict may not know he has the virus and may be unaware of the dangers of continuing to take heroin until it is too late." Dr Cassidy, who has carried out post-mortem examinations on more than 100 addicts, says the new evidence of hepatitis infection may explain an unusual feature of recent deaths in Strathclyde: that many of the victims had not taken large quantities of drugs. She said: "Toxicology tests reveal that many victims have actually consumed relatively low - even therapeutic - amounts of drugs before death. "When I first started carrying out post-mortems, I could not understand why such modest quantities were proving fatal. But now that I and other researchers know of the extent and the cumulative effects of hepatitis, it no longer seems so odd. The virus and its rapid spread in Glasgow could be the key to explaining why deaths here are so common." Drugs counsellors say Glasgow's "culture of injection" has led to the high levels of hepatitis C infection. David Liddell, director the Scottish Drugs Forum, which co-ordinates services for addicts in Strathclyde, said: "Drug users in Glasgow, more than anywhere else, prefer injecting to any other method of drug-taking. "Before needle exchange schemes were set up in the city in the late 1980s, many drug users shared dirty needles and, even today, in spite of all the warnings about the dangers, there is evidence that some sharing still takes place. It's a simple fact that the more injecting and sharing there is, the more viral infection there is." Mr Liddell, who has advised the Government on strategies to combat Glasgow's burgeoning drugs problem, is sceptical about the significance of hepatitis C in explaining the rising death toll. Most deaths are, he insists, the result of "polydrug use": addicts taking lethal heroin and sleeping pill cocktails. But, he says, hepatitis could be a contributory factor.

No cash payout for bad blood victims

BY VERA ORRICE

HAEMOPHILIACS who contracted Hepatitis C through contaminated blood will not receive compensation, the Government announced yesterday.

The decision follows disclosures that 133 patients died from the disease last year.

83 of them were haemophiliacs and 50 patients below the age of 40 contracted the virus while they were children when they were not screened, according to government figures released today.

Treatment

In 1981 the Government set up a special fund of £30m to treat haemophiliacs and their families for the effects of Hepatitis C, but the blood donor charity Medcare added yesterday that this fund is being depleted rapidly.

A spokesman said a haemophiliac who has been diagnosed with Hepatitis C could be given a lump sum of £15,000 to cover treatment costs.

But family will press for £50,000

The family of one of the 133 haemophiliacs who died of the virus have launched a high profile campaign calling for compensation.

They have based a claim that the Government is not doing enough to prevent the disease and should pay £50,000 for the loss of each victim.

The claim is being heard by the Scottish courts.

Last week some after being given the blood infected with Hepatitis C have been offered compensation by the charity Medcare.

Haemophiliac victims will not receive compensation

HAEMOPHILIACS who contracted hepatitis C through contaminated blood will receive no compensation, the Government said yesterday.

Mr Gerald Malone, the Health Minister, said that the Government would not compensate people infected by contaminated clotting agent before 1986, when sterlisation was introduced.

Responding to a report that 12 haemophiliacs had died from the virus, he said that everything possible had been done by the standards of the time.

"I think it would be a significant and unwelcome step if the National Health Service were to move forward to a position of 'no fault' liability and we don't intend to do that," Mr Malone said.

In 1991 the Government paid £42 million compensation to 1,200 haemophiliacs who had contracted the Aids virus HIV through contaminated blood.

Dr Christine Lee, director of the haemophilia centre at the Royal Free Hospital in London, said last night that 3,122 haemophiliacs were infected with hepatitis C before 1986. About 20 per cent of those infected develop symptoms, but the number of deaths is unknown and the total of 12 appears to be speculation.

Dr Lee said she was sure that most of those who died would also have had HIV.

The National Blood Authority said that some people who had been administered clotting factor had died from liver trouble, but the number was unknown.

Dr Lee said there was not a strong case for compensating haemophiliacs. The Government should instead make available genetically engineered clotting factor which, although more expensive than that made from natural sources, was guaranteed free of infection.

The Haemophilia Society said it did not intend to press for cash payments. "Our priority is to ensure help and support for people who are unwell as a result of hepatitis C," said a spokesman. The situation would be kept under constant review.

The British Liver Trust said it was "lamentable" that there had been no national study of the scale of the problem.

Hepatitis C was identified only in 1989. The chronic liver condition can take up to 30 years to develop.
