6 December 1994_1.chunks: _F Yesterday's front-page report about haemophiliacs infected with hepatitis C after treatment with contaminated blood has produced a surprising reaction from the Haemophilia Society. To lay observers, there seems to be a strong analogy between this episode involving about 2,000 people, and the earlier case of 1,200 haemophiliacs infected with HIV in the course of treatment. In 1990, the Government agreed to pay them #42m in compensation. In both instances, those requiring treatment with a blood product picked up a dangerous infection. About half the larger group will develop a chronic form resulting in inflammation of the liver. Only one in five of those - making 8 per cent of the initial total - will develop cirrhosis of the liver, which is not necessarily fatal. Whereas HIV tends to develop into Aids within 10 years, symptoms of liver disease can take 10 to 40 years to develop. Need for research into hepatitis C

SECTION: Features

From Professor Roger Williams
Sir, Recent publicity about the likely means of infection of up to 3,000 haemophiliac patients with hepatitis C (report, November 17) highlights the need for continuing research into this serious disease.
 Clinical illness may not arise until after 20 to 30 years of infection which should give some reassurance to those who have acquired the infection by whatever route. Nevertheless, the hepatitis C virus (HCV) is highly infectious; it leads to much morbidity and mortality in the world, with some estimated 300 million persons affected.
 The virus is transmitted by blood-to-blood contact, mainly via transfusions and injections; but there are still many cases where doctors simply do not know how hepatitis C has been acquired.
 The Times has recently drawn attention to the case of Chiron v Murex, where a biotechnology company is seeking to limit competitors carrying out research into hepatitis C by claiming that it, effectively, ''owns'' the virus (''Blood feud in the High Court'', Mind and Matter, October 31). Already one HCV research project has been dropped because the Chiron patent is so broad that no resulting vaccine could ever be commercialised.
 As a society we cannot afford to be restrictive about scientific knowledge in so vital a field. A vaccine which would protect, say, health workers and those exposed to intravenous infection would be an extremely important advance, and research to achieve this end should not be restricted.
 It is hoped that the current storm, while it may stir up undue alarm, emphasises the fact that excessively broad patents which are used to discourage commercial endeavour must be against the public interest.
Yours sincerely,
ROGER WILLIAMS (Director),
Institute of Liver Studies,

Ms Page is now being investigated for her suitability for treatment with interferon, the anti-viral drug used to treat heptitis C which has proved successful in 25 per cent of cases. "We have made some small adjustments to family life. When I feel tired I have a sleep and I do not feel guilty about it. I pace myself. I refuse to become a failing Victorian lady lying about swooning on a chaise-longue. "The message is that we can get out on the other side of this," she said. - Send SAE to Gabrielle Page, 112 Hunter Avenue, Shenfield, Essex, CM15 8PG.

6 December 1994_1.Title: CONTAMINATED BLOOD KILLS 12.
6 December 1994_1.Author: No author in byline
6 December 1994_1.chunks: _F By CELIA HALL Medical Editor. Doctors believe 5,000 people have caught liver disease from transfusions and clotting agents  Twelve British men with haemophilia have died from the liver disease hepatitis C after they were given contaminated concentrates of blood. All 12 men died last year. At least 2,000 more people are infected, and four have had liver transplants as a result. Another 3,000 adults and children, who are not haemophiliacs but did receive fresh blood transfusions before 1991, may also have been infected, according to the Blood Transfusion Service, but are unaware of their condition. The emergence of these previously unreported deaths echoes the case of hundreds of haemophiliacs who caught the Aids virus from contaminated blood. Haemophilia is an inherited disease whose major symptom is the failure of the blood-clotting mechanism. Haemophiliacs, who are always male, often have to be given blood-clotting agents - called "factors" - which are produced from donated blood. Doctors say 90 to 95 per cent of haemophiliacs who used factors regularly before May 1985 have contracted hepatitis C.  Now the Haemophilia Society is considering seeking redress from the Department of Health. The society is organising meetings to inform haemophiliacs and is in contact with the department. The National Blood Authority is also considering what action to take. Dr Fereydoun Ala, chairman of the Standing Advisory Committee on Transfusion Transmitted Infections, said: "Those working in the field believe we have a duty of care of patients and that we should be open about this. We are deciding how we can best proceed." At the same time, the consultants who head the regional haemophilia centres around the country have their own working party on haemophilia and hepatitis. The hepatitis C virus (HCV) was only identified in 1989. Before that, it was recognised as non-A, non-B hepatitis. It is a slow, chronic condition leading to cirrhosis of the liver in 20 per cent of cases. Ten per cent of these go on to liver failure in five years. Symptoms of liver disease can take 10 to 30 years to develop. Doctors admit they still do not know enough about the progress of the disease. Hepatitis C is transmitted by blood-to-blood contact, mostly via transfusions and injections. In 1985, blood products, including the clotting agent Factor VIII, were subjected to anti-viral heat treatment designed to eradicate HIV. Haemophilic boys up to the age of 10 who use factors are not, therefore, at risk. No cases of hepatitis C in this group have come to light for the past nine years. However, fresh whole blood or fresh parts of blood cannot be treated in the same way. In June 1991, the Department of Health paid out a total of #42m to 1,200 haemophiliacs who caught HIV from factors made from infected blood. In September 1991, on advice from the Department of Health, the Blood Transfusion Service began to screen donors for hepatitis C to protect the blood supply. Simon Taylor, vice-chairman of the Haemophilia Society, said: "At this stage, because the information about hepatitis C is so slight we are not sure which way we should proceed. The difficulty is the vast majority of haemophiliacs have no hepatitis symptoms because the disease could take 30 years to show itself. There is no medical consensus on diagnosis, treatment or prognosis. One thing we are considering is seeking compensation when people become ill."  Haemophilia experts say the true number of patients infected with hepatitis C is not known but 2,000 is a reasonable estimate. There are 10,000 men and boys with haemophilia in the UK. Of these, 2,500 - including 500 boys aged under 10 - need factors regularly, the rest intermittently. Mr Taylor said most of the 2,000 adults had contracted hepatitis C.  The infection rate is very high because between 20,000 and 30,000 donations are pooled to produce the factors. Dr Ala, who is also director of the West Midlands Blood Transfusion Centre, said they were able to arrive at the estimate of the 3,000 transfusion patients with hepatitis C by checking the records of blood donors who were subsequently found to have hepatitis C.  "What we now have to consider is whether we identify the recipients and contact them. These people may have no symptoms at all. These are very difficult issues," said Dr Ala.  A spokesman for the Department of Health said: "We have the greatest sympathy for these people. "There are no plans to extend the settlement scheme for haemophilia patients who are HIV-positive to patients who have been infected with hepatitis C. The Government does not have a policy of no-fault compensation. Patients received the best available treatment in the light of medical knowledge at the time."

6 December 1994_1.Title: THE HAEMOPHILIA CONTROVERSY - MEDICAL EXPERTS DIVIDED OVER EXTENT OF PROBLEM.
6 December 1994_1.Author: No author in byline
6 December 1994_1.chunks: _F By Martin Whitfield. Survey identifies new group at risk as legal dispute jeopardises checks. Medical experts are sharply divided on the extent of infection of hepatatis C among the general population. Estimates vary from as few as 9,000 to more than 500,000. Intravenous drug users and people who received blood transfusions before 1986 are most at risk. However, considerable numbers of people carrying the virus have no known risk factors. The British Liver Trust, the only patient organisation for people with hepatitis C, believes that as many as 1 per cent of the population may be infected. Most would have no idea that they were carrying the virus as the symptoms of liver disease can take up to 20 years to develop. Virtually no research has been carried out to discover the scale of hepatatis-C infection although the first studies among drug users have found a high incidence. The trust is urging the Government to fund a detailed national survey. Professor Peter Scheuer - medical adviser to the trust and a former leading pathologist at the Royal Free Hospital, north-west London, until his retirement in 1992 - said the rate of infection was a serious medical problem. He supported the trust's prediction that up to 500,000 people could be involved. "A common history is someone who may have taken drugs once or twice when they were young," he said. "They may be in their 40s or 50s before they find they are in serious trouble." But Professor Roger Williams, head of the liver unit at King's College Hospital, London, said he believed that estimates of half a million infected people were "much too high". He said latest blood transfusion figures showed that 0.016 per cent of new donors had the viral infection, not 1 in 100. "It is very unlikely that throughout the general population of the UK the figure is more than 0.01 per cent." The National Blood Authority believes that around 3,000 patients may have been infected as a result of transfusions from infected blood donated before 1991. Professor Williams, who is a member of the board of governors of the British Liver Trust, maintained that the level of hepatitis-C infection was lower than in most other countries. The incidence of infection is known to vary considerably between states although there is a world-wide estimate of 300 million people carrying the virus. A large study in Italy found that 1.7 per cent of the population had the virus, while even higher levels are found in Egypt and in the Far East where large-scale "shared-needle" immunisation programmes have been carried out. Professor Williams and Professor Scheuer agreed that blood-to-blood contact is the most likely form of transmission, but there remains a low risk of the virus spreading through sexual intercourse and exchange of body fluids. All blood donations have been screened for hepatitis C since 1991, and about one in 2,000 new donors has been found to be a carrier. Far more people are likely to be infected in the general population as blood donors are a self-selecting group, with most of the high-risk groups explicitly prevented from giving blood. Another unknown factor about the virus - only identified positively in 1989 - is the percentage of carriers who later suffer from liver disease. It is believed that up to 20 per cent could develop cirrhosis, with half of these going on to suffer from liver failure. Heavy drinking, often associated with the onset of cirrhosis, and the added presence of HIV have accelerated liver problems among haemophiliacs. Dr Christine Lee, director of the haemophilia unit at the Royal Free Hospital, said 255 patients attending the unit had hepatitis C, and it was known that virtually all of the 3,122 haemophiliacs who received blood products between 1965 and 1986 would be infected. "There is a probability of some form of sexual transmission but the amount is small. Very few of the sexual partners of haemophiliacs have been affected," she said.

6 December 1994_1.Author: No author found
6 December 1994_1.chunks: Hidden perils of blood transfusion Could it be that the Jehovah's Witnesses are right in refusing blood transfusions? This radical thought is prompted partly by the latest scare: blood contaminated by Hepatitis C. An earlier alert concerned blood donors who were HIV positive. The life-saving blood transfusion is one of the most potent medical images, but infection is only one of a number of dangers that have been described in professional journals. However, studies such as the one that estimated the chances of an adverse reaction to a transfusion as high as 20 per cent are little known to the public. Equally unfamiliar are the studies that have found that having a transfusion is the best predictor of making a poor recovery after abdominal or colon operations. "If blood was a new drug it wouldn't receive a product licence," said Tom Lennard, consultant surgeon at the Royal Victoria Infirmary, Newcastle upon Tyne. "There have never been proper trials to show when it is useful and when not. If blood was a new drug it would not receive a licence, say experts. Transfusion can save lives, but it can also have dangerous side-effects and these are all too often ignored." Even more vehement is Lynne McTaggart, editor of the newsletter What Doctors Don't Tell You. "The latent 'window' period during which no blood tests can detect the presence of HIV in an infected individual can be eight years," she says. She claims that transfusions are dangerous and often given unnecessarily. "One study by the US Office of Technology Assessment Task Force estimated that as much as 25 per cent of the red blood cells and 95 per cent of fresh-frozen plasma transfused into people were not needed." Jehovah's Witnesses maintain that the Bible prohibits transfusions. Media interest concentrates on life-threatening cases where the refusal of a transfusion technically condemns a Jehovah's Witness to death. But in America, researchers found that out of 1,404 operations on Jehovah's Witnesses, a lack of blood was only involved in 20 deaths or 1-4 per cent of them. What is more, survivors had no more post-operative problems than similar patients who did have transfusions. "I think blood should be regarded as a powerful drug," says Mr Lennard. "At the moment most surgeons are far too cavalier with it. I think that is changing, if only through pressures to keep costs down." The disease was first described in the United States in 1982, and since then it has spread to over 15 countries. The illness is believed to be transmitted from organ donor to organ recipient, and can result in death within 18 months of the transplant.

6 December 1994_1.chunks: An edition of Panorama, the BBC's flagship current affairs programme, is to be made by an ITV company. The team which makes Yorkshire Television's factual show 3D is combining with the BBC to produce a Panorama investigation into contaminated blood. It will be the first Panorama under the programme's new editor, Steve Hewlett, who has a brief to increase audiences and widen its popular appeal. The report, Bad Blood, will investigate the spread of hepatitis C. Britain was the last country in Europe to screen for the virus and 3,000 people have been infected by contaminated blood. Panorama examines whether those carrying the virus should be told and whether they should receive compensation. The story was uncovered by 3D producer Roisin McAuley, but it was thought that broadcasting it could not be delayed until the programme's new run, starting on ITV on February 16. A BBC producer is also working on the project. Panorama's viewing figures picked up under former editor Glenwyn Benson, with high-profile investigations into police corruption and the business affairs of England soccer coach Terry Venables, although she had previously said it did not matter if only five people watched. Mr Hewlett, aged 36, spent two years as editor of the BBC1 documentary series Inside Story, where he displayed enthusiasm for a human interest stories. A quarter of the BBC's TV output has to be made by independent companies. Outside producers have made editions of Panorama in the past, but Bad Blood is the first in its 41-year history to come from an ITV company. ITV broadcasters are increasingly seeking commissions from the BBC and satellite channels. Yorkshire has made programmes for Sky One and the Discovery channel. Here, Vicky, 47, charts nine-year-old Lexie's rapid downhill over five weeks after she was prescribed 80mg of corticosteroids a day for a minor eye infection. "Lexie was given a course of antibiotics and steroids to fight an eye infection. It was all over with by Christmas... because she was dead. "We were told the side-effects were perhaps a rash. I pumped 12 pills into her on the Friday, but by Sunday, she started to feel very weak with a severe headache and nausea. During the night, I could see her face swelling. "She went back for check-ups at the hospital. She had put on enormous amounts of weight, found it difficult to move, and had blinding headaches. Towards the end, she started shaking, developed holes in her tongue, couldn't hold a fork, and had to sleep with two pillows to help her breathe properly. "This went on for five weeks until she started having chronic stomach pains and couldn't even walk to the doctor's. Lexie was admitted to hospital on Thursday, where they saw spots on her, which was later identified as chicken pox, when she was barely conscious and in intensive care. "It was then that we were told of the side-effects of steroids and of the destruction to the immune system. She died on Saturday... but she was brave until the very end." An inquest on the nine-year-old, killed by a bout of chicken pox, recorded a verdict of misadventure after hearing how the steroids had suppressed her immune system - and made it impossible for her to put up a fight against the disease. 11 January 1995_1.Title: HUNT FOR 3,000 BLOOD 'VICTIMS'.
11 January 1995_1.Author: By David Brindle, Social Services Correspondent.
11 January 1995_1.chunks: HOSPITAL records are to be trawled to try to trace 3,000 people feared to have contracted hepatitis C through transfusions of contaminated blood, the Department of Health announced yesterday. More than 6,000 people are estimated to have been infected by transfusions before September 1991, when routine screening of blood donations for the hepatitis C virus was begun. At least one in two is assumed to have died since. The department is stressing that people who had a blood transfusion before autumn 1991 run a risk of only one in 2,000 of having contracted hepatitis C - and that very few even of those infected will need treatment. Jeremy Metters, deputy chief medical officer for England, said the department was concerned in case family doctors were besieged by worried patients. "There is no need for those who received blood transfusions to take any immediate action." Ministers have decided to authorise a "look-back exercise" involving transfusion records following concern over hepatitis C infection via transfusions and disclosure that 12 men with haemophilia died from the liver disease in 1993. Previously, the department has argued that it would be technically too difficult to mount such a tracing operation and that no treatment for the disease was available. The policy change has been prompted by the success of a pilot exercise, showing it may be possible to trace many of those infected, and by the licensing of a drug - Interferon Alpha 2a - for use in the treatment of hepatitis C.  The tracing exercise will start by identifying former blood donors discovered since 1991 to have been carriers of the disease. Transfusion centres will then check records and inform hospitals which were sent consignments of blood taken from the donors. The hospitals will seek to establish from their records which patients, if any, received the possibly infected blood and will contact them direct or inform their GPs. Tom Sackville, junior health minister, said: "We shall do all we can to care for patients who have become infected in this way through counselling, and where appropriate, treatment." Health officials estimate that 3,000 people infected before 1991 are still alive. Hepatitis C infection is usually mild in the initial stages. About one in five cases leads to cirrhosis of the liver after 20 years and a few cases lead to liver cancer. A Haemophilia Society spokesman said the society was not seeking compensation across the board. However, it wanted relief of financial hardship on the same terms as those for people infected with HIV.

January 17, 1995, Tuesday

Gaps in the ABC of blood screening

BYLINE: Dr Thomas Stuttaford

SECTION: Features

LENGTH: 605 words

 Dr Thomas Stuttaford explains how some people came to be given blood contaminated with hepatitis C - and what is being done for them.
ABOUT five years ago a young man had his car stolen. Later, by chance, the owner spotted it parked by a building site in central London; he accosted the thief, who drew a knife and stabbed him through the abdomen. Bleeding profusely he was taken to casualty in the nick of time. Resuscitated by transfusions, and repaired by surgeons, he made a good recovery marred only by some slight post-operative jaundice and a recurrent low-grade fever.  Recently he has been complaining of ill health and chronic tiredness; his liver function tests are abnormal and his blood tests show that he has been infected by hepatitis C. 
 In the period when blood could be screened for hepatitis A and B, but not for hepatitis C, the latter accounted for the majority of cases of post-transfusion hepatitis, and it may well be that it was also therefore responsible for many of the cases of inexplicable chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and cancer of the liver.
 The initial symptoms of hepatitis C are mild, but the sting of the disease lies in its tail 50 to 80 per cent of patients who catch it fail to make a full recovery and are likely to develop a chronic infection. In most cases this infection is benign, and is very often free of all discernible symptoms, but in at least 20 per cent of those affected the disease will lead to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis of the liver and, in some cases, malignant disease.
 Treatment with interferon will eradicate hepatitis C in about 35 to 45 per cent of carefully selected cases; but interferon can have unpleasant side effects and is not suitable for every patient. Those in whom eradication fails may well become carriers, and even if they are asymptomatic they will remain capable of infecting others with a potentially deadly virus. In the Victorian era before the days of antibiotics doctors, patients and novelists were not unreasonably obsessed by the carrier state. To be a carrier of any disease, capable of causing sickness and death while remaining healthy, can induce in sensitive people a great sense of guilt. In chronic hepatitis C there is the added burden of never knowing if the condition is likely to deteriorate and lead to irreversible liver damage.
 Now the Government has agreed to make efforts to trace all patients who might have been given blood contaminated by hepatitis C after it could first be detected, but before testing became standard. Controversy surrounds the period between 1989, when the first screening tests for hepatitis C were being developed in America, and 1991, when they became routinely established.  The initial test could detect hepatitis C only several months after the blood had first become infectious, and the numbers of false positive and false negative results were very high. When all factors were taken into account the predictive value of the test was only 50 per cent, and the US Food and Drug Administration did not approve it until 1990. In Britain three different and better tests were approved and introduced in 1991; since then they have been further improved, and now give a 90 per cent predictive value.
 Professor Arie Zuckerman, Dean of the Royal Free School of Medicine, said yesterday: ''There were very sound reasons for the delay in introduction of routine screening. Only the improved tests introduced in 1991 had the sensitivity and specificity which is needed. These screening tests are now, of course, essential for all blood which is going to be used for transfusion.''

No special payments will be made to people who contracted the liver disease hepatitis C from blood products and transfusions, Baroness Cumberlege told the House of Lords yesterday. Lady Cumberlege, Under-Secretary of State for Health, said the Government could not open the floodgates to compensation claims. The Haemophilia Society, which is seeking payments for members with hepatitis C who become ill, immediately said it would continue its fight. "We are not surprised at the stand adopted by the Government. They responded in just the same way at the start of the HIV campaign," a spokesman said. He was referring to the Government's decision in 1990, after a two-year battle, to pay hardship money to haemophiliacs and then to transfusion patients who caught HIV from contaminated blood supplies. After protracted legal arguments, the Government made #42m available in a trust fund. The spokesman added: "The society believes there is a strong moral case and will continue its discussions with the Government." He said it was seeking the same financial treatment for sufferers and their families as achieved by the HIV group. Lady Cumberlege said: "We have great sympathy for those affected, but have no plans to make special payments. "We have to be careful not to open the floodgates to every case that is made for compensation. If we were to do that, we would get into the US situation where doctors are very frightened now to give a medical treatment for fear of being sued. That would actually finish the NHS and we would all be the poorer." The minister told the Lords that HIV differed from hepatitis in that it was a very new disease, believed invariably to be fatal, and with devastating health, social and financial effects. But many hepatitis sufferers "could lead ordinary lives for decades". Lady Cumberlege was responding to Lord Ashley of Stoke, who declared: "Virtually all haemophiliacs who received blood transfusions before 1986 have been infected ... Although no fault is involved, they need payment just the same as those who were infected by the HIV virus through contaminated blood. There is no difference in the principle and there should be none in the practice."

Need for research into hepatitis C

SECTION: Features
11 January 1995_1.Author: No author found
11 January 1995_1.chunks:
The Times

November 19, 1994, Saturday

Need for research into hepatitis C

SECTION: Features

LENGTH: 305 words

From Professor Roger Williams
Sir, Recent publicity about the likely means of infection of up to 3,000 haemophiliac patients with hepatitis C (report, November 17) highlights the need for continuing research into this serious disease.
 Clinical illness may not arise until after 20 to 30 years of infection which should give some reassurance to those who have acquired the infection by whatever route. Nevertheless, the hepatitis C virus (HCV) is highly infectious; it leads to much morbidity and mortality in the world, with some estimated 300 million persons affected.
 The virus is transmitted by blood-to-blood contact, mainly via transfusions and injections; but there are still many cases where doctors simply do not know how hepatitis C has been acquired.
 The Times has recently drawn attention to the case of Chiron v Murex, where a biotechnology company is seeking to limit competitors carrying out research into hepatitis C by claiming that it, effectively, ''owns'' the virus (''Blood feud in the High Court'', Mind and Matter, October 31). Already one HCV research project has been dropped because the Chiron patent is so broad that no resulting vaccine could ever be commercialised.
 As a society we cannot afford to be restrictive about scientific knowledge in so vital a field. A vaccine which would protect, say, health workers and those exposed to intravenous infection would be an extremely important advance, and research to achieve this end should not be restricted.
 It is hoped that the current storm, while it may stir up undue alarm, emphasises the fact that excessively broad patents which are used to discourage commercial endeavour must be against the public interest.
Yours sincerely,
ROGER WILLIAMS (Director),
Institute of Liver Studies,
Bessemer Road, SE5.
November 17.

11 January 1995_1.Author: No author in byline
11 January 1995_1.chunks: _F By CELIA HALL, Medical Editor. More than 60 haemophiliacs have instructed solicitors to seek compensation from the Government after they were infected with the hepatitis C virus from contaminated blood products. According to Graham Ross, one of the solicitors, more are expected to join the litigation since the Independent revealed that thousands have been infected with the virus which causes liver disease. "We have received many calls in the past two days," said Mr Ross, who led the haemophiliacs' case against the Government over HIV infection. This resulted in a #42m settlement in 1991. However, the claims for damages in the hepatitis cases could face a legal difficulty. Mr Ross said that in 1991, as part of the HIV settlement, the clients agreed to a government clause "whereby haemophiliacs would agree not to pursue any claims for hepatitis infection prior to the settlement". He said: "On the basis of present knowledge it is questionable whether haemophiliacs would have accepted at that time the condition attached to the settlement. "The Government claims in the Independent that `patients received the best available treatment in the light of medical knowledge at the time'. "It has to be acknowledged that at the time the HIV settlement was reached the state of medical and scientific knowledge of the relative effects of HIV and hepatitis infections were markedly different to what they are today. "At the time HIV was by far and away the most serious condition and was felt to lead to early death. Hepatitis C was felt to be something that could be lived with. "We now have a situation where HIV is no longer an early death sentence. On the other hand hepatitis C is being seen to be more dangerous than at first felt with 12 haemophiliacs dying last year." About 2,000 haemophiliacs who used the blood-clotting agent Factor VIII, and 3,000 patients who are not haemophiliacs who received transfusions of fresh blood, are said to be infected with Hepatitis C. This happened before the blood transfusion service took steps to protect blood supplies. Mr Ross said that the existence of hepatitis infection in blood products was known about before the HIV problems came to light. "It was an important part of our case. We argued that they were negligent because they knew about hepatitis B and about non-A non-B hepatitis [later indentified as hepatitis C]. Had they stopped importing these blood products from the United States then the HIV infections would not have happened."

11 January 1995_1.Author: Jenny Hope
11 January 1995_1.chunks: by Medical Correspondent SUFFERERS of the mysterious blood disease hepatitis C will now be able to turn to their own support group The Hepatitis C Support Group has recently been set up to deal with the problems of an estimated one in 500 Britons who suffer from the condition. The hepatitis C virus (HCV) was only identified in 1989 and so little is known about the disease. Doctors suggest that 20% of those infected will develop cirrhosis of the liver, possibly resulting in liver failure. In some cases, sufferers will go on to develop liver cancer. Symptoms of liver disease can take 10 to 30 years to develop. The development of a reliable blood test led to the introduction of nationwide screening of blood donors in September 1991 and since that time, donors found to be infected are not allowed to give blood and are offered counselling and treatment. The disease can also be spread by infected needles and, rarely, sharing toothbrushes and razors. Ear piercing and tattoos are other possible sources of risk. There is little evidence in Europe of sexual transmission, nor mother to child transmission. Gabrielle Page, a nurse from Essex, started the first support group in the UK for hepatitis C sufferers last month in association the British Liver Trust. Gabrielle, 42, discovered she had contracted the hepatitis C in November last year. She believes she contracted the virus after a blood transfusion she received while undergoing spinal surgery in August 1991, just one month before the screening programme started. `I had always been a very active person,' says Gabrielle, `ready to throw myself into anything and bursting with energy. After the operation, however, I found myself feeling more and more tired. It was weird, I just wasn't myself at all. I wasn't just tired, I was completely exhausted and found it difficult to do even the smallest things. `I kept going to my GP, but as he could find nothing wrong, in the end he told me that maybe I was trying to do too much. And I tried laughing it off. `Then I had to have a gallstones operation. This was quite unusual because I am quite slim and normally it is overweight people who have this problem. The surgeon agreed, and when he performed the operation he took a liver biopsy. They told me they were testing for hepatitis C but said that I should not worry because they were sure I was negative. `But they were wrong. When the positive result came back, I just thought, `Of course'. All of the signs were there and I had had a blood transfusion.' Gabrielle started receiving drug treatment at the Royal Free Hospital in North London last month. Gabrielle's condition was diagnosed largely by chance but there is mounting concern among experts about the moral dilemma of whether to contact people who could have been exposed to contaminated transfusions. The problem was given fresh impetus two months ago when it was revealed that 12 British haemophiliacs had died from hepatitis C after they were given contaminated blood products and 2,000 others had been infected. Labour peer Lord Ashley of Stoke, a veteran campaigner for the disabled, claims that virtually every haemophiliac who received blood before 1986 will have been infected with the virus. There have already been calls for government compensation to be paid to haemophiliacs affected by contaminated blood products provided by the Health Service - along the lines of the 1990 out-of-court settlement for those infected by the Aids virus. But Dr Metters claims the NHS is not liable. `We do not believe there is any question of fault or negligence in the way the transfusion service screened its donations during that time,' he says. Nevertheless Government health officials are launching a nationwide hunt to trace an estimated 3,000 people who may have contracted hepatitis C after receiving contaminated blood transfusions. After mounting pressure from health experts, a decision has finally been taken to track as many people as possible who may have been infected with a potentially deadly virus which can cause liver disease. Those at risk will have received transfusions prior to September 1991 when all blood donations began to be routinely screened for the virus although health minister Tom Sackville has stressed the chances of any individual being infected are `extremely small'. The UK was the last country in Europe to set up a screening programme. The new `look-back' exercise will concentrate on tracking donations made by 1,000 infected donors picked up under the screening programme. It will use hospital records to trace patients who received a transfusion of blood from an infected donor. The Blood Transfusion Services estimates 3,000 people will have been affected. Dr Jeremy Metters, the government's deputy chief medical officer who is masterminding the operation, admits the exercise might alarm millions of people. `I am afraid that doctors may be besieged by people concerned about being at risk,' he says. It would be a decision for individual GPs whether to order a blood test for someone who was particularly anxious or had been at high risk because of multiple transfusions. Dr Metters advises people to be patient because even those at risk were not in any immediate danger. `The individual risk is very small. There is no need for anyone who received a blood transfusion to take any immediate action - the evidence we have is that it will take a long time for problems to develop. It is better for them to wait until they are called.' * A free helpline has been set up to answer questions from the public on 0800 716197. For details of the Hepatitis C Support Group, send an SAE to Gabrielle Page, c/o The British Liver Trust, Central House, Central Avenue, Ransomes Euro-Park, Ipswich IP3 9QG

11 January 1995_1.Title: VICTIM PLEDGES TO HELP OTHERS WITH HEPATITIS C.
11 January 1995_1.Author: No author in byline
11 January 1995_1.chunks: _F Celia Hall meets a woman determined to form a support group for sufferers of the liver disease caught through infected blood Gabrielle Page has hepatitis C and a mission. Despite her condition, which makes her feel constantly tired, despite her job, her family and her household commitments, she intends to form a support group for sufferers of this liver disease - which thousands of people caught through infected blood supplies. Ms Page and her doctors believe it is likely that she was infected during spinal surgery in 1989 when she received donated blood. Two weeks ago The Independent revealed that before 1985, 2,000 haemophiliacs had been infected with hepatitis C from contaminated Factor VIII, the blood-clotting product. Twelve haemophiliacs died last year as a result. Four have had liver transplants. Since 1985 Factor VIII has been given anti-viral heat treatment. Another group of 3,000 people was also infected from fresh or frozen blood or blood products used routinely in hospitals. This blood cannot be heat treated, so instead since 1991 all blood donors have been screened for hepatitis C. Ms Page said: "Anyone who had a fresh or frozen blood product before 1991 is at risk. There are a lot of people involved here. I don't know at this stage what we will do, but I want people to contact me. "Many need support and to be able to talk about this. We may go for compensation; we may have an educational role. It will be up to the group." Ms Page, 42, a health visitor, is married and has a 12-year-old daughter. She stresses that hepatitis C is not passed on in normal contact, that the infection route is blood to blood, classically by injection and transfusion. "There is no risk to others in the normal course of events," she said. It is still something of a medical enigma. The heptitis C virus was identified in 1989. Six strains have been indentified and it can take 10 to 30 years to produce symptoms of liver damage. It can be hard to detect in the blood or in the liver. Progress of the disease varies from one patient to another. Liver damage can take the form of cirrhosis which can lead to liver failure and the risk of liver cancer is increased. Ms Page's story must mirror the experience of many. "For 18 months to two years I was feeling increasingly tired. I am a very energetic person but I was feeling exhausted all the time. I was getting breathless at the gym. "My GP surgery is very good but they said I was really doing too much; I was getting older." Ms Page also had a longstanding gall bladder problem which caused her pain. In the summer the surgeon she was referred to decided to remove her gall bladder but he was not convinced that her symtpoms related to it alone. So, during surgery, he performed a liver biopsy. "It was all a bit of a puzzle. He suggested that I had a test for hepatitis C," Ms Page said. "To be honest I knew that there was something wrong so when he told me it was not a complete surprise." Ms Page is now being investigated for her suitability for treatment with interferon, the anti-viral drug used to treat heptitis C which has proved successful in 25 per cent of cases. "We have made some small adjustments to family life. When I feel tired I have a sleep and I do not feel guilty about it. I pace myself. I refuse to become a failing Victorian lady lying about swooning on a chaise-longue. "The message is that we can get out on the other side of this," she said. - Send SAE to Gabrielle Page, 112 Hunter Avenue, Shenfield, Essex, CM15 8PG.

11 January 1995_1.chunks: _F By the time the NHS introduced the screening of blood products in 1985, 1,200 haemophiliacs had been infected by the Aids virus, writes Mary Braid. It was 1990 before the Government reached a #42m out-of-court settlement with affected haemophiliacs or their families. By then victims were dying at the rate of one a week. More than 150 adults and children had died of Aids-related illnesses and 210 had developed full-blown Aids. Most had been infected by the anti-clotting agent Factor VIII. The settlement, under John Major, came only two months after Margaret Thatcher and Kenneth Clarke, the then Health Secretary, had ruled it out. But William Waldegrave, Mr Clarke's successor, said he had "seldom seen a stronger humanitarian case". The deal meant #60,000 for married haemophiliacs with children, #32,000 for married childless couples, #23,000 for single men and #21,000 for each of 175 infected children. People infected by haemophiliac partners received #23,000. But the Haemophilia Society argued it was too little, too late. It had demanded #90m on top of #34m ex-gratia payments already made.

11 January 1995_1.Title: EDITORIAL - JUSTICE FOR THOSE THE NHS INFECTS.
11 January 1995_1.Author: No author in byline
11 January 1995_1.chunks: _F Yesterday's front-page report about haemophiliacs infected with hepatitis C after treatment with contaminated blood has produced a surprising reaction from the Haemophilia Society. To lay observers, there seems to be a strong analogy between this episode involving about 2,000 people, and the earlier case of 1,200 haemophiliacs infected with HIV in the course of treatment. In 1990, the Government agreed to pay them #42m in compensation. In both instances, those requiring treatment with a blood product picked up a dangerous infection. But yesterday the Haemophilia Society said it had "no plans to seek compensation". Not enough was known, said the society, about how the disease progresses. This cautious approach has a certain medical logic, since the two infections have very different consequences. Compared with HIV, hepatitis C's advance is far less inexorable. Of those infected, 20 per cent recover quickly, while the rest develop persistent infection lasting many years. About half the larger group will develop a chronic form resulting in inflammation of the liver. Only one in five of those - making 8 per cent of the initial total - will develop cirrhosis of the liver, which is not necessarily fatal. Whereas HIV tends to develop into Aids within 10 years, symptoms of liver disease can take 10 to 40 years to develop. That helps to explain why the Haemophilia Society is playing down the latest scourge to afflict its members. Most of those infected, it pointed out, have had the condition for several decades, and remain well. None the less, 12 men - only males suffer from haemophilia - are understood to have died from hepatitis C as a result of treatment before 1991; four have had liver transplants; and the society concedes that a "small proportion" of others have had severe problems. Their number is likely to increase as the infection takes its course. Furthermore, not only haemophilia sufferers are affected. An additional 3,000 adults and children who received transfusions before 1991 may also be at risk. Hepatitis C is never likely to be as acute a threat for those who have used blood products as HIV has been, and it will not reach its peak for years. Yet when people fall seriously ill as a direct result of NHS treatment, natural justice dictates that some provision should be made to compensate them. That should apply to haemophiliacs and non-haemophiliacs alike. For the Government to rule out all compensation at this stage, as it did yesterday, is both insensitive and unfair.

11 January 1995_1.Title: THE HAEMOPHILIA CONTROVERSY - MEDICAL EXPERTS DIVIDED OVER EXTENT OF PROBLEM.
11 January 1995_1.Author: No author in byline
11 January 1995_1.chunks: _F By Martin Whitfield. Survey identifies new group at risk as legal dispute jeopardises checks. Medical experts are sharply divided on the extent of infection of hepatatis C among the general population. Estimates vary from as few as 9,000 to more than 500,000. Intravenous drug users and people who received blood transfusions before 1986 are most at risk. However, considerable numbers of people carrying the virus have no known risk factors. The British Liver Trust, the only patient organisation for people with hepatitis C, believes that as many as 1 per cent of the population may be infected. Most would have no idea that they were carrying the virus as the symptoms of liver disease can take up to 20 years to develop. Virtually no research has been carried out to discover the scale of hepatatis-C infection although the first studies among drug users have found a high incidence. The trust is urging the Government to fund a detailed national survey. Professor Peter Scheuer - medical adviser to the trust and a former leading pathologist at the Royal Free Hospital, north-west London, until his retirement in 1992 - said the rate of infection was a serious medical problem. He supported the trust's prediction that up to 500,000 people could be involved. "A common history is someone who may have taken drugs once or twice when they were young," he said. "They may be in their 40s or 50s before they find they are in serious trouble." But Professor Roger Williams, head of the liver unit at King's College Hospital, London, said he believed that estimates of half a million infected people were "much too high". He said latest blood transfusion figures showed that 0.016 per cent of new donors had the viral infection, not 1 in 100. "It is very unlikely that throughout the general population of the UK the figure is more than 0.01 per cent." The National Blood Authority believes that around 3,000 patients may have been infected as a result of transfusions from infected blood donated before 1991. Professor Williams, who is a member of the board of governors of the British Liver Trust, maintained that the level of hepatitis-C infection was lower than in most other countries. The incidence of infection is known to vary considerably between states although there is a world-wide estimate of 300 million people carrying the virus. A large study in Italy found that 1.7 per cent of the population had the virus, while even higher levels are found in Egypt and in the Far East where large-scale "shared-needle" immunisation programmes have been carried out. Professor Williams and Professor Scheuer agreed that blood-to-blood contact is the most likely form of transmission, but there remains a low risk of the virus spreading through sexual intercourse and exchange of body fluids. All blood donations have been screened for hepatitis C since 1991, and about one in 2,000 new donors has been found to be a carrier. Far more people are likely to be infected in the general population as blood donors are a self-selecting group, with most of the high-risk groups explicitly prevented from giving blood. Another unknown factor about the virus - only identified positively in 1989 - is the percentage of carriers who later suffer from liver disease. It is believed that up to 20 per cent could develop cirrhosis, with half of these going on to suffer from liver failure. Heavy drinking, often associated with the onset of cirrhosis, and the added presence of HIV have accelerated liver problems among haemophiliacs. Dr Christine Lee, director of the haemophilia unit at the Royal Free Hospital, said 255 patients attending the unit had hepatitis C, and it was known that virtually all of the 3,122 haemophiliacs who received blood products between 1965 and 1986 would be infected. "There is a probability of some form of sexual transmission but the amount is small. Very few of the sexual partners of haemophiliacs have been affected," she said.

11 January 1995_1.Title: THE HAEMOPHILIA CONTROVERSY - HEPATITIS C VIRUS SPREADS AMONG DRUG ABUSERS.
11 January 1995_1.Author: No author in byline
11 January 1995_1.chunks: _F By Jason Bennetto. Survey identifies new group at risk as legal dispute jeopardises checks. An estimated 400,000 people who have injected drugs are infected with hepatitis C, according to an unpublished study. A survey of more than 2,000 intravenous drug users in the United Kingdom found that 60 per cent were hepatitis anti-body positive. Several injectors are believed to have died from the disease, which can destroy the liver. Others are believed to have been infected after just a few injections, which took place as far back as the Sixties. International studies have shown that most people who are anti-body positive are infected, although in many cases the hepatitis C virus may be dormant or non-infectious. Hepatitis C is easily spread by sharing needles contaminated by blood containing the virus. The new two-year study - the first national survey of injecting drug users - was carried out by the West Suffolk Drug Advisory Service. They obtained test results from 2,081 injecting drug users. The authors of the report, Dr Tom Waller and Roger Holmes, say that, at a conservative estimate, there are about 400,000 people infected via injecting. This assumes there are about 150,000 to 200,000 people currently injecting drugs. However, symptons of liver diseases can take 30 years to appear and therefore tens of thousands of former injectors will have been exposed to the virus. Nearly half the 131 respondents who carried out the tests reported difficulty in getting clients tested, or in following up a positive test with further tests or treatment. The new report, which is expected to be published in the next few months, is being presented to the independent Government advisory body, the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs, later today. Studies have shown that the longer someone injects, the more likely he or she is to contract the disease. In an Australian study, 95 per cent of drug users were positive if they had been injecting for more than 10 years. The type of drug affects the degree of risk, as some substances are injected more often. Cocaine addicts who can inject 15 times a day are more likely to be infected than heroin users, who need the drug far less often. Mr Holmes, co-author of the study, said: "Shared needles are the main way the virus is spread, but sharing razors or contaminated tattoo equipment might also be involved." He added that his department knew of a small number of "deaths related to the effects of hepatitis C". The proportion of people who are expected to die after being contaminated is unknown. Mr Holmes said: "Although about 60 per cent of the drug injectors may develop some form of chronic disease, we are not sure how many are life-threatening. There's a possibility that some of the people who are believed to have died from Aids could have been victims of hepatitis C." Because the viral infection was only identified in 1989, many of the people currently infected are likely to have been contaminated by dirty needles from the 60s and 70s. Christopher Tibbs, a specialist at the liver unit at King's College Hospital in London, said earlier this month: "About 10 per cent of the cases referred to me are City yuppies who have had it detected when they had a standard Bupa-type insurance medical. "These people have no idea how they caught it or how long they had it. Most likely it was in their university days in the Sixties. They might have had a wild party and had one or two shots in the arm. "These are middle-aged people whose past history has suddenly been thrown back in their faces."

11 January 1995_1.Title: HEPATITIS C  STILL PASSED IN SURGERY.
11 January 1995_1.Author: No author in byline
11 January 1995_1.chunks: _F By CELIA HALL, Medical Editor. Up to 150 patients a year could be infected with the hepatitis C virus as a result of receiving contaminated blood plasma during surgery, a consultant physician said yesterday. He said patients risked infection because the "safest" product available was not being used. Dr Jonathan Freeman a transplant anaesthetist and intensive care specialist who has himself been involved in the transfusion of more than 20,000 units of blood and blood products, says other countries use treated plasma. He said: "Some countries in Europe such as Belgium and Norway have already switched to the sole use of this specially treated plasma in place of untreated frozen plasma and this is a growing practice." Dr Freeman said that in Germany there is a law which deems it medically negligent if a patient becomes infected after the prescription of a product known to be inferior and to have identifiable risks when a safer product is available. "Are the residual risks acceptable and are we doing enough to reduce them even further in the UK? Infection with hepatitis C is not to be taken lightly," he said. He said that by 2000 the commonest reason for liver transplant could be liver failure caused by hepatitis C.  He has based his estimates on data published in the British Medical Journal in August. It described the risk of being infected with hepatitis C as "less than 1 in 13,000". He says that 2.5 million units of blood are used in England and Wales every year so "anything up to 150 units could possibly be infected with hepatitis C virus [HCV]". Dr Freeman, who works at the prestigious liver unit at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Birmingham, stressed that he was making a personal statement. "I am concerned for my patients. I want to be assured I am giving them the best possible product." Last week, the Independent revealed that 12 patients with haemophilia had died from liver failure caused by hepatitis C. They were infected by contaminated Factor VIII, a blood product. A total of 2,000 haemophiliacs have hepatitis C.  Another 3,000 patients who are not haemophiliacs are estimated to have been infected through blood transfusion. The risk to both groups has diminished since Factor VIII is now treated and donors are screened. But it is accepted that there is a small risk of HCV getting into the blood supply because tests may not detect it in a donor who has been newly infected and has not created measurable anti-bodies. Dr Angela Robinson, medical director of the National Blood Authority which supervises the transfusion service, said: "The screening is 90 per cent effective. We put the risk at 1 in 100,000." She said the authority was "treating the matter urgently", and was considering two courses of action. "Quarantine" of the frozen plasma, would mean that before it was used the donor would have to be recalled for another blood test for HCV 6 to 12 months after the orginal screen. "We are also trialling the treated product, which is not currently licensed for use in this country. We are treatiang this matter urgently," she said. She said that the treated plasma would cost twice as much as the #30 a unit for the untreated product.

Hepatitis C patent

SECTION: Features

LENGTH: 288 words

From Mr Larry Kurtz
Sir, On behalf of the Chiron Corporation, which in 1987 discovered the hepatitis C virus (HCV), I would like to allay the fears of Professor Roger Williams (letter, November 19) that upholding Chiron's HCV patent rights, as the High Court has just done (report, November 30), may limit research.
 Since Chiron's patent application was published (in May 1989) research in the hepatitis C field has burgeoned. In fact, since Chiron's patent was granted in January 1992, more than 4,500 scientific papers related to HCV have been published and more than 350 patent applications related to HCV have been filed (only 20 by Chiron) by at least 25 commercial and research organizations. This puts into context the one project that Professor Williams says has been dropped as a result of our patent.
 Chiron does not ''own'' the hepatitis C virus. The company's patents generally cover reagents based on the HCV genetic sequence and the application of the reagents to diagnostics. Since the invention of those reagents, Chiron has entered into a number of licensing arrangements with international diagnostic companies, three of them in the UK, to supply HCV tests.
 A commitment to research must go hand-in-hand with a commitment to protection of intellectual property rights. Without the reward offered by the patent system, it is doubtful whether companies such as Chiron would make the substantial investments needed to address problems such as HCV. Safeguarding these rewards is vital if future advances in healthcare are to be achieved.
Yours etc,
LARRY KURTZ (Vice-President,
Corporate Communications),
Chiron Corporation,

Emeryville, California.

11 January 1995_1.Title: KENNETH FERGUSON.
11 January 1995_1.Author: By Gillian Bowditch, Scotland Correspondent.
11 January 1995_1.chunks: A boy aged 15 who suffers from haemophilia is planning to sue the Government for negligence after he contracted hepatitis C from contaminated blood products. Kenneth Ferguson, from Strathclyde, was told five months ago that he had the virus. Doctors believe that he had contracted the disease in 1984 from contaminated Factor 9, a blood-clotting agent. If the case comes to court it will be the first of its kind in Britain and its success would open the way for the 3,000 haemophiliacs who have contracted hepatitis C to pursue legal action. A spokesman for the Haemophilia Society said two cases in England had been settled before they reached court. The Government has denied liability for the contamination of haemophiliacs with hepatitis C. In 1991, after a sustained campaign, it paid #42m to patients given blood infected with HIV. The Haemophilia Society is pressing for the same level of compensation for hepatitis C victims. Kenneth suffers from Christmas disease, a form of haemophilia which leads to internal bleeding. When he is ill he needs three injections a week of Factor 9. In 1984 Salisbury Hospital supplied the family with a batch of the blood-clotting agent that doctors believe had come from an infected batch. Kenneth's father Patrick Ferguson, who has retired from the Army, says that he wants his son to be financially secure. "He faces a life of not having children because he must practise safe sex," he said. "He can't have a drink because of the effects on his liver. What are his chances of marrying? His career prospects are hindered." Hundreds of patients of a doctor carrying the hepatitis B virus were urged yesterday to have blood tests. The unnamed doctor is an orthopaedic surgeon for Scarborough and North East Yorkshire Health Care NHS Trust but has stopped clinical work. He previously worked at Castle Hill Hospital, Cottingham, Humberside.

Steve Connor explains On Tuesday, a High Court judge granted a company that "owns" the hepatitis C virus an injunction to prevent rival firms from selling blood tests for the potentially lethal infection. 11 January 1995_1.Title: CHIRON CORPORATION.
11 January 1995_1.Author: By Nigel Hawkes.
11 January 1995_1.chunks: A High Court ruling yesterday confirmed that a common virus is effectively owned by a California biotechnology company. The court backed the claims of Chiron Corporation that two other companies had breached its patents on a stretch of DNA in the hepatitis C virus by marketing test kits. A permanent injunction was granted to prevent Murex Diagnostics and Organon Teknika from marketing the tests. The judgment means, in effect, that a discovery as well as an invention can be patented. Yesterday's ruling is the latest to back the idea that it is possible to patent a stretch of DNA, together with any application to which it may be put. Chiron's British patent covers the use of the DNA from hepatitis C in any test or any vaccine that may be developed. Half a million people in Britain are believed to be infected by hepatitis C. William Burns, managing director of Ortho Diagnostic Systems, Chiron's partner in the development of the hepatitis C test, said that the ruling meant that companies that had invested in research and development in biotechnology could get a fair return. The products sold by Murex and Organon would now have to be withdrawn. The tests have a guaranteed market because all blood donations must be tested for hepatitis C.

11 January 1995_1.Title: THE HAEMOPHILIA CONTROVERSY - PATENT ROW THREATENS BLOOD TESTS.
11 January 1995_1.Author: No author in byline
11 January 1995_1.chunks: _F By Steve Connor, Science Correspondent. Survey identifies new group at risk as legal dispute jeopardises checks. A legal dispute over who "owns" the hepatitis C virus could lead to a third of the blood tests for the disease being banned in Britain by the end of the year. A High Court judge is soon to rule whether to grant an injunction against a company whose blood test for the virus (HCV) accounts for 34 per cent of sales in Britain, including more than one-third of HCV tests used by the national blood transfusion service. The company, Murex, is involved in a patent dispute with Chiron, a biotechnology company based in California, which identified HCV in 1987 and subsequently applied for patents on the virus's entire genetic sequence. Chiron won a legal challenge claiming that Murex has infringed its UK patent, and it wants the High Court to impose a ban on its competitor's blood test. Murex has appealed against the patent-infringement decision and wants to continue selling its blood test until its appeal is heard in about a year's time. Leading liver doctors and transfusion scientists have condemned Chiron's use of its patent to create what they claim is a monopoly. Professor Roger Williams, director of liver studies at King's College, London, said: "It is very dangerous to have any area of research restricted to one company. It's against the public interest because the testing for hepatitis C is many times more expensive than for HIV, which is a similar sort of test, because of the patent. The cost could be greatly reduced if you had free competition." Professor Williams said it would be better for Murex to be allowed to continue selling its HCV test kit and so have the incentive to continue research on the virus. "For a doctor, the most important aspect is that unless you have several groups checking their own ideas and doing the research, you don't get any progress," he said. A transfusion scientist, who wished to remain anonymous, said that competition "has improved the nature of the product", and the broad range of the Chiron patent will eliminate this competition. He said that the cost of the HCV test kit ranges between #1.50 and #2.50, compared with 35p to 50p for the HIV test. "When you get a monopoly situation, there is no way you'll get the prices coming down." About 3 million HCV test kits are used each year in Britain and the National Blood Authority said that about 1 in every 2,000 new blood donors are confirmed as testing positive for the virus. Bob Blackburn, chief patent counsel for Chiron, said the patent on HCV covers the entire genetic sequence of the virus, but insisted that this was normal for viral blood tests. He said the patent dispute did not prevent Murex or any other company from doing research on HCV. "We're not trying to monopolise the virus," he said.

11 January 1995_1.Title: CONTAMINATED BLOOD KILLS 12.
11 January 1995_1.Author: No author in byline
11 January 1995_1.chunks: _F By CELIA HALL Medical Editor. Doctors believe 5,000 people have caught liver disease from transfusions and clotting agents  Twelve British men with haemophilia have died from the liver disease hepatitis C after they were given contaminated concentrates of blood. All 12 men died last year. At least 2,000 more people are infected, and four have had liver transplants as a result. Another 3,000 adults and children, who are not haemophiliacs but did receive fresh blood transfusions before 1991, may also have been infected, according to the Blood Transfusion Service, but are unaware of their condition. The emergence of these previously unreported deaths echoes the case of hundreds of haemophiliacs who caught the Aids virus from contaminated blood. Haemophilia is an inherited disease whose major symptom is the failure of the blood-clotting mechanism. Haemophiliacs, who are always male, often have to be given blood-clotting agents - called "factors" - which are produced from donated blood. Doctors say 90 to 95 per cent of haemophiliacs who used factors regularly before May 1985 have contracted hepatitis C.  Now the Haemophilia Society is considering seeking redress from the Department of Health. The society is organising meetings to inform haemophiliacs and is in contact with the department. The National Blood Authority is also considering what action to take. Dr Fereydoun Ala, chairman of the Standing Advisory Committee on Transfusion Transmitted Infections, said: "Those working in the field believe we have a duty of care of patients and that we should be open about this. We are deciding how we can best proceed." At the same time, the consultants who head the regional haemophilia centres around the country have their own working party on haemophilia and hepatitis. The hepatitis C virus (HCV) was only identified in 1989. Before that, it was recognised as non-A, non-B hepatitis. It is a slow, chronic condition leading to cirrhosis of the liver in 20 per cent of cases. Ten per cent of these go on to liver failure in five years. Symptoms of liver disease can take 10 to 30 years to develop. Doctors admit they still do not know enough about the progress of the disease. Hepatitis C is transmitted by blood-to-blood contact, mostly via transfusions and injections. In 1985, blood products, including the clotting agent Factor VIII, were subjected to anti-viral heat treatment designed to eradicate HIV. Haemophilic boys up to the age of 10 who use factors are not, therefore, at risk. No cases of hepatitis C in this group have come to light for the past nine years. However, fresh whole blood or fresh parts of blood cannot be treated in the same way. In June 1991, the Department of Health paid out a total of #42m to 1,200 haemophiliacs who caught HIV from factors made from infected blood. In September 1991, on advice from the Department of Health, the Blood Transfusion Service began to screen donors for hepatitis C to protect the blood supply. Simon Taylor, vice-chairman of the Haemophilia Society, said: "At this stage, because the information about hepatitis C is so slight we are not sure which way we should proceed. The difficulty is the vast majority of haemophiliacs have no hepatitis symptoms because the disease could take 30 years to show itself. There is no medical consensus on diagnosis, treatment or prognosis. One thing we are considering is seeking compensation when people become ill."  Haemophilia experts say the true number of patients infected with hepatitis C is not known but 2,000 is a reasonable estimate. There are 10,000 men and boys with haemophilia in the UK. Of these, 2,500 - including 500 boys aged under 10 - need factors regularly, the rest intermittently. Mr Taylor said most of the 2,000 adults had contracted hepatitis C.  The infection rate is very high because between 20,000 and 30,000 donations are pooled to produce the factors. Dr Ala, who is also director of the West Midlands Blood Transfusion Centre, said they were able to arrive at the estimate of the 3,000 transfusion patients with hepatitis C by checking the records of blood donors who were subsequently found to have hepatitis C.  "What we now have to consider is whether we identify the recipients and contact them. These people may have no symptoms at all. These are very difficult issues," said Dr Ala.  A spokesman for the Department of Health said: "We have the greatest sympathy for these people. "There are no plans to extend the settlement scheme for haemophilia patients who are HIV-positive to patients who have been infected with hepatitis C. The Government does not have a policy of no-fault compensation. Patients received the best available treatment in the light of medical knowledge at the time."

11 January 1995_1.Title: SIR NICHOLAS FAIRBAIRN
11 January 1995_1.Author: By Dr Thomas Stuttaford.
11 January 1995_1.chunks: The shades of grey which have characterised the House of Commons for the past few parliaments have deepened with the death from hepatitis of Sir Nicholas Fairbairn. Hepatitis is a diagnostic portmanteau within which very diverse diseases can be hidden. Literally translated, hepatitis means inflammation of the liver; inflammation which can follow infection with a wide variety of viruses. As well as hepatitis A, B, C, D, bacteria or spirochaetes, it can result from the ingestion of various liver toxins, of which alcohol is the most common but also includes many pharmaceutical drugs, or by the infiltration of malignant disease. Doctors, and politicians, often use the term to disguise from patients and the public the true nature of their troubles. In Sir Nicholas's case the assumption has been made, possibly unfairly, that his hepatitis stemmed from his convivial lifestyle. Professor Peter Scheuer, an emeritus professor of histopathology at the Royal Free Hospital school of medicine and chairman of the medical advisory committee of the British Liver Trust, said: "The vast majority of drinkers who develop alcoholic cirrhosis are by most people's standards prodigiously heavy drinkers; there are, of course, exceptions that need a minimum of 16 units of alcohol a day for well over five years (a unit is equivalent to a glass of wine, a pub measure of whisky or a half pint of beer). Even then, only a third of these very heavy drinkers will develop cirrhosis." Much is known about the effect of alcohol on the liver's biochemistry, but which particular change it induces in the liver to trigger the start of cirrhosis is unknown. Professor Scheuer said: "This is one of the great unsolved mysteries of modern medicine and one which the trust is trying to unravel. But we do know that gender, ethnic background and probably genetic differences can be important." The type of alcohol, whether wines, spirits or beer, does not make any difference to the prognosis, only the quantity. I first heard of Sir Nicholas's prodigous sexual exploits when he was a successful Edinburgh advocate. There is no evidence that his later liver problems were related to his love life, about which little secret has been made. He even listed it as a hobby in Who's Who. But liver disease always remains a possible danger for the multi-partnered. Contrary to popular beliefs the sexual transmission of hepatitis B, and possibly hepatitis C, as opposed to its transmission by transfusion or injection, is not confined to homosexual sex, about which Sir Nicholas had particularly strong views. Although the sexual transmission of hepatitis B is well proven, the pattern of transmission is still to be mapped. Even after those who are known to have caught it through transfusion or drug abuse have been excluded, there are still a very large number of cases that remain unexplained. Examination of the blood of the sexual partners of known cases of hepatitis C has shown that the majority remain unaffected. As Professor Scheuer says: "The means by which hepatitis C is spread is another mystery of liver disease."

11 January 1995_1.Title: IMPROVING THE NATION'S BLOOD SUPPLY.
11 January 1995_1.Author: No author in byline
11 January 1995_1.chunks: _F After recent scares, Simon Hadlington reports on the quest for safer products  The revelation that an estimated 3,000 people who received blood transfusions before 1991 have been contaminated with the hepatitis C virus has focused attention on the purity of the nation's blood supply. First reports appeared in the Independent last week, describing the spread of hepatitis C through blood or blood products, affecting those who had received fresh blood and another group, haemophiliacs, who received the blood-clotting agent Factor VIII before heat treatment began in 1985. Despite the fact that infections from hepatitis C through contaminated blood have been extremely rare since screening of donors began in 1991, viral contamination of donated blood and its products is a big concern among professionals involved in blood transfusion medicine. The problem is an international one. Earlier this year, Dr Harvey Klein, chief of the Department of Transfusion Medicine at the National Institutes of Health in the US, said, "The risk of infection from hepatitis and HIV, as well as from future unknown viruses, remains a major concern among medical and scientific communities." Dr William Murphy, a senior lecturer in medicine at Edinburgh University and honorary consultant to the Scottish Blood Transfusion Service, says that most people in the medical profession are confident that the blood supply is safe. "You get very little expression of unhappiness and I think that confidence is probably not misplaced. Most of the deaths associated with transfusion are due to things other than viral transmission. Nevertheless, we are constantly on our toes just in case new infective agents appear. There is no room for complacency." In the UK, donated blood is screened routinely for HIV, hepatitis B and C and syphilis, and, in certain situations, for another virus, cytomegalovirus. Procedures for eliminating the risk of HIV infection through contaminated blood appear to have been largely effective. "There is a theoretical possibility of transmission if a donation is made within two to three weeks of the donor having become infected, when sufficient antibodies have not been produced to be detected by the test. So there is a gap in the security," Dr Murphy says. He points out that since 1985 in the UK there has been only one known instance of HIV transmission through blood products. The other big issue is ensuring a regular, consistent supply of blood. Reliance on the goodwill of donors, coupled with the short shelf-life of blood products, can cause shortages. Red cells can survive for between five and six weeks; platelets, which are vital for the clotting process, expire after only five days. The manufacture of artificial blood products could go some way to improving both the purity of supplies and their availability. Researchers have not been slow to recognise the potential of the market. But natural blood is a hard act to follow. One candidate undergoing clinical trials at centres around the world is a group of synthetic organic chemicals called perfluorocarbons, which are capable of carrying oxygen. Their attraction is that being synthetic they are potentially cheap to produce. However, while the perfluorocarbons were initially thought to be largely chemically inert, there have been concerns about what happens to them in the body. If their safety is guaranteed, however, perfluorocarbons would be used principally for providing oxygen to tissues in emergencies, such as at the scene of an accident, rather than for more chronic conditions. A number of companies in the United States are extracting and purifying haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying component of blood, from red cells. The chief problem here is that in the body such "naked" haemoglobin, which is no longer protected within the blood cell, is broken down into its constituent sub-units. These are called alpha-beta dimers, and they can interfere with the function of the kidneys. Furthermore, such "recycled" haemoglobin does not release oxygen as freely as its native counterpart. Work is under way to stabilise the haemoglobin sub-units in the body. Meanwhile, trials of a genetically engineered haemoglobin are being undertaken in surgical patients at the University of Utah in the US. This "recombinant" haemoglobin is being produced in the bacterium Escherichia coli by Somatogen, a Colorado-based biopharmaceutical company, which has signed a marketing agreement with Eli Lilly, the drugs giant. According to Somatogen, its product is comparable to human red cells in its efficacy of oxygen delivery and safety. Also, the company says, it is active for a sufficiently long period to permit its use in surgery. The company further claims that the product has a low risk of being attacked by the body's immune system; it requires no tissue typing or cross-matching, and may release oxygen into the tissues more effectively than transfused red blood cells. Yet another American firm, Delta Biotechnology, is gearing up for human clinical trials of genetically engineered human albumin, which is an important component of blood plasma. The trials are due to begin next year, and will examine the safety and effectiveness of the product as a means of "expanding" blood, to help eke out supplies. Some professionals involved in the field, however, are concerned that it will be difficult to make genetically engineered products sufficiently pure; that they will remain contaminated by tiny quantities of foreign proteins emanating from the organisms which were used to produce them. The fear is that these proteins will trigger the body's defence mechanisms against the blood products. One of the most interesting projects is the development of a "bone marrow bioreactor" by Dr David Wu at the University of Rochester in New York. Bone marrow is the "factory" for the production of all red blood cells and platelets and most white blood cells. "Our overall goal is to develop an artificial bone marrow to support the maintenance of stem cells and their differentiation into mature blood cells," Dr Wu says. Stem cells are blood cells that have been newly produced by the bone marrow and that have not yet been modified (differentiated) to perform specialist functions. The reactor comprises a culture chamber filled with tiny, highly porous spheres that are inoculated with marrow cells. This porous matrix is overlaid with a liquid culture medium containing a cocktail of the nutrients necessary for the cells to grow. "The various physiological parameters, such as nutrient and oxygen levels, can be closely controlled," Dr Wu says. He says the bioreactor can support both human and mouse blood cells, and that a wide range of cell types can be harvested from the system at various stages of their development. "It is different from the traditional flask culture in that it produces almost all the blood cell types and thus resembles much better the marrow tissue in the body. With further study we hope to produce mature blood cells for transfusion."
