11 January 1995_2.Title: HUNT FOR 3,000 BLOOD 'VICTIMS'.
11 January 1995_2.Author: By David Brindle, Social Services Correspondent.
11 January 1995_2.chunks: HOSPITAL records are to be trawled to try to trace 3,000 people feared to have contracted hepatitis C through transfusions of contaminated blood, the Department of Health announced yesterday. More than 6,000 people are estimated to have been infected by transfusions before September 1991, when routine screening of blood donations for the hepatitis C virus was begun. At least one in two is assumed to have died since. The department is stressing that people who had a blood transfusion before autumn 1991 run a risk of only one in 2,000 of having contracted hepatitis C - and that very few even of those infected will need treatment. Jeremy Metters, deputy chief medical officer for England, said the department was concerned in case family doctors were besieged by worried patients. "There is no need for those who received blood transfusions to take any immediate action." Ministers have decided to authorise a "look-back exercise" involving transfusion records following concern over hepatitis C infection via transfusions and disclosure that 12 men with haemophilia died from the liver disease in 1993. Previously, the department has argued that it would be technically too difficult to mount such a tracing operation and that no treatment for the disease was available. The policy change has been prompted by the success of a pilot exercise, showing it may be possible to trace many of those infected, and by the licensing of a drug - Interferon Alpha 2a - for use in the treatment of hepatitis C.  The tracing exercise will start by identifying former blood donors discovered since 1991 to have been carriers of the disease. Transfusion centres will then check records and inform hospitals which were sent consignments of blood taken from the donors. The hospitals will seek to establish from their records which patients, if any, received the possibly infected blood and will contact them direct or inform their GPs. Tom Sackville, junior health minister, said: "We shall do all we can to care for patients who have become infected in this way through counselling, and where appropriate, treatment." Health officials estimate that 3,000 people infected before 1991 are still alive. Hepatitis C infection is usually mild in the initial stages. About one in five cases leads to cirrhosis of the liver after 20 years and a few cases lead to liver cancer. A Haemophilia Society spokesman said the society was not seeking compensation across the board. However, it wanted relief of financial hardship on the same terms as those for people infected with HIV.

11 January 1995_2.Title: BLOOD TEST DELAY `PUT LIVES AT RISK'.
11 January 1995_2.Author: By Nigel Hawkes, Science Editor.
11 January 1995_2.chunks: THE blood transfusion service was accused last night of jeopardising people's health by delaying the introduction of a test for hepatitis C virus for two years. Between 1989 and 1991, thousands of patients received blood contaminated with the virus, according to the BBC1 programme Panorama. The Government plans to trace those who had been infected with contaminated blood to provide counselling and, if necessary, treatment. The service could face legal claims from people infected during the two-year period when the test was available but was not used. Over the period, it is estimated, about 3,600 bags of infected blood were given to patients. Hepatitis C virus can cause liver inflammation which is usually mild but may in about a fifth of the cases lead to cirrhosis of the liver in 20 years. Of these, about a tenth go on to develop liver cancer, which is nearly always fatal. The first test was developed by 1989 and adopted abroad. Dr John Barbara, a consultant at the National Blood Authority, told Panorama that he had not wanted to start screening blood donations then because the test produced too many false positive results. "You have to remember that we are talking about doing a thousand tests a day at this one centre," he said. "So any problems with the test too many complications, too much blood wastage could perversely get you into a situation where you are doing more harm than good." Dr Geoffrey Dusheiko, a liver specialist at the Royal Free Hospital in London, told Panorama: "We were adamant that hepatitis C screening should be introduced and I thought that moment had arrived once a test was authorised in several countries." The Haemophilia Society believes that more than 3,000 people with haemophilia have been infected with the virus, many before any test was available. In Belgium, Panorama said, the problem with false positives was dealt with by a second test. A helpline, on 0800-767800, is open 10am-6pm today and tomorrow.

The Times

January 17, 1995, Tuesday

Gaps in the ABC of blood screening

BYLINE: Dr Thomas Stuttaford

SECTION: Features

LENGTH: 605 words

 Dr Thomas Stuttaford explains how some people came to be given blood contaminated with hepatitis C - and what is being done for them.
ABOUT five years ago a young man had his car stolen. Later, by chance, the owner spotted it parked by a building site in central London; he accosted the thief, who drew a knife and stabbed him through the abdomen. Bleeding profusely he was taken to casualty in the nick of time. Resuscitated by transfusions, and repaired by surgeons, he made a good recovery marred only by some slight post-operative jaundice and a recurrent low-grade fever.  Recently he has been complaining of ill health and chronic tiredness; his liver function tests are abnormal and his blood tests show that he has been infected by hepatitis C. 
 In the period when blood could be screened for hepatitis A and B, but not for hepatitis C, the latter accounted for the majority of cases of post-transfusion hepatitis, and it may well be that it was also therefore responsible for many of the cases of inexplicable chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and cancer of the liver.
 The initial symptoms of hepatitis C are mild, but the sting of the disease lies in its tail 50 to 80 per cent of patients who catch it fail to make a full recovery and are likely to develop a chronic infection. In most cases this infection is benign, and is very often free of all discernible symptoms, but in at least 20 per cent of those affected the disease will lead to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis of the liver and, in some cases, malignant disease.
 Treatment with interferon will eradicate hepatitis C in about 35 to 45 per cent of carefully selected cases; but interferon can have unpleasant side effects and is not suitable for every patient. Those in whom eradication fails may well become carriers, and even if they are asymptomatic they will remain capable of infecting others with a potentially deadly virus. In the Victorian era before the days of antibiotics doctors, patients and novelists were not unreasonably obsessed by the carrier state. To be a carrier of any disease, capable of causing sickness and death while remaining healthy, can induce in sensitive people a great sense of guilt. In chronic hepatitis C there is the added burden of never knowing if the condition is likely to deteriorate and lead to irreversible liver damage.
 Now the Government has agreed to make efforts to trace all patients who might have been given blood contaminated by hepatitis C after it could first be detected, but before testing became standard. Controversy surrounds the period between 1989, when the first screening tests for hepatitis C were being developed in America, and 1991, when they became routinely established.  The initial test could detect hepatitis C only several months after the blood had first become infectious, and the numbers of false positive and false negative results were very high. When all factors were taken into account the predictive value of the test was only 50 per cent, and the US Food and Drug Administration did not approve it until 1990. In Britain three different and better tests were approved and introduced in 1991; since then they have been further improved, and now give a 90 per cent predictive value.
 Professor Arie Zuckerman, Dean of the Royal Free School of Medicine, said yesterday: ''There were very sound reasons for the delay in introduction of routine screening. Only the improved tests introduced in 1991 had the sensitivity and specificity which is needed. These screening tests are now, of course, essential for all blood which is going to be used for transfusion.''

The woman was given a positive diagnosis for hepatitis C virus (HCV) when blood centres began to screen donations in 1991. In April this year, the husband, who had continued to donate, learnt that he too was positive for HCV. "I am not a drug addict, I do not use needles and I have never had a blood transfusion. We were told we did not have to take precautions but there is no other way I could have got it," he said. "I believe they were negligent in the advice they gave us and I have contacted my solicitor." In a letter to him, the patient's consultant accepts his belief that "there is no other way" that he could have caught the virus. However, the consultant adds that sexual transmission is very rare. The man is also concerned that he has not been prescribed the only drug available for hepatitis C, interferon alfa, which his wife has been given. It is likely that his wife became infected when she had a blood transfusion in 1988 during a Caesarean operation. Until 1991, when all donations were routinely tested, doctors estimate that 1 in 2,000 donations was infected. The Department of Health says that about 6,000 people who received whole blood were infected as a result of HCV in the blood supply, half of whom are still alive. As a result, it is in the middle of a "lookback" exercise to trace these former patients. The first of these 3,000 people have been identified and liver and hepatitis support groups say they are "starting to trickle through" their doors. A spokeswoman for the National Blood Authority said they had changed their advice on protected sex and hepatitis C as more information had become available. "Initially we advised that people used condoms, even though the risk is low. But with more knowledge we thought that this approach was conservative and restricting. Then we decided to give people all the information and to leave it to individuals to make up their own minds," she said. Alison Rogers, director of the British Liver Trust, said yesterday that there was a need for coherent national guidelines for testing the progress of disease in patients, for prescribing and for giving them advice about their lifestyle. "We know of the Southend case and have already raised it informally with the Department of Health. We are now writing to the Department about the information given to patients. "Hepatitis C is a very big issue. Patients need maximum information," she said. The American Gastroenterological Association issued a statement in May recommending early and longer treatment of HCV-positive patients with interferon. There is no such agreement in the UK. Hepatitis C is a "silent" disease which may not produce symptoms for 20 years. Without treatment, 25 to 50 per cent of patients will develop scarring of the liver and a proportion of those will have liver failure and some will develop liver cancer. 19 July 2000_1.Author:

19 July 2000_1.chunks: THE NATIONAL Blood Service is being sued by 130 people who contracted hepatitis C between 1989 and 1991 because they believe the service was too slow to introduce tests to screen blood products for the virus. The service will face the group action in the High Court in October. It was revealed last week that as many as 500,000 people could have hepatitis C (HCV) in Britain. HCV was first identified in 1989. Because the only symptom in the initial stages is tiredness, the illness can remain indetected for many years. It is believed to have originated in South-east Asia and was identified by a Briton, Michael Houghton, whose American employer, the Chiron Corporation, began a multi-million dollar project to develop an HCV test for use on blood products. The test was first used by the National Blood Service in September 1991. Critics say the service was slow to introduce a test. In the US and on mainland Europe a less sophisticated test was introduced before 1991, but the National Blood Service claims it was waiting for an "effective and reliable" test to be developed. A spokesman said yesterday: "Because this is litigation we cannot comment any further until the case is heard." Paul Saxon, of Dees Mellen in Newcastle, is the leading solicitor representing the 130 people who claim to have been infected through blood transfusions between 1988 (when the Consumer Protection Act came into force) and September 1991 when tests were finally introduced. The claimants "are essentially claiming compensation because we believe there was an unnecessary delay in introducing tests", Mr Saxon said. He did not reveal how much money his clients were seeking. www.independent.co.uk For further reading, help and advice for people worried about Hepatitis C, go to: www.independent.co.uk/links/.

Transfusion victims open hepatitis court battle

By DAILY TELEGRAPH CORRESPONDENT

MORE than 100 people infected with the Hepatitis C virus through blood transfusions, blood products or transplanted organs during medical treatment started damages claims in the High Court yesterday.

Lawyers for the 112 victims have said the case "stands to set an important precedent by seeking to establish a legal link between medical liability and consumer rights".

Michael Brooke, QC, for the claimants, told Mr Justice Burton that they had been infected with the virus since March 1, 1988, "in a wide range of circumstances".

The claimants, who have been granted anonymity, are claiming against the National Blood Authority (in England) and the Velindre NHS Trust (in Wales).

It is the first multi-party action to go to court under the Consumer Protection Act, which became law in 1988.

Mr Brooke told the judge: "All of these claimants have suffered in one way or another the stigma of being Hepatitis C sufferers."

"The public is often confused about HCV and wrongly believes that it is similar to HIV infection."

19 July 2000_1.Author: No author in byline
19 July 2000_1.chunks: Almost one in a hundred women in the UK may be infected with the potentially fatal hepatitis C virus, according to a study published yesterday. The rate of infection has prompted authorities to call for a national screening programme of pregnant women. Antenatal screening for the hepatitis C virus (HCV) could lead to earlier diagnosis and treatment and reduce long-term complications of the disease, such as liver damage and cancer, said the study, published in the medical journal Gut. About 400,000 people in the UK are diagnosed with hepatitis C, but many more may unknowingly have the virus and show no symptoms. It is transmitted sexually or through blood. Researchers for the study tested more than 4,000 pregnant women for HCV when they went for their first antenatal appointment at St Mary's hospital in London between 1997 and 1999. They found that 0.8% of the mothers-to-be tested positive for hepatitis C infection - and that two thirds of those who were positive did not know they were infected. The report's author, Tina Cotzias, said: `It is noteworthy that a high proportion of our infected mothers attended for further follow-up and treatment, whereas patients with HCV in other settings have a high prevalence of subsequent non-attendance. `Antenatal screening may therefore identify infected women when they are most receptive to medical intervention.' 19 July 2000_1.Title: Nearly 500,000 carrying deadly hepatitis virus.
19 July 2000_1.Author: By Jeremy Laurance Health Editor.
19 July 2000_1.chunks: BRITAIN IS poised on the edge of an epidemic of liver failure caused by hepatitis C that could kill more people than Aids. The virus, spread by blood-to-blood contact and, rarely, through sex, is estimated to have infected 250,000 to 500,000 people. Although symptoms are mild or non-existent in the early stages, 85 per cent become chronically infected and up to one in three of those is expected to develop cirrhosis in 20 to 30 years. A survey of 5,000 women attending a London antenatal clinic found almost one in a hundred infected. The survey, published today in the medical journal Gut, is the largest done in an unselected population and, extrapolated to the whole country, implies 400,000 people may be infected. Graham Foster, of the liver unit at St Mary's Hospital, London, who led the study, said many of those infected had contracted the virus through intravenous drug use years ago. They were mostly professional people who had dabbled in drugs in their 20s. He said: "There has been a big increase in people coming to liver clinics but we ain't seen nothing yet, because most of these people became infected around 20 years ago. We are at the start of a massive surge of cases and we don't know how big it is going to be." In the United States, 4.5 million people are estimated to be infected. If rates in Britain are at the same level, up to 800,000 people could face liver failure, most in their fifties. Everett Koop, the former US surgeon general who has campaigned on the issue, said in April: "We stand at the precipice of a grave threat to our public health ... it affects people from all walks of life, in every state, in every country. And unless we do something about it soon, it will kill more people than Aids." Unlike Aids, hepatitis C is treatable with a combination of the drugs interferon and ribavirin, which can cure 40 per cent of cases. But they cost #7,000 a patient and have to be taken for up to a year. Treatment involves three injections a week and has unpleasant side-effects - chiefly flu-like symptoms - which cause one in five patients to drop out. Many health authorities refuse to pay for the drugs, exposing patients to the mercy of the postcode lottery. The issue has been referred to the National Institute for Clinical Effectiveness (Nice), which is to give its ruling later this year. Howard Thomas, of St Thomas' Hospital, chairman of the Government's advisory group on hepatitis, said hepatitis C was its main focus. "We are working on the premiss that between a half and 1 per cent of the population are infected, between 250,000 and 500,000 people. We know this is a big problem and we are hoping Nice will make the treatment uniformly available across the country." However, he said the case for screening was unproved, because the treatment, though effective in severe cases, remained to be demonstrated in mild cases. People with mild symptoms, who might never suffer liver failure, had to endure an unpleasant treatment, possibly for no benefit. Professor Thomas is co-ordinating a study of the drug treatment in mild cases in 12 centres in Britain, the results of which will be known next year. William Rosenberg, of the liver group at the University of Southampton, says in an editorial in Gut, the gastro-enterology specialists' journal, that the high level of infection shown by the study of pregnant women "establishes hepatitis C as a major healthcare problem for the 21st century and one that cannot be ignored". In America the costs of treating hepatitis C over the next 20 years have been estimated at $85bn (#53bn). Allowing for the lower population and lower infection rate in Britain, that suggests costs here of $9bn. Dr Rosenberg said: "We can make a huge dent in that $9bn by spending something now. We can do a huge amount more about hepatitis C than we can about heart disease or hypertension of diabetes." He added: "The idea that the typical hepatitis C sufferer is someone lying in the gutter injecting drugs is far from the truth. The majority are well-to-do, happy professional people who experimented with drugs in their youth and are paying the price."

19 July 2000_1.chunks: A SURGEON infected with the potentially fatal blood disease hepatitis C could have infected many of his patients, it has emerged yesterday. The senior doctor was diagnosed positive withdrawn from clinical work in February but 749 patients considered at risk were not told of the scare until yesterday. The patients are all adults who underwent surgery, which included breast operations, in Birmingham over the past five years. The identity of the surgeon, based at the Selly Oak and Queen Elizabeth hospitals in Birmingham, has not been revealed. A hospital spokesman said he was having treatment and is entitled to patient confidentiality. It is believed the doctor contracted the virus from a patient but was not aware he had caught the disease. The scare came to light earlier this year when a patient was found to have been infected. A blood screening programme was carried out among staff at both hospitals and the surgeon was discovered to be the carrier. Officials at the hospitals trust insist the risk of transfer of infection to patients is extremely low, but public health officials confirmed the disease is usually transmitted to three in every 1,000 patients. A helpline has been launched and GPs of the patients affected in Birmingham have been contacted. One affected patient, a woman from south Birmingham who asked not to be named, underwent three operations over a period of nine months three years ago after she was diagnosed with breast cancer. Earlier this week, she received a telephone call from her doctor's surgery asking her to come in and have a blood test. 'Having just got over the trauma of breast cancer this has all come as a bit of a shock,' she said. 'All I can do is wait for the results of the blood test, which I'm told will take ten days.' Hepatitis C is a virus which circulates in the blood and can eventually lead to liver damage in about 20 per cent of cases and more rarely, liver cancer. Most people who are infected are unaware of it and will have no symptoms but in some cases the result can be fatal. The disease is frequently transmitted by intravenous drug users sharing injecting equipment. It can be treated in around half of those who contract it. There is no vaccine to counter it spreading. 948142098

19 July 2000_1.chunks: Consumer Act used to press case against blood service. More than 100 people infected with the hepatitis C virus through receiving blood transfusions, blood products or organ transplants launched a high court claim yesterday that could cost the NHS millions of pounds in damages. The case is the first group action to reach court under the 1987 Consumer Protection Act, which came into force in March 1988 and was intended to allow people injured by a defective product to claim compensation without proving that the manufacturer or supplier was negligent. The government eventually settled those claims out of court in the early 1990s but has refused to compensate people infected with hepatitis C. The legal action at the high court in London, brought by 112 people represented by six `lead" cases, is expected to last three months. Michael Brooke QC, for the claimants, told Mr Justice Burton that those bringing the case had been infected over the years since March 1 1988, when the act came into force, and were infected with the hepatitis C virus (HCV) `in a wide range of circumstances". Some had transfusions after childbirth, during planned operations, or during surgery after an accident.

19 July 2000_1.Title: The mystery of hepatitis C - Science Briefing.
19 July 2000_1.Author: Nigel Hawkes.
19 July 2000_1.chunks: "WE stand at the precipice of a grave threat to our public health...it affects people from all walks of life, in every state, in every country. And unless we do something about it soon, it will kill more people than Aids." The apocalyptic words are those of Everett Koop, a former US surgeon-general, and he is talking about hepatitis C.Dr Koop has made it his mission to spread the word about hepatitis C, though happily not all specialists think that the situation is as worrying as he does. Caused by a blood-borne virus, hepatitis C is easily transmitted and has only mild symptoms in its early stages. The infection can, however, become chronic and lead to liver failure and liver cancer many years later.Far more people are infected by hepatitis C than by HIV, the cause of Aids. In the United States, the number is between three and five million; in Britain 400,000; worldwide, it may be 170 million. Eliminating the virus is difficult, so if Dr Koop is correct then we could indeed face a huge increase in liver diseases in the future.The difficulty is working out just how serious the problem is. To investigate this, Dr Leonard Seeff, a liver disease specialist at the Veterans Affairs Medical Centre in Washington, has used blood samples given half a century ago by airforce recruits at a base in Wyoming.Nobody even knew that hepatitis C existed then, but tests on the preserved samples showed that 17 men - out of 8,568 - had been infected by it.Following them up, Dr Seeff discovered that seven had died, one of chronic liver disease, and that two had no known addresses. The other eight were asked to come in for an examination. The first to be tested, Edward Woodland, now 69, was still infected, but perfectly healthy. "I am more amazed by this than by almost anything I have ever seen," Dr Seeff told The New York Times. "This man has 50 years of infection." Yet Woodland has no signs of illness. The conclusion is that there are people, perhaps a large number, who can live with hepatitis C infection without even noticing it.How, then, might the progression of the disease be predicted so that treatment could be targeted at those who really needed it, leaving the likes of Woodland alone? A study conducted by a team lead by Dr Patrizia Farci of the University of Cagliari - reported in last week's issue of Science - throws light on this.The team looked at two genes which are responsible for making proteins that lie on the surface, or envelope, of the virus. In 12 patients examined, they found that those who recovered completely were those in whom the viral genes underwent few changes during the early stages of infection. In contrast, the virus evolved quickly in those who went on to develop the chronic form of the disease, perhaps because it was responding to attacks from the patients' immune systems.These changes, the researchers suggest, could be used to monitor the disease, and maybe even to develop possible treatments, if the infection is acute enough to be detected in its early stages. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2000.Not Available for Re-dissemination.

19 July 2000_1.Title: Hepatitis warning over body piercing
19 July 2000_1.Author: No author in byline
19 July 2000_1.chunks: WOMEN who have body piercings or tattoos are being warned that they are twice as likely to contract hepatitis C as drug users. Researchers have found that almost one in 100 women in the UK may be infected with the potentially fatal blood disease many as a result of socalled body jewellery or tattoos. Celebrities including Scary Spice Mel G and Princess Anne's daughter Zara, who both have tongue studs, have helped make piercing highly fashionable in recent years. But a new study warns that body jewellery puts women at a much-increased risk from the blood-borne virus which can cause cirrhosis of the liver and liver cancer. The worrying rate of infection has prompted calls for a national screening programme of pregnant women, who can pass it on to babies. Antenatal screening could lead to earlier diagnosis and treatment and reduce long-term complications of the disease, said the study published today in the medical journal Gut. About 400,000 people in the UK are diagnosed with hepatitis C (HCV), but many more may unknowingly have the virus. Researchers for the study tested more than 4,000 pregnant women when they went for their first antenatal appointment at St Mary's Hospital, in Paddington, London, between 1997 and 1999. They found that 0.8 per cent of the mothers-to-be tested positive for hepatitis C and that two thirds of those who were positive did not know they were infected. Many carriers often mistake the initial symptoms for flu or tiredness. The study also concluded that women who had undergone previous surgery were at greater risk. The researchers said that newly available treatment can cure four-inten of those with chronic hepatitis C.  The report's author, Dr Tina Cotzias, of St Mary's Hospital, added: 'We believe that large-scale, randomised controlled trials of screening for HCV in pregnancy should now be considered.' In a separate study, the researchers found that as few as four out of 80 NHS hospitals which specialise in treating hepatitis C are able to prescribe a powerful combination drug therapy which costs Pounds 10,000 a year. More than 40 clinics said they had no budget from their health authority to pay for treatment with interferon and ribavirin which kill the virus in 40 per cent of sufferers. 947404873

19 July 2000_1.Title: Man sues over blood infection.
19 July 2000_1.Author: By Annie Flury.
19 July 2000_1.chunks: A haemophiliac who claims that he was infected with the potentially lethal hepatitis C virus from a blood transfusion has won the right to sue the Government (Annie Flury writes). The 42-year-old father, who does not want to be named, is the first person in England and Wales to be granted legal aid for such litigation. The man, who is also calling for a public inquiry to find out where the contaminated blood came from and why patients were not told of the risks of acquiring the disease, said: "I have watched my brother and scores of other haemophiliacs die after becoming infected with viruses through NHS treatment." In 1990 haemophiliacs who contracted HIV through contaminated blood products received compensation from the Government for the prejudice that had been caused by the Aids advertising campaigns. However, the deal included a waiver to prevent them from taking action over "other blood-borne viruses" that they might contract in the future. In this case, legal aid was granted so that the waiver can be challenged.

19 July 2000_1.Title: The creeping virus; Thousands unaware they have hepatitis C
19 July 2000_1.Author: MARK AITKEN
19 July 2000_1.chunks: SCOTLAND is suffering an epidemic of hepatitis C virus with thousands unaware they are infected, health experts warned yesterday. Official statistics show more than 10,000 people with the disease, but a medical research group said the true number could be more than three times higher. The Scottish Needs Assessment Programme's hepatitis C working group, which carried out a yearlong study into the virus, said the figure could be as much as 35,000. Professor Peter Hayes, of Edinburgh Royal Infirmary's liver transplant unit, said: 'People are used to hearing shocking stories about how an epidemic might happen. 'What we've got to realise is that there is a hepatitis C epidemic in this country right now. The official figure is 10,000, but I would be extremely surprised if the figure is not up to 35,000 because there are so many people who have it but who have not been tested. 'We have to find these people and treat them and, at the same time, stop more cases from happening.' Hepatitis C is a contagious disease which is spread through blood-to-blood contact. The virus is spread through blood transfusions, body-piercing and tattooing. Heroin addicts sharing infected needles are particularly at risk. The working group's recommendations include an extension of needle exchange programmes. It has also called for more money to be made available for further research. The statistics were last night described as worrying by opposition politicians and medical experts, who called for an investigation by the Scottish Executive. Scottish Conservative health spokesman Mary Scanlon said: 'If the suggestion that 35,000 people have hepatitis C is confirmed, Health Minister Susan Deacon should sit down as a matter of urgency with health trusts to work out a protocol for giving them the care and support they need.' Dr Charles Saunders, chairman of the British Medical Association Scotland's public health committee, said: 'This report demonstrates the need for a coherent Scotland-wide strategy to tackle hepatitis C. 'Funding must now be made available to allow full implementation of the report's very sensible recommendations.' Kate Grainger, a spokesman for C Change, a hepatitis C umbrella group, said: 'These figures are worrying, but I do not think they will surprise people working in the field. 'There is a huge epidemic and an urgent need for research to find out what the true level is.' A Scottish Executive spokesman last night expressed 'great concern' and said it would urgently consider the report. He said it plans to give more than Pounds 6million to health boards for HIV prevention. He added: 'This will include the provision of needle exchange facilities which may assist in reducing the transmission of such viruses.' Trapped in his own home WHEN John McAughey, pictured left, was diagnosed with hepatitis C he was told by doctors he had 'nothing to worry about' that symptoms would be no worse than a dose of the flu. Nine years later Mr McAughey, 60, is now housebound and often needs a wheelchair. He suffers from acute liver damage, constant exhaustion, sore joints, night sweats and intolerance to alcohol. Mr McAughey from Stanley, Perthshire, said: 'Every joint and muscle aches. Hepatitis C has been likened to having your power supply switched off.' He has suffered from haemophilia from childhood and contracted hepatitis after being infected with contaminated blood used to treat him. He has difficulty enjoying simple things such as playing with his three grandchildren. He questioned if the Scottish Executive would follow recommendations in yesterday's report. He said: 'The Government has consistently failed to take action. It has known about this problem for years. Lack of cash is what is behind this epidemic.'

19 July 2000_1.Title: Tribunal told of rows over blood agent.
19 July 2000_1.Author: By NICOLA TALLANT.
19 July 2000_1.chunks: THE Lindsay Tribunal was yesterday told about a row between doctors and the Blood Transfusion Service over which products should be used to treat haemophiliacs. Professor Ian Temperley, former director of the National Haemophilia Treatment Centre who treated haemophiliacs in the 1970s and 1980s, was questioned about the choosing of clotting agents for patients. Commercial blood products are believed to have been mostly responsible for infecting more than 220 haemophiliacs with HIV and Hepatitis C.  Professor Temperley agreed the procedures stated doctors would agree on a product and consult with State bodies before a separate consultative committee agreed the decision. Pressed by Tribunal counsel that the doctors rather than the medical staff at the BTSB were making the decisions, Professor Temperley said no-one felt the need to challenge it. The Tribunal has already heard that Dr Jack O'Riordon, national director of the BTSB, was opposed to concentrates as they were made from the blood of "skid row" types in the US. Professor Temperley said he went to London where imported concentrates were being used and was of the view that if it was good for the people in the UK it was good for Ireland too.

19 July 2000_1.Title: Drugs kill up to 60 users a week, say official advisers.
19 July 2000_1.Author:
Ian Burrell.
 The Independent - London
19 July 2000_1.chunks: UP TO 60 people a week are dying drug-related deaths in Britain, an official report warned yesterday. As the Government promised action to cut the toll, it was warned of a new "public health time bomb" in the form of thousands of drug users infected with the potentially deadly hepatitis C virus. The report published yesterday by the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs said there were between 1,076 and 2,997 drug-related deaths in England and Wales in 1998.

19 July 2000_1.Title: Mum not told about disease.
19 July 2000_1.Author: By PAT FLANAGAN.
19 July 2000_1.chunks: A MOTHER of three yesterday told the Lindsay Tribunal that she was not told about her sons' infections until five years after they were diagnosed. Using the name "Felicity", she told the tribunal that her sons had been diagnosed with Hepatitis C 1990. However despite ten visits to the hospital she was never once told of their condition. "Felicity" said that Professor Ian Temperly of the hospital told herself and her husband in 1985 that HIV was no longer an issue and that Factor 9 blood-clotting agent was safe. She added that she believed all three had been infected by the same batch of Factor 9, which was produced by the Blood Transfusion Service Board. And she told the Tribunal that if she had been told about her first child's infection, she would have stopped using the same batch on the two other children later that year. She also told Judge Alison Lindsay that she was now "very, very angry". The Tribunal also heard that her three sons, now aged between 12 and 15, were never registered with the Heptology clinic and their condition went unmanaged. She told the tribual that her sons had said that they wished they had cancer, because then they could tell their friends about their diseases. She said they were still afraid that their friends would not like them anymore if they knew the truth about their condition, she explained. And for the first time the National Children's Hospital offered an apology to the woman and her three children. Mel Christle, counsel for the hospital said that he wished to offer a humble apology to the family on behalf of the hospital. He said that this was on the basis that it is clear, that she, her husband and her children were not informed that they had contracted Hepatitis C as far back as 1991. Mr Christle said he hoped that the apology went someway towards easing the pain, and he blamed the tragedy on a lapse in communication. (c) Mirror Group Ltd, 2000.

19 July 2000_1.Title: It took me 12 years to discover what was destroying my life.
19 July 2000_1.Author: By KEN FOXE.
19 July 2000_1.chunks: HEARTACHE OF BLOOD TRANSFUSION VICTIMS  BLOOD tribunal witness Bernard Smullen's family life was destroyed when he was infected with Hepatitis C from faulty blood products, he said yesterday. Bernard, 52, a father-of-five from Newbridge in Co Kildare, said he still wakes up in fear of the virus. Incredibly, it took 12 years for him to learn about the diagnosis, despite the fact that doctors knew much earlier. By that stage, his family life and career had almost been destroyed. Haemophiliac Bernard explained: "I was suffering from unbearable depression and mood swings. "My family life suffered, my work suffered. It got to the stage where some of my older children wouldn't even stay in the room with me. I was that bad. "My relationship with my wife suffered. Luckily it's much better now and she's very supportive. "I needed to know what was wrong. I found out that it was Hepatitis C. It almost came as a relief. At least I knew what had been causing my problems." Bernard also revealed how his brother, also a haemophiliac, contracted the same disease. He said: "As a consequence, he had to sell out his business. He had a nervous breakdown and has been in and out of psychiatric hospitals. "That fear is always with me, that it would affect me in the same way." Bernard, who works with the Turf Club, told how the illness had nearly wrecked his own career. He added: "My quality of work was dreadful. Concentration was very difficult. Major tasks became impossible and minor tasks became major tasks. "The racing industry is part of my life, a 24-hour part of my life and my colleagues are now very understanding." Bernard contracted the illness in 1980 when he received treatment following a road traffic accident. It was 12 years before he finally found out and only then because a doctor was doing a study on the incidence of viral illnesses among haemophiliacs. "I really didn't understand very much about it. No-one had explained it to me. "It was like being ambushed. What's going to be the next virus, what's going to be the next infection?" Bernard was the first victim of infected blood products to go public for the Lindsay Blood Tribunal of Inquiry, currently sitting in Dublin. The Tribunal has already heard evidence that the Blood Transfusions Service, represented by Chief Executive Officer Martin Hynes, did not do its job properly in distributing blood products. Bernard said: "I felt that I was in a position to come forward because all my friends and neighbours already know what's wrong. "There is a fear, there will always be a fear. "We started out with HIV, then Hepatitis C. Now we hear that CJD, mad cow disease, has an incubation period of 20 years. "I'd like to go further in my career, I'd like to live without the fear of further infection, for my family and for myself." Bernard is anti-body positive and has been told by doctors that he will never develop the full-blown virus. But Hepatitis still has a massive impact on his life, causing mood swings and lethargy. Three other people told their heart-breaking stories yesterday on the third day of the tribunal. Amazingly, all four found out that they had Hepatitis C either by accident or indirectly. One woman described how her husband slowly slipped away and died from Hepatitis C.  They found out about the illness through a letter in the post. The couple had tied the knot in 1972 after a "whirlwind romance". They had three children. By the start of the 90s, the woman's husband had suffered severe liver failure. He was put on a waiting list for a transplant. She said: "At about 11 o'clock on a Sunday evening, we got a call to say that a liver may be available. "Within about 20 minutes, we found out that the liver was not suitable." A fortnight later, her husband's condition deteriorated and he was taken into hospital. Tests were carried out and cancer of the liver diagnosed. Within 36 hours he was dead. She told the tribunal: "My son was in college about 20 or 30 miles away. "He had to travel in a taxi on a black November night. "His older sister kept her dad alive until my son arrived. He'll be here soon, dad, she said. "He got there, his dad opened his eyes. He died about seven minutes later. "Where does the buck stop? Who is taking responsibility?" Under cross-examination from St James' Hospital, she was asked whether she knew that they had actively sought to appoint counsellors. She was told that two were appointed from lottery funds. Disgusted, she replied: "That's about the size of it, lottery funds." Another haemophiliac, Oliver (not his real name) from Cork, told how he had waited for 17 years before he found out that he had Hepatitis C.  When he went to see the Blood Transfusions Services Board, they asked whether he was an intravenous drug user, whether he had his body pierced or whether he had tattoos. He was told that his wife may need a test and that both his wife and his daughter would be removed from the blood transfusion register. Six months later, a letter arrived at their home requesting that the two women donate blood. At first they kept their problems private. But then one of his daughters heard a rumour in college that her dad had Aids. Oliver said: "A friend of my daughters had said that I had Aids and that I had two months to live. "Then they were saying that I had an alcohol problem." In reality, Oliver had stopped drinking because of his illness. He said that the only way to put a stop to the rumours was to make sure that all family, friends and neighbours knew exactly what was wrong. The Lindsay Tribunal will sit again next Monday when the victims of HIV and Hepatitis C will continue with their testimonies.

19 July 2000_1.Title: Treatment for cancer.
19 July 2000_1.Author: By Dr Tom Waller, Dr Chris Ford, Gerry Stimson.
19 July 2000_1.chunks: Other government policies pull in the opposite direction to the cancer policy. Hepatitis C is not mentioned in the new national drugs plan. The Government's obsession with drugs and crime will lead to more drug users in our prisons - which are notorious for high levels of risky drug use. The drugs strategy excludes and marginalises the very population that a hepatitis-prevention strategy needs to reach. We have prevented HIV in drug users. It's now time for some joined-up thinking between the Home Office and the Department of Health to prevent and treat hepatitis C.  Dr TOM WALLER  Chair, Action on Hepatitis C  Dr CHRIS FORD  Chair, Methadone Alliance  Professor GERRY STIMSON  Chair, UK Harm Reduction Alliance  Imperial College School of Medicine  London SW6.

19 July 2000_1.Title: 600 offered virus test after surgeon infected patients.
19 July 2000_1.Author: By Andrew Mullins.
19 July 2000_1.chunks: MORE THAN 600 patients of a heart surgeon have been offered tests for hepatitis B after he was found to have accidentally infected two of his patients with the potentially fatal virus. Ajay Singh Geholt, 42, performed open-heart surgery on patients across Britain before DNA tests showed beyond any doubt that he had infected two patients at the Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, where 128 patients have already been tested. Yesterday Broad Green Cardiothoracic Centre in Liverpool, where Mr Geholt worked between July 1996 and September 1998, disclosed that it had written to more than 500 people - mostly from Merseyside, but including 81 from North Wales and 15 from the Isle of Man - to advise them to contact their GPs. Mike Bone, the chief executive of the centre, said: "Because it is some years since the exposure, it is a very, very small chance that anybody could still be infected. Some people who catch the infection do not have any signs; that is why we are offering the blood test to see if anybody does have a continuing infection." The letters arrived at the homes of former patients yesterday morning. After testing, patients will have to wait aboutone week for the results. Mr Geholt, who trained in India, is now believed to be living in the United States and has stopped working as a surgeon. Throughout his time working for the NHS, managers were aware of his condition, but guidelines introduced by the Department of Health in 1993 meant he was not precluded from being a surgeon. Hospitals were informed of new and more stringent rules, prompted by Mr Geholt's case, via a circular released on 23 June this year. Professor Tony Hart, consultant microbiologist at the Liverpool centre, said: "When the surgeon came to work here he told us he had hepatitis B but at the time was graded as a low-risk carrier. Our understanding of the disease has since changed and, under new Department of Health guidelines, we have undertaken this look-back procedure to identify those patients." In May last year the Aberdeen Royal Infirmary tested 127 patients operated on by Mr Geholt between September 1998 and June 1999 after one of his patients was readmittedwith the virus. One other of the 127 patients was also found to have been infected. In Hull, where the surgeon worked at the Castle Hill Hospital between 1 March 1990 and 31 January 1991, 139 patients have also been contacted. Dr Richard Charles, the centre's medical director, said: "The chance of any patient contracting hepatitis B during surgery is remote, but we want to do all we can to give patients reassurance and peace of mind." Hepatitis B and hepatitis C are the most common forms of the virus in the UK. It is passed between humans through blood, and is fatal in about one case in 100. Health officials said any patients of the hospitals who had not received a letter had already been eliminated from the list of potential carriers.

19 July 2000_1.Title: Death row blood man 75th to die
19 July 2000_1.Author: Ronan O'Reilly
19 July 2000_1.chunks: A HEPATITIS C victim has died - just months after telling an inquiry he was "on death row". Haemophiliac John Berry, 62 - who died two days ago - contracted the deadly liver disease from contaminated blood products. He had been given a tainted clotting agent for a nose bleed. He was infected in 1971 but discovered he had it nine years ago. Four months ago, he told the Lindsay Tribunal that he felt like he was "on death row". The married father-of-three, from Athy, Co Kildare, couldn't work and slept two hours a night. Mr Berry also told Judge Alison Lindsay that every time he felt pain he expected to die. The inquiry will resume tomorrow. Mr Berry is the 75th Irish haemophiliac to die from infected blood products. The inquiry is investigating more than 220 infected haemophiliacs. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2000

19 July 2000_1.Title: We were told to be safe and use condoms - but they were'nt on sale in Ireland;Blood tribunal
19 July 2000_1.Author: Michael Devine
19 July 2000_1.chunks: WIFE'S SHOCK AFTER HIV TEST RESULT. Blood tribunal THE wife of a haemophiliac told a judge yesterday the amazing advice they were given when her husband was diagnosed HIV positive. After they got the test results at St James's Hospital, Dublin, the couple were told: 'Make sure to have safe sex - use condoms'. But the victim's wife added: "The irony of that was that you couldn't even purchase condoms in this country at that time." The woman, given the pseudonym Ann to protect the family's identity, was giving evidence at the tribunal of inquiry into Ireland's contaminated blood scandal. Abandoned Ann went on to claim that the family never received any counselling and they weren't told that she or her children should be tested for HIV. She accused the authorities of taking advantage of the fact that they could not go public about their situation. "We were abandoned by the State and the doctors," she claimed. They did not get a medical card entitling them to free care until 1996 when her husband tested positive for hepatitis C. "It seemed that it was a far cleaner thing to have hepatitis C than HIV," she said. Ann said their lives had "somersaulted" since her husband became infected. "We have no life just now," she added. Infected Ann's husband, using the name Dominic, told the tribunal he was "stunned and shocked" when he became HIV positive from blood provided by the State. "I felt I had possibly five years to live," said the middle-aged father of four. He was given the grim news that he was HIV positive in 1985. Later he contracted the liver illness hepatitis C from the infected blood products supplied by the State-run Blood Transfusion Board. He said that when the full impact of his condition hit him, it changed his whole outlook on life. "I sold my house in Dublin and moved with my wife and children to the country and set up a business," he said. "It was tough going. But we burned all our bridges and got on with life. Secret "I started the business because I didn't want to go on social welfare. I couldn't let my kids see me on social welfare." Dominic spoke of the pressure of living in a small rural town with his diseases. "You keep your head down and don't discuss them and hope people don't find out," he said. "I feel I'm living a secret," he added. He told the tribunal that the Blood Transfusion Board imported the Factor 8 blood concentrate he was treated with from the United States where people sold their blood. The product he had been treated with previously, cryoprecipitate, was manufactured mainly in Ireland. Dominic said he did not believe the Blood Transfusion Board checked the imported product. "I don't believe they did their job. I think it's disgusting and appalling that so many have died because somebody didn't do the job they were paid to do." Dominic said he had decided to testify at the tribunal "because I want to know what happened". He said: "Somebody did something wrong and covered it up and it caused deaths." Dominic's daughter, who used the name Barbara, told the tribunal she was 16 years old when she was told her father was HIV positive. "Life went from being carefree to thinking my father was going to die," she said. "There was a huge stigma about HIV at that time and we had to become very secretive. It put a lot of pressure on us." Responsible Barbara told the tribunal that she hoped the people responsible for her father's illness would be held accountable. "I want names named and I want to know the reason why it happened." The tribunal, headed by Judge Alison Lindsay, is investigating how more than 300 haemophiliacs became infected with HIV and hepatitis C from contaminated blood products in the 1980s. Seventy-four victims have since died. Paddy Clancy - Page Six (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2000

19 July 2000_1.Title: Blood sick to reveal all.
19 July 2000_1.Author: No author in byline
19 July 2000_1.chunks: THE harrowing stories of 22 gravely ill victims of HIV and Hepatitis C will be heard at the first sitting of the Blood Tribunal today. Speaking of the 15-year battle to get the case into court, Haemophilia Society chairman Brian O'Mahony said: "People with haemophilia need to know what happened. "The truth has to come out - 74 people have died without knowing the circumstances of their infection," he added. Of the 400 people with haemophilia in Ireland, some 221 were infected with Hepatitis C or HIV through contaminated blood products. (c) Mirror Group Ltd, 2000.

19 July 2000_1.Title: Bite cop's health fear.
19 July 2000_1.Author: No author in byline
19 July 2000_1.chunks: A COP fears he may have hepatitis after being bitten during an arrest. The un-named officer was attacked by Steven Murray, 37, who tested positive for hepatitis C.  The cop now faces tests to discover if he caught the disease during a drugs "bust" in March. Murray, of Falkirk, yesterday admitted struggling with the officer and having heroin.

19 July 2000_1.Title: BLOOD HERO DIES.
19 July 2000_1.Author: By KEN FOXE.
19 July 2000_1.chunks: Victim who took on State loses his final battle  A HEP C blood victim who pioneered the campaign for justice has died, it was revealed yesterday. John Berry, 62, started the movement that led to the haemophilia tribunal. He lost his battle for life on Sunday. Mr Berry told the Lindsay Tribunal that he was on "death row" since contracting Hepatitis C.  The Kildare man had battled with the liver disease for more than 20 years. The Times (London)

September 21, 2000, Thursday

 XTL confirms flotation plans

BYLINE: Mark Court

SECTION: Business

LENGTH: 210 words

 
 XTL PHARMACEUTICALS, the Israeli drug discovery and development company, yesterday confirmed its intention to float this month after raising Pounds 28.3 million in an institutional placing of 19.4 per cent of its shares.
 The shares were placed at 150p, valuing XTL, which focuses on developing human antibodies for use as drugs, at Pounds 162 million. 
 XTL had attempted to float earlier this year but the float was pulled because of uncertain market conditions. However, it successfully raised $ 17 million (Pounds 12 million) this summer in a private funding round.
 The company's Trimera technology enables the introduction of human tissue into mice for the production of fully human antibodies to fight infectious diseases and cancer.
 Its lead products are treatments for hepatitis B and hepatitis C and it is also developing treatments against bacterial and fungal infections.
 XTL, whose chief executive is Martin Becker, is in the same research area as the highly rated companies Cambridge Antibody Technology and, in the US, Medarex and Abgenix. However, XTL is distinct in that it can produce fully human antibodies within mice.
 Trading in its shares will begin on Tuesday on both the full list and the techMARK index.

19 July 2000_1.Title: XTL Pharmaceuticals.

19 July 2000_1.chunks: XTL PHARMACEUTICALS, the Israeli drug discovery and development company, yesterday confirmed its intention to float this month after raising #28.3 million in an institutional placing of 19.4 per cent of its shares. The shares were placed at 150p, valuing XTL, which focuses on developing human antibodies for use as drugs, at #162 million. XTL had attempted to float earlier this year but the float was pulled because of uncertain market conditions. However, it successfully raised $17 million ( #12 million) this summer in a private funding round. The company's Trimera technology enables the introduction of human tissue into mice for the production of fully human antibodies to fight infectious diseases and cancer. Its lead products are treatments for hepatitis B and hepatitis C and it is also developing treatments against bacterial and fungal infections. XTL, whose chief executive is Martin Becker, is in the same research area as the highly rated companies Cambridge Antibody Technology and, in the US, Medarex and Abgenix. However, XTL is distinct in that it can produce fully human antibodies within mice. Trading in its shares will begin on Tuesday on both the full list and the techMARK index.

26 March 2001_1.Title: PATIENTS' HEPATITIS FIGHT ENDS IN
26 March 2001_1.Author: MICHAEL DAY HEALTH EDITOR
26 March 2001_1.chunks: CONSUMERS won a landmark victory yesterday when more than 100 patients infected with Hepatitis C through blood transfusions, blood products or transplants won a GBP7million compensation battle in the High Court. Lawyers said the judgment confirmed the existence of a "no fault" regime under the Consumer Protection Act and the EU Product Liability Directive - on which it is based. It protects "anyone damaged by a defective product, in other words a product which is not as safe as the general public is entitled to expect." Anthony Mallen, of Newcastle solicitors Deas Mallen which led the campaign, said: "This is a landmark decision for consumer rights and shows that the effect of the EU directive has been significantly to strengthen product liability law in the UK and throughout Europe. "Producers are not liable for risks which are genuinely unknown to exist, but as soon as the possibly dangerous nature of the product has been discovered by someone somewhere they will be liable if they continue to supply dangerous products." Actor Timothy Pearce, who became infected with the virus after a hip replacement, yesterday spoke of his anger. Mr Pearce, 65, of Highgate, North London, was the only victim to attend court. He said: "I feel bitter that I may have been given a death sentence and that it could have been avoided by the introduction of a screening test that was in use in other countries." During the three-month case Mr Michael Brooke QC, for the claimants, said: "All of these have suffered in one way or another the stigma of being Hepatitis C sufferers. "The fact that a person is infected with HCV attracts stigma which is objectively unwarranted. The public is often confused about HCV and wrongly believes that it is similar to HIV infection. Mr Brooke explained that hepatitis meant inflammation of the liver - Hepatitis C was an illness with a "complex natural history which defies precise prognosis". Nicholas Underhill QC, for the National Blood Authority, told Mr Justice Burton: "As with any other form of medical treatment, blood transfusion cannot be made absolutely risk-free. "But the National Blood Authority are most anxious that patients should realise that the current risks are extremely remote. Claimants sadly suffering this infection from products given in the course of their medical treatment does not of itself mean that they are legally entitled to compensation. "That has never been the rule in this country, and the defendants do not believe it has now become the rule." The judge said he would decide whether to grant permission to appeal next month. Lawyers for the 114 claimants put the value of their claim at between GBP6million and GBP7million, plus costs of up to GBP2million.

26 March 2001_1.Title: BAD BLOOD COSTS NHS #10M.

The trial concerned claims for damages arising out of infection with Hepatitis C - which affects the liver - "from blood and blood products through blood transfusions from March 1 1988". 26 March 2001_1.Title: BLOOD MONEY.
26 March 2001_1.Author: By JILL PALMER Medical Correspondent.
26 March 2001_1.chunks: Hepatitis C victims win massive payouts for transfusion blunder  PATIENTS who caught Hepatitis C through infected blood transfusions were yesterday awarded compensation. In a landmark High Court ruling a judge decided 114 victims were entitled to payouts that could cost the NHS up to #10million. The patients, treated in the late 1980s and early 90s, included mothers giving birth, accident cases and those having surgery. Several children contracted the virus from blood products given to fight leukaemia. One woman infected during an operation needed a liver transplant to save her life. Yesterday's ruling, hailed as victory for consumer rights, came after six test cases had been heard before Mr Justice Burton in London. He awarded them compensation from #10,000 to more than #210,000 plus costs, put at between #2million and #3million. The victims had brought the action against the National Blood Authority in England and the Velindre NHS Trust in Wales. Both bodies had argued they took reasonable steps to avoid contamination. But the judge ruled the NHS was aware of the risk of infection but did not introduce blood screening until September 1991, long after many other countries. One victim Jane Lindley, of Rexford, Notts, waived her anonymity after getting a payout of #200,000. She was infected by a blood transfusion in 1990. Lawyers have put the value of the victims' claims at between #6million and #7million plus costs. A second group of nine patients, including haemophiliacs, will have their cases heard in May. After yesterday's hearing Antony Mallen of Newcastle solicitors Deas Mallen, who led the case, said: "This is a landmark decision for consumer rights. "Producers are not liable for risks which are genuinely unknown to exist. "But once the danger has been discovered they will be liable if they continue to supply the product." Haemophilia Society president and Labour peer Lord Morris added: "This gives renewed hope of much-needed help to the dependents of haemophiliacs who have already died of the infection." Potentially fatal, hepatitis C can cause major liver damage including cirrhosis and cancer. Blood donor screening has dramatically cut the risk of cross-infection.

26 March 2001_1.Author: No author found
26 March 2001_1.chunks:
The Times (London)

March 27, 2001, Tuesday

 Hepatitis cases land NHS with Pounds 10m bill

BYLINE: Helen Studd

SECTION: Home news

LENGTH: 797 words

 
 THE NHS was facing a Pounds 10 million compensation bill yesterday after more than 100 people who contracted the hepatitis C virus through medical treatment won an unprecedented High Court battle for damages.
 In six lead cases, chosen to give general guidance on damages, the judge awarded sums of up to Pounds 210,000 per person, while leaving the way open for victims to make further claims if their condition deteriorated. The NHS is now preparing itself for a flood of similar claims from sufferers of CJD and recipients of the MMR vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella, who will be able to apply the same criteria to win compensation.
 Yesterday's multi-party hearing is the first time since its introduction in 1988 that the Consumer Protection Act has been tested on medical products in the UK. At least another 2,500 hepatitis C sufferers who contracted the virus after 1988 are believed to be eligible to bring similar cases. 
 Many of the 114 claimants were young children or pregnant when they contracted the potentially fatal liver disease through blood transfusions, blood products or organ transplants following routine operations or road accidents. Some have not yet developed long-term symptoms of the condition, which may limit their life expectancy.
 The other 108 claims are expected to be along similar lines to yesterday's awards and will be decided in coming months. Crucially, however, the arguments behind yesterday's ruling can be applied to any medical product that is deemed to have put people at risk and the NHS is now bracing itself for thousands of new claims from CJD sufferers and recipients of the MMR vaccine who are able to prove that they were infected by defective medical products after 1988.
 Scientists claim that 10,000 people in Britain are harbouring CJD, which can be contracted through surgical instruments, while 2,000 children are estimated to have suffered adverse effects as a result of the MMR vaccine.
 Ruling in favour of the victims, Mr Justice Burton said: "Such infected blood did not provide the safety which persons generally are entitled to expect." He said routine screening "ought to have been introduced by March 1, 1990". It was finally introduced in the UK in April 1991, despite being used in other countries long before this date.
 The initial 114 victims took the action last year against the National Blood Authority and Velindre NHS Trust in Cardiff. They set out to prove the existence of a no-fault regime "for anyone damaged by a defective product".
 Lawyers for the group put the value of their claim at about Pounds 7 million yesterday with Pounds 3 million in costs.
 The initial six claimants included a mother in her mid-thirties who became infected by a blood transfusion during childbirth, and a young man infected after a road accident when he was nine years old.
 A man in his seventies who contracted the disease following heart surgery was awarded Pounds 53,000, while Jane Lindley, 56, a married mother of three, was awarded Pounds 210,000 after becoming infected during routine surgery to remove a cyst.
 Anthony Mallen, the solicitor who led the litigation, said the ruling had been a landmark decision that would open the way for a variety of similar claims.
 He added: "This shows that producers are not liable for risks which are genuinely unknown to exist, but as soon as the possibly dangerous nature of the product has been discovered by someone somewhere, they will be liable if they continue to supply dangerous products. The judgment is an important contribution to both UK and European law."
 The Haemophilia Society said last night that the ruling would give renewed hope to the dependants of the more than 100 people, suffering from haemophilia, who have already died of the infection.
 Mr Justice Burton is due to preside over a preliminary hearing involving another nine claimants including haemophiliacs and a woman who became infected after a heart transplant in May. He will decide whether to grant the National Blood Authority and the Velindre NHS Trust leave to appeal on April 10. A similar case is being prepared in Northern Ireland while one in Scotland has so far been blocked.
 Hepatitis C causes inflammation of the liver that can lead to liver disease, cirrhosis and liver cancer. While some of those infected would, in due course, spontaneously clear the virus from their systems, many others experienced symptoms a number of years after contracting the infection.
 Nicholas Underhill, QC, for the defence, told the court that the risk of patients contracting hepatitis C was tiny and was expected to reduce further with advances in medical science.

 Liability for defective blood products

SECTION: Features

26 March 2001_1.chunks:
The Times (London)

April 4, 2001, Wednesday

 Liability for defective blood products

SECTION: Features

LENGTH: 1372 words

 
 QUEEN'S BENCH DIVISION. Published April 4, 2001. A and Others v National Blood Authority and Another. Before Mr Justice Burton. Judgment March 26, 2001.
 When determining, under article 6 of the Product Liability Directive (85/374/EEC), what degree of safety the public were entitled to expect in a product, the impossibility of avoiding a harmful characteristic in the product by taking precautions was irrelevant.
 If the existence of a defect generally was known or should have been known in the light of accessible information, then a producer could not rely on the defence under article 7(e), regardless of whether it was possible to identify in which if any of his products that defect would occur. 
 Mr Justice Burton so held, in the Queen's Bench Division, giving judgment for A and 113 other claimants, on their claims for damages under the Consumer Protection Act 1987, made against the National Blood Authority and Velindre NHS Trust in respect of their infection with hepatitis C contracted from blood and blood products used in blood transfusions.
 Article 6 of the 1985 Directive (OJ 1985 No L210 p29) provides: "1 A product is defective when it does not provide the safety which a person is entitled to expect, taking all circumstances into account..."
 Article 7 provides: "The producer shall not be liable as a result of this Directive if he proves ... (e) that the state of scientific and technical knowledge at the time when he put the product into circulation was not such as to enable the existence of the defect to be discovered."
 Mr Michael Brooke, QC, Mr Stuart Brown, QC, Mr Ian Forrester, QC, of the Scots Bar, and Mr Jalil Asif for the claimants.
 Mr Nicholas Underhill, QC, Mr Philip Brook Smith and Ms Louise Merrett for the defendants.
 MR JUSTICE BURTON said that the 114 claimants had all been infected with the hepatitis C virus as a result of being given infected blood in transfusions for which the defendants were responsible.
 Section 2 of the Consumer Protection Act 1987 imposed strict liability on the producer of a defective product which caused damage.
 The claimants' case was that all those who received blood infected by hepatitis C after the Act came into effect on March 1, 1988 were entitled to recover damages, irrespective of any fault of the defendants.
 It was agreed that although the medical profession had known since the 1970s that there was a problem of infection by hepatitis C in transfused blood, no screening test to discover the presence of the virus in a donor's blood was even known of until Spring 1989.
 Following the introduction of screening tests throughout England and Wales in September 1991 the problem of infection through blood transfusion had been all but eliminated.
 The 1987 Act had been passed in order to implement the Product Liability Directive and, as had been held in European Commission v United Kingdom (re Product Liability Directive) (Case C-300/95) ((1997) ECR I-2649), was to be construed so as to be consistent with the Directive. Consequently both parties during the trial had concentrated on the terms of the Directive itself.
 Article 6 The parties agreed that the question to be resolved, when deciding whether a product was defective within the meaning of article 6.1, was the degree of safety which persons generally were entitled to expect.
 The claimants asserted that the conduct of the producer was irrelevant to that question, and the avoidability of the virus, whether it was possible to take any steps by way of prevention or avoidance, did not arise.
 The defendants argued that avoidability was a relevant circumstance under article 6. They submitted that avoiding the risk had been impossible and it was not legitimate for the public to expect the unattainable; all they were entitled to expect was that all reasonably available precautions had been carried out.
 His Lordship did not consider that the legitimate expectation of the public at large was that legitimately expectable tests would have been carried out or precautions adopted. Their legitimate expectation was as to the safeness of the product (or not). It was inappropriate to propose that the public should not expect the unattainable, in the sense of precautions which were impossible, at least unless it was informed as to what was unattainable or impossible.
 In his Lordship's judgment "all circumstances" in article 6.1 meant all relevant circumstances. It was quite plain that the 1985 Directive was intended to eliminate proof of fault or negligence.
 It was intended to make it easier for claimants to prove their case, so that a consumer would not have to prove that the producer did not take all legitimately expectable steps.
 His Lordship concluded therefore that "avoidability" was not one of the circumstances to be taken into account within article 6, because it was outwith the purpose of the Directive.
 His Lordship set out what he considered to be the structure for consideration under article 6.
 The first step must be to identify the harmful characteristic which caused the injury, article 4.
 The next step would be to conclude whether the product was standard or non-standard, which would be done most easily by comparing the offending product with other products of the same type or series produced by that producer.
 If the respect in which it differed from the series included the harmful characteristic, then it was non-standard.
 If it did not differ, or if the respect in which it differed did not include the harmful characteristic, then it was to be treated as a standard product.
 The primary issue in relation to a non-standard product was whether the public at large accepted the non-standard nature of the product, that is whether they accepted that a proportion of the products would be defective. They did not in this case.
 The question was one of legitimate expectation. The avoidability of the harmful characteristic, the impracticality of taking precautionary measures, and the benefit to society or utility of the product were all irrelevant considerations.
 With a standard product the sole question would be safety for the foreseeable use. "Avoidability" was again irrelevant.
 Article 7(e) The parties agreed that the defence must be based on the most advanced scientific and technical knowledge available to anyone at the time when the product was put into circulation, as long as it was accessible.
 The claimants argued that, in order to establish the defence, it was necessary to show that there was no such knowledge which had identified the problem.
 On that basis, the defendants would have no defence, since it was common ground that the existence of the hepatitis C virus in blood generally was known at all relevant times.
 The defendants argued that it was enough to show that, although the existence of the defect was known, there was no such knowledge which would have enabled a producer to discover the existence of the defect in a particular product.
 In his Lordship's judgment, the analysis of article 7(e) was entirely clear.
 If the existence of the defect was known or should have been known in the light of accessible information, then the producer continued to produce at his own risk.
 It would be inconsistent with the purpose of the 1985 Directive if a producer, in the case of a known risk, continued to supply products simply because he was unable to identify in which if any of his products that defect would occur.
 Result In his Lordship's judgment, the infected bags of blood were non-standard products since they were different from the norm which the producer intended for use by the public.
 They were defective because his Lordship was satsified that the public at large was entitled to expect that the blood transfused to them would be free from infection.
 The defendants had no defence under article 7(e), since the existence of hepatitis C in blood was known at the relevant time. Therefore the claimants succeeded.
 Solicitors: Deas Mallen, Newcastle upon Tyne; DMH, Brighton; Evill & Coleman; Freeth Cartwright, Nottingham and Howard Cohen & Co, Leeds.

26 March 2001_1.Title: SCOTS HEPATITIS VICTIMS FACE WAIT ON
26 March 2001_1.Author: ANGUS MACLEOD SCOTTISH POLITICAL EDITOR
26 March 2001_1.chunks: SCOTS infected with the Hepatitis C virus through blood transfusions will have to wait to find out whether they are going to get similar compensation to English victims. It follows a High Court ruling in London yesterday which left the NHS south of the Border facing a bill of up to GBP10million to compensate more than 100 people infected with the virus. In a judgment hailed as a landmark decision, Mr Justice Burton concluded that 114 claimants, who have been granted anonymity, should receive damages. In six lead cases, chosen to give general guidance on the levels of damages, the judge awarded sums ranging from more than GBP10,000 to in excess of GBP210,000. Afterwards, lawyers for the victims put the value of their claim at between GBP6million and GBP7million. The claimants were also awarded costs, of between GBP2million and GBP3million. But in Scotland, victims were left disappointed last year when Scottish Executive health minister Susan Deacon ruled out compensation. Last night a spokesman for Ms Deacon said she would now be studying the English judgment and its implications. The court ruling on the first multi-party action to go to court under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 sets an important precedent by establishing a legal link between medical liability and consumer rights. The judge said the trial concerned claims for recovery of damages arising out of infection with Hepatitis C, which affects the liver, "from blood and blood products through blood transfusions from March 1 1988". "The 114 claimants received blood transfusions or blood products usually in the course of undergoing surgery, whether consequent upon having suffered an accident or otherwise, or immediately after childbirth or in the course of treatment for a blood disorder," he said. The action was against the National Blood Authority (in England) and the Velindre NHS Trust (in Wales), who contested the action. The defendants are the NHS bodies answerable today for the production and supply of blood and blood products over the period since March 1 1988, by the National Blood Transfusion Service. Anthony Mallen, of Newcastle solicitors Deas Mallen, who led the litigation, said: "Producers are not liable for risks which are genuinely unknown to exist, but as soon as the possibly dangerous nature of the product has been discovered by someone somewhere, they will be liable if they continue to supply dangerous products." Actor Timothy Pearce, 65, of London, said: "I feel bitter that I may have been given a death sentence which could have been avoided by a screening test used in other countries."
