26 March 2001_1.Title: Holyrood
26 March 2001_1.Author: By Fraser Nelson Scottish Political Correspondent.
26 March 2001_1.chunks: THE Scottish National Party yesterday claimed a small victory in its attempts to secure compensation for haemophiliacs infected with hepatitis C by infected blood products. Malcolm Chisholm, the Deputy Health Minister, headed off an SNP motion in the Scottish Parliament with a promise "to examine constructively the implications" of a recent English High Court judgment. This was taken as a hint that the the Executive may support Scottish victims who may wish to sue the NHS after becoming infected. Nicola Sturgeon, the SNP's Shadow Health Minister, told the Parliament she was "greatly encouraged" by Mr Chisholm's amendment to her motion. She had expected complete opposition, with no undertaking to recognise the award of #2.5 million to six plaintiffs who sued the National Blood Authority in England. "This amendment takes us further than the Scottish Executive have gone before, and I can only encourage this as a step in the right direction," she said. "It is still a fair bit away from where we want to be." Ms Sturgeon was moving a debate on the need for compensation to be paid to haemophiliacs who contracted the disease through NHS treatment during the 1970s and 1980s. She called for a no-fault compensation scheme where all victims would be compensated by the Executive without the need to sue the NHS. This would go a stage further than England, where government compensation is refused. Mr Chisholm said that Ms Sturgeon's proposal would set a dangerous precedent for other legal action to be taken against the NHS. "Would we want to create a climate in our health care system which made it risk averse?" he said. "Would we want to see new treatments denied to people because they might involve a risk?" In England, hepatitis C victims who had contracted the disease through blood transfusion managed to sue, claiming that that contaminated blood should be categorised as a faulty product. Six plaintiffs, on behalf of 114 other victims, had sued under the Consumer Protection Act of 1987 and were awarded average compensation of #24,200. Ms Sturgeon said the ruling should hold good for Scotland, and be taken further into government policy. The Scottish Parliament has been petitioned by a group of hepatitis victims who contracted the disease in the mid-1980s. They cannot sue as they were infected before the Consumer Protection Act came into effect (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

26 March 2001_1.Title: Dublin's record hepatitis payout.
26 March 2001_1.Author: By John Burns.
26 March 2001_1.chunks: A WOMAN suffering from hepatitis C has been awarded almost #2.5m in damages, the highest compensation payment ever made to a sufferer. The settlement was made last November by the hepatitis C tribunal, which has paid out a total of #217.8m in compensation to 1,418 women suffering from the incurable disease. The woman was represented by Patrick A Hurley, a Cork solicitor. The previous record award was #1.6m. The tribunal was set up in 1995 after 1,600 women were infected with hepatitis C during pregnancy by a contaminated anti-D blood product. More than #35m has been paid by the state to legal firms representing hepatitis C victims. Almost a third of that figure - #10.7m - was earned by Ivor Fitzpatrick & Co. Figures obtained by The Sunday Times for the past six months reveal that the Fitzpatrick practice earned almost #550,000 in that time, representing 16 clients who got compensation from the tribunal, at an average of #34,375 per case. Fitzpatrick was the first legal firm to represent hepatitis C victims and did all the preliminary research. "The amount of work devoted to this research was enormous in terms of time and staff resources and was carried out at a stage when there was no guarantee of any form of professional remuneration," the firm has said. The #10.7m fees paid to Fitzpatrick include payments to barristers and accountants, as well as actuarial, medical and other professional costs incurred in making a claim to the tribunal or to the High Court on appeal. The next highest earning legal practice is Malcolmson Law, which has been paid #5.1m in fees for representing hepatitis C sufferers. More than #900,000 of this was paid in the past six months for representing 20 clients, at an average of #45,000 per case. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

26 March 2001_1.Title: Compensation for NHS mistakes - Letter.
26 March 2001_1.Author: No author in byline
26 March 2001_1.chunks: From Professor John A. DavisSir, With a judge's decision (report, March 27; see also law report, April 4) that the NHS must pay damages to patients infected with the hepatitis C virus by blood transfusions, albeit at the time there was no way of checking for its presence, we have reached an important crossroads in our attitude to such accidents.One road leads to ever-increasing demands for compensation and the attribution of blame, with no great gain to anyone bar lawyers and leading to the practice of defensive medicine and the milking of public money. The other leads to the recognition that, regardless of who or what may have been responsible, persons who suffer loss or injury through no fault of their own should be helped out of public funds as a form of national insurance to recoup the strictly financial costs of their misfortune.When someone clearly was to blame, it would then be up to the relevant authority, not the injured party, to recover some or all of the cost of compensations already claimed and paid out according to need. This would save a lot of time and money for all concerned without in any way diminishing the sense of responsibility of those who hold our lives in their hands, whether they be surgeons, the drivers of motor vehicles or Railtrack.If we do not take the bull by the horns now, we shall be faced in the future with the absurdity of a patient suing a blood or organ donor (or their kin) for illness inadvertently caused by their being carriers of - for instance - BSE. Do we need more doctors or more lawyers?Yours faithfully,JOHN DAVIS,1 Cambridge Road,Great Shelford, Cambridge CB2 5JE.April 5. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

26 March 2001_1.Title: Health: Infected blood has ruined the lives of many haemophiliacs. So why are they denied the safe, synthetic alternative?
26 March 2001_1.Author: No author found
26 March 2001_1.chunks:
The Guardian (London)

February 8, 2001

Health: Infected blood has ruined the lives of many haemophiliacs. So why are they denied the safe, synthetic alternative?

BYLINE: James Meikle

SECTION: Guardian Features Pages, Pg. 15

LENGTH: 682 words

 
 The NHS has accidentally infected 4,800 British haemophiliacs with the hepatitis C virus. Of these, 1,200 have also been infected with HIV; a third of them remain alive. Now there is a theoretical risk that the NHS has infected some of these people with the human form of BSE, the fatal variant CJD.
 No wonder many haemophiliacs are angry. As many as 5,000 people in Britain need a "clotting factor" (made from blood plasma) to treat the painful, excessive bleeding that swells their muscles as a result of haemophilia. Imagine finding out that these products were made from contaminated blood. 
 And it is no wonder adult haemophiliacs in England are demanding the same "safer" synthetic alternative (known as recombinant) that is on offer to child sufferers throughout Britain, and to older patients in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. You might think any government, having seen the effects of two previous mistakes involving tainted blood supplies, would be keen to cough up the extra cash for such treatment.
 But not a bit of it. Ministers, under pressure from the Haemophilia Society's campaign for recombinant and a public inquiry into the overall safety of blood products, appear more worried about the effect "sensationalist" press coverage would have in further distressing patients.
 Decisions on providing recombinant should be made on clinical grounds, not on whether a fuss is made. Haemophilia doctors say recombinant should be on offer, although British-sourced products, which might carry vCJD infection from donors, were replaced by US plasma in 1998. Paul Giangrande, at the Churchill centre in Oxford, says this could cost an extra pounds 23m a year.
 He, like many other centre directors, is ignoring general NHS guidance not to tell patients they have been treated with products that included material donated by someone who went on to develop vCJD. The third warning of this type, relating to treatments given before the switch to US human product, was sent out by the blood service before Christmas. Dr Giangrande has informed 85 of his patients.
 Three years ago, batches involving other vCJD patients had to be recalled. Then, some directors, including Dr Giangrande, told; some did not. Now the NHS is reviewing that don't-tell policy, implemented because vCJD cannot be detected before symptoms are evident. It is also untreatable and incurable. Some haemophiliacs are convinced they have been infected again, and some of the most militant sufferers believe they are acting the canaries in the coal mine in an experiment to see if vCJD can be transmitted through blood.
 Reassurances from officials may have little impact. Sufferers know that the NHS, worried enough to have changed the source of most plasma and to have introduced other blood controls at a combined cost of pounds 83m a year in England and North Wales, has been further alarmed by evidence from an experiment with sheep that showed BSE can be transmitted by transfusion. Now officials are considering whether anyone who has received a blood transfusion should be allowed to donate blood themselves.
 It could be years before we know if there has been human transmission. The incubation period of vCJD is unknown, and the disease has been identified for less than five years. If most of the current 94 victims were infected by cheap meat products in the mid-80s, how much longer before we know the condition's eventual scale?
 Thirteen victims so far have been blood donors, their donations transfused into 23 people, as well as going into blood products used by thousands at home and abroad. The government should be desperately seeking to shore up confidence in blood transfusion, but when it is gearing up to spend pounds 200m on new hospital sterilisation measures, pounds 30m on disposable instruments for tonsillectomies and, if necessary, a great deal more on changing other surgical procedures, can they blame haemophiliacs for thinking another pounds 23m is small change?
 James Meikle is the Guardian's health correspondent. Sarah Boseley is away.

26 March 2001_1.Title: JUSTICE FOR SCOTS VICTIMS
26 March 2001_1.Author: No author in byline
26 March 2001_1.chunks: Scotland's Health Minister, Susan Deacon, says she will study an English court ruling that Hepatitis C victims are entitled to compensation from the NHS. Last year she ruled out paying damages, which was then the official Government line or, at least, the line that ministers were being told to follow by their officials. The English judge has accepted that, since the victims contracted the illness through NHS treatment then they were entitled to compensation. Ms Deacon says she will look at the financial implications of the ruling for Scotland. Surely she must already know how much this will cost, as it would have been imprudent for officials to assume that the claimants would lose. So why is there a delay? Why has Ms Deacon chosen to give the impression of being a Scrooge? You could bet your lottery winnings that, if she were a member of the Opposition, she would be on her feet demanding justice to the victims. She would have been right, too. Ms Deacon should do the right thing and announce that she will act on what the English court has said. *** BRS DOCUMENT BOUNDARY ***

26 March 2001_1.Title: DOCTOR'S FURY AT BLOOD DEATHS
26 March 2001_1.Author: MARK BLACKLOCK
26 March 2001_1.chunks: A DOCTOR yesterday blamed the Government for killing 77 of his patients with infected blood products. Dr Peter Jones, a world haemophilia expert, called for a public inquiry into the scandal of sufferers of the illness who were treated with contaminated supplies from abroad. He said the authorities were responsible because the transfusion service in Britain had been underfunded for decades, forcing doctors to seek products from overseas to meet demand. Thousands of people may have contracted HIV or hepatitis C viruses as a result. Dr Jones, an executive member of the World Federation of Haemophilia, was head of a regional treatment centre at Newcastle upon Tyne's Royal Victoria Infirmary during the Seventies and Eighties. The transfusion service could not meet demand for blood products, and doctors all over the country used imported supplies of the clotting agent Factor VIII. But that was made from blood bought from drunks and drug-addicted prisoners in the United States and from the slums of South Africa. One infected donor could contaminate thousands if suspect blood was used to make the clotting agent. Today only 18 of the 105 patients Dr Jones treated on Tyneside are still alive because 95 of them became infected with HIV and hepatitis C.  "We were all devastated when the true horror of what had happened started to unfold in the mid-Eighties," he said. "At the haemophilia centre we were like one big family and myself and my colleagues had always tried to be completely open and honest with our patients. "The Government promised us that Britain would be self-sufficient in blood products by 1977 but in fact we have never been able to meet demand and we are still importing plasma from the US. "So many of my patients died, as they did at centres across the UK, and as their doctor I felt responsible." Public inquiries into the safety of blood supplies have been started in Ireland, Canada, and Germany. "It is a basic human right that patients have their questions about their treatment answered and that accidents occurring in the course of that treatment are explained," he said. Dr Jones spoke out before addressing the inquiry in Dublin. A Department of Health spokeswoman said the Government did not believe it would be "in anybody's interests" to hold a public inquiry. "Little was known about HIV and Aids at the time and a test did not exist until 1985," she said. "Factor VIII was in great demand from haemophiliacs."

26 March 2001_1.Title: Haemophiliac refuses surgery in vCJD protest.
26 March 2001_1.Author: By Oliver Wright.
26 March 2001_1.chunks: A HAEMOPHILIAC who contracted both HIV and hepatitis C from contaminated blood supplies has refused further treatment after being told his medication may also have given him variant CJD. Mark Payton, 39, told doctors he is not prepared to have any more blood transfusions despite needing an operation and suffering from bleeding. He has also accused Worcestershire Health Authority of discriminating against him by refusing access to a safe synthetic blood product available only to haemophiliacs aged under 16. "If no one says anything, nothing will ever change," he said. "My life has already been devastated with the diseases I have contracted. My marriage has broken up, I've lost my job and I've had cancer. I am not prepared to put up with any more." The latest blow to Mr Payton, from Rubery, in Worcestershire, came in a letter from his specialist at Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Birmingham telling him he had received blood products from a man who later developed variant CJD. Mr Payton said that he was devastated by the latest news and called for the synthetic treatments to be made available to all haemophiliacs. Under the present regulations haemophiliacs aged under 16 in England, and all those with haemophilia in Wales and Scotland are treated with recombinant Factor 8 which is made from synthetic proteins. However, this treatment is twice as expensive as the blood-derived product. But Mr Payton added: "Human blood-derived products are cheaper but more expensive in the long term because we have to be treated for the diseases we get." A spokesman for the Queen Elizabeth Hospital claimed that while Mr Payton's treatment had been contaminated with vCJD there was no medical evidence to suggest that he would develop the disease. Worcestershire Health Authority, said that providing recombinant Factor 8 for all haemophiliacs would mean taking away money from other services. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

 Victim was told that she had ten years to live
26 March 2001_1.Author: No author found

The Times (London)

March 27, 2001, Tuesday

 Victim was told that she had ten years to live

BYLINE: Helen Studd

SECTION: Home news

LENGTH: 531 words

 
 WHEN Jane Lindley had a routine operation to remove a cyst 11 years ago she had never heard of hepatitis C and hailed her blood transfusion as a life-saver.
 Four years later she was told that she had ten years to live, the beginnings of cirrhosis of the liver and would need a liver transplant. "No one told me about the risks of a blood transfusion and I had never even heard of hepatitis C," she said. 
 Subsequent medical tests showed that Mrs Lindley, 56, a mother of three children, had cirrhosis of the liver, a condition normally suffered by alcoholics. At a time when hepatitis C was little-known even among the medical profession, her doctor assumed that heavy drinking was to blame.
 It was then in 1994 that doctors told her the prognosis. From contracting the disease she had just ten years to live. She had been living with hepatitis C for four years but despite a painful course of Alfa-Interferon injections to help to suppress the virus, her condition deteriorated.
 By 1998 she was virtually housebound, unable to muster the energy to carry out even the simplest household chores.She suffered from excruciating joint and stomach pain and her skin turned a sallow shade of yellow. That March she was told that she needed a liver transplant or would die.
 Luckily for her the transplant was successful and Mrs Lindley found herself with a new lease of life and the energy to do things on her own for the first time in years.
 Yesterday she was awarded more than Pounds 210,000 in compensation from the National Blood Authority.
 "The prognosis is uncertain and I could start rejecting at any time," she said. "My faith and my family have got me through."
 Less optimistic, however, was Timothy Pearce, 65. As he left the High Court after the hearing yesterday, the bitterness and pain of the past nine years was etched on his face.
 Mr Pearce had broken down as he told how the disease, which he had contracted during a hip operation in 1991, had become an "early death sentence".
 He claims that he has been drained of his vitality. He has lost his job, been inflicted with endless bouts of flu and had been forced to resign as a coach for his local football team.
 Despite previous appearances in the film Jesus of Nazareth, and the television shows Minder and EastEnders, he has also been unable to get a manager to promote his career and more recently has had trouble getting insurance.
 "I am frightened about what the future holds," he said outside the High Court yesterday. "I am not confident that there will ever be a cure.
 "Ever since the operation, I've never really felt like myself. I am just not the person I was before. I have become increasingly tired and lethargic. I am now very susceptible to colds, flu and have massive problems with my teeth."
 Mr Pearce, of Highgate, North London, first became aware of the infection in 1995 when he was traced as part of a "look-back" programme by the National Blood Authority.
 He is one of 30 people who were infected on or after the beginning of April 1991 whose claims were settled shortly before the trial began. Their claims will be assessed later in the hearing.

26 March 2001_1.Title: This careless error has wrecked our lives.I'm here for justice
26 March 2001_1.Author: No author in byline
26 March 2001_1.chunks: HAEMOPHILIACS infected by hepatitis C through tainted blood products renewed their demands for compensation yesterday as they gave evidence to a committee of MSPs. About 400 haemophiliacs in Scotland have contracted the disease and at least 15 have died in the last 15 years. The Scottish National Blood Transfusion Service insisted there were technical reasons why the service was 18 months behind England in producing treated blood product which eliminates the virus. Its arguments have satisfied Health Minister Susan Deacon but sufferers have waged an angry campaign for compensation. Here we tell the moving story of how a wife has coped with her haemophiliac husband's suffering. PAT McAUGHEY is not fainthearted. She is a nurse. She has seen patients die, burn victims weep in their sleep, children so sick they need tubes to breathe. And although she has done her best to help them all, human misery is nothing new to her. It is something to be borne bravely. But when she tells how her gentle, doting husband cannot dare even to pick up his beloved grandchildren for fear of infecting them with the hepatitis C that courses through his veins, she has to squeeze her eyes to stop herself from crying. She simply feels he has been robbed. John McAughey, 60, was born a haemophiliac. After years of blood infusions and spontaneous, painful bleeding, he had it under control. Once o r twice a month he would visit Ninewells Hospital in Dundee. It was no more than an inconvenience and he felt safe there, knowing his wife was nearby, comforted by the fact that the regular doses of Factor 8 would help his blood clot and ease the agony in his joints. Little did he realise that the very infusions designed to save life would in fact result in destroying it. In 1991 he was, without his knowledge, tested twice for HIV and hepatitis C after an influx of infected blood polluted the health service. He was found positive for the latter on both occasions but, incredibly, he and his family were not told until 12 months later. Fortunately, he did not pass on the virus which is so infectious that a spot of blood can remain 'active' for three months. But he easily could have done. He and his wife have had to practise safe sex ever since and will have to do so forever more. Their one glint of hope is that the haemophilia will die with them. Only men can contract haemophilia, but it is carried by women. The couple's sons John, 32, and Tommy, 33, are safe. Their daughter Wendy, 30, had a 50 per cent chance of passing it on. But her two sons, aged 18 months and four years, were both, joyfully, given the all-clear. Mrs McAughey, 54, travelled to Edinburgh alone from the family home in Perth to give evidence to the Scottish parliament's health and community care committee as part of a bid by the Haemophilia Society for compensation. There are 6,000 haemophiliacs in Britain, 600 in Scotland. And 4,800 300 north of the Border were infected by HIV or hepatitis C, or even both. They are grim statistics, but Mrs McAughey is determined to be more than just a number. She says: 'There is a terrible stigma attached to hepatitis C. People seem to think it's like Aids. It's not. But it's a life sentence all the same. John had enough problems with the haemophilia. But he coped. We coped. 'He should never have been given hepatitis. What makes me even angrier is that measures were brought in south of the Border to screen blood products in 1985, yet nothing was done in Scotland for another two years. That is criminal in my book. 'We don't know when John was infected, but that could have saved him. The cruelty is that we will never know.' Mr McAughey is at home, too sick to travel. The internal bleeding caused by his haemophilia is getting steadily worse because he is now wary of blood infusions. A bad bleed can confine him to bed for up to three weeks, and this occurs on average every other month. He has had to give up his job as an antiques dealer as a result. The bleeds, left unchecked, have given him chronic arthritis, which has crippled his shoulders, fingers, hips, knees and ankles. And the hepatitis is also getting worse as his liver slowly packs up. He has never been a drinker but he cannot now have so much as a glass of wine with a meal because his liver could not cope. The future is uncertain. Cirrhosis is a probability, a transplant possible. Mrs McAughey says: 'John has no appetite. The hepatitis is always there and the symptoms are horrendous headaches, dizziness, loss of concentration, memory lapses, muscular pain, fatigue, anorexia, nausea and insomnia. 'He is tired all the time. He only sleeps for three hours a night. We have been married for 35 years. We are a normal, healthy couple and still share a bed but this thing has disrupted both our lives, and affects the children. Our eldest grandchild is 11 and he is old enough now to understand that his grandad is poorly. 'But it's heartbreaking to see the two younger ones. They'll go bounding up to him but John is nervous. He can't hug them and show affection as he should, as he would like to. If one of them falls over and cuts their knee, he can't help. It's a terrible, terrible disease. And there's such a lot of ignorance surrounding it. Our friends and neighbours have been wonderful, but you hear these terrible stories of the children of infected haemophiliacs being shunned in the playground. Taunted for having "dirty blood". 'At least we haven't had to go through that. But we do want justice. 'Our life has been stolen from us and nothing can ever get it back. At the very least we deserve some compensation, some recognition. 'No amount of money can ever make John well again. But it would help us feel happier about the future. At present we are just living day-today, and that is not easy.' The committee's findings are expected to be released in the next few months, but already 900 of the 4,800 haemophiliacs who were infected in the Seventies and Eighties are dead, and that figure is rising. Mrs McAughey only hopes her husband will still be alive when the hoped-for judgment finally comes. 'It's like playing Russian roulette,' she says sadly, walking away. 'Every day.'

26 March 2001_1.Title:
, Tuesday

 Race to find patients at risk of CJD
26 March 2001_1.Author: No author found
26 March 2001_1.chunks:
The Times (London)

January 30, 2001, Tuesday

 Race to find patients at risk of CJD

BYLINE: David Charter, Health Correspondent

SECTION: Home news

LENGTH: 667 words

 
 THE Government was trying last night to trace scores of haemophiliacs at risk from catching the human form of "mad cow" disease after admitting that NHS patients were treated with blood products from a man who died of vCJD.
 Ministers immediately announced counselling arrangements for patients and their families who will face an agonising wait to learn if they received the infected treatment.
 The admission last night by Lord Hunt of Kings Heath, the junior Health Minister, will alarm Britain's 10,000 haemophiliacs. The incident echoes the 1980s blood contamination scandals when 4,800 haemophiliacs contracted hepatitis C and 1,200 caught HIV. 
 The disclosure came as one of the Government's advisers on vCJD accused ministers of "seriously misleading" the public over the safety of hospital treatment. Michael Banner, the chairman of a group of experts set up to control vCJD, considered quitting the CJD Incidents Panel over his concerns about surgery.
 In a letter to Liam Donaldson, the Chief Medical Officer, he accused the Government of not taking the panel seriously. Civil Service support of the panel was a "shambles", he said. He did not know from one day to the next which official he would be dealing with because none was assigned to the panel. His letter landed on Professor Donaldson's desk as Parliament heard that scientists were combing hospital records to find how many haemophiliacs were given a clotting agent made from a blood donor in 1996 or 1997 who later learnt that he had vCJD.
 The Government banned the use of British plasma in the manufacture of blood products in 1998 as a precautionary measure against the risk that vCJD can be transmitted in this way. Lord Morris of Manchester, the Labour peer who is honorary president of the Haemophilia Society, said: "This has come as a devastating shock to the haemophiliac community who have already been stricken by HIV and hepatitis C infection in the course of NHS treatment."
 He added: "I will be discussing the minister's reply very urgently with the Haemophilia Society. No one seems to know how many people may be affected but the society is doing all it can to counsel families that have cause to believe they were affected. The implications are very serious."
 Lord Hunt admitted that it was too early to tell how many haemophiliacs might have been affected but sought to play down the risks. He said: "We would stress that any risk of transmission of vCJD through blood products is theoretical. There have been no reported cases of vCJD among the haemophilia community."
 Professor Banner, of King's College London, criticised just such reassurances as "seriously misleading" in his letter, saying the incubation period was too long to be at all certain.
 He took issue with a statement from John Denham, the Health Minister, who said: "We have no evidence of any patient being infected with variant CJD in hospital. But while we are still learning about the progress of vCJD we should take precautions to reduce the theoretical risk of transmission."
 Professor Banner said that "simply overlooked" the fact that the vCJD incubation period could be 20 years and was therefore "not as reassuring as it may seem".
 Earlier this month ministers announced Pounds 200 million to improve hospital sterilisation, including Pounds 25 million for disposable instruments for all tonsillectomies. Professor Banner implied that all high-risk operations should be performed with disposable instruments.
 He said: "While no one within the Department of Health would intend to mislead the public, it is a matter of great concern if the public is misled, even as a result of lack of care in setting out the current state of knowledge in a clear and frank form."
 In the letter he added: "The course of events up to this point may suggest to the public that the Department of Health is not taking seriously the very important issues of public health which are the concern of the panel."

26 March 2001_1.chunks: Steen v HM Attorney-General  Court of Appeal (Civil Division)  Lord Phillips MR, Simon Brown and Longmore LLJ  March 23, 2001  Contempt of court - security service - injunction enforcement  S, the editor of the magazine, Punch, appealed against a decision that an article written by David Shayler, a former security service employee, had been published in contempt of court. After newspaper articles about the service based on information provided by Mr Shayler, the Attorney-General had obtained an injunction prohibiting, pending trial, the publication of any information that Mr Shayler had gained during his employment. Allowing the appeal, the court held that while publication of the article defeated the purpose of the injunction, it had not been shown that S had been aware that it would do so. A proviso to the injunction requiring anyone wishing to publish material within its ambit to obtain the AG's consent was disproportionate to any public interest and contrary to the European Convention on Human Rights 1950 Art. 10. A & ors v National Blood Authority & ors  Queen's Bench Division  Burton J  March 26, 2001  Personal injury - consumer protection - defective blood  After their infection with Hepatitis C from blood transfusions, a number of claimants sought damages under the EC Council Directive 85/374 and the Consumer Protection Act 1987. They argued that the National Blood Authority, which had assumed responsibility for administering blood transfusions, was liable under Art. 6 of the Directive, despite the absence of fault, and that it could not rely on Art. 7(e) by contending  that it had taken all possible steps to avoid infection. Giving judgment for the claimants, the court held that  the blood had been defective within the meaning of Art. 6  and that where a known risk had existed, a producer  could not evade responsibility by arguing that he had  been unable to identify the products in which the defect would occur. 26 March 2001_1.Title: Hepatitis jabs for court staff as heroin bust junkie is jailed.
26 March 2001_1.Author: By DONNA CARTON.
26 March 2001_1.chunks: EXCLUSIVE  A COURTHOUSE went on hepatitis alert last week when it was discovered a heroin junkie had been diagnosed as having the virus. Thomas Morgan was in front of a magistrate facing charges of having heroin. A probation report revealed that he had Hepatitis C and possibily the more dangerous Hepatitis B. His condition was referred to the Northern Ireland Court Service who took medical advice. As a result, all staff at Newtownards Courthouse were told to attend their GP and have injections against both Hepatitis C and B. And the alert was later widened to include police and prison staff who had been in contact with Morgan during the case. A legal source said: "The court staff were advised to visit their GP and receive injections. "Because they are not free on the NHS, the staff each had to pay out #41.50 for the injections. However, they will be reimbursed." Court officials were so concerned about the spread of the virus that anything Morgan touched in court was thrown out. Hepatitis C is the less serious strain of the virus, affecting the liver and be caught from a blood transfusion and injecting from illegal drugs. Hepatitis B, caught in the same way, is regarded as much more serious. Morgan pleaded guilty last Tuesday to having eight grammes of heroin with an estimated street value of around #1,500. Magistrate John Fyffe sentenced Morgan to six months in prison and said he should seek rehabilitation on release. Before being led away, Morgan told the RM: "God sparing, you will not see me within the next 10 years."

26 March 2001_1.Title: Haemophiliacs risk deathin blood treatment protest.
26 March 2001_1.Author: By LORRAINE FRASERMedical Correspondent.
26 March 2001_1.chunks: HAEMOPHILIACS are refusing to take a life-saving - though potentially deadly - treatment in protest at the refusal of the NHS to pay for them to receive medication free from the risks of them contracting HIV or vCJD.Dozens of sufferers have stopped using a standard NHS treatment and risk bleeding to death. They say they would rather suffer the pain of their illness or die, than continue to take it.The "treatment strike" only applies to sufferers in England, where health authorities are refusing to find the #23 million a year to switch from blood-derived treatment to a genetically engineered treatment, which is safer.Most of the men on strike are ill with HIV and hepatitis C virus infection, contracted from the contaminated blood clotting treatment they received on the NHS in the 1970s and 1980s. Now many have been told they are among hundreds, including children, to have received treatment made from the blood of a victim of vCJD, the human form of BSE.Marc Payton, 40, from Worcestershire, said last night: "It's time to make a stand. The pain is horrific without treatment and people are afraid to go back to that, but I feel that if we don't nothing will get done. "People with haemophilia are unable to make their own supply of key blood clotting proteins, most commonly Factor VIII, and unless they get this through treatment they can suffer painful bleeding into the joints and potentially fatal internal haemorrhage. A death among the protesters, which is possible, would provoke an outcry.The drastic protest is a measure of the anger many haemophiliacs now feel towards the Government and the NHS. Of 1,200 sufferers who contracted HIV from blood-derived treatment, 800 have died. Hundreds are living with hepatitis C or both viruses, contracted before heat treatment to destroy them was introduced in the mid-1980s.Those who have survived blame the Department of Health for their illnesses, saying it has failed repeatedly to recognise the risks of contamination in the Factor VIII made from human blood plasma, and continues to do so. Even now, blood-derived Factor VIII is known to be contaminated with viruses which can be harmful to individuals with a damaged immune system.Mr Payton, who has HIV and hepatitis C and has had cancer because the Aids virus has damaged his immune system, said the possible vCJD contamination was the last straw. He sent back his supply of plasma-derived Factor VIII to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Edgbaston, three weeks ago.He said: "It has destroyed my life and I am not prepared to take any more. Every time you inject it you are injecting something that is supposed to be life-saving but effectively it's a killer. It is slowly poisoning us. "Health ministers are struggling to explain why English haemophiliacs are discriminated against. Lord Hunt, the health minister, met their representatives a fortnight ago but has yet to make an announcement.

26 March 2001_1.Title: I've lost a brother and an uncle because of contaminated blood, now my son Jordan could ...
26 March 2001_1.Author: By ALEXANDRA WILLIAMS.
26 March 2001_1.chunks: I've lost a brother and an uncle because of contaminated blood, now my son Jordan could be dying from vCJD. AN Irish mother who lost two members of her family because of contaminated blood transfusions is living with the fear that her haemophiliac son may have CJD. Eight-year-old Jordan Mc-Envoy was given blood from a man who died from the human form of mad cow disease. Now his mother Susan says he risks contracting the killer illness. And she claims cost-cutting led to him being given inferior treatments in the first place. Susan, 36, said: "I am so angry. This could have been prevented. But now my son's at risk from variant CJD and nobody can tell me for sure that he hasn't contracted it. There's no test for it." Susan's agony is compounded by the fact that three haemo-philiac members of her family were given HIV-contaminated blood in Dublin in 1984. Her eldest brother Gerard died of Aids in 1992 at the age of 33, and her uncle Benny McEnvoy died in 1989. Another brother still in Dublin is being treated with drugs to stave off Aids. Susan, who lives in London, spoke out after haemophiliac Marc Payton from Rubery, Worcestershire, revealed last week that contaminated blood had exposed him to vCJD. Marc, 39, also has hepatitis and HIV. Susan said: "It's like genocide. That man has been cheated out of a life just to save money." Jordan was born in 1992, three months after the death of his uncle Gerard. Haemophilia is a hereditary condition passed through the mother, who has a 50 per cent chance of passing it to her sons. Because the blood is stopped from clotting naturally, a cut can mean bleeding to death and a bruise can lead to internal haemorrhaging. Susan injected Jordan every other day with a clotting factor made from blood plasma. But when he was five she learned that the blood product he had been given from London's Royal Free Hospital came from a vCJD sufferer. Susan, a single mum who moved from Dublin to Clapton 15 years ago, said: "I nearly had a heart attack when the hospital told me. "After what happened with the Aids virus I was scared stiff. "They patronised the life out of me at the hospital. "The doctor was like a robot reading a memo when he told me that the risks of Jordan getting vCJD from the blood were theoretical. "When I asked him how he knew, he couldn't tell me. I want to know the full details. "I was treated like an idiot but it's simple for the doctor to blurt out what he wants when it's not his son." A year before the hospital discovered Jordan had been treated with a contaminated batch they had already switched him to man-made blood products (recombinant). Susan said: "I'm relieved that Jordan has recombinant. The risk of viral infection through a genetically engineered product is greatly reduced. "All haemophiliacs should have it. The British government pumps money into futile projects like the Dome but penny pinches when it comes to health. "I feel like it's a wait and see situation with Jordan's health. "Every time he's ill and it's not a cold I get worried that it could be symptoms of vCJD. If he has a headache I make him lie down because I just don't know what I'm dealing with. I am waiting on tenterhooks until someone develops a test for vCJD." In Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland all haemophiliacs are given recombinant, but in England it is only prescribed to children under the age of 16. A spokesman from The Haemophilia Society, which is campaigning for recombinant and a public inquiry in England into the safety of blood products, said: "It is illogical to make them available for under-16s only. "If cost is the reason it's being withheld then it's a false economy." He said more patients were refusing treatment with a clotting factor from human sources. Instead, they joined networks that allowed patients who do get recombinant to send their doses to others without it. One patient who did this last year forced his health authority to pay for the treatment. There are 10,000 haemophiliacs in Britain. The vCJD scare echoes the 1980s blood contamination scandals when 4,800 haemophiliacs were accidentally infected with the hepatitis C virus. Of these, 1,200 were infected with HIV, and only a third of them are still alive. It could be years before doctors know if there has been human transmission. The incubation period of variant CJD is unknown and the disease has been identified for less than five years. When questioned in January, Britain's Junior Health Minister Lord Hunt said it was too early to assess the extent of any infection. He said: "We would stress that any risk of transmission of vCJD through blood products is theoretical. "There have been no reported cases of vCJD among the haemophiliac community." But Michael Banner, the chair of a group of experts set up to control vCJD, criticised such reassurances as "seriously misleading". Susan said: "I am angry. I have watched my brother die over five years from Aids after he had contaminated blood. It has to stop. It's pure and simple penny-pinching but it could be costing lives." A spokeswoman for Britain's Department of Health said they now have safeguards against vCJD transmission. In 1998 they stopped using plasma from UK donors. She said: "There is no evidence worldwide that vCJD of any type has been transmitted via blood or blood products, although the possibility cannot be ruled out. "Since 1998, as a precaution against this theoretical risk, no blood products have been manufactured using plasma from UK donors. US donors are now used. "All children under 16 and all new patients receive recombinant. "The Haemophilia Society has now asked the government to provide recombinant clotting factors for all haemophiliacs but there is currently a worldwide shortage of recombinant. "Ministers are now giving this careful consideration."

26 March 2001_1.Title: Acambis - Tempus.
26 March 2001_1.Author: Robert Cole.
26 March 2001_1.chunks: ACAMBIS, the biotechnology company formerly called Peptide Therapeutics, has made an impressive fightback from the failure of its overambitious vaccine against all allergies.Yesterday the company unveiled positive early trial results for a vaccine against Japanese encephalitis - a mosquito-borne viral disease afflicting up to 100,000 people, mostly in Asia. The data appear to validate both the ChimeraVax technology platform from which the vaccine was developed, and the logic of acquiring the US company OraVax, which owned it.The results were early stage, but showed that the vaccine produced a good antibody response. Moreover, it is possible that vaccines for hepatitis C and other conditions can be developed from the same platform.Acambis has developed a strong intellectual property position in vaccines and the harnessing of the immune system to prevent and treat disease. Both are hot areas of medical research. A strategic alliance last year with Baxter Healthcare, which agreed to invest #28 million, underpins confidence in Acambis. Baxter brings technological and distribution skills and will give invaluable help to Acambis in its quest to bring its products to market. Baxter's presence also creates takeover excitement.The firm already has products enough to commend the stock. But it is also likely to seek acquisitions that will strengthen its position. The share price, however, fails to reflect the company's progress and potential. Buy. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

26 March 2001_1.Title: Lover with HIV guilty of risking woman's life.
26 March 2001_1.Author: Gillian Harris Scotland Correspondent.
26 March 2001_1.chunks: A WHIRLWIND romance that began at a party led yesterday to Britain's first court conviction for knowingly infecting a lover with the HIV virus.Stephen Kelly, 33, was found guilty of culpable and reckless conduct by having unprotected sex knowing that he was risking the life of his lover, Anne Craig, 34.Miss Craig, from Manchester, found that she had become HIV positive within three months of first sleeping with him. After the verdict, she said: "I am delighted that justice has been done and hope this will be a deterrent to others. If the verdict saves one life from the misery I have been through then it will all have been worthwhile. "Over the last few years I have fought to get my life back together but it can never be the same. Similarly, the lives of my children, other family and close friends have been damaged. "Sentencing of Kelly was deferred until March 16. During the nine-day trial at Glasgow High Court, the jury was told that the couple met at a Glasgow party in January 1994. Before they slept together for the first time, within hours of meeting, Miss Craig asked him if there was any reason other than pregnancy why they should not have unprotected sex. Kelly replied: "No. "In fact, Kelly, a heroin addict from Provanmill, Glasgow, had contracted HIV after sharing dirty needles with other prisoners while serving a sentence for assault and attempted robbery in Glenochil jail, Clackmannanshire.Kelly, a widower with two children, had received his HIV test results in July 1993. He was tested as part of the prison's voluntary screening programme, prompted by an outbreak of hepatitis. He was advised about the importance of practising safe sex.Anne Thompson, a nurse from Ruchill Hospital in Glasgow, who talked to Kelly about his condition, said that he seemed intelligent and aware of the potentially devastating consequences of unprotected sex. Kelly told Miss Craig that he had been tested negative for HIV.Evidence that Kelly was the likely source of her infection was given by Andrew Leigh-Brown, Professor of Evolutionary Genetics at Edinburgh University, an expert on HIV. He told the court that the strain of the virus uncovered at Glenochil prison was the same one which showed up in Miss Craig's blood sample from March 1994.Kelly later claimed to have caught the virus from a former girlfriend.Donald Findlay, QC, defending Kelly, suggested to Miss Craig that she had been fully aware of Kelly's condition but had unprotected sex with him because of the obsessive nature of their relationship.Miss Craig, a mother of three, denied the claim but admitted that after her diagnosis she continued to see Kelly. She said that her family had disowned her and she was afraid of dying alone. Her solicitor, Cameron Fyfe, said she would now pursue a claim for criminal injuries compensation to help support her children aged 16, 14 and nine.The case was brought under Scottish common law because there is no criminal charge of deliberately infecting a person with the HIV virus in Scotland. In England and Wales, it became a criminal offence in 1997. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

26 March 2001_1.Title: Wonder drug not for the poor.
26 March 2001_1.Author: No author in byline
26 March 2001_1.chunks: Biotechnology company Acambis is set to announce startling results from trials of a pioneering vaccine for deadly Japanese encephalitis, using technology which could tackle other viral diseases such as dengue fever, hepatitis C and West Nile fever, writes Andrew Clark. In a study using 36 volunteers, Acambis achieved 100% success in stimulating antibodies to counter Japanese encephalitis - a mosquito-borne virus which kills 10,000 people annually. Acambis, formerly called Peptide Therapeutics, intends to target its vaccines initially at backpackers visiting developing countries rather than sell to the `at-risk' local population. The Cambridge-based company, which has struggled due to several product failures over the last two years, is unlikely to make much money out of sales in poor countries, who are unable to afford hi-tech medicines.

26 March 2001_1.Title: Cure that kills - Drug patents must stay while prices must fall - Leading Arti cle.
26 March 2001_1.Author: No author in byline
26 March 2001_1.chunks: The 41 pharmaceuticals companies that have filed suit against the South African Government for violation of patent rights have been denounced worldwide. Their chief executives knew that they would be. They are seen as corporate Scrooges who are prepared to let the sick and indigent die without medicines rather than sacrifice a mite of their profits.This is damage the companies cannot ignore; in a global market, bad publicity can outweigh the most elaborate advertising. The risk of consumer boycotts is all the greater when the South African law in question, the Medicines and Related Substances Act of 1997, was signed into law by the universally revered Nelson Mandela, the country is afflicted by an Aids pandemic and the law is presented as essential to reducing the costs of treatment.Why then has the industry, led by South Africa's own pharmaceuticals manufacturers, grimly gone to court? Its case is that this particular law is so sweeping that, were it to be copied by other countries, global patent protection would be dead. That would undermine the financial basis of research and development of new drugs because the costs, which can be huge, are recouped through international patents on successful medicines. Under World Trade Organisation rules, these last for 20 years.There are also, however, generic versions of most patented drugs on the market, which can cost as little as a tenth of brand-name products. The South African law would enable the Health Minister either to import or to order the domestic manufacture of generic drugs, overriding both domestic and international patent laws, whenever it was held that this would "protect the health of the public". That could apply to any medicine. It is defended by a vocal lobby, which argues that poor countries ought to be able, regardless of patent law, to shop around for the cheapest available drugs and which accuses the industry of obstructing the fight against Africa's alarming Aids pandemic.That charge is ill-founded. South Africa can already legally use generic drugs to treat Aids. Existing WTO rules expressly permit the licensing of drugs by poor countries without the patent-holder's consent, for public use or when they face a "national emergency". Some of the biggest companies have offered South Africa massive discounts on Aids drugs, to about 20 per cent of the market price; it has not taken them up. It has also resisted treatments for HIV-positive pregnant women costing a mere #2.50, standard in the US, that can halve the transmission rates to babies. President Thabo Mbeki has even questioned whether Aids is linked to the HIV virus. That undermines the campaign to raise public awareness which is vital in a continent where only 3 per cent of people with HIV report to clinics and many do not know they have the disease.Blaming the pharmaceuticals industry for Africa's ills is as easy as it is dishonest. The past year has seen a massive drive, starting in the US, to tackle the biggest Third World killers. Four major companies have donated more than #100 million in vaccines against malaria, hepatitis and polio as well as Aids. The US Government gives $1 billion in tax incentives to stimulate vaccine research. Led by the Gates Foundation, American charities are pouring money into medical research and subsidised drugs. There are loopholes enough in patent law to give the poor access to cheap medicine. South Africa would do better to use them intelligently than to challenge the system of property rights that alone makes research viable. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

26 March 2001_1.Title: Needles, the deadly threat on NHS wards; Scandal of 100,000 accidents a year that could be avoided
26 March 2001_1.Author: BEEZY MARSH
26 March 2001_1.chunks: DOCTORS and nurses are being put at risk of life-threatening illnesses because the NHS does not have enough money to provide safer needles. More than 100,000 needle injuries occur every year on Health Service wards, exposing medical staff to incurable diseases such as HIV and hepatitis C. Nearly every doctor and nurse in Britain can expect to be accidentally jabbed by a needle in any three-year period. Experts say many of these incidents could be avoided by using needles fitted with safety guards, which close around the tip on withdrawal from the patient's arm. Such devices a legal requirement in all hospitals in the United States cost twice as much as regular needles. The most sophisticated kits cost ten times more. Campaigners believe the Department of Health is reluctant to introduce them because using safety needles for taking blood or giving injections would add between Pounds 25million and Pounds 40million a year to health service costs. The full extent of needle injuries in the NHS is due to be revealed at a conference on occupational blood-borne viruses in London later this month. Researchers at the newly- formed Safer Needles for Safer Health Care Network audited accidents at 14 hospitals throughout Britain. Preliminary results show that at least 100,000 injuries are occurring every year, though the true figure could be higher because many staff fail to report the accidents. Consultant anaesthetist Philip Bickford Smith, chairman of the campaign group, said: 'There is a fear among managers that the costs for safer needles could spiral out of control. 'We don't think that is the case, and they have to offset that against the cost of counselling and treating those who have suffered such an injury.' A Department of Health spokesman said few safer needles had been identified that could be supplied under medical devices regulations. MARTIN Alster, above, faced the nightmare prospect of being infected with hepatitis C which can cause total liver failure after injuring himself on a needle. The 37-year-old nurse from King's Lynn, Norfolk, pricked his finger after taking blood from a drug abuser who was carrying the infection. The married father of one underwent an immediate blood test, but faced a three-month wait for the results. A second, quicker test wrongly gave a false positive result because it had been taken too early. He was later given the all-clear. Mr Alster, a mental health specialist, said: 'I went through agony. Some of my patients were infected with hepatitis C and it was very difficult to hear what they were going through knowing it could be me.'

10 August 2001_1.Title: Schering hepatitis drug gets go
10 August 2001_1.Author: By ADRIAN MICHAELS.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: Schering-Plough announced yesterday that a more convenient and effective version of its successful hepatitis C treatment had been approved by US regulators. The approval by the Food and Drug Administration is a welcome piece of good news for the US pharmaceuticals company which is otherwise in trouble with the FDA over manufacturing quality deficiencies. Many large pharmaceuticals companies have suffered setbacks in drug approvals at the FDA this year. However, Schering said that a sustained-release, once-a-week, version of Intron-A - called Peg-Intron - had been approved in combination with another drug, Rebetol. The combination has been more effective in the treatment of hepatitis C than previous formulations and also involves fewer injections. Intron-A and related drugs are Schering's second-biggest sellers after Claritin, its allergy blockbuster. They are also used in the treatment of some cancers and last year earned revenues of $1.4bn. "Ten years ago, there were no approved therapies for hepatitis C. Today ... physicians have an improved treatment regimen that is more convenient for patients," said Richard Zahn, president of Schering Laboratories. Roche, the Swiss pharmaceuticals company, has seen its competitor to Peg-Intron, called Pegasys, held up by the FDA. It was approved in Switzerland this week. Schering's FDA problems have caused large disruption to production, resulting in profit warnings and stifled growth. The manufacturing issues have also held up approval for the successor drug to Claritin, its allergy blockbuster.

10 August 2001_1.chunks: Schering-Plough, US pharmaceuticals company, has had approval from regulators of a more convenient and effective version of its hepatitis C treatment. Page 27.

10 August 2001_1.Title: Roche acquires  Hepatitis C  drug rights from ICN.
10 August 2001_1.Author: By DAVID FIRN IN LONDON.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: In a move to beef up its product pipeline, Roche, the Swiss healthcare group, has acquired the rights to levovirin, an experimental treatment for hepatitis C, from ICN Pharmaceuticals of the US. The decision to license levovirin, a follow on product to ribavarin, ICN's leading antiviral treatment, is the first sign that Roche is serious about its recently-announced strategy of acquiring products to fill the gaps left after a number of its own medicines failed. Levovirin is a "cleaned-up" version of ribavirin with fewer toxic side effects. The acquisition is also a coup in Roche's battle with Schering-Plough, the US group, over dominance of the hepatitis market. Schering-Plough had the right to license levovirin from ICN, but did not take it up. Roche and Schering-Plough are both poised to launch new hepatitis treatments based on interferon. Roche's candidate, Pagasys, seems to have the edge over Schering-Plough's PEG-Intron in clinical trials. However, the launch of Pegasys has been held up by closer than expected scrutiny from US regulators, giving Schering-Plough a head start in the market. Roche faces a lean year following a fall in pharmaceutical sales in 2000. Pegasys is one of the few major product launches planned for this year. Analysts expect it to have peak sales of $900m. Mark Booty of Commerzbank said levovirin could give Roche the edge it needed to catch up with PEG-Inton. "Combining Pegasys with a cleaned up version of ribavirin has the hallmarks of turning it into a very serious competitor to Schering Plough," he said. Roche will pay ICN a one-time licensing fee, as well as milestone payments, and a royalty on sales. Roche will also give ICN a compound at a similar stage of development. Separately Roche has signed a five year agreement with deCode, the Icelandic genomics company, to develop tests for genetic diseases. It follows an earlier agreement to hunt for the genes that cause conditions such as cardiovascular disease and schizophrenia. The new deal could be worth up to $300m in research payments and royalties to deCode.

10 August 2001_1.Title: COMPANIES &FINANCE EUROPE - Roche drug delay takes edge off growing sales.
10 August 2001_1.Author: DAVID FIRN and WILLIAM HALL.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: Roche, the Swiss pharma-ceutical company, said it expected full-year operating profit to equal last year's SFr4.3bn ( $2.6bn), after reporting a 7 per cent rise in sales for the first nine months yesterday.However, delays to the launch of Pegasys, its hepatitis C treatment, overshadowed accelerating pharmaceutical sales.Franz Humer, chairman and chief executive, said the core pharmaceuticals operation outgrew the market for the second quarter in a row. "In the last six months the world pharma market was growing at 10 per cent and we were growing at 12 per cent," he said.However, growth is expected to slow in the fourth quarter, and Mr Humer refused to say whether Roche would outpace competitors in 2002.Roche is under pressure to launch new medicines because the US patent on its number-three drug, acne treatment Roaccutan, expires in February.However, the launch of Pegasys has been put back to the second half of next year, following modifications to the production process, giving a head start to Peg-Intron, the Schering-Plough treatment.Mr Humer played down the problem saying Roche would also launch a new type of HIV treatment, T-20, next year.Sales for the nine months to September 30 were SFr21.6bn up from SFr20.2bn a year ago. Diagnostics sales climbed 12 per cent - outpacing the market by a considerable margin. Sales of vitamins and fine chemicals, seen as a possible divesment, were up just 4 per cent, missing analysts' forecasts.Mr Humer said the pharmaceutical figures showed that plans to shed 3,000 jobs - the biggest cutbacks in Roche's 105-year history - were having an effect. "We are focusing our resources on the key products in terms of promotion, advertising and marketing," he said.However, Denise Anderson, analyst at Julius Baer in Zurich, said growth in pharmaceuticals would remain below average for the foreseeable future. Margins were low and the pipeline weak, she said.Last year the pharmaceuticals division had an operating margin of 18 per cent compared with 30.7 per cent at Novartis, its arch rival.Roche also said that it did not expect any contribution from financial operations in the second half.Last year financial income, which has underpinned growth for several years, was SFr1.7bn. Financial income was SFr1.5bn in the first half of 2001.

10 August 2001_1.Title: Roche.
10 August 2001_1.Author: No author in byline
10 August 2001_1.chunks: Roche seems to be responding to treatment better than expected. The 5 per cent growth in first-half pharmaceutical sales - 11 per cent in the second quarter - and jump in operating margin to 19 per cent all beat forecasts. But Kytril, a drug acquired from GlaxoSmithKline, contributed half the sales increase - and last year's second quarter was particularly weak. While an improving product mix helped the margin, cost-cutting was the biggest factor. The success of the restructuring at least suggests Roche can achieve its planned SFr600m annual savings by 2003 - and get its operating margin into the 20-25 per cent range. But it remains difficult to see how Roche can meet its other target: matching industry sales growth. It has only one big drugs launch planned - Pegasys, a hepatitis C drug that will come up against Schering-Plough's PegIntron. A merger or acquisition looks the only way to resuscitate the top line. Speculation over a Bayer tie-up has intensified since the latter's withdrawal of Baycol. This might be a good cultural and therapeutic fit. But it would not solve Roche's sales growth and late-stage pipeline problems. Novartis, with 20 per cent of voting shares, could also hardly be expected to sit back and watch Roche get together with Bayer. And a cross-Basle merger still looks the best option. It would have huge cost-cutting potential, and put Roche back among the drugs industry giants. Unless its family shareholders show they are open to such a move, Roche's shares, on 23 times 2002 earnings, look unlikely to narrow their discount to the sector.

10 August 2001_1.Title: COMPANIES &FINANCE UK - XTL develops hepatitis method NEWS DIGEST.
10 August 2001_1.Author: DAVID FIRN.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: XTL develops hepatitis methodA new type of treatment developed by XTL Biopharmaceuticals, the London-listed Israeli biotechnology company, could make hepatitis treatment much more effective, according to preliminary trial data released today.XTL has developed a way of transplanting human immune cells into mice to produce antibodies, against a variety of infectious diseases.The new hepatitis treatment uses a mixture of two synthetic antibodies that stick to the hepatitis B virus and flag it up for destruction by the body's immune system. 10 August 2001_1.Title: Tough medicine but recovery not assured.
10 August 2001_1.Author: By DAVID PILLING.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: COMPANIES &FINANCE EUROPE - Tough medicine but recovery not assured - The Swiss group is cutting costs but few believe that the measures will work, writes David Pilling. Roche was yesterday dressing up its long-awaited cost-cutting initiative as a "strengthening of its pharmaceuticals division". But nobody was fooled. The Swiss group's plans to slash 3,000 jobs, about 8 per cent of its pharma workforce, are a last-ditch attempt to realign its cost structure to a new, painful, reality. That is one of declining sales and the prospect of further falls as a number of important drugs come under generic onslaught. Cost cuts aim to restore the drug unit's measly margins to a half respectable 20-25 per cent by 2004. They will bear down heavily on UK operations, where research and manufacturing is to be ended in Welwyn, and in the US, where at least 1,100 jobs will go at Roche's sites in Nutley, New Jersey, and Palo Alto, California. Costs will be drastically reduced at the company's lavish headquarters in Basle, Switzerland, where 600 redundancies - including in chemicals production - will be pushed through. The company will also reorganise global manufacturing to reflect its slim portfolio of drugs. The vital US marketing division will be restructured, with more than 300 jobs going in the primary care division. William Bruns, head of the pharmaceuticals division, said the company did not need to match the mega salesforces of companies selling mass-market heart and blood-pressure medicines. Roche said it intended to license in new compounds from other companies - a tacit admission of shortfalls at its own laboratories. But potential partners may question its credentials as a marketing powerhouse. Analysts say yesterday's excercise is a necessary scaling back, but few believe it will be enough to address the group's fundamental problems. The underlying difficulty at the pharma division, by far the most important contributor to group earnings, is that it is being driven by three drugs launched in 1982. All, to some degree, face pressure from generics. According to Cheuvreux, the brokers, Dormicum (an anaesthetic), Rocephin (an antibiotic), and Roaccuatane (an acne medication), accounted for nearly SFr3bn ( $1.68bn), or a whopping 65 per cent of pharma operating profits in 2000. Cheuvreux's most optimistic forecast is that more than half of those profits will be lost by 2005. By contrast to these cash cows, which require very little marketing effort, profits on Xenical, an expensive drug to manufacture and advertise, are much smaller. Tamiflu, an influenza pill licensed from Gilead, looks unlikely to become a big earner. And the only other drug with big potential, Pegasys for hepatitis C, faces a potentially damaging delay after rigorous questioning from the US Food and Drug Administration. That leaves Franz Humer, Roche's embattled chairman, needing to do something strategic. Analysts say he may seek to bolster diagnostics, the group's most successful business. Alternatively, he may try to dispose of vitamins. But none of this would bolster pharma performance. Unless Roche can sign a marketing collaboration for a real money-spinner - such as AstraZeneca's Crestor, a cholesterol drug - it may have to take more drastic action. One option would be to emulate its corporate raids of the 1990s, which saw it pick up such sterling assets as Genentech, arguably the world's most productive biotechnology company, and Boeringer Mannheim, the diagnostics group. But such companies are not easy to find and, notwithstanding Roche's substantial cash-pile, are generally expensive. Names such as Schering of Germany and Biogen of the US have been mentioned by analysts scratching around for a possible target. The other possibility is a full-scale merger, though given Roche's decline of recent years it could well have to settle for being the junior partner. That would be tough to accept for descendants of the founding Hoffmann family, who have maintained independence for 105 years. Even if - as some people close to the company say - the family is for the first time contemplating a merger, the current state of the share price hardly makes this a propitious moment. Nor is it clear quite who would want to merge with Roche. AstraZeneca might be attracted by its oncology franchise and the fit between cholesterol and obesity drugs. Eli Lilly of the US could conceivably see Roche as a way of bolstering its European presence. And there is always Novartis, the rival Swiss company that stunned the industry this month by purchasing 20 per cent of Roche's voting shares. An all-Swiss solution would appear the most logical. But for the proud Hoffmann family, surrender to the rival across the Rhine could be the hardest pill to swallow.

10 August 2001_1.Title: USFDA panel split on Lilly sepsis drug.
10 August 2001_1.Author: By ADRIAN MICHAELS IN NEW YORK AND VICTORIA GRIFFITH IN BOSTON.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: Eli Lilly on Tuesday suffered a setback in efforts to have its breakthrough treatment for sepsis, or septic shock, approved by regulators. An advisory panel to the US Food and Drug Administration was split over whether to recommend approval of the drug, originally known as Zovant and now called Xigris. The FDA, which normally follows panel advice, could be prompted to delay approval after 10 of 20 panel members voted against. Xigris has already been held up by the FDA once this year over manufacturing quality concerns. In addition, Tuesday's panel hearing had been delayed by the September 11 terrorist attacks. The drug was hailed by some analysts as the most exciting expected approval this year. Sepsis is an often fatal condition that affects 1.5m people worldwide. Tuesday's split decision surprised analysts, who had expected Xigris to be recommended. Some panel members urged more clinical studies, unconvinced that the drug had demonstrated a clear benefit. Lilly says it saves the lives of a significant number of patients. The FDA could decide to limit severely the number of situations for which the drug's administration is approved. Such limitations, stated on the drug's label, could mean that as few as 25 per cent of sepsis patients would be prescribed the drug, so cutting into Xigris sales. "Restrictive labelling often does not have the desired effect, but in the case of Xigris it may, because of stringent enforcement by hospitals due to its high expected cost," said Barbara Ryan, analyst at Deutsche Banc Alex Brown. Lilly had been hoping for more positive news from the panel and its shares may come under further pressure on Wednesday. The company has already suffered at the hands of investors this month. It scaled back earnings forecasts in response to competition from generic equivalents to Prozac, the anti-depressant drug. Roche, the Swiss pharmaceutical company, said it expected full-year operating profit to equal last year's SFr4.3bn ($2.6bn), after reporting a 7 per cent rise in sales for the first nine months on Tuesday. However, delays to the launch of Pegasys, its hepatitis C treatment, overshadowed accelerating pharmaceutical sales.

10 August 2001_1.Title: 60 BLOOD VICTIMS GIVEN #5M.
10 August 2001_1.Author: By FIONA WYNNE.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: Drug firms agree payout  SIXTY haemophiliacs last night won settlements of up to #80,000 each after being infected with HIV and Hepatitis C.  The #5million agreement was made with five international drug firms. The case, which began more than eight years ago, was settled outside the High Court, but full details are not being disclosed. Only one out of the 60 people involved in the proceedings chose not to accept the deal. The proceedings were also mentioned at the Lindsay Tribunal. Jerry Durcan, SC for the Tribunal, revealed that his team is seeking access to results of HIV tests conducted on haemophiliacs who are involved in the case against the drug firms. These results will show which particular company products infected which people. The five drug companies involved include Armour Pharmaceutical, Baxter Healthcare Corp, Bayer and Immuno. And a breakthrough in amending legislation has also been announced. Haemophiliacs infected with HIV may soon be able to claim compensation from the state. Talks between the Irish Haemophilia Society and the Department of Health have been deadlocked for months, but a new offer from the department means that discussions are likely to restart and compensation may finally be paid. Further statistics revealed at the Tribunal yesterday show that 30 more haemophiliacs were infected by blood products than previously known. Seamus Dooley of the Virus Reference Lab at UCD said that according to his studies, 252 haemophiliacs were infected with HIV and Hepatitis C.  The Irish Haemophilia Society had thought that 221 haemophiliacs were infected. Health Minister Micheal Martin said: "We're committed to introducing a compensation scheme. "Talks have been going on for some time. "Logjams developed but we're setting up parameters for renewed discussion."
