10 August 2001_1.Title: Shire - Sharewatch.
10 August 2001_1.Author: Edited by David Parsley.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: TURNING a drugs minnow into a #5 billion company in the space of seven years has given Rolf Stahel a big City following. After finally completing the acquisition of BioChem Pharma, Merrill Lynch reckons the shares in Shire Pharmaceuticals can race ahead to #18.25 over the next 12 months. But Nick Woolf at ABN Amro is sceptical. He says Shire's Adderall treatment for hyperactive children is facing tough competition; that Reminyl for Alzheimer's disease will struggle to displace the market leader; and that royalties from a hepatitis-B drug rely on unstable Asian markets. Woolf says: "The historic 40%-50% growth is going to go to zero over the next four years. A lot of the stuff coming through is me-too." With the shares at #11.95, ABN Amro says sell. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

10 August 2001_1.Title: XTL shares rise on  hepatitis C  drug data.
10 August 2001_1.Author: By DAVID FIRN.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: Shares in XTL Biopharmaceuticals, rose over 10 per cent after the London-listed Israeli biotechnology company said its new hepatitis C drug could make treatment of the potentially fatal liver disease much more effective. XTL has developed a synthetic human antibody that attacks the hepatitis C virus. A single dose was sufficient to reduce the levels of the virus in half of a group of 15 hepatitis patients, according to preliminary trial data released by the company on Monday. Hepatitis C, a sexually-transmitted virus, is difficult to treat and potentially fatal. The US Center for Disease Control has forecast that deaths caused by hepatitis C will surpass those from Aids by the end of the decade. XTL's breakthrough follows the creation of mice with human livers. That allowed the company to test potential drugs extensively before moving to human trials. Analysts said the data was encouraging, but still preliminary and needed confirming by larger trials. Antibodies are one of the fastest growing classes of medicines. XTL's treatment, known as XTL-002, is the first against hepatitis C. Last month the company reported encouraging data from a combination of two other antibodies that attack hepatitis B, which is caused by a different virus. The shares were up 5p at 51p in morning trading on Monday.

10 August 2001_1.Title: GSK regains Glaxo's old steadfast reputation - Tempus - GlaxoSmithKline.
10 August 2001_1.Author: Robert Cole.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: GlaxoSmithKline yesterday staked its claim to be the UK's greatest exporter. More than half the company's #20 billion-a-year turnover is in the US, the world's largest, most profitable and fastest-growing prescription drug market.The US exposure comes with risk. The political environment is uncertain and drug prices may be undermined. Meanwhile the Food and Drug Administration appears to be adopting a toughening stance on drug approvals. However, these concerns should not overshadow GSK's success in the US or the attractive fundamentals of the pharmaceutical sector there. GSK's 13 per cent earnings growth in the second quarter was fuelled by US sales, which were up 20 per cent, compared with 12 per cent for the whole group.The US launch of Advair - the asthma drug called Seretide in Europe - looks particularly promising. Blockbuster status seems assured, as does the future of GSK's respiratory franchise, which had sales growth of 21 per cent to almost #1 billion in the second quarter. If GSK broke itself up, the respiratory franchise would be a substantial standalone business.Avandia, the adult-onset diabetes drug, showed 84 per cent sales growth at #220 million and is also destined for blockbuster status. Hepatitis sales were disappointing, however, and the consumer healthcare division would have shown lower sales if not for the acquisitions.GSK has suffered some high-profile product and earnings setbacks in the past. But it is delivering on its promises to fill its new product pipeline and deliver double-digit growth in earnings. The joint venture with Japan's Shinogi may also open a promising new geographic market.GSK shares are on a forward p/e of 28, in line with the European pharmaceutical sector but at a justifiable premium to US peers. Hold.

10 August 2001_1.Title: Acambis - Tempus.
10 August 2001_1.Author: Robert Cole.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: ACAMBIS, the biotechnology company formerly called Peptide Therapeutics, has made an impressive fightback from the failure of its overambitious vaccine against all allergies.Yesterday the company unveiled positive early trial results for a vaccine against Japanese encephalitis - a mosquito-borne viral disease afflicting up to 100,000 people, mostly in Asia. The data appear to validate both the ChimeraVax technology platform from which the vaccine was developed, and the logic of acquiring the US company OraVax, which owned it.The results were early stage, but showed that the vaccine produced a good antibody response. Moreover, it is possible that vaccines for hepatitis C and other conditions can be developed from the same platform.Acambis has developed a strong intellectual property position in vaccines and the harnessing of the immune system to prevent and treat disease. Both are hot areas of medical research. A strategic alliance last year with Baxter Healthcare, which agreed to invest #28 million, underpins confidence in Acambis. Baxter brings technological and distribution skills and will give invaluable help to Acambis in its quest to bring its products to market. Baxter's presence also creates takeover excitement.The firm already has products enough to commend the stock. But it is also likely to seek acquisitions that will strengthen its position. The share price, however, fails to reflect the company's progress and potential. Buy. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

10 August 2001_1.Title: Xenova shares up 18% on cancer licensing deals.
10 August 2001_1.Author: By FT.COM STAFF IN LONDON.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: Xenova, the UK drug development company which recently took over its rival Cantab Pharmaceuticals, on Tuesday said it had signed two collaboration agreements worth about $130m, sending shares up by nearly 18 per cent. The UK drugs company said it had signed a $105m licence agreement with Canada's QLT to develop and market XR9576, Xenova's cancer drug treatment, in the US, Canada and Mexico. Under the terms of the agreement, QLT would take responsibility for Phase III trials and the manufacturing of the product in those areas. In early London trading, shares in Xenova rose by 7p to 46-1/2p. In a separate move, Xenova said Phogen, its joint-venture company it acquired in its merger with Cantab, had signed a $21m licensing agreement with Genencor International. The deal involves the development of a number of therapeutic vaccines for certain infectious viral diseases including hepatitis C and hepatitis B. Xenova also said the completion of its merger with Cantab had hit profits. For the six months to June 30, Xenova reported a pre-tax loss of GBP7.39m ($10.5m) compared with a loss of GBP3.59m in the same period last year. The Cantab acquisition contributed to a net loss per share of 6p, which compares with a net loss last time of 7p. As part of a strategic review following its merger with Cantab, Xenova cut a quarter of its workforce. Xenova said the combined company would focus on therapeutic cancer drugs.

10 August 2001_1.Title: Vaccine sales give Chiron a strong boost.
10 August 2001_1.Author: By MATTHEW LEISING.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: Chiron, the biotechnology company, yesterday beat firmly its third-quarter earnings estimates on strong vaccine sales and said next year would see strong growth. Shares of Chiron, which closed up 75 cents at $47 on the Nasdaq exchange, were lifted after hours by the news, climbing another $1.35 to $48.35. Chiron reported pro forma earnings from continuing operations of $58m, or 30 cents a share, versus $43m, or 23 cents a share, in the same period a year ago. Analysts were expecting 25 cents per share. Total revenues increased 37 per cent to $302m, compared with $221m in the third quarter of 2000 and higher than analysts' estimates of $278m. Sean Lance, chief executive, said Chiron would come in on the high side of its year total earnings per share estimate of 90 to 95 cents, raised from 85 cents in July. Sales of TOBI, an inhalable treatment for cystic fibrosis that Chiron acquired in its takeover of PathoGenesis, helped to boost third-quarter results as TOBI, which brought in $34m this past quarter, was not owned by Chiron in the third quarter last year. Sales of Chiron's vaccine products jumped 47 per cent to $115m compared with $78m in the same quarter a year ago. Menjugate, Chiron's vaccine against meningitis, sold strongly in Canada, at $23m against $7m in the third quarter last year. Chiron is eagerly awaiting FDA approval of its Nucleic Acid Testing system for blood donations, which could come by the end of the year and affect 2002 revenues, the company reported. The NAT tests, which screen blood donations for HIV and Hepatitis C, are used throughout the world. Yet lacking FDA approval, the tests sell at generic prices, roughly $4 per test. With FDA approval, Chiron could sell the tests for $8 to $10. It is estimated there are roughly 50m blood donations a year in the US alone.

10 August 2001_1.Title: Shire - Tempus.
10 August 2001_1.Author: Robert Cole.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: SHARES in Shire Pharmaceuticals have been knocked hither and thither since it proposed a merger with Canada's BioChem Pharma last December. At first the price fell as concerns circulated about whether the two made a suitable partnership and whether existing Shire shareholders were diluted too far in order to get the deal done.Most of the falls were recovered in January as Rolf Stahel, Shire's respected chief executive, went on an investor roadshow. He eased fears about whether Shire would be overexposed to research risks. But, as well as early-stage stuff, BioChem has two promising products for Aids and hepatitis, which are already marketed with GlaxoSmithKline assistance.However, the shares came under attack again in February as the short-selling arbitrage community got stuck in. They hoped to make a turn playing the difference between the price of BioChem and Shire shares over the period that the deal was finalised. It also looks suspiciously as if the short-sellers were artificially depressing Shire's share price in the process. Any delay in completing the merger, however, would hurt the arbs and yesterday's news that the Canadian authorities had put a spanner in the works confirmed the speculators' worst fears. In rushing to cover positions, arbs bought Shire, squeezing the price up.It is an episode saying more about the risks of arbitrage and short-selling - a technique often used by hedge funds. The Shire/BioChem deal is still on course and there are plenty of concomitant reasons to hold the FTSE 100 company's shares.

10 August 2001_1.Title: XTL welcomes positive trials for hepatitis drug.
10 August 2001_1.Author: By Rosie Murray-West.
10 August 2001_1.chunks: XTL, the biotechnology company, will announce today that its hepatitis C treatment, XTL-002, has tested positively in clinical trials. The company, which is listed in the UK but based in Israel, produces human monoclonal antibodies. It owns a technology called Trimera, which allows it to change an ordinary mouse into a living test tube with functional human tissues. XTL-002 was originally tested in the Trimera system, and found to reduce levels of the virus. The latest trials indicated a similar effect in more than half the patients tested. Martin Becker, president and chief executive officer of XTL, said: "We are pleased that the clinical results with XTL-002 suggest that it is active against the HCV virus. XTL-002 is the most advanced drug in our broad hepatitis C programme." Hepatitis C is a major public health concern, with the World Health Organisation estimating that 170 million people are chronic carriers. Of these, some 25pc to 35pc may go on to develop serious liver diseases. It is predicted that the number of deaths caused by hepatitis C in the US could start to surpass those from AIDS. XTL shares reached as high as 153p last year. Last week they stood on 46p, having been hit by the slump in biotechnology stocks.

16 October 2002_1.Title: LEX COLUMN - Roche.
16 October 2002_1.Author: No author in byline
16 October 2002_1.chunks: This week, the pharmaceuticals sector has received its own dose of combination therapy. First AstraZeneca took revenge on generic competitors, winning a US patent case on ulcer drug Prilosec. Then Roche reminded the market that potential blockbusters could make it past the US Food and Drug Administration. Its Pegasys drug, to compete with Schering-Plough's PEG-Intron for Hepatitis C, was approved for monotherapy without a hitch. This increases hopes that a more attractive combination with ribavirin will win FDA approval in December.The combination is expected to have sales of about $1bn by 2006, provided it can knock Schering-Plough off its perch. Pegasys also provides a boost to morale. It is Roche's first home-grown drug since Xenical, the obesity drug that fizzled out prematurely several years ago. And it will help counter-balance the importance of Genentech and Chugai to Roche's sales growth - without them, Roche's pharmaceuticals sales would have fallen recently.The victory will be sweeter because Novartis - Roche's cross-town rival and 20 per cent shareholder - yesterday dished out bad news. It put back the launch of its potential blockbuster, Prexige, until 2004. But even if Roche's success now puts it a step beyond Novartis' clutches, it cannot relax. Its controlling bearer shares have shot up to a 66 per cent premium to non-voting shares - close to their long-run average but well above 1999-2001 lows. Some may still savour an end to its independence.Europe Edition 1.

16 October 2002_1.Title: Roche drug is given go-ahead.
16 October 2002_1.Author: GEOFF DYER IN LONDON.
16 October 2002_1.chunks: Roche received a welcome boost on Friday when European regulators approved Pegasys, the Swiss healthcare group's new treatment for hepatitis C.Pegasys is the group's only important new drug launch this year and is critical to Roche's efforts to revive the fortunes of its pharmaceuticals division.The drug has been approved by the European Medicines Evaluation Agency (EMEA) as a therapy on its own and in combination with ribavirin, an existing treatment.Hepatitis C, an infection of the blood that attacks the liver, has affected more than 170m people in the world, the company said, making it more common than the HIV virus. Analysts said winning European approval was a significant milestone for the company, although the more important market opportunity was in the US.The company said it still expected to win approval for Pegasys from the US Food and Drug Administration later this year.Roche had hoped for an earlier approval in the US. However, regulators insisted on changes to the manufacturing process, which has given Schering Plough's Peg-Intron, a similar drug, a year's head start in the US market over Pegasys. "The real crunch issue will be getting approval in the US," said Duncan Moore, an analyst at Morgan Stanley in London. "Given the disappointments so far, there will be a big sigh of relief when it goes through." Analysts estimate the Roche drug could achieve peak sales of $1bn a year.Roche is hoping the launch of Pegasys will help boost pharmaceuticals sales growth next year to the industry average of about 10 per cent. However, the expiry of the patent on its Accutane acne treatment is likely to limit the increase in sales this year to mid-single digit.While Roche's diagnostics business has produced strong results in recent years, the group was forced to restructure its pharmaceuticals unit last year with the loss of 3,000 jobs.Roche is hoping to hear from European regulators soon about Tamiflu for influenza and anti-obesity treatment Xenical.Roche certificates increased SFr0.75 to SFr111.75 on Friday.

16 October 2002_1.Title: Merck and Schering-Plough gain drug approval.
16 October 2002_1.Author: CHRISTOPHER BOWE IN NEW YORK.
16 October 2002_1.chunks: Merck and Schering-Plough, two US pharmaceutical groups, on Thursday said German regulators approved their new co-developed cholesterol drug seen as key to each one's future profit prospects.Germany is the first country to give such approval and foreshadows eventual mutual marketing approval across the European Union plus an expected decision soon by US regulators. Analysts expect a potential US Food and Drug Administration approval this quarter, and possibly later this month.The drug - to be called Ezetrol in Germany, and Zetia in the US - is one of the handful of potential catalysts for a US pharmaceutical industry rebound. The industry has seen a dearth of new drug discoveries that could plug lost sales to generic competition after older drugs lose their patent protection.Moreover, it sets in motion a drug seen as a potential blockbuster in a $19bn market and important to the growth prospects of both Merck and Schering-Plough. Each has seen little luck recently in the laboratory to fully replenish their pipelines.Schering-Plough is counting heavily on the drug to revive earnings per share increases estimated to be 20 per cent in 2004. Earlier this month, it slashed profit estimates for this year and the next due to its Claritin allergy drug reaching the end of its patent lifeManagement credibility could get a boost from the new cholesterol drug as well. Schering-Plough currently faces a Securities and Exchange Commission probe into circumstances surrounding its profit warning a few weeks ago.The two companies' new cholesterol drug is a new class of chemical compound designed to work alone to lower cholesterol or in conjunction with current blockbuster drugs called statins.Statins, including Pfizer's Lipitor and Merck's Zocor, reduce cholesterol often times in heart patients and have become widely prescribed. Pfizer's Lipitor saw sales grow 22 per cent to more than $2bn in the third quarter. Merck reports third quarter earnings Friday.Schering-Plough also faces increased competition on its second-best drug franchise that treats hepatitis. Roche, the Swiss group, has received approval for its Pegasys combination treatment for hepatitis C which analysts expect to agressively compete with Schering-Plough's drugs. Merck shares rose 2 per cent to $50.67 and Schering-Plough's increased 2 per cent to $19.35 in lunchtime trading in New York.

16 October 2002_1.Title: WORLD STOCK MARKETS - Roche shines out on drug approval - EUROPE.
16 October 2002_1.Author: ALEXANDER ISAAC
16 October 2002_1.chunks: Europe's best performer in a rather flat market yesterday was Swiss drug stock Roche which rose 8.3 per cent to SFr195. An advisory panel at the Food and Drug Administration in the US unanimously urged approval for Roche's drug Pegasys which is used to treat the liver disease hepatitis C. Other drug stocks were mixed, with Aventis down 1.3 per cent to Euros 58.40 but Sanofi up 2 per cent to Euros 59.60.French caterer Sodexho jumped 7.6 per cent to Euros 24.94 after reassuring investors with results largely in line with expectations. In September the shares plummeted after the company issued a profits warning and said it had found "serious errors of management" and "accounting anomalies" at its UK operations. Sodexho said it was raising its dividend by 9 per cent to Euros 0.61 compared with last year.Electronics group Thales was also firm as it reported sales at the top end of expectations. Nine-month figures were up 18 per cent to Euros 7.56bn. Growth came largely from the defence side which rose 37 per cent, compared with 1 per cent growth for aeronautics. The shares closed up 3 per cent at Euros 25.08 while aerospace group EADS slipped 1.1 per cent to Euros 10.67.European stocks which have been battling the threat of exposure to asbestos claims took heart from hopes for a settlement at the US group Halliburton. An analyst said he thought a settlement could be reached within a month.Investors continued to push up the price of Richemont, the luxury goods company, as the market expects increased activity ahead of next week's float of the remaining 33 per cent of the company. The shares closed up 5.7 per cent at SFr26.95.Traders think it is likely the float will lead the Swiss Market Index to increase the weighting of the company, and encourage tracker-funds to purchase the stock. The shares had already rallied on Thursday after the company, which owns Cartier and Montblanc, revealed better-than-expected results.Italy's Bulgari dazzled the market with improved sales and a rise in third-quarter next profit of 75 per cent. Shares in the company, Regular world stock markets updates at www.ft.com/markets which have lost almost half their value this year, soared 7.9 per cent to Euros 4.50.UBS Warburg lent further support, raising its price target from Euros 5 to Euros 5.20 and maintaining its buy recommendation.Elsewhere in the luxury goods sector, Gucci closed flat, Hermes was up 0.2 per cent at Euros 149.8, while Swatch Group rose 2.3 per cent to SFr123.Engineering group ABB, which faces potentially crippling asbestos-related claims, gained 6.8 per cent to SFr3.29, Alfa Laval rose 4.2 per cent to SKr61.50, Saint Gobain rose 2.2 per cent to Euros 26.30 and Hanson was up 1.7 per cent to 281p.Media company Vivendi Universal continued its campaign for Cegetel, the mobile operator it is seeking to control fully. It told regulators in France its special purpose vehicle for the bid could include Euros 1.3bn of bank debt. Vivendi, which already has 44 per cent of Cegetel, is competing against Vodafone, which has offered Euros 6.77bn for Vivendi's stake.Vivendi shares, which have been on the ropes all week, fell another 2.1 per cent to Euros 11.55. Vivendi Environnement, the utility it controls, fell 6 per cent to Euros 22.21 on a report that the parent group was having difficulty finding institutional buyers for its Environnement stake.Utilities Eon and RWE came under pressure as investors queried how much the companies have paid for recent acquisitions. Shares in Eon fell 1.7 per cent to Euros 45.65 and RWE dropped 3.1 per cent to Euros 30.35.Earlier this year Eon bought UK electricity company Powergen and its smaller rival RWE acquired Innogy. Results from companies this week have raised the question of value for money.Eon surprised the market on Thursday by writing down Euros 2.4bn for its purchase of Powergen, and warned that it might have to write down other investments, including its stake in HVB. A writedown was expected but most analysts thought it would be in the region of Euros 1.5bn.Earlier in the week RWE increased goodwill on Innogy to Euros 7.8bn, equivalent to more than 90 per cent of the price it originally paid.Schroder Salomon Smith Barney cut its price target on Eon had from Euros 70 to Euros 65. 16 October 2002_1.Title: COMPANIES &FINANCE INTERNATIONAL - Zetia news lifts Schering-Plough and Merck.
16 October 2002_1.Author: CHRISTOPHER BOWE.
16 October 2002_1.chunks: Shares of Merck and Schering-Plough rose yesterday as investors got their first chance to react to US regulatory approval of a new cholesterol drug that is critical to both companies' future profits.On Friday, the two US pharmaceuticals groups said the Food and Drug Administration approved Zetia, a cholesterol-lowering drug co-developed by them. US approval follows earlier go-ahead by German regulators this month, paving the way for European market launch.Schering-Plough's shares increased 8 per cent, or $1.66, to $22.01, while Merck's traded 3 per cent higher, or $1.54, at $54.45 in lunchtime trading in New York.Both shares are significantly off their highs at the beginning of last year, as concerns over a lack of new products to maintain sales growth weighed upon them.The worldwide launch of Zetia brings a new type of cholesterol-fighting drug to a huge market dominated by cholesterol drugs called statins. Some analysts estimate Zetia sales hitting $2bn to $4bn by 2006 out of the current statin market of $19bn.Such sales potential could not come at a better time for either company. Both are expected to report no profit growth this year having seen sales of key drugs evaporate due to patent expiries and launches of cheaper generic versions of their drugs.Schering-Plough also sees earnings next year significantly below this year's. The decline of sales for allergy drug Claritin continue to cloud its profit outlook. "Zetia is indeed promising and has the ability to save Schering-Plough in the long run, but throughout the rest of this year and next Schering faces several major challenges to lead franchises like allergy and hepatitis," said Timothy Anderson, analyst at Prudential Securities.Mr Anderson said Merck also needs Zetia to be a success. The high stakes are likely to prompt the companies' joint venture to spend heavily to promote the drug, potentially with one of the most expensive marketing campaigns in the industry's history, he said.London Edition 1.

16 October 2002_1.Title: Market forces - Weston therapy.
16 October 2002_1.Author: No author in byline
16 October 2002_1.chunks: Market professionals with an eye for oversold situations were taking a close look at Weston Medical yesterday. Weston fell 11p to 51.5p - an all-time low - as an alliance with Swiss drug maker Roche to develop a needle-free delivery system for its new hepatitis C treatment, Pegasys, appeared to have hit legal problems. On Monday, a Californian biotech company named Ribapharm said it filed a patent lawsuit to prevent Roche from marketing Pegasys with another medicine, ribavirin. But sector specialists said Weston was not developing a delivery system for the combination product and there was no reason to suppose the lawsuit would delay US approval for the product, expected later this year. Ribapharm would struggle to defend its patent, they thought, as ribavirin had been around for 40 years; even if it did, Pegasys was not important to Weston's prospects. "The market has got his one wrong. It has made a mountain out of a molehill," said one analyst.

The Guardian (London) - Final Edition

January 28, 2004

Go ahead for hepatitis C drug

BYLINE: James Meikle, Health correspondent

SECTION: Guardian Home Pages, Pg. 6

LENGTH: 296 words

 
 Thousands of patients who developed chronic liver disease after being infected with hepatitis C will be switched to more effective and expensive treatments. The decision was announced as the government steps up its battle against hepatitis C, a potential killer which has shown alarming increases over the last decade. 
 Official endorsement for the drug pegylated interferon, usually taken in combination with another anti-viral drug, could significantly increase the drugs bill for fighting one of Britain's most serious public health threats.
 But the drug's success in treating many patients has meant that the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (Nice), the government's good-practice watchdog in England and Wales, has backed its far greater use.
 Only about 2,000 patients are thought at present to use either pegylated interferon or the more standard interferon alpha, but that number is expected to grow rapidly, using regimes which could be £3,200 more expensive for each patient. Even conservative estimates put the extra cost at around £11m a year.
 People infected with hepatitis C often carry it unknowingly for years. Between 50,000 and 500,000 people may have the virus. If the higher figure is accurate, far fewer than one in 10 people with the disease is diagnosed.
 Around one in five known to have been exposed to the virus will eventually develop acute hepatitis, which can take more than 20 years to become evident.
 Graham Foster, consultant hepatologist with Barts and the Royal London NHS trust, said: "This is the first positive step which will allow patients in the UK to receive the same treatment choice which has been available to patients in other parts of the world for many years."

28 January 2004_1.Title: New treatment for hepatitis C.
28 January 2004_1.Author: No author in byline
28 January 2004_1.chunks: A new drug may help those with hepatitis C. The molecule, called BILN 2061, slams the brakes on virus replication, and has performed well in a preliminary trial. Some 170 million people worldwide are infected with the hepatitis C virus, which can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer. The new treatment could help those who carry strains that are resistant to current drugs - around half of all sufferers. In the trial, eight patients took doses of the new drug for two days. After 24 hours, their viral levels had plummeted up to 1,000-fold, Nature reports. "The drug appears to be safe and well tolerated," says Paul Anderson, senior vice president of Boehringer-Ingelheim in Quebec, Canada, the company that developed the new treatment. Longer, larger trials are needed to see whether problems develop over time, says Ralf Bartenschlager, who studies virus replication at the University of Heidelberg, Germany. Even so, "the short-term data are extraordinary", he says.

28 January 2004_1.Title: NHS hepatitis victims to get up to Pounds 45,000
28 January 2004_1.Author: Sam Lister
28 January 2004_1.chunks: PATIENTS infected with hepatitis C after being given blood by the NHS will receive payments of up to Pounds 45,000 each, the Government said yesterday. The scheme, outlined by John Reid, the Health Secretary, will also include patients cleared of the virus through treatment and others who caught the virus from someone infected by NHS blood or blood products. But the Department of Health, which plans to start the scheme in April, was accused last night of a gross oversight for excluding widows of haemophiliacs who had died from the disease as a result. Lord Morris of Manchester, the Labour peer and president of the Haemophilia Society, said that the omission was symptomatic of a scheme that fell far short of the benefits offered by other governments around the world. Dr Reid announced his intention to award ex-gratia payments to British hepatitis C victims last August. Announcing details of the scheme yesterday, he reiterated his belief that patients should receive payments on compassionate grounds. "I believe that these are fair and reasonable payments and I hope that they will help to alleviate some of the problems," Dr Reid said. Under the deal, every person in Britain who was alive on August 29, 2003, and whose hepatitis C was caused by NHS treatment with blood products before September 1991 will be eligible for an initial lump sum of Pounds 20,000. Patients with more advanced stages of the illness will get a further Pounds 25,000. The total payout is expected to be Pounds 100 million. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2004

28 January 2004_1.Title: Hepatitis C, The silent killer;Health
28 January 2004_1.Author: No author in byline
28 January 2004_1.chunks: NINE out of ten people with the hepatitis C virus in the United Kingdom are unaware that they have this tiny ticking time bomb coursing through their veins and infecting their livers. Hepatitis C is a virus that takes time to make its presence felt: its initial symptoms are so trivial as to go unnoticed, and the patient may not realise that the incident which caused the trouble could give rise to a potentially fatal liver condition 20 or 30 years later. The first symptoms are often tiredness, listlessness and lethargy, a more literary way of describing the diagnostic term TATTY: doctors' shorthand for patients who complain that they are tired all the time. There is an increasing demand for patients who could have been at risk of catching hepatitis C to be tested if they have these symptoms. It is shaming that whereas in France doctors have diagnosed the disease in half the estimated number of patients -and they have a government plan to identify the rest within the next two years -in the UK 90 per cent remain undetected. Only by uncovering the presence of hepatitis C while it is still asymptomatic will many thousands of patients avoid a premature death following a lengthy and expensive illness. Any occupation or habits that might bring people into contact with someone else's blood or body fluids increases the chance of catching hepatitis C. Although blood is the most important vector, and in the past cases were spread by blood transfusion and blood products, these sources are now eliminated (although not all those who were infected before blood screening will yet have been uncovered). Fifty per cent of regular intravenous drug-users become infected, and others may become positive through contact with other body fluids. One new development is that the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (Nice) approves of the use of pegylated interferons and decrees that these should be made available as they are clinically effective and highly cost-effective. And today the results of an international trial were announced: when patients with hepatitis C who also have HIV took a treatment that combined Pegasys peginterferon alfa 2a 40kDa with Copegus ribavirin, it was found that the chances of ridding the body of hepatitis C were trebled, or even quadrupled, when the most resistant forms of hepatitis C were involved. One in three of the HIV-positive people in the UK also suffers from hepatitis C. Complications of the liver are their most common cause of death. 28 January 2004_1.Title: The Sex Doctor - THE SILENT KILLER.
28 January 2004_1.Author: DR Catherine Hood.
28 January 2004_1.chunks: ISSUE OF THE WEEK: HEPATITIS C HEPATITIS C BAYWATCH beauty Pamela Anderson says she got Hepatitis C from sharing a tattoo needle with ex-husband Tommy Lee. But it isn't just a disease of the rich and famous - the silent viral killer is predicted to claim more victims in the West than AIDS. WHAT IS IT? HEPATITIS C is a lethal virus carried in the blood which affects the liver. It's estimated that 200,000 people in the UK might be infected. WHAT DOES IT DO? THE virus causes inflammation of the liver. Twenty per cent of sufferers will recover quickly but one in five will develop liver cirrhosis or even cancer. WHAT ARE THE SYMPTOMS? THE infection can be silent or cause mild tiredness, loss of appetite, flu-like symptoms, nausea and anxiety. HOW IS IT SPREAD? THE virus is mainly spread by blood-to-blood contact. It is believed that the majority of drug abusers who inject drugs and share needles are infected. Hep C can also be passed by sharing toothbrushes, razors or, as in Pamela Anderson's case, tattoo needles. Transmission through sex is possible but not common. CAN I GET TESTED? ANTIBODIES to the Hepatitis C virus can be detected by a blood test that is freely available on the NHS. CAN IT BE TREATED? A COCKTAIL of antiviral drugs can help prevent liver damage in around 60 per cent of cases. HOW CAN I PROTECT MYSELF? STICK to your own toothbrush and razor, and always practise safe sex. - FOR information visit www.britishlivertrust.org.uk.

28 January 2004_1.Title: Drug injectors still sharing equipment
28 January 2004_1.Author: James Meikle Health correspondent
28 January 2004_1.chunks: A third of those who inject drugs are still sharing equipment, posing a health hazard to themselves and others, the government's Health Protection Agency said in a report yesterday. Two in five injectors have been exposed to hepatitis C and are at risk of becoming chronically ill and developing cirrhosis and liver cancer. Many of them do not know they have been infected, even though testing and effective treatments are available, the report, Shooting Up, says. Most of the 50,000 laboratory-confirmed cases of hepatitis C last year are thought to have been drug users. Hepatitis B, a condition for which there is a vaccine, con tinues to be transmitted: more than one in five injectors display antibodies produced in response to the infection. There is an increasing number of patients with hepatitis A. The danger of HIV infection continues: more than 100 cases were diagnosed as being acquired though drug use last year, although in most instances this seems to have happened abroad. There have also been worrying outbreaks of wound botulism and tetanus. The agency suggests that there are not enough needle and syringe exchanges. It wants health services to take advantage of a recent change in the law, which allows other equipment - such as sterile water, swabs, spoons, bowls, cups and dishes - to be provided.

28 January 2004_1.Title: Virus sufferer is forced to wait three years for treatment.
28 January 2004_1.Author: Jeremy Laurance Health Editor.
28 January 2004_1.chunks: HEPATITIS C One of the 200,000 people caught in a silent epidemic  IN THE three years since Brenda Binge was diagnosed with hepatitis C, she has seen a doctor once, a nurse twice and had an ultrasound test but she is still waiting for treatment. The 57-year-old former hotelier has been married for 30 years, never dabbled in drugs, and suspects she became infected through a blood transfusion in the early 1980s. She is angry at the lack of urgency shown by the NHS to people in her predicament. "It is very distressing because I feel I have a death sentence hanging over me," she says. "Although there are drugs that can treat hepatitis C I am denied them. You can have cirrhosis, liver cancer and liver failure and no one is doing anything." After being diagnosed in 2000, Mrs Binge moved from Bath to Sussex where she was referred to a liver specialist only after "constant pestering". Her appointment has been cancelled twice and she has not yet seen him. A week before Christmas she received a letter telling her that the kind of hepatitis C she had - genotype 1B - was one of the hardest to treat. "To say I am upset is to put it mildly," she says. "I was going to call my MP. The Government is burying its head in the sand. A lot of people don't know they have got it and because no one makes a fuss no one is doing anything. It's a shocking neglect of the nation's health.This is a very nasty illness." Mrs Binge, who serves as a councillor on Mid-Sussex District Council and once stood as a Tory parliamentary candidate, has been told that after treatment starts with a cocktail of drugs she will need an injection once a week and pills each day for a year. The cost of the drugs is about 7,000. "What are they waiting for?" she asks. "Perhaps if I die they can save money and won't have to treat me." Although her marital status was known to the NHS, she had never been given any advice about how to prevent her husband, Rod, 59, a financial adviser, becoming infected. "We never had any advice about protective sex even though the virus can be passed on that way," she adds. "I am anxious now to do anything I can to get this issue more widely known." More information on hepatitis C can be found at  www.hepcuk.info.

28 January 2004_1.chunks: The cholesterol drugs market is set to heat up in the summer when Merck and Schering-Plough launch a new product, but the groups' first-quarter earnings reflected US drugmakers' efforts to restructure to bridge long gaps for new drugs.Merck, the world's third largest drugmaker, yesterday reported a 7 per cent rise in profits to Dollars 1.6bn, or 73 cents per share, from Dollars 1.54bn, or 68 cents, in the period a year ago. Merck is restructuring its wholesaler distribution system to cut costs and reducing inventories to three-week supplies.Schering-Plough is streamlining operations under one global operating company, but also faces expense burdens for regulatory problems and preparation for a critical new product.Merck and Schering-Plough are anxiously awaiting Vytorin, a combination of Merck's Zocor cholesterol drug and Zetia, co-developed by the two groups. Approval for the drug could come as soon as July or August.A recent study has shown that Vytorin is as good as, if not better than, Pfizer's Lipitor, a cholesterol treatment that is the world's biggest drug with Dollars 10bn sales. Drugs to lower cholesterol are a big and growing market, with up to Dollars 30bn sales.The companies said they expected their joint venture for Vytorin and Zetia to generate income this year. Zetia sales were Dollars 190m in the first quarter.While they wait, Merck and Schering-Plough said they would continue to look to license drugs from smaller companies to fill the void. Merck's first-quarter earnings were hurt by a Dollars 70m fee paid to Lundbeck of Denmark and Dollars 125m in research expenses for a small biotech acquisition. That was offset by gains on investments.Merck said it expects 78-82 cents per share in the second quarter, which is higher than Wall Street's forecast of 77 cents.But it reiterated expectations of Dollars 3.11 to Dollars 3.17 per share this year.

28 January 2004_1.Title: LETTER - A healthy life is the best medicine.
28 January 2004_1.Author: Dr Richard Halvorsen.
28 January 2004_1.chunks: Sir: Your report (8 December) that a senior GlaxoSmithKline executive has admitted that 90 per cent of the company's drugs only work in 30-50 per cent of people is alarming and has profound implications for future health care. We in the medical profession understand that pharmaceutical companies are commercial organisations with an obligation to maximise their profits. We understand that the company must market its drugs aggressively; after all there's tough competition out there. We are constantly being bombarded by promotional material extolling the benefits of their products. It may be reasonable to accept poor efficacy if there are no serious side-effects to a drug. But when I am told that less than half my patients with hepatitis C or incontinence will be helped by their drug treatment and that three quarters of my patients taking anti-cancer drugs, all of which have unpleasant and sometimes life-threatening side-effects, have no chance of benefit because the drugs are ineffective, I become concerned. It makes me ask whether there may be other ways that we can treat diseases that are safer, cheaper and, dare I say it, more effective. Drug companies are furiously promoting statins, a new class of drug widely and increasingly used to lower cholesterol and prevent heart disease. But nobody points out that eating one portion of fish a week reduces the risk of dying suddenly from heart disease by over 50 per cent - with no side-effects. Dr RICHARD HALVORSEN  London WC1.

August 23, 2006_1.Title: Hepatitis C patients offered new drugs
August 23, 2006_1.Author: Celia Hall
August 23, 2006_1.chunks: PATIENTS with hepatitis C will be able to get an effective drug on the NHS before too much liver damage is caused by the potentially fatal disease. The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (Nice) has approved the use of the drug, Pegasys, making 15,000 more patients eligible for the pounds 800-a-week combined treatment. Hepatitis C, a virus that attacks the liver is a known as a silent killer. People can be infected for 20 or 30 years before they begin to feel ill by which time considerable damage has occurred and 20 or 30 per cent will develop serious disease or liver cancer. The Government estimates that between 200,000 and 500,000 people have hepatitis C, which is passed on through contact with infected blood. However, only 47,000 have been diagnosed and around 7,000 treated. Until the new ruling, the combination therapy was only available for people with advanced disease confirmed by liver biopsy. Nice recommended that people with mild chronic hepatitis should be offered combination therapy with peginterferon alfa (Pegasys) and ribavirin, an anti-viral drug. The recommended treatment has a cure rate of between 60 and 80 per cent, depending on the strain of the virus. Treatment lasts for 24 to 48 weeks, depending on the virus. Large numbers of people were infected through medical blood products and transfusions before 1989 and drug addicts who share equipment are at high risk. Close family members of infected people are also at risk when the disease has not been diagnosed. Prof Graham Foster, professor of hepatology at Queen Mary, University of London and a consultant hepatologist at Barts and the London NHS Trust, said: "This new guidance means that more patients, regardless of where they live in the UK, can have an increased chance of avoiding serious liver damage.''

It is not known whether they have hepatitis.John Forsythe, a transplant surgeon at the unit, said all prospective recipients had to have a 50% chance of surviving five years after the operation and that the HIV patient met the criterion. "Sadly, there are fewer organ donors than we need and donation rates across the UK are below those of other countries. "However, concerns have been raised about the long-term benefits because of complications that can arise when HIV patients are also infected with hepatitisC.Last night Margaret Watt, chairman of Scotland Patients Association, expressed reservations about the decision. August 23, 2006_1.Title: The ticking time bomb of liver disease;Health
August 23, 2006_1.Author: Dr Thomas Stuttaford
August 23, 2006_1.chunks: A new form of treatment for hepatitis C promises a cure within 24 weeks, says Dr Thomas StuttafordLast week, amid the former imperial glories of Vienna, and its still glorious shops and cafes selling sacher torte and other cakes oozing cream, hepatologists from all over the world gathered for the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Liver Diseases. Between mouthfuls of cream they discussed the prognosis of patients suffering from hepatitis C infection and the incidence of alcoholic hepatitis and cirrhosis in young South Asians who drink only in moderation.The incidence of cirrhosis is increasing and greater knowledge of its pathology has shown that, contrary to popular opinion, most cirrhosis is not the result of excessive alcohol. Research has also emphasised the difficulty of knowing which drinkers will suffer alcoholic cirrhosis and the variability of the amount of alcohol needed to cause it. Forty years ago hepatitis A, B, C (in all there are six genotypes of hepatitis C), D, E and G were all lumped together under the diagnosis of viral hepatitis or viral jaundice. Once hepatitis A and B had been recognised the rest were known as hepatitis non A and non B. Hepatitis C was identified only in 1989.Hepatitis A, the most common hepatitis caused by virus, can be totally disabling in its acute phase, but it is clinically less important as sufferers recover and it never leads to cirrhosis. Immunisation against it is possible and indicated for all those who travel overseas.Hepatitis B is a problem that was previously confined to those in the developing world, or to people whose work exposed them to contaminated blood or body fluids.Easy travel and mass migration has now made this a global problem and the immunisation programme needs to take account of these changes.Delegates at the conference heard that an increasing number of patients are showing a long-term sustained response to treatment -the earlier it is started the better -with a comparatively new drug, Pegasys. Fortunately, therefore, treatment of hepatitis B is improving just as its pathology in the UK is altering for the worse.The great worry is now the ubiquitous but frequently hidden hepatitis C. Between 270 million and 300 million people worldwide, 3 per cent of the world's population, are infec-ted with one of the six genotypes of hepatitis C. The numbers in the UK are unknown as nine out of ten people carrying the virus are unaware that they have it. It is estimated that there are at least 450,000 people with it.Most are unaware that they have hepatitis C because its onset is insidious, hence the comparison with a ticking time bomb. Twenty to 50 years after some long-forgotten exposure to someone else's blood or body fluid, 20 to 30 per cent of infected cases will suddenly find out the cause of their symptoms. Initially these may be no more troublesome than tiredness, increasing lethargy and general listlessness. Only when these feelings of general malaise are investigated by a blood test will the true diagnosis be made and treatment started.The severity of the hepatitis C infection and its ease of treatment is likely to be related to the genotype. Genotype 1 is the most common in Britain and is also the most difficult to treat. Type 2 and 3, sometimes referred to as non-type 1 hepatitis C, respond more rapidly and more completely to modern treatment.Genotype 4, like genotype 1, is difficult to treat.The good news announced in Vienna is that research has shown that the long term treatment of genotype 2 and 3 with Pegasys (peginterferon alfa-2a) and Ribavirin will now give optimum results with only 24 weeks' treatment. This combination will, in two thirds of cases, clear the virus from the blood of a patient with hepatitis C. In patients who haven't genotype 1 or 4, results of combination therapy are even better. In some trials more than 80 per cent of cases have now been cured. Eight years ago the overall percentage of cures when considering all the genotypes combined was only 6 per cent.The next stage in beating hepatitis C is to produce an approved programme that will detect the disease at an earlier stage. We can learn from other countries where early diagnosis of hepatitis C is much better. This is one disease where early treatment would be a saving.More prompt diagnosis would not only spare the minority who are going to develop cirrhosis and eventually die from liver failure after years of ill health; it would also save the NHS the bills that are associated with any chronic disease, and the social services the cost for caring for patients when they are no longer capable of work.www.timesonline.co.uk/health (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2006

"Novartis is committed to achieving a leadership position in infectious diseases, particularly by building a strong portfolio...to help patients with hepatitis," said Thomas Ebeling, chief executive officer of Novartis Pharma.Hepatitis C is a liver disease caused by infection with the hepatitis C virus (HCV), which lives in the liver cells and causes the liver to become inflamed. August 23, 2006_1.Title: Why is my liver in trouble when I am a moderate drinker?;Letter;Health
August 23, 2006_1.Author: Dr Thomas Stuttaford
August 23, 2006_1.chunks: Answers your health questionsA reader, who spends much of his time overseas as an aid worker in Africa, India and Pakistan, has written to say that a recent blood test revealed abnormal liver function. He assures us that he is only a moderate drinker and hasn't had any blood transfusions at any time of his life. He did, however, have major orthopaedic surgery in Africa 15 years ago.When he goes to a malarial zone he takes Malarone. He has never used illegal drugs.Patients who are found to have raised liver enzymes during a routine examination present their doctors with a difficult problem. The easy, idle, thoughtless way of dealing with an unexplained small increase in one or more of the liver enzymes in a patient is to suggest that he or she is being dishonest about their alcohol intake and accept that this is the explanation. Recent research has shown that modest drinkers are, like problem drinkers, likely to under-report their intake.Our reader is obviously well informed. He has already considered many of the points in his medical history that could be relevant. We have to accept that he is accurate about his alcohol intake.He has obviously understood the importance of blood-borne hepatitis B and C and has told us that he has never had a transfusion or used injectable drugs. There are many other ways that hepatitis C might be transmitted other than by contact with contaminated blood or through transfusions or by drug abuse.It is noteworthy that he had major surgery before this danger was recognised. He hasn't mentioned tattooing or body piercing that are occasional causes of transmission of hepatitis C, nor acupuncture, although reputable acupuncturists are as conscientious about sterility as doctors.Medical staff, care workers, boxers, rugby footballers, other contact sports athletes and even kindly people who bind up the minor injuries of children are all at some slight risk of being contaminated with infected blood. In an appreciable proportion of cases of hepatitis C the source of the infection is never traced.Very rarely, Malarone, an excellent anti-malarial, may cause an increase in liver enzymes. This is one possible cause, even perhaps the probable cause of the minor liver function changes. Another consideration in his case is that several tropical diseases may cause liver damage. Should he be worried? Not worried, but certainly he needs careful monitoring, and should have immediate blood tests to see if he has ever had hepatitis B or C.If the liver function tests don't return to normal he should ask his GP if it would be wise to consult a hepatologist, who may seek a second opinion from a specialist in tropical diseases.Anyone and everyone who has abnormal liver function of unknown origin wherever they live, and whatever their lifestyle, needs to have their blood tested to make certain that they haven't picked up hepatitis C.There are somewhere between 400,000 and 900,000 people in Britain with hepatitis C who are unaware that they carry this potentially lethal virus, but are initially free of symptoms.There are also 200,000 who have the diagnosis. It is important to detect hepatitis C at an early stage before there is appreciable liver damage and at a time when it is more easily treated.Overall, when taking into account the varying response to treatment of the many different types of hepatitis C, combined anti-viral therapy will now clear the body of any detectable hepatitis C virus in 40 per cent of cases. The Times (London)

September 21, 2006, Thursday

Drug-taking kits for inmates to reduce spread of infections

BYLINE: Angus Macleod Scottish Political Editor and Ben Hoyle

SECTION: HOME NEWS; Scotland; Pg. 4

LENGTH: 665 words

PRISONERS will be given personal drug-taking kits under a controversial new scheme to tackle the spread of HIV and hepatitis C in British jails.
Inmates at Craiginches Prison in Aberdeen, where drug-taking among prisoners was particularly high, will be the first to receive the kits. They include syringes, swabs, filters and a sharps disposal box.
The Scottish Prison Service (SPS) has confirmed that the pilot programme was planned for early next year, following a Glasgow Caledonian University report. It concluded that prisoners regarded the drug problem in Scotland's jails as unstoppable. 
Their views echoed a Home Office report last month, which confirmed that drug use was commonplace within prisons in England and Wales.
That study stated that some supposedly drug-free wings were awash with illegal drugs and depicted a world where heroin, cannabis, crack and non-prescribed medications all circulated freely.
Interviewees said that obtaining drugs was relatively straightforward. Drugs entered prisons by social visits, in the mail, through new prisoners, via contact with friends on the outside after court appearances, or even in bundles thrown over the perimeter wall. They were then exchanged in prison churches, gyms, workshops, education classes, during visits and in queues.
With the continued proliferation of illicit drug-taking in prisons has come a serious infection problem, which the Craiginches pilot scheme aims to address.
The SPS said yesterday that if the behaviour of prisoners taking drugs could not be changed, the service had a responsibility both to inmates and to prison staff to ensure their safety. A decision to introduce the kits will be taken by the prison service and will not have to be approved by Scottish Executive ministers.
The SPS added that the kits would reflect needle exchange programmes that existed in the community and would be modelled on similar schemes in the Republic of Ireland, Switzerland, Germany and Spain.
The Court of Appeal in London has already dismissed a case brought by an English prisoner under human rights laws to have needle exchange programmes introduced in jails south of the border.
The SPS spokesman added: "We've looked at international research which shows the introduction of the safe injection programmes reduces drug injecting." Last year alone, nearly 2,000 drugs packages were intercepted on their way to Scottish prisoners. Officials claim that human rights laws allowing contact between prisoners and their families mean that the authorities could never halt the flow of drugs into jails.
Annabel Goldie, the leader of the Scottish Tories and a campaigner for more treatment centres for drug addicts, said that she could understand why the move was necessary, given the alarming levels of drug abuse in Scottish jails. "But we need a radical overhaul of rehabilitation structures in our jails. We should be helping prisoners get off drugs rather than helping them take them," she said.
Investigations at prisons have illustrated the scale of the problem. Last month 14 officers at Pentonville prison, North London, were suspended in a corruption investigation involving the alleged smuggling of drugs into the jail.
The Home Office has given no indication that it will adopt the scheme for England and Wales if the pilot in Scotland proved successful.
A HABIT IN JAIL
* Prison needle exchange programmes in Ireland, Switzerland, Germany and Spain have reduced dramatically HIV and hepatitis transmission rates
* A recent study in Canada claimed that giving drug kits to prisoners did not lead to an increase in drug taking or cause needles to be used as weapons
* A recent Home Office study suggested heroin, cannabis and crack were freely available in English and Welsh jails
* A survey of 6,200 in Scottish jails showed that a third had used drugs in the previous month with 128 injecting. Seventy-eight of those had shared needles
Last year nearly 2,000 drugs packages were intercepted on their way to Scottish prisoners

The files provide vital evidence about what has been described as one of the worst medical disasters in the history of the NHS. Earlier this year, the Department of Health said that around 600 sensitive files had been 'inadvertently destroyed' by an inexperienced civil servant. However, in a striking new development it has emerged that several solicitors have copies of the documents, which detail meetings between the blood transfusion service, health boards, government officials and consultants. Some of the files were returned to the department of health last Tuesday. During the late Seventies and early Eighties, thousands of people, including nearly every haemophiliac in the country, were infected with deadly viruses such as Hepatitis C and HIV through infected blood. At least 800 have already died from Aids-related illnesses and hundreds more from chronic liver disease caused by hepatitis. Investigations into tainted blood scandals in other countries have revealed evidence of wrongdoing on the part of government and pharmaceutical companies. Campaigners in the UK have accused authorities of an extensive cover-up. It is understood that other solicitors have been contacted and urged to return any files they have about the case. Senior legal figures who have seen the documents told The Observer they contain evidence of 'significant knowledge of risk and fault'. In particular, they claim that officials knew of the risks of contracting deadly diseases such as HIV and hepatitis from contaminated blood products years before they alerted patients. The latest development comes as a complaint was lodged with the parliamentary ombudsman seeking an investigation into the destruction of the original documents, which should have been stored for at least 25 years. Campaigners said they were delighted that copies of the paperwork still existed. 'We have waited more than 20 years to find out what happened,' said Carol Grayson, whose husband died after receiving contaminated blood imported to the UK from high-risk prisoners in America. 'We cannot turn the clock back but at last we have some hope in our search to find out the truth.' However, she expressed concerns that they had been returned to the department which had appears to have accidentally destroyed the original files. 'We would have preferred these copies to have been held by some independent or neutral body,' she said. Her solicitor has written to the DoH asking them to provide an undertaking to preserve the documents. A spokeswoman for the DoH confirmed that documents relating to the contaminated blood case had been received last week. 'The department will consider these papers in light of the Freedom of Information Act,' she added. < THE NUMBER of young people in Scotland languishing on 'hidden' waiting lists for NHS treatment has increased dramatically, according to new figures, which also show a significant cut in hospital beds available to treat sick children. August 23, 2006_2.Title: Tainted blood victims 'were not informed'

August 23, 2006_2.chunks: CONCERNS about Britain's contaminated blood scandal escalated yesterday after it emerged that thousands of people who were infected with hepatitis C have still not been informed. The Observer has obtained evidence from solicitors representing scores of victims which appears to confirm claims that efforts to trace those infected with the deadly virus from transfusions and blood products were 'restrictive, passive and inadequate'. It has also emerged that no efforts were made to contact relatives of those who died as a result of the disaster despite the fact they could have unknowingly passed it on. The virus can lie dormant for over 20 years, but then lead to severe liver damage and cancer. Solicitors acting for some of the 30,000 people in the UK believed to have been infected with hepatitis C by contaminated blood and products during the 1980s said only about 15 per cent had been contacted as part of the official 'lookback' programme. 'Nearly every week I receive clients who inform me that they have just found out, usually because of incidental treatment, that they have hepatitis C,' said Frank Maguire, a legal adviser for the Haemophilia Forum. Routine donor screening began in 1991 and a two-year 'look back' exercise began four years later to trace those infected. But it focused on those who returned to the blood transfusion service. Charles Gore, chief executive of the Hepatitis C Trust, said: 'It is absolutely appalling that health and government officials are deliberately not doing anything about this and are deliberately letting people die. It is a major public health issue.' In another development, The Observer has seen documents which reveal panic and chaos in the transfusion service as the scale of contamination emerged. In a letter of May 1991, the director of the transfusion service in Newcastle said that since the ability to test for hepatitis C was available it would be 'indefensible' not to introduce it immediately. In a response, another regional director stated that such 'unilateral action is both disgraceful and mischievous'. A Department of Health spokeswoman said there was great sympathy for people who were infected with hep C and HIV from contaminated blood during the 1970s and 1980s. Those patients who were considered to be most at risk were counselled, offered testing and referred for further assessment . She added: 'It is our belief that everything was done to identify and trace patients who had received blood before September 1991.' In Scotland, Health Minister Andy Kerr is still considering calls from the influential health committee to hold an independent inquiry into the scandal. Join the debate at www.observer.co.uk/blog

August 23, 2006_2.Title: Blood scandal families' fury at inquiry refusal
August 23, 2006_2.Author: No author in byline
August 23, 2006_2.chunks: SURVIVORS of Scotland's contaminated blood scandal have written to the Health Minister seeking an urgent meeting after he dismissed recommendations from parliament for a public inquiry. Thousands of people across the UK had pinned their hopes on Andy Kerr to trigger an investigation into what they believe is one of the worst disasters in the history of the NHS. But Kerr said it would not add significantly to an understanding of how blood supplies came to be contaminated with deadly viruses. Critics, however, said it was a 'cowardly decision' and accused him of showing contempt for the health committee, which strongly recommended an inquiry into the tragedy. During the late Seventies and early Eighties, thousands of people, including nearly every haemophiliac in the country, were infected with deadly viruses such as Hepatitis C and HIV through infected blood. At least 800 have already died from Aids-related illnesses and hundreds more from chronic liver disease caused by hepatitis. Investigations into tainted blood scandals in other countries have revealed evidence of wrongdoing on the part of government, health officials and pharmaceutical companies. Campaigners in the UK suspect a massive government cover-up. Hundreds of critical documents were said to have been 'inadvertently destroyed' by an 'inexperienced civil servant'. However, copies later turned up. Senior legal figures have told The Observer there is evidence of 'significant knowledge of risk and fault' and, in particular, claims that officials knew of the risks of contracting deadly diseases from contaminated blood years before they alerted patients. There are thousands of people who are believed to have been infected with Hepatitis C, which can lie dormant for as long as 20 years, but who have still not been informed. Philip Dolan, chairman of the Scottish Haemophilia Society, said he had asked for an urgent meeting with the Health Minister and would urge him to reverse his 'cowardly decision'. He said: 'We are so angry that he has failed this vulnerable group of people. Once again he offers his sympathy. We don't want that. We want answers and we want to make sure that something like this will never happen again. The safety of our blood is a matter of critical importance. Yet politicians continue to stick their heads in the sand, pretend that it was all in the past and pretend that everything's OK.' Roseanna Cunningham, convenor of the health committee, said survivors and relatives of the bereaved from across the UK had been looking to the Scottish Executive to hold an inquiry. She said: 'I am extremely disappointed that Andy Kerr did not accept our recommendations, but the issue is not going to go away. The executive is not doing itself any good whatsoever. There is a huge issue of public safety.' Kerr said that he did not believe a public inquiry would uncover any new evidence or information that is relevant to the causes of the infection of NHS patients through blood and blood products, or lead to significant lessons for the future. 'It would be a diversion of effort from delivering and improving health services today,' he said. 'I cannot see that there is any possible justification for the efforts and costs that would be involved, or that this would bring any benefit to the patients involved.'

August 23, 2006_2.chunks: Dear Dr Cath AN ex-boyfriend of mine has Hepatitis C. We split up a while ago, but should I be worried? HEPATITIS C is a virus carried in the blood which affects the liver. A staggering 200,000 people in the UK might be infected - but symptoms often don't show, so people don't get tested. Hep C causes inflammation of the liver. Twenty per cent will recover quickly, but some will have longer-term liver problems, including cirrhosis and cancer. The virus is mainly spread by blood-to-blood contact. It is possible to get it through sex, but this is uncommon. You'd be more at risk if you were an injecting drug user or had received a blood transfusion before 1991, when blood started to be screened for Hep C. It can also be passed by sharing toothbrushes or razors, which may sometimes explain why the virus spreads to sexual partners. Foreign workers at risk in Libya

LENGTH: 319 words

Sir, We are deeply concerned over the fate of six medical workers who have been in a Libyan prison since 1998 on charges of deliberately infecting more than 400 children with HIV, more than 40 of whom have died of Aids.
The charge is against five Bulgarian nurses and a Palestinian doctor who worked in the al-Fateh Hospital in Benghazi. President Gaddafi alleged in 2001 that the HIV infection of the Libyan children was a plot by the CIA and Mossad. In May 2004 the six workers were sentenced to death, but a supreme court questioned the conviction after international protests. 
The Libyan authorities invited Professor Luc Montagnier, the co-discoverer of HIV at the Pasteur Institute, in Paris, and Professor Vittorio Colizzi, an Aids and infectious diseases authority at Rome University, to report on the outbreak of HIV infection. They concluded that many of the children contracted HIV before the accused staff arrived and that many of the children were also infected with hepatitis B and C, which pointed to poor medical practice and hygiene at the hospital. The report stated that all the evidence indicated that the six accused were innocent of the alleged crime.
However, the court dismissed this report in favour of an investigation by Libyan doctors whose impartiality and scientific credentials must be in doubt. A retrial was ordered and the verdict is expected next month. The fear is that all six will be condemned to death.
We ask the medical and scientific authorities of the United Nations, Arab countries, United States and European Union (Bulgaria will join the EU in three months) to exert their utmost influence on President Gaddafi to prevent what might amount to judicial murder.
PROFESSOR LORD REES, President, Royal Society
PROFESSOR SIR KEITH PETERS, President, Academy of Medical Sciences

August 23, 2006_2.Title: 400,000 Britons don't know they have a deadly disease
August 23, 2006_2.Author: Victoria Fletcher Health Editor
August 23, 2006_2.chunks: BRITAIN faces a health timebomb with at least 400,000 people unaware they are carrying a deadly disease that is costing the NHS 150million a year.Lives are being put at risk because sufferers of Hepatitis C face a postcode lottery of care, MPs claim in a new report.Around 400,000 people are thought to be undiagnosed and carrying the disease in the UK, but estimates go as high as 900,000.And as Health Secretary Patricia Hewitt faces increasing criticism as jobs are cut in a struggling health service, the MPs are demanding urgent action to prevent a future burden on hospitals.Hepatitis C, which is mostly transmitted through infected blood transfusions, attacks the liver and can lead to cirrhosis or cancer.The MPs said: "A failure to act now will inevitably create for the future huge numbers requiring enormously costly treatments for advanced liver disease." A second report out today, for the Hepatitis C Trust, added that immediate action is needed to prevent an "unacceptable burden" all round.It said the UK has not responded as well as its European neighbours and that management of the virus in the UK was "both unstructured and under-funded".And it said there is evidence that ineffective treatment and diagnosis cost the NHS around 150million a year.The Trust urged the Government to take action on the disease by raising awareness, improving testing and establishing a "diagnosis to treatment highway" for rapid referral and treatment.Chief executive Charles Gore said: "We have an opportunity to reverse this spiralling epidemic and avoid not just the unnecessary deaths of thousands but also a financial crisis for the NHS. If we do not seize this opportunity, we will look back and know that by our inaction we let it happen." The Department of Health insisted it is tackling the disease with its Hepatitis C Action Plan for England.A spokeswoman said: "We have set a clear national framework for action to improve the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of Hepatitis C."In addition, alongside unprecedented increases in NHS funding, we have provided central support for key aspects of implementation of the Hepatitis C Action Plan for England, such as raising awareness and improving surveillance." Hepatitis is caused by one of five viruses A, B, C, D and E. It can cause sudden illness or more long-term problems. Hepatitis A and E are caused by poor hygiene, B is transmitted through blood, and D is usually attached to the B virus.

The Times (London)

September 21, 2006, Thursday

Drug-taking kits for inmates to reduce spread of infections

BYLINE: Angus Macleod Scottish Political Editor and Ben Hoyle

SECTION: HOME NEWS; Scotland; Pg. 4

LENGTH: 665 words

PRISONERS will be given personal drug-taking kits under a controversial new scheme to tackle the spread of HIV and hepatitis C in British jails.
Inmates at Craiginches Prison in Aberdeen, where drug-taking among prisoners was particularly high, will be the first to receive the kits. They include syringes, swabs, filters and a sharps disposal box.
The Scottish Prison Service (SPS) has confirmed that the pilot programme was planned for early next year, following a Glasgow Caledonian University report. It concluded that prisoners regarded the drug problem in Scotland's jails as unstoppable. 
Their views echoed a Home Office report last month, which confirmed that drug use was commonplace within prisons in England and Wales.
That study stated that some supposedly drug-free wings were awash with illegal drugs and depicted a world where heroin, cannabis, crack and non-prescribed medications all circulated freely.
Interviewees said that obtaining drugs was relatively straightforward. Drugs entered prisons by social visits, in the mail, through new prisoners, via contact with friends on the outside after court appearances, or even in bundles thrown over the perimeter wall. They were then exchanged in prison churches, gyms, workshops, education classes, during visits and in queues.
With the continued proliferation of illicit drug-taking in prisons has come a serious infection problem, which the Craiginches pilot scheme aims to address.
The SPS said yesterday that if the behaviour of prisoners taking drugs could not be changed, the service had a responsibility both to inmates and to prison staff to ensure their safety. A decision to introduce the kits will be taken by the prison service and will not have to be approved by Scottish Executive ministers.
The SPS added that the kits would reflect needle exchange programmes that existed in the community and would be modelled on similar schemes in the Republic of Ireland, Switzerland, Germany and Spain.
The Court of Appeal in London has already dismissed a case brought by an English prisoner under human rights laws to have needle exchange programmes introduced in jails south of the border.
The SPS spokesman added: "We've looked at international research which shows the introduction of the safe injection programmes reduces drug injecting." Last year alone, nearly 2,000 drugs packages were intercepted on their way to Scottish prisoners. Officials claim that human rights laws allowing contact between prisoners and their families mean that the authorities could never halt the flow of drugs into jails.
Annabel Goldie, the leader of the Scottish Tories and a campaigner for more treatment centres for drug addicts, said that she could understand why the move was necessary, given the alarming levels of drug abuse in Scottish jails. "But we need a radical overhaul of rehabilitation structures in our jails. We should be helping prisoners get off drugs rather than helping them take them," she said.
Investigations at prisons have illustrated the scale of the problem. Last month 14 officers at Pentonville prison, North London, were suspended in a corruption investigation involving the alleged smuggling of drugs into the jail.
The Home Office has given no indication that it will adopt the scheme for England and Wales if the pilot in Scotland proved successful.
A HABIT IN JAIL
* Prison needle exchange programmes in Ireland, Switzerland, Germany and Spain have reduced dramatically HIV and hepatitis transmission rates
* A recent study in Canada claimed that giving drug kits to prisoners did not lead to an increase in drug taking or cause needles to be used as weapons
* A recent Home Office study suggested heroin, cannabis and crack were freely available in English and Welsh jails
* A survey of 6,200 in Scottish jails showed that a third had used drugs in the previous month with 128 injecting. Seventy-eight of those had shared needles
Last year nearly 2,000 drugs packages were intercepted on their way to Scottish prisoners

August 23, 2006_2.Title: Hepatitis C patients offered new drugs
August 23, 2006_2.Author: Celia Hall
August 23, 2006_2.chunks: PATIENTS with hepatitis C will be able to get an effective drug on the NHS before too much liver damage is caused by the potentially fatal disease. The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (Nice) has approved the use of the drug, Pegasys, making 15,000 more patients eligible for the pounds 800-a-week combined treatment. Hepatitis C, a virus that attacks the liver is a known as a silent killer. People can be infected for 20 or 30 years before they begin to feel ill by which time considerable damage has occurred and 20 or 30 per cent will develop serious disease or liver cancer. The Government estimates that between 200,000 and 500,000 people have hepatitis C, which is passed on through contact with infected blood. However, only 47,000 have been diagnosed and around 7,000 treated. Until the new ruling, the combination therapy was only available for people with advanced disease confirmed by liver biopsy. Nice recommended that people with mild chronic hepatitis should be offered combination therapy with peginterferon alfa (Pegasys) and ribavirin, an anti-viral drug. The recommended treatment has a cure rate of between 60 and 80 per cent, depending on the strain of the virus. Treatment lasts for 24 to 48 weeks, depending on the virus. Large numbers of people were infected through medical blood products and transfusions before 1989 and drug addicts who share equipment are at high risk. Close family members of infected people are also at risk when the disease has not been diagnosed. Prof Graham Foster, professor of hepatology at Queen Mary, University of London and a consultant hepatologist at Barts and the London NHS Trust, said: "This new guidance means that more patients, regardless of where they live in the UK, can have an increased chance of avoiding serious liver damage.''

"You can get Hepatitis C from blood transfusions, from tattoos, from doing coke if you share the same note with someone else when you're snorting coke. ''You can even get it from using someone else's toothbrush." Hepatitis C is known as a silent epidemic as sufferers may have it for years without knowing.
