29 August 2003_1.Title: News - Payouts for victims of infected NHS blood.
29 August 2003_1.Author: Celia Hall.
29 August 2003_1.chunks: Medical Editor  SEVERAL thousand people infected with the potentially fatal liver disease hepatitis C through contaminated NHS blood supplies are to receive "financial assistance" from the Government in a surprising reversal. John Reid, the Health Secretary, announced yesterday that a payment scheme would be established on compassionate grounds after eight years of refusal by the Government to help. It is likely to follow Scottish proposals of giving 20,000 to people infected with hepatitis C and up to 45,000 to those who have developed serious health problems as a result. It is unlikely that the families of people who have died will receive any money. The Department of Health says the payments are not "compensation" since little was known about the condition at the time of the contamination. Hepatitis C was first recognised in the 1980s and blood supplies were contaminated until 1985. Then, when blood was treated to remove traces of HIV, by chance the hepatitis C virus was also eradicated. About 5,000 people with haemophilia who use a blood-clotting product, Factor VIII, and an unknown number of people who had blood transfusions were infected. Among haemophiliacs, 1,200 were also infected with the Aids virus HIV. Overall 1,000 haemophiliacs with hepatitis C, or hepatitis C and HIV, have died. Hepatitis C is a slow, chronic disease that attacks the liver and is most commonly transmitted by blood contact. It can lead to liver failure and in some cases liver cancer. Mr Reid said: "After becoming secretary of state, I looked at the history of this issue and decided on compassionate grounds that this was the right thing to do in this situation. "I have therefore decided in principle that English hepatitis C sufferers should receive ex-gratia payments from the Department of Health." Lord Morris, president of the Haemophilia Society, said: "The acceptance of the principle of giving financial assistance on a no-fault basis is a major breakthrough by any standards. "The haemophilia community is a small and stricken community. Because of infection by NHS blood transfusions, well over 1,000 people have died and many are seriously ill."  Last year a report from the society called on the Government to make 52.6 million available for the infected people, but this was refused. Ireland, Canada, Italy, Hungary, Spain and Sweden are among the countries that have already given financial help to sufferers infected through national blood supplies. Karen Pappenheim, chief executive of the Haemophilia Society, said: "This was quite unexpected and is fantastic news." It was not known how many people who had received blood transfusions during surgery or because of accidents had also been infected or had since died. "We will have to see how many come forward." Some hepatitis C patients are treated with interferon drugs but they can have substantial side-effects. A liver transplant may be the only way to save a patient's life.

29 August 2003_1.Title: Judge tells ministers 'find cash for victims of hepatitis'
29 August 2003_1.Author: EDDIE BARNES
29 August 2003_1.chunks: MINISTERS responsible for spending 400million on the Holyrood parliament should pay full compensation to people who contracted hepatitis C from infected blood, a judge declared yesterday. Lord Ross, who chaired the Scottish Executive group on the hepatitis C blood scandal, said the spiralling cost of the parliament proved governments could find cash if the political will was there. He also believed there could be no excuse for denying funds to the 500 people infected with the deadly liver disease in the 1980s after they were given blood products that had not been screened for the condition. Health Minister Malcolm Chisholm has announced pay-outs of up to 45,000 to compensate victims for their suffering. But the 15million set aside is only a sixth of what Lord Ross recommended. Yesterday he stepped up his call for more to be done, contrasting the Executive's tight approach on this issue with its profligacy on the Holyrood project. The row is set to become a major headache for Mr Chisholm, with campaigners insisting they won't back down. They are furious not only over the level of compensation, but the fact it does not extend to families of victims who have already died. The Executive said yesterday: 'The scheme would make lump sum payments of 20,000 to those who now have hepatitis C, with a further 25,000 for those at a more advanced stage of the illness. The minister believes this is a fair and reasonable settlement in light of other competing priorities on the health budget.' But SNP health spokesman Shona Robison said: 'The Executive owes the victims of this scandal the truth. These latest allegations make a public inquiry essential.'

29 August 2003_1.Title: Families 'excluded from hepatitis payouts'.
29 August 2003_1.Author: James Meikle Health correspondent.
29 August 2003_1.chunks: Widows and children of haemophiliacs who died from hepatitis infection caused by contaminated blood products could be excluded from a government aid package for i nfected patients, campaigners warned last night. The Haemophilia Society fears that ex gratia payments promised to infected patients in England and Wales will go no further than a package outlined for Scotland, where the executive has proposed 20,000 payments, with an extra 25,000 to those with an advanced condition. The society believes more generous payments should be made, the final size depending on the number of dependants. More than 210 of around 5,000 Britons infected with hepatitis C in the 70s and 80s after being given contaminated blood-clotting concentrates have died from liver cancer and other liver diseases. Haemophilia is a condition that affects men, although women can carry the gene responsible. The government package is expected to include related, less common conditions, which can affect women. Dependants, and many patients who have been successfully treated for the virus after years of suffering, are unlikely to benefit from the "compassionate" payments. It is also unclear whether the 500 people co-infected with HIV and hepatitis C, or surviving close relatives, would get the award. In all, 1,240 patients infected with HIV have received payments totalling 33.5m since 1988 but only 400 of these are still alive. Patients given payments for HIV infection had to sign a waiver promising not to pursue compensation for hepatitis, but campaigners argue that such a waiver was unfair. Society representatives are meeting the health minister Melanie Johnson today to press for a better settlement. The organisation's chief executive, Karin Pappenheim, said: "Surely those who have died from this terrible virus have suffered the most serious consequences of the contaminated blood disaster. It seems inconceivable that the government could even consider excluding their dependants from this scheme, yet we fear this is what is being considered." The government has never accepted responsibility for the infections, but John Reid, the health secretary, is keen to end the embarrassing row with the haemophiliac community. guardian.co.uk/medicine.

29 August 2003_1.Title: Blood risk for haemophiliacs 'covered up'
29 August 2003_1.Author: Sue Leonard
29 August 2003_1.chunks: THE danger of using infected blood products on haemophiliacs was known to government officials more than 20 years ago, newly uncovered documents reveal.Papers seen by The Sunday Times show doctors had linked cases of hepatitis C to specific brands of blood-clotting agents during a monitoring project in the 1970s.The study, funded by what was then the Department of Health and Social Security (DHSS), found that 197 cases of hepatitis C were reported by haemophilia centre directors between 1974 and 1979.Thousands of haemophiliacs in Britain contracted hepatitis C from contaminated blood-clotting products used in their treatment in the 1970s and 1980s. The condition attacks the liver and can cause cirrhosis, liver failure and cancer.The government has always insisted it could not have known that people were being infected because the heat treatment to deal with the contamination was not available until the mid-1980s, and a test for hepatitis C was only introduced in 1991.The documents were uncovered by the Haemophilia Action UK group. Scottish campaigners for compensation for haemophilia sufferers now say they will use the new evidence in private court cases and will renew calls for a public inquiry.They will also use the evidence to put pressure on the Scottish executive to make higher pay-outs to sufferers. Scottish ministers announced last week they would go ahead with ex-gratia payments of up to Pounds 45,000 to those who contracted hepatitis C as a result of their NHS treatment.Financial assistance is also being provided to people in England by the Department of Health at Westminster.The unearthed documents include a report from the haemophilia centre directors' hepatitis working party for the year 1980-81. It says of the number of hepatitis cases: "Current investigations are attempting to relate the results in different groups of patients to their transfusion history, and there is strong evidence that different types of non-A, non-B hepatitis (now known as hepatitis C) are related to different products. "In 1982, Dr John Craske, of the Public Health Laboratory Service, recommended that the surveillance should continue. "He thought it might be necessary to again ask for details of all patients who had received treatment with a particular 'suspect batch'," the report said.Phil Dolan, chairman of the Scottish Haemophilia Forum, said the documents provided compelling evidence that information had been kept quiet. "I think it may push the government into reviewing its position because obviously that information has been around. It has been hidden. It is further evidence that we need a public inquiry. "Dolan plans to raise the issues with the Scottish health minister, Malcolm Chisholm.Carol Grayson, co-ordinator of Haemophilia Action UK, who uncovered the documents, said: "We were told nothing. They knew there was another type of hepatitis that was attacking the liver whether there was a test or not. "Haemophiliac Andy Gunn, who is pursuing legal action in America against plasma manufacturers over alleged contamination, said he would ensure his lawyers were aware of the documents.Chisholm will be put under new pressure this week by members of the Scottish parliament's health committee, who will question why the payments are much lower than the amount recommended by the executive's own expert group, led by Lord Ross.Sufferers in the republic of Ireland are believed to have received an average of about Pounds 300,000.Christine Grahame, convenor of the Scottish parliament's health committee, said she did not think the amount being offered was enough. "I want to know why Scotland is being so shabby compared with Ireland," she said. Frank Maguire, solicitor advocate with Thompsons Scotland, who was on the expert group, said he was preparing a number of cases against the NHS in Scotland which, if successful, could cost the executive millions.The executive said: "We are not currently aware of these documents and would not therefore wish to comment on them. The test used to detect hepatitis C was introduced in the UK in September 1991. The development and introduction of this test marked a major advance in microbiological technology and could not have been implemented before this time. "(C) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2003

29 August 2003_1.Title: Lost records blow for Scots patients seeking damages.
29 August 2003_1.Author: Shirley English.
29 August 2003_1.chunks: PATIENTS infected with deadly viruses from contaminated NHS blood products have missed out on the chance of compensation because hospitals have lost or destroyed their medical records, it has been claimed.More than 200 British haemophiliacs are involved in a class action in the United States which is about to be lodged against four large pharmaceutical companies who allegedly supplied blood plasma from high-risk donors, including prisoners, to the NHS in the late 1970s and early 1980s.British haemophiliacs who subsequently received the US blood products, namely a clotting agent called Factor 8, went on to develop hepatitis C and HIV.The class action is being co-ordinated by a firm of solicitors in San Francisco and evidence from affected British patients was meant to be submitted by tomorrow.But scores of patients, particularly those in Scotland, have had difficulty accessing their complete medical records - vital to prove that their infection was caused by imported American blood plasma.Some patients have been told by hospitals that their records have been lost, or destroyed, while others have received documents with huge gaps in data, invariably involving the years 1980-85 when the mass contamination of 3,000 haemophiliacs (568 in Scotland) is thought to have taken place.The blunder over archiving of records has proved remarkably consistent across Scotland, raising suspicions among haemophiliacs that it may be more than coincidence.It came to light after American lawyers visited Scotland last November to talk to haemophiliacs about the class action and patients began requesting their medical records. At the time, Malcolm Chisholm, Health Minister, instructed hospitals to co-operate. He has now asked haemophiliacs whose records are missing or incomplete to contact his department. It is understood that medical records of people with long-term illnesses should be kept more than five years after their death.Philip Dolan, chairman of the Scottish Haemophiliacs Forum, said: "One hospital's failure to keep adequate medical records could be put down to poor administration.But when the same thing has happened at hospitals in Glasgow, Aberdeen, Edinburgh and Dundee, and the same sort of vital information is missing over the same period of time, it seems a wee bit suspicious. 29 August 2003_1.Title: Inquiry into infected blood that killed 1,000 ; MoS campaign for haemophiliacs is vindicated as GMC finally tackles 20-year scandal
29 August 2003_1.Author: JO KNOWSLEY; DOMINIC TURNBULL
29 August 2003_1.chunks: A NEW inquiry has been launched into the scandal of haemophiliacs who died after being treated with HIV-infected blood first revealed by The Mail on Sunday 20 years ago. The General Medical Council is seeking to establish exactly when doctors first became aware of the dangers of controversial Factor VIII and Factor VIX blood-clotting products imported from the US. And they have also been asked to investigate whether there were any financial links between British haematologists and the American firms which supplied them. The GMC investigation follows a decade of tireless campaigning by Carol Grayson, whose husband Peter, a haemophiliac, was found to have been infected with HIV and hepatitis C. Mrs Grayson claims that the Public Health Laboratory Service warned the Department of Health in 1983 about the risk of AIDS, advising in a letter that all blood products manufactured in the US after 1978 should immediately be withdrawn. Mrs Grayson says this proves consultants were aware of the risks from infected blood and wants the GMC to find out why the withdrawal of stocks apparently did not happen. Mrs Grayson, who set up a pressure group called Haemophiliac Action UK ten years ago, said: 'This has been a tragic conspiracy of silence.' Last night a spokesman for the GMC said: 'We are looking into the actions of doctors responsible for the treatment of blood- borne diseases.' Two haemophiliacs had already contracted HIV when The Mail on Sunday published its original expose on May 1, 1983, a week before the PHLS sent its warning letter. But our attempts to protect a highly vulnerable section of the public were blocked after a complaint was made to newspaper watchdog the Press Council alleging that our report was 'sensational and highly exaggerated'. Opponents said our story would scare haemophiliacs into rejecting essential blood clotting products and that the risk of contracting a disease through blood plasma was lower than dying of an uncontrolled bleed. That claim was upheld by the Press Council, effectively preventing the media from reporting on this vital issue. Two decades on, however, it is The Mail on Sunday which has been proved right, albeit at immense human cost. In the following years about 4,500 more haemophiliacs are thought to have been diagnosed with AIDS and hepatitis C after being treated with contaminated clotting agents. Of these more than 1,000 later died. The dangers of paying blood donors from Third World countries or from underprivileged sections of society had been outlined by the World Health Organisation as early as 1975. That year, a report in the influential medical journal The Lancet condemned paying blood donors as encouraging a 'traffic in blood'. Yet this is what four American plasma companies continued to do throughout the late Seventies and Eighties, until the number of haemophiliacs developing AIDS began attracting international attention. Documents seen by The Mail on Sunday reveal that the four American companies accepted blood from prisoners, homeless people and homosexuals, who were paid about 8. None of them was screened. At the time Britain was importing 70 per cent of its blood products and the one which later proved so deadly was used in Britain until 1986, when it was finally withdrawn after it was proved that it had infected two boys at a Birmingham hospital. A court action has now been launched in America on behalf of infected haemophiliacs, including 150 British victims, to seek compensation from the companies. Lawyers allege they knew the risks at the time they were exporting the blood products. In Britain there was a no-fault compensation payment made by the Government in 1991 to hundreds of haemophiliacs who had been infected with HIV. The money about 23,000 for a single man was provided on the grounds that they signed a waiver ruling out future payments if they became infected with any other viruses. Campaigners claim doctors knew at the time that the majority of these people were already infected with hepatitis C. Any doctor found guilty by the GMC of serious misconduct could be struck off but the Press Council judgment against this newspaper made in 1984 cannot be reversed. Meanwhile the problems associated with plasma and donor blood products are not over yet. In November last year hundreds of haemophiliacs were warned they might have vCJD, the human form of mad cow disease.

29 August 2003_1.Title: News - Doctors defuse hepatitis C timebomb.
29 August 2003_1.Author:
Roger Highfield.
 The Daily Telegraph
29 August 2003_1.chunks: Science Editor DOCTORS have found a way to help defuse the "timebomb" of hepatitis C, a disease that may affect as many as 400,000 people in Britain. Only a small proportion are diagnosed because people can live with the hepatitis C virus (HCV) for more than 20 years before serious health concerns make them aware they are infected. The drug Pegasys - pegylated interferon alfa-2a, where pegylated refers to the use of the antifreeze chemical, polyethylene glycol - can get to the liver, the primary site of infection, more easily than conventional interferon. As a result, it can cut the virus to undetectable levels in 61 per cent of all patients and a study reported yesterday that more than 99 per cent will remain virus-free up to four years later. The results were announced by Dr Mark Swain, associate professor of medicine, University of Calgary, at the annual meeting of the European Association for Study of the Liver in Geneva. Dr Graham Foster, consultant hepatologist, Royal London Hospital, said: "These results are very encouraging. This suggests that patients who eliminate the virus when therapy is stopped may be totally cured. "It is estimated that 200,000 to 400,000 in Britain are living with hepatitis C, although 90 per cent are unaware they are affected. This is a critical message for patients - whether they are newly diagnosed or in the midst of therapy - the end result may be lifesaving." Hepatitis C affects the liver and is caught through blood-to-blood contact. Many Britons were infected through blood transfusions before screening began in 1992. However an even larger number may have contracted the virus through intravenous drug use, sharing cocaine equipment, body piercing, tattooing or possibly even sharing an infected person's razor or toothbrush.

29 August 2003_1.Title:
Features - Health & Wellbeing - I caught hepatitis C first - but Guy
died Sandra Waters had no idea that ...
29 August 2003_1.Author:
CHRISTINE DOYLE.
 The Daily Telegraph
29 August 2003_1.chunks: Features - Health & Wellbeing - I caught hepatitis C first - but Guy died Sandra Waters had no idea that a blood transfusion had given her a killer disease until tragedy hit her family. Christine Doyle reports. Fifteen years ago, Sandra Waters had a successful operation to remove a ruptured spleen. During the surgery, doctors transfused eight pints of donated blood and one pint of plasma. The blood saved her life but, many years later, it was to have tragic consequences for her family. Not only did Waters develop severe liver disease, which was likely to have been caused by a virus carried in the donated blood, but the operation also led indirectly to the death of her boyfriend of 21 years, Guy Norman. Norman developed cirrhosis of the liver five years ago and, within two months, had deteriorated so quickly that a transplant was out of the question. When Norman was acutely ill in intensive care, Sandra, 41, discovered, from reading his notes, that he was infected with hepatitis C, a deadly liver virus known to be passed through donated blood and blood products. "At the time of my operation, virtually nothing was known about hepatitis C. I had always been relatively fit and healthy, knew very little about hepatitis C and never imagined that I might have been infected or that I might pass on a deadly virus. "Guy's death was a huge shock, and I felt, for the sake of our son, William, who was then only 11, that I should find out more about the virus. I could not take any risk that William might be left an orphan. So I asked to be tested." Two initial tests proved positive. "I was shaking and my heart was pounding when I got the result - just as I felt when Guy died." Two months later, a biopsy showed that her liver was moderately inflamed with fibrosis. Luckily, cirrhosis had not yet developed. But it took six months of gruelling treatment to clear the virus from her body, and she is still having check-ups. In Norman's memory, Waters, who works with community health councils, is speaking out to support the first annual National Hepatitis C Awareness Day, which is today. The aim is to highlight the widespread lack of knowledge about hepatitis C. "We know that at least 200,000 people could be infected with the virus and that only about one in 10 has been diagnosed. Up to a third of these could be at risk of potentially fatal disease," says Nigel Hughes, of Mainliners National Hepatitis C Resource Centre, which, with the Hepatitis C Trust, has launched the campaign. One major issue is the virus's legacy, says Hughes. "Donated blood has been screened since 1991, but the virus has a long latency period and the effect on the liver might become obvious only years later." Another is that many people are unaware of how the virus is transmitted or how they might have picked it up years ago, says Charles Gore, director of the Hepatitis C Trust, which is launching a new website. "Many people are still not aware of the possible risk of medical treatment or emergency dental treatment in countries where sterility standards are lax." Alan James, 50, who is in arts management, was horrified when he tested positive for hepatitis C three years ago. "I had been run down and lacking my usual energy for some time," he says. "The only explanation is my wild youth. I injected smack - heroin - intravenously and, crucially, shared needles. It was more a weekend than a serious habit, but enough to pick up hepatitis C. The infection probably lay dormant for years. No one knew about the risk at the time, and I would say to anyone now, avoid any possible risk and never share needles." So far, Alan has opted not to have the "toxic treatment" necessary to clear the virus. "I am waiting for something gentler to come along, and am trying to minimise symptoms by being kind to my liver with a very low fat diet." By contrast, having seen how swiftly Norman's liver succumbed, Waters was determined to rid her body of the virus as quickly as possible. "I had a very potent cocktail of alpha interferon and a drug called ribavirin," she explains. "It has a similar affect to chemotherapy for cancer. Half my hair fell out, I lost weight and had to take three months off work. But, wonderfully, the virus has gone. Alternative treatments, such as acupuncture, evening primrose oils and some Chinese herbal remedies, have helped." Britain has not yet woken up to the hidden risks of undetected hepatitis C, says Professor Roger Williams, director of the Foundation for Liver Research in London. "The virus is more common than many people realise. It is becoming the commonest reason for liver transplants, and will be for the next 13 to 14 years, as people who were infected in the past come forward. Treatment is effective, if given early." There are several different viral genotypes and treatment success varies from 50 to 80 per cent. Williams and Mainliners are highly critical of government inaction. "The issue has largely been pushed to one side," says Hughes. "The Government produced a hepatitis C strategy. Although the document, which was published a year ago and late, contained a promise for an action plan, nothing has yet appeared." Compared with many other EU countries, we treat less than one tenth of the proportion of infected patients, says Hughes. Williams points to a potential hepatitis C epidemic among immigrants. "Leaving aside asylum seekers, each year for the past four years an estimated 6,000 to 7,000 infected immigrants have moved to Britain," he explains. "These figures are based on the prevalence rates in the countries of origin. I believe we must carry out checks for the virus, preferably in the country of origin." This includes southern Europe, Africa, south-east Asia and countries in the former Soviet Union. "In most similar EU countries, there are already procedures in place," says Hughes. "We don't want any discrimination, but, if immigrants' health needs are catered for, it is better for them and helps to prevent the virus spreading."

29 August 2003_1.Title: News roundup - Americas - Law suit for infected blood.
29 August 2003_1.Author:
Duncan Campbell.
 The Guardian
29 August 2003_1.chunks: An American firm has launched a law suit on behalf of haemophiliacs and survivors of haemophiliacs who were supposedly infected by contaminated blood products. The plaintiffs were allegedly infected with HIV or Hepatitis C after being given the product in the early to mid-80s. "Tens of thousands of haemophiliacs globally were infected with HIV or HCV af ter receiving blood products from blood plasma that was originally manufactured in the US," said attorney Robert Nelson of the San Francisco-based firm Lieff Cabraser, which is bringing the action on behalf of clients. At present, 15 people from the United Kingdom, Italy and Germany are named in the action. A spokesman for the Lieff Cabraser said yesterday that they were seeking an order from the court which would turn the suit into a class action. According to the suit, there were four major firms in the US involved in the production and sale of the products concerned, Factor VIII and Factor IX: the Bayer Corporation and its Cutter Biological Division, Armour Pharmaceutical Company, Baxter Healthcare Corporation and its Hyland Pharmaceutical division and Alpha Therapeutic Corporation. The suit follows reports that Bayer knowingly sold blood-clotting agents infected with HIV to Asia and Latin America months after it withdrew the products from Europe and the US. "Bayer has always behaved responsibly, ethically, and humanely," said the company in a statement from its base in Leverkusen, Germany. The other companies named in the suit had not responded to Lieff Cabraser yesterday.

29 August 2003_1.Title: New treatment for hepatitis C.
29 August 2003_1.Author: No author in byline
29 August 2003_1.chunks: A new drug may help those with hepatitis C. The molecule, called BILN 2061, slams the brakes on virus replication, and has performed well in a preliminary trial. Some 170 million people worldwide are infected with the hepatitis C virus, which can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer. The new treatment could help those who carry strains that are resistant to current drugs - around half of all sufferers. In the trial, eight patients took doses of the new drug for two days. After 24 hours, their viral levels had plummeted up to 1,000-fold, Nature reports. "The drug appears to be safe and well tolerated," says Paul Anderson, senior vice president of Boehringer-Ingelheim in Quebec, Canada, the company that developed the new treatment. Longer, larger trials are needed to see whether problems develop over time, says Ralf Bartenschlager, who studies virus replication at the University of Heidelberg, Germany. Even so, "the short-term data are extraordinary", he says.

29 August 2003_1.Title: Women in virus alert ; Surgeon who did caesareans has hepatitis C
29 August 2003_1.Author: ADAM POWELL
29 August 2003_1.chunks: HUNDREDS of women need urgent blood tests after a surgeon was diagnosed with the potentially fatal hepatitis C virus. Health bosses have recalled 343 patients who underwent caesarean sections or hysterectomies at the doctor's hands and could be infected. There is no cure for hepatitis C, which can cause liver failure and organ cancer and is spread through blood and bodily fluids. The surgeon was found to have the virus during tests for an unrelated condition, according to senior management at Tameside and Glossop Acute NHS Trust in Greater Manchester. He works in the obstetrics and gynaecology department at Tameside General Hospital and has not performed an operation since he was found to be infected three months ago. Trust medical director Tim Dunningham insisted the recall is 'simply a safety precaution'. He said: 'Patients have a right to know about risks to their health. However, I stress that the chance of anyone having picked up the hepatitis C infection from this doctor is extremely unlikely.' The virus could spread only if the doctor, described by colleagues as being 'meticulous', had cut himself and bled during surgery. The recall concerns women treated in the last three years. Mr Dunningham said the doctor would not be named because it could put the patients' confidentiality at risk. There are 19 doctors in the department. Dr Jennifer Hill, consultant in communicable disease control at the Greater Manchester Protection Unit, said: 'We are confident we have identified all patients who need to be contacted. Those who have not received a letter may be assured they are not included in this investigation.' a.powell@dailymail.co.uk

29 August 2003_1.chunks: Arrow Therapeutics has raised 21m in the largest private finance round in the UK biotechnology sector this year.Arrow, which scans the genomes of bacteria and viruses to find new types of anti-infective medicines, plans to use the money to fund trials of experimental treatments for hepatitis C and respiratory syncitial virus.The fundraising, which Arrow hopes will net up to 25m when the second round closes this year, follows closely on a 20m venture capital financing by Ardana, a Scottish drug development company, and is further evidence of a return of investor enthusiasm for cash-hungry biotechs.Several US biotech companies are preparing to float on Nasdaq, including Myogen, which recently raised $40m ( 24m) in venture funding, as well as Aderis, Cancervax and Affibody. 29 August 2003_1.Author: James McNamara
29 August 2003_1.chunks: GBH charge after cops raid homesTWO top doctors from the blood transfusion service appeared in court yesterday after being dramatically arrested over the 1970s contamination scandal.Former chief medical consultant Terry Walsh and ex-senior biochemist Cecily Cunningham were charged with causing grievous bodily harm to patients.They appeared at Dublin District Court after cops called at their homes at 8am and took them away for questioning yesterday.The arrests came five years after gardai launched a probe into how patients, including haemophiliacs, were given blood infected with hepatitis C.The case against the doctors involved pregnant women given a blood product called anti-D immunoglobulin, which prevents their newborns developing blue baby syndrome.It emerged in the mid-Nineties that 1,200 women given anti-D were infected with the Hepatitis C virus. which can cause fatal liver cancer.NoxiousYesterday it was alleged in court that the doctors "unlawfully and maliciously caused a noxious thing, namely infected anti-D immunoglobulin, which caused grievous bodily harm to seven women" between 1977 and 1992.Dr Walsh's solicitor Padraig Dwyer asked why 26 years had elapsed before the case had been brought before the court.Mr Dwyer also demanded to know why his client had not been kept up to date with developments in the case more than four years after making a statement to cops.Both Dr Walsh, from Dublin's exclusive Foxrock neighbourhood, and Dr Cunningham, from Clontarf, Dublin, were smartly dressed in suits.They were remanded on their own bail to appear before the district court on September 24.Hepatitis C support group Positive Action said it welcomed the first prosecutions in the controversy.  Clampdown on health tourists
29 August 2003_1.Author: No author found
29 August 2003_1.chunks:
The Times (London)

July 29, 2003, Tuesday

 Clampdown on health tourists

BYLINE: Oliver Wright Health Correspondent

SECTION: Home news; 1

LENGTH: 496 words

 
 Health tourists who use bogus business trips to get thousands of pounds worth of free health service treatment are to be banned under a government crackdown.
 Ministers intend to stop foreign businessmen and their families from receiving free treatment unless they can prove that they work full time in the country, The Times has learnt.
 At present, foreign citizens can run up huge healthcare bills by getting a business visa to visit the UK and applying for treatment for themselves and their families. No official figures are available, but the total cost is thought to run into millions of pounds a year. 
 A Department of Health review, to be published today by John Hutton, the Health Minister, uncovered dozens of examples of abuse.
 One sports presenter covering Wimbledon this year used it as an opportunity to bring his son to Britain for a complicated operation that would have cost thousands of pounds in his home country.
 The wife of a businessman working temporarily in the UK flew into the country days before she was due to give birth and presented herself at a London hospital, which had to admit her. She flew home shortly after the birth.
 The Government intends to ban relatives of foreigners working full time in the UK from receiving treatment unless they can prove that they are also full-time residents.
 At present, anecdotal evidence from doctors suggests that many relatives fly to Britain when they get ill. The sister of a businessman who arrived in Britain for a wedding was diagnosed with Aids within days of arrival. Patients have turned up at hospitals with advanced hepatitis B and C when they had come to Britain "on holiday" to see a family member. At present all must be treated on the NHS.
 At present any foreign citizen and dependants in Britain are entitled to treatment if they are "engaging in employment as an employed or self-employed person".
 That will be changed to include only people working full-time for a UK company.
 Relatives will only be covered if they live in Britain full time. At the same time, the Government will publish guidance on how to spot abuses.
 Some doctors, particularly in London, have complained that they have to treat many patients who should not be entitled to use the health service.
 Professor Roger Williams, the haematologist at University College London who supervised George Best's liver transplant, said that he saw many patients who were in Britain only for its healthcare service.
 "The system has been abused for years," he said. "It is getting worse and worse.
 The whole thing is monstrous and I would personally welcome any moves to tighten up the regulations."
 But Tauhid Pasha, Legal Policy and Information Director of the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants said that the new policy would be counter productive.
 "The Government seems to be going against its own policy of making the UK a versatile labour market," he added.

29 August 2003_1.Author: No author found
29 August 2003_1.chunks:
The Guardian - Final Edition

September 23, 2003

Insurers issue new rules on gays

BYLINE: Jill Treanor

SECTION: Guardian City Pages, Pg. 15

LENGTH: 351 words

 
 Male ballet dancers, hairdressers and cabin crew should no longer face discrimination from insurance companies assessing risks of HIV/Aids as a result of new proposals published yesterday.
 The Association of British Insurers has issued five principles that insurers should follow when considering applications for life cover and other protection.
 The ABI is trying to prevent insurers from making assumptions about applicants' risk of HIV/Aids or sexuality as a result of their occupation. 
 The industry group is also trying to enforce a requirement that applicants are not asked whether they have been tested for HIV but only if they have tested positive or are awaiting the result of a test.
 The ABI is suggesting new wording for application forms about tests for HIV, hepatitis B or C and visits to countries where there might be a risk of HIV infection.
 Richard Walsh, the ABI's head of health, said the proposals were intended to make customers feel they were being treated with respect and not being overcharged for their policies.
 The proposals, which are out for consultation in the industry, have been put together with the support of the Terrence Higgins trust and pinkfinance.com.
 The ABI is looking for views from other relevant organisations, such as gay and African rights lobbies, doctors, patient support groups and financial advisers, before publishing a final version of the code.
 Chris Morgan of pink-finance.com said the guidelines demonstrated a "new level of respect towards gay men". He noted a clause had been introduced for a "new respectful and relevant question" about safe sexual behaviour that was applicable to all risk groups, not only gay men.
 Martin Kirk of the Terrence Higgins trust welcomed a pledge from insurers to conduct a review of policies on HIV/Aids in three years. The ABI's first statement on the issue was published in 1994 and updated in 1997.
 The proposals recommend that when communicating with applicants' GPs, insurers should not ask them to speculate on whether the applicant is at higher risk than normal.

29 August 2003_1.Title: Drugs deal 'not viable'.
29 August 2003_1.Author: Nick Mathiason.
29 August 2003_1.chunks: RECRIMINATIONS erupted last night over an international trade agreement to provide cut-price copies of life-saving drugs for the world's poorest countries  Amid jubilation in Geneva, where yesterday trade negotiators thrashed out a compromise they hope will avert a series of health catastrophes afflicting huge parts of Africa and Asia, fears are growing that the agreement will be unworkable. Under the intellectual property deal, poor countries, can now issue a compulsory licence to import low-cost copies of expensive branded drugs owned by powerful pharmaceutical firms. But according to trade analysts, the deal will be unable to provide the quantities of drugs needed to combat the world's growing deadly infections. '[The] deal was designed to offer comfort to the US and Western pharmaceutical industry,' said Ellen 't Hoen of Medecins Sans Frontieres. 'Unfortunately, it offers little comfort for poor patients. Global patent rules will continue to drive up the price of medicines.' The principal concern is that it will be uneconomic for manufacturers of cheap copies of expensive drugs to export them to countries that need it. Pharmaceutical firms, whose collective profits run into tens of billions of pounds, have largely failed to reduce the price of their products, making them unaffordable to developing countries. A deal has been held up for two years over concerns by pharmaceutical companies, led by American giant Pfizer, that generic drug companies, who copy patented products, will make huge profits from health crises. The major firms also fear medicines meant for the poor will 'leak' into the West. Campaigners dismiss that as exaggeration. 'This is a historic agreement for the World Trade Organisation,' said its director general Supachai Panitchpakdi. 'It proves the organisation can handle humanitarian as well as trade concerns.' There has been immense pressure for poor countries to adopt the deal. Had it collapsed yesterday it would have derailed next week's trade talks in Mexico. The agreement comes as a new study reveals a massive outbreak of hepatitis C in Africa. Oxfam reveals that 170 million globally are infected, with 150 million of them living in poor countries. The disease is labelled 'Africa's silent killer'. Cases progress slowly resulting in chronic liver diseases, cirrhosis and cancer. But the overwhelming number of sufferers have no access to medicines to combat the disease  Hepatitis C is most prevalent in Egypt where up to a fifth of its 70 million population suffer from it, according to the campaign group. Two pharmaceutical companies produce drugs to combat the disease - Hoffman-La Roche and Schering-Plough. A Hoffman La Roche spokesman was unaware of any discount schemes by his firm to poor countries. Mohga Kamal Smith of Oxfam, who wrote the report, said: 'The world is focused on HIV, TB and malaria but hepatitis C affects tens of millions. The medicines are unaffordable. Yesterday's agreement may be seen as a breakthrough, but the reality is the drugs will not be affordable for the millions who need them. The tragedy is this is a missed opportunity. '.

29 August 2003_1.Title: Health service to test recruits for HIV
29 August 2003_1.Author: Sue Leonard
29 August 2003_1.chunks: ALL new doctors, nurses and dentists involved in invasive procedures will have to take an HIV test before being allowed to work in the National Health Service in Scotland.They will also have to test negative for hepatitis B and C under new guidelines drawn up by the Scottish executive.Ministers have accepted the recommendations from a group of UK experts which was set up by the Department of Health in England. It has just published draft guidance for consultation north of the border.The disclosure follows the publication last week of a report into the case of a doctor who had worked in the obstetrics and gynaecology department at Raigmore hospital, Inverness, from February 1999 to February 2000 while he was HIV positive.More than 60 women patients who he had treated had to be tested after his illness was discovered. A baby who had been nicked by a scalpel while being delivered by caesarean section was also tested. None tested positive for the virus.The report concluded that had a proper screening policy of NHS staff been in place, the doctor would not have been allowed to put the lives of patients at risk.The doctor, who has never been named, became ill while working at a hospital in Hull but the report reveals that he was infected with HIV when he was working in Scotland.A blood sample from Raigmore's virology laboratory which was taken to test for hepatitis B in October 1999 was subsequently tested for the HIV virus and found to be positive.The case involving the doctor was the third scare about HIV-positive hospital doctors in 10 years in Scotland.The report calls for the mandatory health clearance for HIV to be "implemented forthwith".In 1993 a junior doctor in Argyll & Clyde was found to have the virus after he became ill. Some 39 obstetric patients were contacted but the scare prompted 604 calls to the helpline that was set up to offer advice to patients.A year later it emerged that Professor George Browning, an ear, nose and throat surgeon in Glasgow had the virus. Two years later Browning was allowed to perform operations deemed to be "risk-free" by the Department of Health.There have been only two cases worldwide in the past 20 years of HIV transmission from healthcare workers to patients, neither of them in Britain.Dr Ken Oates, consultant in public health medicine in the Highland Health Board and who was chairman of the incident team, said that while it was extremely unlikely that a health worker would pass infection on to a patient, public anxiety was caused by such scares. "We live in a society that does not accept any risk," he said. "If there is any remote possibility of a healthcare worker passing it on to a patient that is unacceptable. 29 August 2003_1.Title: JIMMY YOUNG.
29 August 2003_1.Author:
JIMMY YOUNG.
 The Express on Sunday
29 August 2003_1.chunks: WHY IS it seemingly impossible for anyone to raise perfectly legitimate questions about asylum seekers in this country without having the Left throw charges of racism at them? Quicker than you can say "health checks", up come the trigger words and accusations of racism, fascism, naked hate, xenophobia, diseased aliens and BNP sympathies. Last week all those insults were hurled at Dr Liam Fox, the Conservative health spokesman, when he declared that under a Conservative Government all immigrants and asylum seekers would be screened for infectious diseases. They would be barred if they were considered to be a possible burden on the National Health Service. Statistics tell us that imported infections have doubled our rates of HIV and TB and some doctors estimate that undiagnosed cases of hepatitis C have increased 20-fold. Imported diseases are a problem for the country as a whole and for the NHS in particular. Predictably Dr Fox was accused of trying to score political points and I don't doubt that the measures he was proposing would be popular with many. However, the fact that the proposals that might be advantageous for his party does not mean they are wrong. One Left-wing newspaper described the proposals as a disingenuous stunt that demeans the Conservative Party. It declared that the health of an asylum seeker should be irrelevant to the outcome of their application. Have you ever heard such nonsense? We have an NHS that is already straining to keep up with demand. We certainly don't need to put further burdens on it by importing problems from abroad. There is even a suggestion that the Government is considering mass vaccination against hepatitis C to protect us. Surely it would be better all round - especially for the continuity of harmonious community relations with immigrants already happily living here - if we tried to prevent diseases such as HIV and TB from coming here in the first place. Australia insists on three tests for would-be immigrants. They must not pose a risk of transmitting an infectious disease to the public, create undue demand on restricted health resources or create a long-term drain on the public purse by bringing elderly relatives. In fact, Canada and the US also insist upon health tests for would-be immigrants. To propose such measures is not racist, it is not pulling up the drawbridge. It is eminently sensible and, just for once, the Conservatives are perfectly in order to say so.

29 August 2003_1.Title:
People assume that liver disease is always the result of too much
boozing.. and that's ...
29 August 2003_1.Author:
MAEVE QUIGLEY.

29 August 2003_1.chunks: People assume that liver disease is always the result of too much boozing.. and that's so upsetting. FASHION GURU TRIONA TELLS OF FAMILY'S LOSS A YOUNG woman has become the first person to set up a charity in Ireland to benefit research into liver disease. Fashion guru Triona McCarthy held the first event to raise money for her charity For Frock's Sake last week. And the following morning Triona had to bury the second aunt she lost to the killer disease. Triona explained: "I have lost two aunts to non-alcohol related liver disease and wanted to do something to raise awareness about it in Ireland. "My aunt Brida passed away a year ago, and tragically the day before we held our first fashion show in aid of the charity, her twin sister Anne passed away. "Liver disease is often asymptomatic and can therefore go undiagnosed for 10 or 20 years before a patient received medical attention. "Decompensated liver disease from any cause is a very aggressive illness and it is surprising how common it is and how little people here know about it. "Most people are aware of the effects of alcohol abuse on the liver but they do not realise that chronic liver disease is not caused simply by alcohol abuse and that there are many different types. "Brida left behind four children while Anne's two boys, who are only 15 and 17, have also been left without a mother. "Neither of them touched alcohol because they knew their livers were already compromised and the automatic assumption that drinking was involved in their illnesses upsets me." Triona, who is manageress of upmarket boutique Khan in Blackrock, is set to launch a fashion book with pictures of Irish celebrities later this year. She said: "It will be a coffee table book which will feature Irish celebrities from all walks of life photographed wearing their favourite dress and explaining why they like it so much." Triona said that since word of the fashion show spread, a vast number of people had contacted her to discuss ideas or to tell their own experiences. "Some kind of central support group for chronic liver disease sufferers and their families needs to be set up. "I don't have any knowledge about this except for my own family's experiences, but it was something I felt very strongly about and something I wanted to do. "A helpline or support group needs to be set up to address the problems of the many Irish sufferers and their families." Dr Shiobhan Weston, an RCSI graduate and specialist in transplant hepatology explained: "Worldwide there has been an increase in Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) which can manifest itself as simple fatty liver or lead to Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH). This can eventually progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer. "People who carry fat around their middle - even though they may not be clinically obese - are more at risk, as are those with type two diabetes, dyslipisemia, coronary heart disease and hypertension - all of which are common in Ireland. "In the past NAFLD was ignored. It does not really have any symptoms so many people don't realise they have this disease until they have developed NASH or cirrhosis. "People do not generally get their liver blood checked and so do not realise that they have this disease which progresses very slow but can be fatal. "In Dublin's Beaumont Hospital alone there are now about four new cases of NAFLD evaluated in the outpatient department each week - which is 200 people in that one hospital alone every year. "There is no approved medical treatment for NASH except for transplantation." Dr Weston said people in Ireland need to be more aware of NAFLD and how to prevent it through lifestyle modification - dietary changes and exercise - as well as aggressive management of diabetes and lipid abnormalitis. "There is no specific public policy in Ireland and, apart from Hepatitis C, there is no central registry or database for any other types of liver disease here. "For Frock's Sake is the first charity that has been set up specifically to raise funds for more research into liver disease. "It is crucial that more is done to raise public awareness of this potentially life-threatening disease."

29 August 2003_1.Title: It would be unethical not to talk about imported diseases - Comment - Opinion.
29 August 2003_1.Author: Anthony Browne.
29 August 2003_1.chunks: There are some awkward problems that will go away if ignored. Some, however, thrive out of the spotlight, growing worse until a crisis forces us to confront them. The problem of imported diseases is one such. While Britain has high levels of immigration without health checks from regions with high levels of disease and little treatment, it is inevitable that much of the illness will end up here.The statistics bear repeating: imported infections have doubled our rates of HIV and TB, and doctors estimate that undiagnosed cases of hepatitis C have increased twentyfold. TB rates in London are higher than in much of the Third World. More African immigrants than gay men are diagnosed with HIV each year in Britain. Each costs 10,000 to 15,000 a year to treat. The infection is spreading to the host population, with about 200 people a year getting HIV through sex with infected immigrants.We may decide to curb this by introducing health tests for immigrants. Or we may decide it is a price worth paying. But we should at least decide, not bury our heads, fearful of accusations of "racism".When I first broke the taboo on this page and set out the need for immigrant health tests, I unleashed paroxysms of denunciation. The Home Secretary accused me in Parliament of "bordering on fascism". The New Statesman magazine couldn't challenge my figures and so decided to libel me as a supporter of the British National Party, while The Guardian accused me of "naked hate".I was not fuelled by hatred but by extensive discussions with government medical advisers who were frustrated that the excellent work they had done over previous decades at controlling HIV and TB was being undone.The Government has now launched a review of immigrant health tests. Yesterday, the Conservatives bravely pre-empted its conclusions by adopting the tests as official policy, suggesting that anyone wanting to move to Britain would have to pay to have them in their home country before they leave.The Liberal Democrats' health spokesman, Evan Harris, demeaned himself by denouncing the proposals as "unnecessary, extremist, unethical and unworkable".But nothing can make them more necessary than our imported HIV epidemic. There is nothing extremist about adopting the policies of the most immigration-friendly liberal democracies in the world, America, Canada and Australia, all of which insist upon pre-departure health tests.As for unethical - not giving someone a student visa or work permit because they are HIV positive is troubling, but there is nothing ethical about trying to combat the HIV holocaust in Africa by treating those who can afford the plane fare to Britain. I am a trustee of a charity that works to prevent HIV in Africa, and know too well that if the vast sums spent treating Africans on the NHS were spent in Africa itself, they would save millions of lives, not just thousands.I was accused of stirring up racial hatred, but what could possibly be worse for race relations than importing HIV and TB epidemics from Africa and Asia? The Government is considering mass vaccination against hepatitis C to protect people against infected immigrants, but it would be better for community relations if it prevented the disease coming here in the first place. There is no greater gift you could give to BNP recruiters than ensuring that immigrants endanger the lives of British people and burden the NHS. The accusations of racism silence debate and succeed in the incredible feat of making the white supremacist BNP sound reasonable to ordinary voters.Immigration policy should balance the interests of immigrants with those of the host community. The public will be far more welcoming of immigrants if they believe the Government has ensured they are a boon, not a burden. But if the Government rejects health tests, it will be showing that it cares more for the rights of immigrants than the rights of the public. It shouldn't be surprised if the public ends up caring neither for the Government nor the immigrants.

29 August 2003_1.Author: STUART WINTER.
29 August 2003_1.chunks: BATTLING Pamela Anderson has received a double boost in her fight against the disease that she fears will kill her in five years. A revolutionary medicine has been invented that could save her from the "silent killer" hepatitis C.  And at the same time Pammy has made up with ex-husband Tommy Lee. She was pictured yesterday kissing the former Motley Crue drummer at their children's football training session in Malibu, California. Brave Pam said last week that she may have as little as five years left to live after contracting the liver disease. She is reported to be quitting the limelight to spend more time with her family. But as the former Baywatch actress, wearing a tight white top and trousers, spent the weekend with Lee and her children, doctors revealed they had made a major breakthrough in the fight against hepatitis C.  The drug blocks an enzyme that is needed by the hepatitis C virus to reproduce. It is the first of its kind to be tested by patients - and the results were dramatic. Eight people infected with hepatitis C drank four liquid doses of the drug, codenamed BILN 2061, over 48 hours. Two days later, their virus levels had dropped by 100 to 1,000-fold. In most patients, the virus could no longer be detected by standard tests and no side effects were reported. An estimated 170 million people worldwide have the disease. In most cases, there are no symptoms until it is at an advanced stage, which is why it is called the "silent killer". The virus is transmitted in the same way as HIV - through sexual intercourse and in the blood. MAKING UP: A kiss for her ex husband Tommy.

29 August 2003_1.chunks: Schering-Plough's second-quarter profit warning was disappointing precisely because it contained no surprises. Everyone knows that sales of Claritin, its allergy drug, are tanking now that patent protection has been removed. And everybody knows that Roche is providing stiff competition with its treatment for hepatitis-C.For Fred Hassan, Schering-Plough's new chief executive, there is no upside in underestimating the extent of the problems he has inherited. But it will be a relief when management can confidently assess the depth of the malaise.For now, investors are left only with this statement of the obvious: the second half of the year could be even worse than the first.With both allergy and hepatitis franchises in trouble, an investor would need the patience of Job to look ahead with any enthusiasm to the results of the cholesterol drug joint venture with Merck. This should make some contribution to profits next year, but not enough to offset declines elsewhere until 2005 at the earliest.Even putting aside all the regulatory and pipeline problems, that leaves Schering-Plough looking expensive based on price/earnings comparisons. On consensus forecasts, its dividend is uncovered this year and next. With the liquidity position so precarious, a dividend yield of around 3 3/4per cent still provides little inducement to hold the stock.Mr Hassan, who turned Pharmacia round before selling it to Pfizer, has the right pedigree and is taking the right steps, including centralising the management structure. He is also right that there are no quick fixes. Therein lies the rub: an investment in Schering-Plough looks like dead money. Everyone loves a turnround story, but we are still at the beginning of chapter one, and it is a heavy volume.London Edition 1.

29 August 2003_1.Author:
Andrew Buncombe in Washington.

29 August 2003_1.chunks: THE BUSH administration has criticised as "immoral" a plan in Canada to open North America's first legal safe-injection zone for drug addicts. The "shooting gallery" is due to open later this year in Vancouver, where up to 12 addicts at a time will be given the equipment to inject safely, under the supervision of nurses. The scheme - to open in the city's impoverished Eastside - is federally funded by about C$1.2m (500,000) a year. Viviana Zanocco, of the Vancouver Coastal Health Authority, said the gallery would be exempt from federal drug laws, allowing heroin and cocaine users to visit without fear of arrest. "They would shoot up under supervision," she said. "It makes us the first health authority in Canada to have this exception, that hopefully will allow us to establish scientifically whether supervised injection sites can improve health outcomes and reduce harm to drug users." Similar safe-injection programmes have been set up across Europe and in Australia, and have reduced deaths from accidental overdoses. But John Walters, the White House "drugs czar", has criticised the plan, claiming it will lead to more deaths. "Drug abuse is a deadly disease. It's immoral to allow people to suffer and die from a disease we know how to treat. There are no safe injection sites." Canada already angered the US by planning to decriminalise possession of small amounts of marijuana. Asa Hutchinson, an undersecretary in the Department of Homeland Security, said this week that it was tightening border controls. "We're concerned about the increased drug activity," he said. "[The US] is adjusting as necessary our border inspections." Ann Livingston, of the Vancouver Area Network of Drug Users, said letting addicts inject at such sites would reduce the spread of HIV/Aids and hepatitis. "It is simply a public health initiative to do what's logical and compassionate and effective," she said. About 4,000 addicts live in the downtown area where the gallery is to be sited. It has one of the world's highest HIV infection rates.

29 August 2003_1.chunks: HEALTH tests for immigrants would be a practical, cost-effective policy that would stop the spread of diseases in Britain, a former Australian Health Minister has said (Anthony Browne writes).The Government is examining the feasibility of immigrant tests because health workers are worried about the dramatic rise in the number of HIV, TB and Hepatitis B cases being reported.The Conservatives recently adopted immigrant tests as official policy, but the proposal was denounced by HIV activists and the Liberal Democrats for being extremist, unethical and unworkable.However, Michael Wooldridge, Australia's Health Minister from 1996 to 2001, said that requiring immigrants to show that they will not be a threat to public health or a burden on the health service was supported across the political spectrum. "There isn't a debate about it, it is completely uncontroversial and just isn't a Left-Right issue," Dr Wooldridge said. "It would be controversial if the Government tried to get rid of them. "Australia has a target of 110,000 immigrants a year, but requires everyone who wants to move there to pay for a medical test with a doctor accredited by the Australian Government. The results of the test are then considered as part of a visa application.Those affected by HIV or TB are not automatically kept out if there are strong reasons for their being allowed into the country. "It's a very fair system that works perfectly. It means we know what's going on and the Immigration Minister can make an informed decision," Dr Wooldridge said.Critics say that the policy is unworkable because people would simply bribe doctors to give them a clean bill of health.Dr Wooldridge said: "It's perfectly workable, there's no corruption at all. There was a black market in fake X-rays from South East Asia 15 years ago, but it was cleaned up quickly. It's almost certainly cost-effective, and it's a very effective way of reducing the burden on the health system. "(c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2003

29 August 2003_1.Title: Sickly immigrants 'are adding pounds 1bn to costs of the NHS' pounds 130,000 cost of flying six Afghans home
29 August 2003_1.Author: STEVE DOUGHTY
29 August 2003_1.chunks: THE health service faces a bill of an extra pounds 1billion every year to treat immigrants and asylum seekers, medical analysts warned yesterday. Taxpayers are likely to face a huge and ever-increasing burden because of the growing flow of migrants from countries where complex infectious diseases are common, they said. Their report highlighted Aids, hepatitis B and C and tuberculosis as diseases that are spreading fast in countries from which large numbers of immigrants come to Britain. The cost to the NHS of treating new arrivals with Aids alone threatens to amount to pounds 900million each year, according to the analysis for the Migrationwatch UK think tank. It called for screening of immigrants before they leave their home countries to stop those with infections coming to Britain. Asylum seekers should be given health tests on arrival to reduce the risk of spreading infection, the report added. Roger Williams, professor of hepatology at University College London and a Migrationwatch adviser, said: 'The potential cost to the NHS is enormous in both financial and staff terms. It is absolutely essential that firm action be taken to prevent any further increase in this growing pool of potential infection. 'Even a fraction of the money spent in the UK would treat a far larger number of patients in their own countries.' A breakdown of potential costs carried out for the report examined the prevalence of serious infectious diseases in countries from which many immigrants come. Based on 2002 Home Office immigration figures and World Health Organisation estimates of the prevalence of disease, it calculated that immigrants brought in 25,000 cases of hepatitis B, 10,000 of hepatitis C and around 8,500 Aids cases. Analysts left dependants out of the reckoning and excluded students on the grounds that they are likely to return to their home countries before developing full symptoms of diseases. Nevertheless, the report said the cost of treating those with work permits and asylum seekers would be pounds 300million a year for hepatitis B and pounds 90million for hepatitis C. Treatments for both cost the NHS between pounds 10,000 and pounds 12,000 a year for each case. Every case of Aids costs pounds 15,000 a year. The report assumed immigrants with Aids will be treated for ten years, which means 6,000 cases arriving each year will cost the taxpayer pounds 900million. It said: 'Adding these sums together would suggest that each year's intake of asylum seekers and work permit holders could involve a potential cost to the NHS of pounds 1,290million. 'Such calculations cannot be precise but they certainly indicate that the potential costs are huge. This suggests an urgent need to introduce testing, at the very least for those, including students, who come from areas of high risk for those diseases.' The report said tuberculosis is becoming a major health problem in some areas by transmission from immigrants to the local population. The growing numbers of health care workers recruited from abroad should also be tested for infections, the report said. Migrationwatch UK chairman Sir Andrew Green said: 'It is clear that the introduction of pre-entry checks for work permit applications and students is an urgent priority. There are few other countries in the world where they are not already in place.' Last week senior doctors warned that hospitals in some parts of the country are being overwhelmed by asylum seekers with HIV. The Department of Health has said it is reviewing the need for compulsory screening of immigrants from countries with high levels of Aids.

29 August 2003_1.Title: Features - Health & Wellbeing - Who's at risk and what does it do?
29 August 2003_1.Author: No author in byline
29 August 2003_1.chunks: How does hepatitis C damage the health? The virus replicates in the liver, which becomes inflamed as the immune system fights to quell it. This leads to scarring and fibrosis and, if not detected, life-threatening cirrhosis and possibly cancer. The virus has a long incubation, possibly of more than 15 years. Liver damage often develops slowly with no obvious symptoms until disease is advanced. In some, the virus never causes problems but can be transmitted. How is the virus transmitted? Hepatitis C is carried in the blood, and those infected pass it on if their blood gets under the skin, or is mixed with the blood, of someone else. Sexual transmission is low. The virus is thought to be 10 times more infectious than HIV and can be passed through sharing a razor or toothbrush. Waters believes that that is how Norman became infected. Who is most at risk? Those who received blood transfusions before 1991. Drug users who inject and share needles. The problems caused by one-off needle-sharing in the Seventies are still emerging. A surgeon or health worker can pass blood to a patient's wound: there have been several hospital scares in this country. Patients can also infect health workers. Those who have an injection, transfusion, dental treatment or tattoo in a country with a high rate of hepatitis C and poor health standards. There is a five to seven per cent chance of transmission from a pregnant mother to her baby. What are the symptoms? At first, there may be vague feelings of malaise and lethargy, aching muscles, nausea and loss of appetite. In retrospect, Waters says she had all these and a feeling that her memory and concentration were fading. "I thought it must be a sign of age," she says. Other symptoms include joint pains and signs of jaundice. How is the virus tested? A blood sample is taken to check for antibodies to the virus. This indicates that an infection occurred at some time, though at least one person in five gets rid of the virus within a few months. If this result is positive, a second test checks for the presence of the actual virus. Blood tests will also be done to check liver function. What are the other hepatitis viruses? Hepatitis A is usually transmitted by contaminated food or water, although it can be transmitted in blood. It is infectious only for a short incubation period, and is not passed on by carriers. Hepatitis B can take much longer, possibly months, to incubate, and is transmitted through unsterile hypodermic needles, exchange of blood and sexual intercourse. Mainliners National Hepatitis C Resource Centre, helpline: 020 7582 5226. Hepatitis C Trust, www.hepcuk.info.

29 August 2003_1.chunks:
The Times (London)

October 18, 2003, Saturday

 Would the criminalisation of knowingly passing on an STI change attitudes to sex?

BYLINE: Anna Shepard

SECTION: Features; Body & Soul 4

LENGTH: 701 words

 
 Mohammed Dica was sentenced on Tuesday for inflicting "biological" grievous bodily harm, by infecting two women with HIV. Aids groups claim this will further stigmatise the disease and other sexually transmitted infections, as well as reducing honesty about sexual health.
 MICHELLE REID, chief executive of George House Trust, an Aids charity.
 "It will worsen attitudes rather than improve them. Fewer people will be prepared to be open about their sexual health, take tests or come forward for treatment. 
 This adds up to an environment of blame and ignorance. Every adult should be responsible for his or her own consenting sexual behaviour."
 ROWAN PELLING, editor of The Erotic Review.
 "Yes. It is entirely right that those responsible should have to face some kind of punishment. This should make sex safer, as people will think twice before passing on an STI. Herpes, for example, is only infectious during a flare-up, yet I know a couple of people who have recently contracted it from partners who must have been aware they had it. Criminalisation aims to prevent this kind of situation.
 However, legislating for sex is difficult; one cannot be too literal. I would impose a fine system. Between £10,000 and £20,000 compensation for passing on herpes would seem fair."
 TRIS REED SMITH, editor of the Pink Paper.
 "I fear the dangers resulting from criminalisation outweigh the protection it offers for a small number of cases. It will encourage the abdication of the shared responsibility of consensual sex. It could lull people into a false sense of security as they might think 'If my partner had an infectious disease, they would have been obliged to tell me'. The law can't act as a safety barrier because people might not even be aware they are infected. Where would you draw the line? People knowingly pass on infectious diseases all the time, from the common cold to herpes and hepatitis."
 DR THOMAS STUTTAFORD, The Times doctor and former STI clinician.
 "Yes. People who knowingly have sex to infect others have always shocked me; it shows a blatant disregard for someone else's health and life. But it does happen. There is an element of vindictiveness, an 'I've suffered, so you can bloody suffer' kind of thing. The thought of a sentence will encourage people to discuss things with their partners. You cannot compare Aids with other STIs because others can be cured. Even herpes can be kept at bay.
 Purposefully infecting someone is a psychopathic trait. People with psychopathic personalities can be controlled if the penalties are high enough."
 EUGENIE HOWARD-JOHNSTON, 22, student.
 "I hope so. So many people of my age and younger are reckless about unprotected sex and its consequences; the morning-after pill has reduced the risk of unwanted pregnancy, which seems to be everyone's prime concern, and they forget, or choose to ignore, that STIs have serious consequences too. It's as if we are all just crossing our fingers and hoping it won't happen to us. If only STI-testing was made compulsory, then we'd all have to know our status, rather than ride on the wave of blissful ignorance."
 HELEN AXBY, deputy chief executive of Marie Stopes International.
 "What would have a more beneficial affect on attitudes to sex is to focus upon the need for safe sex. Awareness is growing, but criminalisation might lead to the stigma that is attached to HIV spreading to other STIs. Chlamydia is a particular concern. The Department of Health's campaign has highlighted the infection's implications for fertility. If the criminal issue is highlighted, people may decide they would rather not know."
 GUS CAIRNS, living with HIV.
 "I think Aids is in a category of its own, but passing on diseases such as Hepatitis C, for which there is no cure, should be taken equally seriously. My main worry, as an HIV carrier, is that this poses a serious dilemma about disclosure. Automatic honesty in this kind of situation is not always realistic.
 There have been times when admitting you were HIV meant rejection and celibacy.
 The important message is: 'Ask if you're negative, tell if you're positive, and above all don't lie'."
