The Times (London)

November 19, 2003, Wednesday

 Hepatitis fear stalks suburbs of Pittsburgh

BYLINE: James Doran in Beaver, Pennsylvania

SECTION: Overseas news; 14

LENGTH: 751 words

 
 THE stench of chlorine disinfectant at the Beaver Valley Mall's deserted food court is almost unbearable.
 Every inch of it is scrubbed many times a day because three people who ate Mexican food at the shopping centre have died of hepatitis A and another 510 are infected.
 The smell of fear among residents of Beaver, Aliquippa and a string of other working-class suburbs of Pittsburgh affected by the outbreak is almost as strong.
 Earlena Powell, 72, often shopped and ate at Beaver Valley, but she will not go near the mall now and is terrified that she or one of her friends might contract the virus. 
 She is not alone. Sales of food at the mall have fallen by 40 per cent since the outbreak began, with total sales down 25 per cent.
 "I am very scared," Mrs Powell said. "Everybody is. Nobody wants to go up to the mall because the numbers of people with hepatitis are rising every day. Today it's 510, tomorrow it will be more. I can't believe so many cases are coming from Chi-chi's (a restaurant in the mall). There must be some other reason."
 Health officials are puzzled by the virulence of the outbreak, which started last month at Chi-chi's, as hepatitis A is rarely fatal.
 Last Friday John Spratt, 46, of Aliquippa, a small town a few miles down the road from the mall where Mrs Powell also lives, became the third person to die from the virus.
 Jeff Cook, 38, of Aliquippa, and Dineen Wieczorek, 51, of Hopewell Township, also died this month. It is unusual for people so young, and in seemingly good health, to die from hepatitis A.
 Mr Cook, the first to die, was a healthy father of two. On October 6 he ate a plate of chicken and beef fajitas at Chi-chi's and soon after came down with what he thought was flu. He was sent home from hospital twice as his symptoms were not very bad. Hepatitis was not diagnosed.
 Mr Cook was nauseous and had a fever, but did not immediately develop the yellowed skin and eyes of jaundice associated with hepatitis A. By November 2, his condition had worsened. His temperature soared, his skin turned yellow and he became delirious.
 Within two days he was told that he would undergo liver transplant surgery. On November 7 he died as the new organ failed to save him.
 The death toll could rise to five this week as two more victims were admitted to hospital in Pittsburgh on Saturday. One of them is said to be in a critical condition.
 The epidemic is far from over, as about 55 more people every day have had the virus diagnosed.
 Contaminated spring onions used to make Chi-chi's famous salsa are the most likely cause of the outbreak, but an investigation spanning another four American states is continuing. In September 280 people from Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio and Tennessee contracted the virus after eating raw spring onions at 12 restaurants.
 It has been suggested that a sewer pipe could have burst near to where the vegetables are grown in Mexico, contaminating an entire crop, but the investigation is not yet complete. Chi-chi's, a chain based in Kentucky, is co-operating with the investigation and has stopped using spring onions at its 100 restaurants.
 So far, 9,600 people in the Pittsburgh area have been tested for the virus and 8,600 have been inoculated. Health officials expect the number of cases in Pittsburgh to continue to rise, as hepatitis A has a month-long incubation period.
 The local health department started to offer antibody inoculations on November 5 to anyone who had visited Chi-chi's after October 22. This reduces the risk of hepatitis A, but it must be administered within two weeks of exposure to the virus.
 Chi-chi's is closed until January 2 while the US Centres for Disease Control and health department officials conduct their investigations. So far 12 members of staff have tested positive for the disease and all 60 employees remain under medical supervision.
 THE DISEASE.
 * Hepatitis A is one of a set of viral diseases of the liver, of which five - hepatitis A to E -have been identified.
 * Unlike hepatitis B and C, which are contracted from contaminated blood, hepatitis A is present in faeces and is most commonly transmitted via contaminated food, which has been prepared by an infected person with unwashed hands .
 * Symptoms include severe nausea, diarrhoea and jaundice. There is no chronic long-term infection, but the symptoms may last for weeks. Once recovered, patients must allow several months before drinking alcohol

29 August 2003_1.Title: A small victory for research.
29 August 2003_1.Author: CLIVE COOKSON and GEOFF DYER.
29 August 2003_1.chunks: A small victory for research - There is still no cure for the disease, but the three-month scientific onslaught has found out much, say Clive Cookson and Geoff Dyer.Sars, the first serious new disease of the 21st century, has so far made 8,300 people ill, killed 750 and disrupted the lives of countless more. The World Health Organisation estimates that its initial economic cost in east Asia, the region most affected, exceeds $30bn ( 18bn).But the scientific response to the emergence of this respiratory illness has been something of a triumph for medical research - and an important preparation for more dangerous infections, natural or artificial, that are bound sooner or later to sweep across the globe.In early March, when the world's microbiologists started to investigate an atypical form of pneumonia that had spread from mainland China to Hong Kong and Vietnam, its cause was a complete mystery. Since then a three-month scientific onslaught has revealed: the virus responsible, down to the last letter of its genetic code; its weak points that could be exploited to produce drugs and vaccines; the likely origin of Sars; the way infection spreads between people; and epidemiological predictions about the future course of the disease.A previously unknown member of the coronavirus family turned out, surprisingly, to cause Sars. For example, a German team has built a molecular model of a vital enzyme that Sars uses to infect cells. The structure suggests that an experimental drug used to treat the common cold - AG7088, developed by Agouron, a biotechnology subsidiary of Pfizer, the US pharmaceuticals group - could be adapted to block the Sars enzyme.The US Army's infectious disease unit and the NIH are screening many existing drugs to see if they might help treat Sars, including several Aids medicines that have been developed in recent years.BrioCryst, an Alabama company, is testing a drug under development for hepatitis C against Sars, while Medarex from New Jersey is trying to generate antibodies - one of the tools of the immune system - to Sars.With the outlook for the Sars epidemic size - and therefore the market for drugs and vaccines - so uncertain, public bodies such as the NIH will inevitably take a leading role in the early stages of the process.Meanwhile, there is one undoubted beneficiary of Sars: Asian wildlife. Last week, scientists confirmed suspicions that Sars originated in the preparation of wild animals for human consumption in south China, by detecting signs of infection in three species - palm civet, raccoon dog and ferret badger - obtained from a market in Guangdong.The Chinese authorities are cracking down on the wild animal trade, although it will be hard to stamp out an ancient culinary tradition.London Edition 1.

January 24, 2004, Saturday

 NHS hepatitis victims to get up to £45,000

BYLINE: Sam Lister

SECTION: Home news; 17

LENGTH: 256 words

 
 PATIENTS infected with hepatitis C after being given blood by the NHS will receive payments of up to £45,000 each, the Government said yesterday.
 The scheme, outlined by John Reid, the Health Secretary, will also include patients cleared of the virus through treatment and others who caught the virus from someone infected by NHS blood or blood products. 
 But the Department of Health, which plans to start the scheme in April, was accused last night of a gross oversight for excluding widows of haemophiliacs who had died from the disease as a result.
 Lord Morris of Manchester, the Labour peer and president of the Haemophilia Society, said that the omission was symptomatic of a scheme that fell far short of the benefits offered by other governments around the world. Dr Reid announced his intention to award ex-gratia payments to British hepatitis C victims last August.
 Announcing details of the scheme yesterday, he reiterated his belief that patients should receive payments on compassionate grounds.
 "I believe that these are fair and reasonable payments and I hope that they will help to alleviate some of the problems," Dr Reid said.
 Under the deal, every person in Britain who was alive on August 29, 2003, and whose hepatitis C was caused by NHS treatment with blood products before September 1991 will be eligible for an initial lump sum of £20,000.
 Patients with more advanced stages of the illness will get a further Pounds 25,000. The total payout is expected to be £100 million.

The Guardian (London) - Final Edition

January 24, 2004

Fury at abysmal level of payouts in blood scandal

BYLINE: James Meikle Health correspondent

SECTION: Guardian Home Pages, Pg. 5

LENGTH: 473 words

 
 Haemophiliacs and others infected with hepatitis C through contaminated blood products expressed outrage last night at the level of government ex gratia payments and the exclusion of widows and families from help.
 Payments of up to £45,000 were said to be barely a tenth of some awards in Ireland. Well over 200 Britons have already died from liver cancer or other illnesses caused by the hepatitis infection. 
 About 7,000 people may benefit from payouts later this year - many of them haemophiliacs infected by clotting factors before a satisfactory test for detecting the virus was introduced in 1991. The government accepts no responsibility for the infections and wants to settle the long-running dispute on compassionate grounds.
 Many clotting factors were imported fromAmerica, but some people were infected from transfusions carried out in this country before 1991.
 Others who can prove they contracted hepatitis C through close contact - such as sharing toothbrushes or having sex - with a person infected in this way will also receive payments, which in many cases will not exceed £20,000. But widows and dependants will not receive any aid otherwise.
 One widow, Harriet Bullock, said: "This is unbelievable. If I was a farmer and my husband was a sheep, I would have been compensated. I am so angry."
 Ken Bullock died five years ago, leaving three children and three grandchildren. He had continued to work as a civil engineer despite failing health.
 "The disease left him exhausted almost all the time," said his widow. "He couldn't play with the children or go for walks at the weekend."
 Other campaigners pointed out that some carers had given up jobs or could not start them because they were caring for sick patients. Haemophilia is a condition that affects only men. Those with families did get higher awards in the early 1990s when a similar scheme was announced for those accidentally infected with HIV.
 About 500 people are co-infected with the two diseases.
 Carol Grayson, a spokeswoman for Haemophilia Action UK whose husband Peter is one of these, said: "This is abysmal. It is a terrible illness and those women who gave up a career to care for their husbands are being treated in a disgusting manner."
 Karin Pappenheim, the Haemophilia Society's chief executive, said the exclusion of bereaved families was "a bitter blow to those who surely have suffered the worst harm from this tragic treatment disaster".
 The payments, announced by John Reid, the health secretary, amount to £20,000 per person plus £25,000 for those living with advanced stages of the disease. This falls short of the £50,000 recommended by a Scottish inquiry and is far less than the average £140,000 suggested by the society, based on a scheme in Canada.

January 2004_1.chunks: PATIENTS may soon be encouraged to provide their own mini-blood bank before undergoing surgery to counter the danger of contracting variant Creutzfeldt Jakob disease (vCJD).The move reflects growing concern about the safety of blood supplies after the Department of Health announced last week that a man had died after being given blood by a person incubating vCJD. Go ahead for hepatitis C drug

BYLINE: James Meikle, Health correspondent

SECTION: Guardian Home Pages, Pg. 6

LENGTH: 296 words

 
 Thousands of patients who developed chronic liver disease after being infected with hepatitis C will be switched to more effective and expensive treatments. The decision was announced as the government steps up its battle against hepatitis C, a potential killer which has shown alarming increases over the last decade. 
 Official endorsement for the drug pegylated interferon, usually taken in combination with another anti-viral drug, could significantly increase the drugs bill for fighting one of Britain's most serious public health threats.
 But the drug's success in treating many patients has meant that the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (Nice), the government's good-practice watchdog in England and Wales, has backed its far greater use.
 Only about 2,000 patients are thought at present to use either pegylated interferon or the more standard interferon alpha, but that number is expected to grow rapidly, using regimes which could be £3,200 more expensive for each patient. Even conservative estimates put the extra cost at around £11m a year.
 People infected with hepatitis C often carry it unknowingly for years. Between 50,000 and 500,000 people may have the virus. If the higher figure is accurate, far fewer than one in 10 people with the disease is diagnosed.
 Around one in five known to have been exposed to the virus will eventually develop acute hepatitis, which can take more than 20 years to become evident.
 Graham Foster, consultant hepatologist with Barts and the Royal London NHS trust, said: "This is the first positive step which will allow patients in the UK to receive the same treatment choice which has been available to patients in other parts of the world for many years."

25 March 2004_2.Author: No author found

The Guardian (London) - Final Edition

January 24, 2004

Fury at abysmal level of payouts in blood scandal

BYLINE: James Meikle Health correspondent

SECTION: Guardian Home Pages, Pg. 5

LENGTH: 473 words

 
 Haemophiliacs and others infected with hepatitis C through contaminated blood products expressed outrage last night at the level of government ex gratia payments and the exclusion of widows and families from help.
 Payments of up to £45,000 were said to be barely a tenth of some awards in Ireland. Well over 200 Britons have already died from liver cancer or other illnesses caused by the hepatitis infection. 
 About 7,000 people may benefit from payouts later this year - many of them haemophiliacs infected by clotting factors before a satisfactory test for detecting the virus was introduced in 1991. The government accepts no responsibility for the infections and wants to settle the long-running dispute on compassionate grounds.
 Many clotting factors were imported fromAmerica, but some people were infected from transfusions carried out in this country before 1991.
 Others who can prove they contracted hepatitis C through close contact - such as sharing toothbrushes or having sex - with a person infected in this way will also receive payments, which in many cases will not exceed £20,000. But widows and dependants will not receive any aid otherwise.
 One widow, Harriet Bullock, said: "This is unbelievable. If I was a farmer and my husband was a sheep, I would have been compensated. I am so angry."
 Ken Bullock died five years ago, leaving three children and three grandchildren. He had continued to work as a civil engineer despite failing health.
 "The disease left him exhausted almost all the time," said his widow. "He couldn't play with the children or go for walks at the weekend."
 Other campaigners pointed out that some carers had given up jobs or could not start them because they were caring for sick patients. Haemophilia is a condition that affects only men. Those with families did get higher awards in the early 1990s when a similar scheme was announced for those accidentally infected with HIV.
 About 500 people are co-infected with the two diseases.
 Carol Grayson, a spokeswoman for Haemophilia Action UK whose husband Peter is one of these, said: "This is abysmal. It is a terrible illness and those women who gave up a career to care for their husbands are being treated in a disgusting manner."
 Karin Pappenheim, the Haemophilia Society's chief executive, said the exclusion of bereaved families was "a bitter blow to those who surely have suffered the worst harm from this tragic treatment disaster".
 The payments, announced by John Reid, the health secretary, amount to £20,000 per person plus £25,000 for those living with advanced stages of the disease. This falls short of the £50,000 recommended by a Scottish inquiry and is far less than the average £140,000 suggested by the society, based on a scheme in Canada.

July 2006_1.Title: Copies of lost 'blood row' papers found: Families' delight as vital documents thought to have been destroyed turn up in solicitors' offices
July 2006_1.Author: No author in byline
July 2006_1.chunks: CRITICAL DOCUMENTS about Britain's contaminated blood scandal, which the government said had been accidentally shredded, are still available, The Observer has learned. The files provide vital evidence about what has been described as one of the worst medical disasters in the history of the NHS. Earlier this year, the Department of Health said that around 600 sensitive files had been 'inadvertently destroyed' by an inexperienced civil servant. However, in a striking new development it has emerged that several solicitors have copies of the documents, which detail meetings between the blood transfusion service, health boards, government officials and consultants. Some of the files were returned to the department of health last Tuesday. During the late Seventies and early Eighties, thousands of people, including nearly every haemophiliac in the country, were infected with deadly viruses such as Hepatitis C and HIV through infected blood. At least 800 have already died from Aids-related illnesses and hundreds more from chronic liver disease caused by hepatitis. Despite public health concerns over the contaminated blood, successive governments have refused to hold an inquiry into the tragedy. Investigations into tainted blood scandals in other countries have revealed evidence of wrongdoing on the part of government and pharmaceutical companies. Campaigners in the UK have accused authorities of an extensive cover-up. It is understood that other solicitors have been contacted and urged to return any files they have about the case. Senior legal figures who have seen the documents told The Observer they contain evidence of 'significant knowledge of risk and fault'. In particular, they claim that officials knew of the risks of contracting deadly diseases such as HIV and hepatitis from contaminated blood products years before they alerted patients. The latest development comes as a complaint was lodged with the parliamentary ombudsman seeking an investigation into the destruction of the original documents, which should have been stored for at least 25 years. Campaigners said they were delighted that copies of the paperwork still existed. 'We have waited more than 20 years to find out what happened,' said Carol Grayson, whose husband died after receiving contaminated blood imported to the UK from high-risk prisoners in America. 'We cannot turn the clock back but at last we have some hope in our search to find out the truth.' However, she expressed concerns that they had been returned to the department which had appears to have accidentally destroyed the original files. 'We would have preferred these copies to have been held by some independent or neutral body,' she said. Her solicitor has written to the DoH asking them to provide an undertaking to preserve the documents. A spokeswoman for the DoH confirmed that documents relating to the contaminated blood case had been received last week. 'The department will consider these papers in light of the Freedom of Information Act,' she added. < THE NUMBER of young people in Scotland languishing on 'hidden' waiting lists for NHS treatment has increased dramatically, according to new figures, which also show a significant cut in hospital beds available to treat sick children. More than 1,000 children are on deferred waiting lists, meaning they do not qualify for treatment within the current 'guarantee' of six months. At the same time the number of paediatric beds across the country has fallen by almost 15 per cent.

July 2006_1.Title: Comment: Leading article: These victims deserve justice
July 2006_1.Author: No author in byline
July 2006_1.chunks: ANDREW Evans was infected with HIV and hepatitis C by contaminated NHS blood products when he was five. At 16, he developed Aids, extinguishing his dreams of becoming a doctor. As we report today, in the following four years, his parents were repeatedly told that each next infection would be his last. He is now 29; thanks to medical advances, a powerful combination of drugs keeps the virus at bay, but brings horrendous side effects. As compensation for this error or, as the government refers to it, this 'unavoidable inadvertent systematic failure', he was awarded pounds 21,000 plus a monthly allowance of around pounds 300. A thousand others, most of them haemophiliacs, received similar payments. When the settlement was agreed, it was based on the belief that victims were facing imminent death. No one thought then there would be survivors in 2006, but there are - around 400 with HIV and thousands more living with hepatitis C. Many now find themselves in a dire financial position. These largely forgotten victims of one of the worst medical blunders in NHS history deserve help now. The Haemophilia Society has sent the Department of Health a detailed compensation plan for a second payment, along with increases in the monthly allowance. It deserves a generous response. Government has a moral responsibility to those who placed their faith in the national blood supply system that became infected with a deadly disease. It is unacceptable for these survivors to be left in poverty. As part of the original settlement, the victims were required to waive their rights to take any further action against the government. Because they were told they had only a few years to live, the last thing on their mind was their long-term financial security. Ministers should ignore this legal waiver and act humanely. An estimated 640 patients in Scotland were infected with hepatitis C through contaminated blood and have been been paid a total of Pounds 12 million in compensation, on average Pounds 18,000 each in a no-fault compensation deal. Hepatitis C is a life-threatening condition that can lead to liver cancer.But MSPs from the SNP and Scottish Socialist Party claim that only a full public inquiry will establish who knew what and when about the affair. Victim support groups have spent years calling for a public inquiry and compensation.The Scottish Executive says the science of hepatitis C and the blood product, Factor 8, was not fully understood until 1989 and denies the NHS was at fault or that patients were not informed of the risk. "One would have expected them to go to donors and recipients and go to the blood products and destroy them.The only thing they did was wait until donors came back between 1995 and 1997 and (then) told them they had tested positive for hepatitis C," he said. July 2006_1.Author: Eddie Dougall
July 2006_1.chunks: Mrs Thatcher's crucial role in introducing contaminated blood products into this country has never been given the prominence it deserves ('Tainted blood victims allege official cover-up', News last week). It was she who, for the saving of a pounds 1m or so in the Eighties, closed down our only laboratory producing factor-8 from donated blood, opting, instead, to import cheaper products from the US. At that time, Aids was almost unknown in Britain, but already appearing in some particular categories in the US, including intravenous drug users. As blood from the US was sold rather than donated, it was received disproportionately from those of this group with nothing left to sell to feed their habit. So haemophiliacs and others in this country infected with HIV and hepatitis C as a result of medical treatment, especially in the Eighties, have a lot to thank Maggie for. I do not think the continuing secrecy and heartless penny-pinching regarding just compensation would be part of a legacy Tony Blair wishes for. Eddie Dougall Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk

July 2006_1.Title: Hepatitis scourge
July 2006_1.Author: No author in byline
July 2006_1.chunks: A Pounds 4 million drive to reduce hepatitis C infection rates was launched by the Scottish Executive. About 1 per cent of the population -50,000 people -have the blood-borne virus, mainly through injecting drugs, compared with 0.5 per cent of the UK as a whole. An individual can be infected for decades before it is discovered.

July 2006_1.Title: Star to battle disease
July 2006_1.Author: No author in byline
July 2006_1.chunks: ROCK star Damien Dempsey wants to raise awareness of the deadly blood disease Hepatitis C - so others do not have to suffer the same fate as some of his friends. Hepatitis C causes liver cirrhosis and even cancer and is so easily spread it can be caught just by using someone else's toothbrush. Now Damien hopes a new campaign, called Hepatitis C - You Have Options, will encourage others to seek treatment before it is too late. Damien said: ''I've known a couple of people who've contracted the disease. "You can get Hepatitis C from blood transfusions, from tattoos, from doing coke if you share the same note with someone else when you're snorting coke. ''You can even get it from using someone else's toothbrush." Hepatitis C is known as a silent epidemic as sufferers may have it for years without knowing.

July 2006_1.Title: Lags 'infected' Brits;Exclusive
July 2006_1.Author: Emma Morton
July 2006_1.chunks: HUNDREDS of Brits were sentenced to death by US drug addicts and murderers who sold their Aids- ridden blood for just over Pounds 1.The full horror of the story unfolded yesterday as the movie Factor 8: The Arkansas Prison Blood Scandal hit the UK.In the film, US inmates reveal how criminals openly injected hard drugs -then flogged their blood. They had NO medical tests. The lags were asked if they were gay, a drug user or had hepatitis.Ex-prisoner Hezil Earl said: "People were shooting up drugs then going to the blood bank. One needle was used 20 or 30 times." The Haemophilia Society which screened the film -urged Health Secretary Patricia Hewitt to open an inquiry.In January, we told how the NHS gave 3,000 people infected blood from drug addicts and prostitutes in the 1970s and 1980s. Just 384 are still alive.

July 2006_1.Title: Aids scandal survivors demand new payout
July 2006_1.Author: Lorna Martin
July 2006_1.chunks: HUNDREDS OF survivors of one of the worst medical disasters in the history of the NHS are demanding millions of pounds in compensation from the government to alleviate the acute poverty in which many of them are now living. Haemophiliacs and other patients who were infected with HIV and hepatitis by contaminated blood have presented a detailed case to the Department of Health for one-off payments of up to pounds 750,000 each and a rise in monthly allowances they are already being paid. They say initial compensation paid in the early Nineties, ranging from pounds 21,000 to pounds 80,000, was calculated on the assumption - widely held by doctors then - that they were facing imminent death. Their request comes amid growing accusations of a massive cover-up after officials admitted that hundreds of crucial documents about their case had been destroyed by a civil servant. This issue is due to be discussed in the House of Lords on Wednesday when there will be calls for a government statement to explain why the paperwork was shredded. While the vast majority of those infected during the scandal in the late Seventies and early Eighties have died, around 380 haemophiliacs and 20 other patients given contaminated transfusions during surgery are still alive. An investigation by The Observer has found that many are living in extreme poverty on state benefits and a trickle of cash from a trust fund. All those infected were urged to accept the original settlement because fighting on through the courts for more would have taken years. They were required to sign away their right to take future legal action against the government. Survivors and their supporters say this has left them in impossible hardship. They point to a recent case in which a man infected with a variant HIV virus from contaminated blood during surgery at the private Nuffield Hospital in Birmingham was awarded pounds 750,000 after a seven-year court battle. Lord Morris of Manchester, the campaigning former Labour MP who is president of the Haemophilia Society, said a grave injustice had been committed and he urged the government to act with 'decency and humanity' to alleviate the survivors' suffering. 'The lives of these people have been absolutely devastated by what is without doubt the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS,' he said. 'These people and their dependants urgently need more help. The money they have received so far goes nowhere near compensating them for the damage inflicted on them by the NHS.' Martin Harvey, chief executive of the Macfarlane Trust charity, which assembled the funding request, said: 'No one expected, nearly 20 years on, that there would have been any survivors of this terrible error. However there are many living in acute poverty. 'The capital payments given to them in the early Nineties, which were in any case small, have long since been spent, often on the advice of consultants on the basis of their likely imminent deaths.' Gary Kelly, 43, who was infected with HIV during treatment for leukaemia, said the mistake had left him struggling financially, physically and emotionally. 'The NHS cured me of cancer, which was wonderful, but in the process, they infected me with HIV. Since that day 20 years ago, I've been unable to work, form a relationship and have sometimes struggled to pay bills,' he said. He was awarded pounds 43,500 in 1992 but, having been told he had no more than five years to live, spent it on clearing his debts and taking a holiday. Haydn Lewis, a haemophiliac, was infected with HIV and hepatitis C by the tainted blood and passed the HIV to his wife, Gaynor. In 17 years he has attended more than 150 funerals for fellow haemophiliacs given tainted blood. 'Money is important but much more than that I want an explanation,' he said. 'It is absolutely scandalous that the government refuses both to compensate victims or hold an inquiry into what happened. I want to be able to tell my sons and my wife who was responsible.' Margaret Unwin, chief executive of the Haemophilia Society, said the patients had been treated 'disgracefully and with a lack of respect'. 'When the payments were initially made it was on the assumption that people would not live for long. Some still are alive, and they are living with unpleasant illnesses because of an NHS blunder. There has never been an apology and to add insult to injury these people are increasingly existing in hardship.' They needed a decent standard of living. A spokeswoman for the Department of Health said the patients' request had been received and was being considered.

July 2006_1.Title: Midwife's legal bid
July 2006_1.Author: No author in byline
July 2006_1.chunks: A MIDWIFE is to sue the hospital where she works over the death of her son.Carol Holland, 50, says doctors gave David four times the recommended dose of drugs after misdiagnosing his condition.David, 28, was admitted to Whiston Hospital in Merseyside with alcoholic hepatitis but died after being given drugs for heart failure.Carol said: "I want to make sure it does not happen to any other family. "(C) The Sun, 2006

July 2006_1.Title: Horror testers' NHS job
July 2006_1.Author: Emma Morton
July 2006_1.chunks: THE company which ran the disastrous "Elephant Man" drugs trials has been hired by the NHS - to run more tests on human guinea pigs.American-based trial company Parexel plans to use a potentially risky blood-clotting treatment on 60 sick British patients.A drug called Fybex - manufactured with blood from US donors - will be given to humans for the first time. Patients volunteering for the trials will be warned that the treatment carries a slight risk of passing on viruses - including HIV and Hepatitis C - if the blood is not screened properly.In March six patients fell critically ill at the Parexel private trial centre at Northwick Park Hospital in North WestLondon.All were given injections of an anti-inflammatory drug, TGN1412.One victim, Nav Modi, 24, likened himself to the Elephant Man after suffering grotesque swelling of his head and neck.A letter inviting patients to take part in the new trials warns: "Fybex is an investigational new treatment, which has not yet been given to humans. "Parexel has sent the letter to patients awaiting operations. Some are to undergo major surgery including double hip replacements. No patients have been offered cash.The Hammersmith NHS Trust in West London is being used as a recruitment centre for the volunteers.A woman awaiting an op, who asked not to be named, said: "When those blokes fell seriously ill the Government said it was a private matter and nothing to do with the health service. Here's proof that they are cap in hand with Parexel.

July 2006_1.Title: Shocking rise in sex diseases
July 2006_1.Author: No author in byline
July 2006_1.chunks: SEXUALLY-transmitted infections in Ireland have nearly TREBLED over the past decade, it was revealed last night.More than 10,000 Irish people caught diseases through unsafe sex last year.But many more people with STIs have no idea they are infected.A staggering 3,000 Irish people were infected with chlamydia alone last year - ELEVEN times the number ten years ago.Another 2,899 contracted genital warts, the highest on record.Half of men and 26 per cent of women said drink contributed to them having sex without condoms.The National Women's Health Council, which carried out the research, called on the Government to launch a screening programme.Its report said: "The role that alcohol plays in risky sexual behaviour is alarming. "Meanwhile, Bob Geldof launched Global Hepatitis C Week and warned 20,000 people here are infected by the disease.He added: "Stigma, shame and fear can suffocate awareness. "(C) The Sun, 2006

July 2006_1.Title: Crazy payouts;Sun says;Leading Article
July 2006_1.Author: No author in byline
July 2006_1.chunks: BRITAIN has managed to avoid the worst excesses of the compensation culture - up until now.A Glasgow man is set to receive a six-figure payout after being dismissed eight days into a new job.The tribunal believed he had been subjected to discrimination on the grounds of his sexuality.A person's sexuality should NEVER preclude them from employment.But what about the other cases that are far more deserving?Is contracting hepatitis C through an infected blood transfusion really worth less than losing your job?Can losing your baby be less traumatic than being on the receiving end of jibes?We have to structure compensation correctly and cap these crazy payments. (C) The Sun, 2006

July 2006_1.Title: Letter: SEX DOCTOR - Does lover's Hep C put me at risk?
July 2006_1.Author: Dr Catherine Hood
July 2006_1.chunks: Dear Dr Cath AN ex-boyfriend of mine has Hepatitis C. We split up a while ago, but should I be worried? HEPATITIS C is a virus carried in the blood which affects the liver. A staggering 200,000 people in the UK might be infected - but symptoms often don't show, so people don't get tested. Hep C causes inflammation of the liver. Twenty per cent will recover quickly, but some will have longer-term liver problems, including cirrhosis and cancer. The virus is mainly spread by blood-to-blood contact. It is possible to get it through sex, but this is uncommon. You'd be more at risk if you were an injecting drug user or had received a blood transfusion before 1991, when blood started to be screened for Hep C. It can also be passed by sharing toothbrushes or razors, which may sometimes explain why the virus spreads to sexual partners. I don't think you should worry too much, but it is worth asking your doctor for a blood test. For more information visit www.britishlivertrust.org.uk

July 2006_1.Title: HIV test for lags' fight jail officer
July 2006_1.Author: Sun Reporter
July 2006_1.chunks: A PRISON officer splattered by a fighting lag's blood is being tested for HIV.The staff member at Limerick Prison is waiting anxiously for results of blood tests following the brawl.He is being checked for HIV, Hepatitis A and Hepatitis B after coming into contact with blood from one of three prisoners.Three officers stepped in to break up the fight between the men -all in their 20s and from the city.The officers were treated at the scene for shock, bruising and blood splattering.They also received a course of medication.Prison chiefs are worried that one officer may have come into direct contact with blood during the brawl on Friday.Results of the blood tests are not expected until next week. The fighting inmates were confined to isolation units at the jail.It was the second violent incident at the jail in less than a week. Last Wednesday two officers were treated in hospital after being attacked by two inmates.

July 2006_1.Title: Doherty's 'jab' girl AIDS fear
July 2006_1.Author: Tony Bonnici
July 2006_1.chunks: THE GIRL pictured with rocker Pete Doherty as he stuck a syringe into her arm has told how she feared she had caught AIDS.And pretty Laura McEvoy accused the Babyshambles junkie of using her for a sick publicity stunt.The photo was taken in Doherty's filthy East London flat in March. Its publication sparked outrage. Essex girl Laura, 21, below, who had a one-night stand with the star, said: "Getting involved with him was so dangerous. "He never told me he was going to put the syringe in my arm. I'd never have agreed. When I realised I was horrified. "He apologised and said he thought I knew what he was going to do. I asked if the needle was clean and he said it was. But I had an AIDS test and a vaccination for hepatitis. I was very scared and upset. "She said Kate Moss's on-off boyfriend Doherty, 27, wanted her blood for a bizarre art work - he created it by spraying blood on the walls. (C) The Sun, 2006

July 2006_1.Title: 'Shared banknote' health warning to cocaine users
July 2006_1.Author: Lauren Veevers
July 2006_1.chunks: Experts are warning of a potential "health time bomb" from drug users snorting cocaine through banknotes, threatening to infect thousands with hepatitis C. They fear that the sharing of banknotes by cocaine users will cause the numbers of those infected with hepatitis C to soar. They are particularly concerned because eight out of 10 carriers don't know they have the virus. The disease is carried through the blood, and users can easily fail to notice small traces of blood on their banknotes, which are then passed around a group. Without treatment, hepatitis C can lead to chronic liver disease. The Department of Health estimates that there are 200,000 people infected with hepatitis C in Britain, but the Hepatitis C Trust fears the number could be much higher. Charles Gore, the chief executive of the trust, said: "Estimates show that around 5,000 new cases of hepatitis C are diagnosed every year - but they are mainly through chance. Because so many are undiagnosed we can't tell what kind of problem we are looking at. When 5,000 banknotes were tested in London [in 2000], 99 per cent of them had traces of cocaine on them. That tells us that there is potentially a massive problem in diagnosis and people's awareness of how easily hepatitis C can be contracted. "We are concerned that if more is not done to alert people to the dangers of sharing, then what is already a big problem risks being turned into a health time bomb." Professor Graham Foster, of St Mary's Hospital, London, said: "Sharing banknotes or straws is a significant risk factor that people need to be more aware of . Although the risk of contracting hepatitis C through snorting is lower than through sharing a needle, it is still there." He added: "We can detect levels of hepatitis C for weeks after it has been on a surface, [but] infectious levels will only remain for a few hours, maybe more." The trust has set up a campaign entitled What Not to Share, and is asking for donations to mark World Hepatitis Awareness Day today. THE FACTS According to the latest Home Office figures 750,000 Britons take cocaine every year. In an American study last year 4.7 per cent of people who sniffed or snorted cocaine or heroin tested positive for hepatitis C. There is no vaccine for the hepatitis C virus. Cocaine costs around 30 per gram. According to health charity Drug Scope it's cheapest in Liverpool and Birmingham.

July 2006_1.Title: Children who have liver transplants commonly get chronic hepatitis that is not detected by routine blood tests;New medical research;Health
July 2006_1.Author: No author in byline
July 2006_1.chunks: Children who undergo liver transplants commonly have chronic hepatitis that is not detected by routine blood tests, claims a study in Hepatology (May) by British researchers. The Birmingham Children's Hospital study followed children for ten years after their transplants and found that those with chronic hepatitis developed scarring on their livers which may threaten the long-term success of their transplants. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2006

July 2006_1.Title: Wake-up call as a million drug needles are missing
July 2006_1.Author: Jude Sheerin
July 2006_1.chunks: DRUGS experts have warned that figures revealing heroin addicts have dumped up to one million dirty needles in the last year were a "wake-up call" to the authorities. More than 2.9 million clean needles were issued to drug users in Scotland in 2004/5 - but only 1.9 million were returned, according to Scottish Executive figures. Professor Neil McKeganey, director of the Centre for Drug Misuse, said an urgent review is needed of procedures at some 200 drug clinics across Scotland to find out how such a large number of syringes could disappear. Prof McKeganey added: "These are shocking figures and these needles are undoubtedly being dumped in areas where children and other people can get access to them and catch hepatitis C. "It's a dangerous and unacceptable situation. "We really need to look closely at what staff in these needle exchanges are doing to ensure drug users return their syringes and find out where these discarded needles are ending up. "This is really a wake-up call because a shortfall of one million needles indicates that something is going very wrong here." The Executive figures show that in 2004/5, of 539,896 needles issued in Greater Glasgow just 327,381 were returned. In Lothian, more than 279,000 were given out but only 82,262 were returned over the same period. Grampian gave out the second highest number of needles - 520,096 - and 357,991 were handed back. The Executive advises drug workers to give addicts new needles in exchange for dirty ones to prevent them from sharing and spreading hepatitis C. The strategy is supposed to stop used needles from being dumped in streets and parks where they are a danger. The Executive insisted many dirty needles dumped in specially provided safe bins were not counted. A spokeswoman said: "Needle exchanges are an essential part of strategies aimed at preventing spread of blood-borne viruses. Public safety is always of paramount importance. "That's why guidance makes clear that there should be a requirement to return used equipment for safe disposal at exchanges before fresh equipment is issued. "Drug workers do, however, need the flexibility to use their professional judgment when dealing with people who have chaotic lifestyles." There are an estimated 51,000 heroin addicts in Scotland and 30,000 people with the highly infectious hepatitis C.

July 2006_1.Title: Why is my liver in trouble when I am a moderate drinker?;Letter;Health
July 2006_1.Author: Dr Thomas Stuttaford
July 2006_1.chunks: Answers your health questionsA reader, who spends much of his time overseas as an aid worker in Africa, India and Pakistan, has written to say that a recent blood test revealed abnormal liver function. He assures us that he is only a moderate drinker and hasn't had any blood transfusions at any time of his life. He did, however, have major orthopaedic surgery in Africa 15 years ago.When he goes to a malarial zone he takes Malarone. He has never used illegal drugs.Patients who are found to have raised liver enzymes during a routine examination present their doctors with a difficult problem. The easy, idle, thoughtless way of dealing with an unexplained small increase in one or more of the liver enzymes in a patient is to suggest that he or she is being dishonest about their alcohol intake and accept that this is the explanation. Recent research has shown that modest drinkers are, like problem drinkers, likely to under-report their intake.Our reader is obviously well informed. He has already considered many of the points in his medical history that could be relevant. We have to accept that he is accurate about his alcohol intake.He has obviously understood the importance of blood-borne hepatitis B and C and has told us that he has never had a transfusion or used injectable drugs. There are many other ways that hepatitis C might be transmitted other than by contact with contaminated blood or through transfusions or by drug abuse.It is noteworthy that he had major surgery before this danger was recognised. He hasn't mentioned tattooing or body piercing that are occasional causes of transmission of hepatitis C, nor acupuncture, although reputable acupuncturists are as conscientious about sterility as doctors.Medical staff, care workers, boxers, rugby footballers, other contact sports athletes and even kindly people who bind up the minor injuries of children are all at some slight risk of being contaminated with infected blood. In an appreciable proportion of cases of hepatitis C the source of the infection is never traced.Very rarely, Malarone, an excellent anti-malarial, may cause an increase in liver enzymes. This is one possible cause, even perhaps the probable cause of the minor liver function changes. Another consideration in his case is that several tropical diseases may cause liver damage. Should he be worried? Not worried, but certainly he needs careful monitoring, and should have immediate blood tests to see if he has ever had hepatitis B or C.If the liver function tests don't return to normal he should ask his GP if it would be wise to consult a hepatologist, who may seek a second opinion from a specialist in tropical diseases.Anyone and everyone who has abnormal liver function of unknown origin wherever they live, and whatever their lifestyle, needs to have their blood tested to make certain that they haven't picked up hepatitis C.There are somewhere between 400,000 and 900,000 people in Britain with hepatitis C who are unaware that they carry this potentially lethal virus, but are initially free of symptoms.There are also 200,000 who have the diagnosis. It is important to detect hepatitis C at an early stage before there is appreciable liver damage and at a time when it is more easily treated.Overall, when taking into account the varying response to treatment of the many different types of hepatitis C, combined anti-viral therapy will now clear the body of any detectable hepatitis C virus in 40 per cent of cases. In patients carrying some types of hepatitis C the percentage is appreciably greater.timesonline.co.uk/talkingpoint E-mail Dr Stuttaford your questions on ovarian cancer(c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2006

July 2006_1.Title: A HEPATITIS CURE ON NHS; DAILY MAIL REPORTER
July 2006_1.Author: No author in byline
July 2006_1.chunks: A BREAKTHROUGH treatment for hepatitis C is to be offered on the Health Service, it was announced yesterday. It means hundreds of thousands of people could be cured of the infection that can lead to fatal liver disease. The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence approved the use of two drugs - Pegasys and Ribavirin - to be offered as a combination therapy for those suffering from mild hepatitis C. Trials show the drugs can cure the disease in more than 80 per cent of such cases within a year and that treatment with the two drugs can 'cure' two genetic types of the infection after 24 weeks.

July 2006_1.Title: Lag drug kits
July 2006_1.Author: No author in byline
July 2006_1.chunks: PRISONERS are to be handed drug-taking kits in a move to stop needle-sharing among addicted inmates. Last year alone, nearly 2,000 drugs packages were intercepted by warders and a report by boffins said drug taking behind bars was "impossible" to stop. Now, Scottish Prison Service health chief Dr Andrew Fraser has ordered an experiment at one jail in a bid to cut the spread of Hepatitis C and HIV. The trial, at Aberdeen's Craiginches Prison, does not need approval by the Scottish Executive.

July 2006_1.Title: Needle horror at new flat;Exclusive
July 2006_1.Author: Annabelle Steggles
July 2006_1.chunks: A HORRIFIED dad told last night how he was jagged by a junkie's needle - just hours after he moved into a council flat. Matt Smith, 23, pricked his finger on the syringe, which had been shoved down the side of an armchair at the flat in Ibrox, Glasgow. The incident happened as he placed four-week-old daughter Erin on the seat to change her nappy. Matt said: "I saw what looked like a Biro tucked down the side so I went to pull it out. "Suddenly I felt a sharp pain on one of the fingers on my right hand and then I realised it was a needle. Blood  "I've now got to have blood tests as I could have HIV or hepatitis - it's really scary. "But my main concern was for Erin. What if she'd been scratched by the needle and not me?" Matt then searched the the room and uncovered dozens more syringes and two plastic boxes stuffed full of used needles. He and partner Sarah McBride, 20, moved into the filthy property on Tuesday. A spokesman for Glasgow City Council said: "We are sorry for any distress suffered." (C) The Sun, 2006

19 February 2007_1.Title: Contaminated blood inquiry
19 February 2007_1.Author: No author in byline
19 February 2007_1.chunks: An independent public inquiry is to be held into the supply to haemophiliacs of contaminated NHS blood (a correspondent writes).The Labour peer Lord Archer of Sandwell, a former Solicitor-General, is to conduct the inquiry after a campaign by Lord Morris of Manchester, president of the Haemophilia Society and a former Minister for the Disabled, who said that 1,757 haemophilia patients who were exposed to HIV and/or hepatitis C-contaminated NHS blood and blood products had died since being infected. "Many more are now terminally ill," the peer claimed.Lord Morris said that, of 4,670 such patients exposed to hepatitis C, 1,243 were also exposed to HIV and that, notwithstanding improvements in treatments, only 2,552 patients with hepatitis C and 361 with HIV were still alive. The situation has been described by Professor Lord Winston as "the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS".

19 February 2007_1.Title: Aids hell probed
19 February 2007_1.Author: No author in byline
19 February 2007_1.chunks: AN official probe into how thousands of Brits got Aids and hepatitis from infected blood was announced yesterday.Almost 1,800 people - mostly haemophiliacs - died after receiving tainted products from the NHS in the 1970s and 80s. At least 3,000 were infected in total.Last year The Sun revealed that some of the blood came from Aids-ridden US prisoners.Campaigners spent 20 years calling for a public inquiry - which Health Secretary Patricia Hewitt agreed to yesterday.Haemophilia Society chairman Roddy Morrison said: "It's an historic day. "(C) The Sun, 2007

19 February 2007_1.Title: SEX DOCTOR: Am I just like Anita?
19 February 2007_1.Author: Dr Catherine Hood
19 February 2007_1.chunks: I'M 46 and have just heard that an ex-boyfriend I was with 12 years ago has hepatitis C. Now I'm worried I may have caught it just like the Body Shop's Anita Roddick. HEPATITIS C is a virus transmitted in blood. You can become infected from an infected blood transfusion, like Anita Roddick did, or from injecting drugs and sharing needles. The virus is in semen so it's possible to catch it through sex. There are thousands of people in the UK who are infected with the virus but don't know it, as they may not get symptoms for years. But long-term the virus can damage the liver. It's unlikely you caught the virus from sex but it is worthwhile going to your doctor for a check-up. The virus can be easily detected with a blood test. If you do have the virus you may need no immediate treatment, with your doctor keeping an eye on how your liver is functioning through regular blood tests. For more info see www.hepc.nhs.uk

19 February 2007_1.Title: Anger as 'hep C widows' left out in the cold: Around 200 women living without financial aid
19 February 2007_1.Author: Lorna Martin
19 February 2007_1.chunks: WIDOWS WHOSE husbands died after receiving contaminated NHS blood are urging the government to close a loophole which denies them access to financial assistance. Around 200 women in the UK, many of whom are pensioners and living in severe hardship, are excluded from the fund because their partners, who all suffered from haemophilia, died from hepatitis C complications before an official cut-off date to be considered for compensation. Had they died later or from an HIV-related illness, they would have been entitled to support. The women are stepping up their campaign after the announcement on Monday that there is to be an independent public inquiry into the supply of tainted blood products to haemophiliacs in the UK. For the past 15 years, The Observer has supported calls for an inquiry and adequate compensation for those affected in what the Labour peer Lord Robert Winston has described as the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS. More than 4,800 haemophiliacs in Britain were infected with hepatitis C, and 1,200 of those also contracted HIV after being given contaminated blood products during the Eighties and early Nineties. More than 1,700 have since died, and many more are terminally ill. Campaigners say they have suffered extreme financial hardship because most of them are uninsurable, unemployable and unable to make adequate provision for their dependants. Successive governments have ruled out inquiries but they have established two funds to help those affected - the Skipton Fund for those infected with hepatitis and the MacFarlane Trust for those who contracted HIV. All but the group of women known as 'hep C widows' have received or are entitled to some form of financial assistance from one of the funds. The anomaly in the scheme is highlighted by the case of Maureen Murphy, a 69-year-old widow from Liverpool. Her husband, William, was one of three brothers with haemophilia who died after receiving contaminated blood. The widows and dependants of his two brothers, who contracted HIV, have received support. However, because her husband contracted hepatitis C, which is now regarded as a more deadly disease in the western world than HIV, from the tainted blood and died before August 2003, Mrs Murphy is not entitled to any form of financial help. 'This is such an unjust and indefensible situation,' Mrs Murphy said. 'This is a dreadful thing to say but in the lottery of NHS blood infection, it would have been easier if my husband had got HIV rather than hepatitis C.' Mrs Murphy gave up her work to become a full-time carer for her husband. Because of the problems surrounding haemophilia, they were unable to take out insurance policies or mortgage protection. Greg Murphy, her son, said the government had created a 'deplorable caveat'. 'Unlike widows of HIV victims, who were rightly compensated my mum has never received a penny. She has suffered the same pain at the loss of her husband. How can the government possibly decide that her suffering is less because he died from hepatitis rather than HIV?' Harriet Bullock, who is in her seventies and who lost her husband, Ken, eight years ago, said the situation had devastated her family's life . 'I feel so angry that there is a small group of us who are excluded sim ply because our husbands died before the government decided to create the fund. No one has ever said sorry. I can't yet begin to mourn Ken.' Lord Morris of Manchester, president of the Haemophilia Society, who initiated the public inquiry after years of campaigning, said: 'It is a gross anomaly that widows of those infected with hepatitis C are excluded. It illustrates the piecemeal way this tragedy has been dealt with.' A spokesman for the Department of Health said there were no plans to offer financial support to the widows, and stressed that the scheme was designed to make lump sum payments to those living with hepatitis C and not to compensate for bereavement.

19 February 2007_1.Title: HEPATITIS C: THE SILENT KILLER
19 February 2007_1.Author: REBECCA SMITH
19 February 2007_1.chunks: AT least 5,000 people in Britain have contracted hepatitis C from infected blood transfusions. Blood bought in from America in the Seventies and Eighties came from prisoners or donors who were paid and was found to be infected with both hepatitis C and HIV. Only 3,000 of the affected patients are still alive, but it is feared that even now there may be more who were infected but still do not know. GPs are testing for the disease more often, but campaigners say this is still not enough - if caught early it can be successfully treated, but of the estimated 231,000 Britons with hepatitis only 7,000 have received treatment. Most carriers will have no symptoms. One in four people with the disease will clear it naturally from their body and only one in five of the remainder will suffer severe liver damage. Until recently only those with moderate to severe infections were treated, but health bosses now say patients with a mild case should also be considered for treatment. Hepatitis C is passed on by sharing bodily fluids. This can occur through blood transfusions, unprotected sex and using dirty hypodermic needles, but also through unhygienic body piercing and even sharing a toothbrush.

The Guardian - Final Edition

February 15, 2007 Thursday

Anita Roddick reveals she has hepatitis C: Entrepreneurs condition leads to disease of liver Virus transmitted through blood transfusion

BYLINE: Sam Jones

SECTION: GUARDIAN HOME PAGES; Pg. 5

LENGTH: 478 words

Dame Anita Roddick, the founder of the Body Shop, revealed yesterday that she is carrying hepatitis C and has cirrhosis of the liver, one of the condition's long-term effects. The 64-year-old entrepreneur said she had contracted hepatitis C through a blood transfusion while giving birth to her youngest daughter, Sam, in 1971. 
"I have hepatitis C. It's a bit of a bummer but you groan and move on," she said yesterday. "I had no idea that I had this virus. I was having routine blood tests when it showed up."
Hepatitis C causes inflammation of the liver, and can eventually lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer. But in a posting on her website yesterday, Dame Anita said she remained phlegmatic about the future.
"I do have cirrhosis. I could still have a good few years - maybe even decades - of life left but it's hard to say. I could be facing liver cancer tomorrow."
She also announced that she had become a patron of the Hepatitis C Trust, a UK charity she discovered to two years ago when she first found out she had the virus. She called for hepatitis C to be taken more seriously as a "public health challenge" and questioned the success of a government awareness campaign.
"Having hep C means that I live with a sharp sense of my own mortality, which in many ways makes life more vivid and immediate," she said.
"It makes me even more determined to just get on with things."
Dame Anita said that more public money needed to be spent on raising awareness of the disease, which is thought to affect more than 230,000 adults in England alone. "I've always been a bit of a 'whistleblower' and I'm not going to stop now," she said.
"I want to blow the whistle on the fact that hep C must be taken seriously as a public health challenge and must get the attention and resources that it needs."
A Department of Health spokesman said the government recognised the virus as "an important public health issue", and was spending £4m on campaigns to raise awareness of the threat posed by hepatitis C. "It is encouraging that these campaigns appear to be leading to increased diagnosis of hepatitis C," she said.
"The Health Protection Agency in England has recorded a rise of around 5,600 (cases) in 2002 to around 7,600 in 2005."
Charles Gore, the chief executive of the Hepatitis C Trust, said: "We are absolutely delighted that someone so dynamic and with such a history of fighting passionately for important causes has agreed to support us."
guardian.co.uk/health
At a glance
The hepatitis C virus is transmitted through blood-to-blood contact, and more than 90% of cases arise in injecting drug users. It can also be passed through transfusions and from mother to baby, before or during birth. Unprotected sex carries a small risk and sharing razors or toothbrushes can also be risky. The virus is not transmitted through normal social contact such as touching, hugging or kissing.

19 February 2007_1.Title: The question How serious is hepatitis C?
19 February 2007_1.Author: Sarah Boseley
19 February 2007_1.chunks: Very - although you might, like Anita Roddick, not find this out for over 30 years. "I could still have a good few years, even decades, of life left, but it's hard to say. I could be facing liver cancer tomorrow," she said yesterday after blood tests revealed she had been carrying the disease since 1971. Hepatitis C is often described as a silent pandemic. The Health Protection Agency recorded 7,600 cases of infection in 2005, but only about one in 10 of those who have it have been diagnosed. Roddick is not unusual. The virus, which causes liver damage that can result in cirrhosis (as Roddick's has) and cancer, has non-specific symptoms and often goes unnoticed until things get serious. Roddick says it is a scandal that the government hasn't tried harder to make people aware of hepatitis C. They have spent pounds 40m advertising the switchover to digital television but only pounds 3m warning us of this potentially deadly virus. One reason few people know about it is stigma. While Roddick was infected through a blood transfusion in the era when the NHS did not test donated blood for the virus, many others have picked up hepatitis C through injecting drugs with shared needles (it does not seem to be easily passed on through sex). After much wrangling and delay, the government agreed a compensation scheme for those infected with hepatitis C through blood transfusion. The Skipton Fund pays pounds 20,000 to all who are eligible, with pounds 25,000 more when their illness becomes "advanced" - cirrhosis or worse. There are vaccines for hepatitis A and B, but none against C, the most dangerous. Treatments have improved but are only 50% effective. Survival rates for those who develop liver cancer are low. For those whose cirrhosis gets so bad that the liver cannot function, a transplant is the only option. Sarah Boseley

19 February 2007_1.Title: Celebrity carriers could raise awareness
19 February 2007_1.Author: Jeremy Laurance Health Editor
19 February 2007_1.chunks: HOME  Dame Anita Roddick is the biggest British celebrity so far to declare she has hepatitis C but she is by no means the only one infected with the virus. It is prevalent in the music industry, among rocks stars who dabbled in drugs decades ago (it is transmitted through shared needles) and have now discovered their livers are slowly rotting. Name any major band from the 1960s and 1970s and the chances are that at least one of their number will be carrying hepatitis C.  The need for greater awareness is urgent. Estimates of the numbers infected in the UK vary from 200,000 to twice that. But despite a campaign launched by the Government, the numbers coming forward for testing have fallen, to little more than 1,000 a quarter. The disease is treatable with drugs if detected early but many are diagnosed late and it is already the main cause of liver transplants. Professor William Rosenberg of Southampton University describes hepatitis C as a public health epidemic and Charles Gore of the Hepatitis C Trust has appealed for other celebrity carriers of the virus to join the Body Shop founder in her campaign. If they were to do so, we might see real results. Dame Anita, 64, has adopted an attitude of extreme pragmatism to her illness. Instead of letting it get on top of her, she is treating it as an opportunity. Having known little about hepatitis C before she was diagnosed, she declares herself outraged by what she has found and excited by the opportunity to do something about it. Campaigning is in her DNA, she says, and here is a chance to help. Like Jane Tomlinson, the 42-year-old mother diagnosed with terminal breast cancer in 2000 who has defied her doctors and raised more than 1m for charity through her feats of physical endurance, Dame Anitas positive outlook and fighting spirit command admiration. It may not make a difference to the outcome research shows that the widespread belief that thinking positively prolongs survival is a myth. But it can make a big difference to the quality of life remaining. Some people cope with adversity better than others. Doctors never like to admit this for fear of adding to the burden on patients. Dame Anita has found an amazing way of taking her mind off things with, we must hope, amazing benefits for others. Her determination not to tell her mother of her plight is part of her pragmatic approach. Why upset an elderly lady in the evening of her life, for whom she is planning a joyful exit? But most parents want to know about the trials and tribulations of their offspring, so that they may share them. It is why they brought their children in to the world.

19 February 2007_1.Title: Resistance movement: viruses that have yet to be conquered
19 February 2007_1.Author: KATE RAVILIOUS
19 February 2007_1.chunks: EXTRA  HEPATITIS C  Spread by blood-to-blood contact, this liver-damaging virus currently infects around 200 million people. It is unlikely that one vaccine will ever protect against all strains. PANDEMIC INFLUENZA  The vaccine for HN15 (bird flu, above) is updated as the virus mutates. Scientists expect a flu pandemic, but do not know which strain will attack. A vaccine will take six months to develop. RESPIRATORY SYNCYTIAL VIRUS (RSV)  This virus, the most common cause of respiratory infections, can be life-threatening to babies. A vaccine is high-priority, but nothing is available yet. CYTOMEGALOVIRUS (CMV)  Every year around 300 babies in the UK are born handicapped as a result of CMV. It spreads in bodily fluids, and most adults are unwittingly infected at some point. No vaccine exists. GENITAL HERPES  Carriers of genital herpes appear to be more susceptible to infection from HIV. A vaccine for genital herpes could help prevent the spread of HIV.

Another previous partner warned any woman who had a relationship with him to immediately contact a doctor.The High Court at Glasgow heard Mola's victim, who cannot be named for legal reasons, tell how he refused to wear condoms and never told her he was infected with HIV and Hepatitis C.The woman, known as Miss X, said her life had been ruined and she had kept her illness a secret, telling only her sister.Yesterday it took a jury of eight women and seven men 80 minutes to find Mola guilty by a majority verdict of culpably and recklessly failing to disclose to Miss X that he was infected with the viruses.The offence was committed between September 2003 and February 2004 in Edinburgh.Mola, who fled Scotland after he was charged and had to be extradited from Italy, showed no emotion as the verdict was read out.Judge Lord Hodge told him: "While you have been struck by tragedy in acquiring HIV and Hepatitis C from a former girlfriend, it is deeply disturbing you should have been prepared to show such an indifference to the health and welfare of Miss X." Afterwards Lord Hodge explained why he had banned any information identifying the woman. He said she was devastated and her mental health would have been put at serious risk if her name was revealed. She also insisted that if her identity wasn't protected she wouldn't give evidence.Miss X and Mola met when he chatted her up outside a grocery store in Edinburgh in the summer of 2003. At first he was affectionate and caring, but she told the court that as their relationship developed Mola was like "Jekyll and Hyde". Miss X said: "If I asked too many questions he said I talked too much. After sex he could be moody and distracted." In court she told Dorothy Bain, prosecuting, that if she had known Mola was infected with HIV and Hepatitis C she would never have had sex with him. She said she always made sure she had condoms and begged him to use them, but he refused, sometimes aggressively. The only times he agreed to wear a condom were the first and last occasion they had sex.Outside court, Detective Chief Inspector Adrian Lawrie, of Lothian and Borders Police, said: "Police were as impressed by the victim's quiet dignity and courage as they were horrified by the complete and utter disregard shown by Mola. He is despicable." Last night Aids campaigners called on those who have the disease to inform new partners of their condition. A spokeswoman for Avert, an organisation that aims to prevent HIV and Aids worldwide, said: "Avert strongly recommends that wherever possible an HIV-positive person embarking on a new relationship should inform their partner of their HIV status, and as such we do not condone Mr Mola's failure to tell his partner of his infections." 19 February 2007_1.Title: BLOODY HELL
19 February 2007_1.Author: Dame Anita Roddick
19 February 2007_1.chunks: HOME | Body Shop founders new battle++Dame Anita Roddick is on the warpath again. But this time her fury is driven by a personal trauma . She has been diagnosed with hepatitis C and is on a new crusade to highlight the disease and the urgent need for greater awareness  I am a campaigner. Ive always felt that activism is my rent for living on this planet. Now I am campaigning on hepatitis C. Its different because its personal about my health. The more I learnt about it, the more outraged I became. I discovered I was infected by chance three years ago when I went for an insurance medical. I didnt take it seriously at first. I felt so fit it didnt seem to matter; it was all insinuations. Doctors tell you the good things I could be fine for another 10 years. Only when I went for another blood test and found that my viral load had increased did I begin finding out about the disease. I started listening to my body I hadnt noticed anything up to that point. I was 61 and if I felt tired, I put it down to ageing. Now I have definitely started to have symptoms. I get itching on my wrists and ankles, fatigue and sometimes I get brain fog. There is a real reduction in the ability to concentrate at least thats what I have found. My liver is damaged I have cirrhosis. The next stage is cancer. I could be in perfect health for another 10 years, or I could be gravely ill tomorrow and need a transplant. I go every three months for a blood test and an MRI scan. I have been to see the liver transplant team at Addenbrookes hospital in Cambridge. When the time comes, I hope to God there is a liver available. There is a drug treatment interferon and ribivarin and when the doctors suggest it, I will have it. But its debilitating and, because of my age and high blood pressure. which I have lived with for years, it may not work for me. The doctors say lets wait and watch to see what happens with the disease. I wasnt upset when I found out I was infected. It was not like being told you are diabetic. Everyone in my family reacted in the same way by saying, Whats that? I think I was affected by the general air of indifference that hangs over the disease. It progresses so slowly. I cant emphasise enough how I was not shocked. I am a terribly pragmatic person. I thought, Oh, I have got that, now lets move on. I am a pathological optimist. Its because I am Italian and I eat a lot of tomatoes. I have never met a depressed Italian. I have not told my mother and I am not going to. She is 92 and lives in sheltered housing in Littlehampton. When she dies she wants her ashes to be fired into space on a rocket, to the theme tune from The Godfather. I have found a firework company that will do it. It is going to be spectacular. The last thing you want to do to a 92-year-old is worry them. That is why I wont tell her. She doesnt listen to the radio or read the newspapers. I just want to make her exit joyful. My family are so supportive of me. I have two daughters and three grandchildren. They want me to be as I am. They know I am a survivor and that I will do the best thing for myself and if I am persuaded this is the best thing for me they know that is right. It wasnt any big decision to declare that I was infected. It was a case of when the time was right. I had to campaign on it. Its in the DNA. My life hasnt changed. The only thing that has changed is the amount of energy I can put into things. Time for me is a real currency now. I am going to spend it doing the things where I can have a real effect. I have dispensed with the tedious stuff. I was invited to an event the other day to celebrate leading businesswomen. Uh, I havent time for that any more. I am campaigning on this because I cant understand how the Government can spend 40m to tell the population about going digital but only 2m raising awareness about hepatitis C. I dont understand why, with the amazing health service we had when I was growing up, we are lagging behind Europe. And I dont understand why there is no information in GPs surgeries. It is conspicuous by its absence. I caught the virus from a blood transfusion at the birth of my younger daughter, Sam, in 1971. It was a really difficult birth in the maternity home at Littlehampton and they gave me a lot of blood. I am so lucky the doctors kept the medical report so I was able to trace the cause. The Government pays compensation of 20,000 to people who contracted hepatitis C from a blood transfusion and 25,000 when they develop cirrhosis but only if they can prove it with the paperwork. I received both payments and gave them to the Hepatitis C Trust. I have become a patron of the trust because it is so important people are aware of the risks. If you had a blood transfusion before 1991 [when screening for hepatitis C was introduced] or if you think you have been in contact with contaminated blood, then go and get tested. It will free you of worry if negative and you will be in control of your life if its positive. Since I sold the Body Shop to LOral I have been working as a consultant to the companies, but I am reducing that to about 25 days this year for each of them. My foundation, which I put 30m into, is working to develop leaders in social justice and human rights. I am involved in projects to rebuild New Orleans and with prisoners in Angola and against sweatshop labour in Bangladesh. There are other projects in Darfur, east Africa, India and Canada. When I was first diagnosed with hepatitis C, I contacted the Hepatitis C Trust and they never asked if I could do something for them. They said, What can we do to help you? Only later they suggested that by speaking up I could help save lives. Most people just dont know that this virus exists, or what its impact is. Its not taken seriously. Hepatitis C has been called a silent killer, because you can go for years with no symptoms. It is also a silent killer because its just not being diagnosed and dealt with in an effective way. Nine out of 10 of us who have hepatitis C simply dont know theyve got it. If you look at somewhere like France, half the people with the virus have already been diagnosed. But in this country were way behind; only one in 10 people with hepatitis C have been diagnosed. Ive always been a bit of a whistle-blower and Im not going to stop now. When I worked in the Body Shop we used to ask ourselves, If we do this, will it benefit them? If you can affect one persons life, its worthwhile.
