19 February 2007_1.chunks:
The Times (London)

March 12, 2007, Monday

The 'tummy bug' that can prove fatal

BYLINE: Dr Thomas Stuttaford

SECTION: FEATURES; Times2; Pg. 11

LENGTH: 809 words

John Inman suffered from hepatitis -but it is preventable, says DR THOMAS STUTTAFORD
The TV programme Are You Being Served? was always compulsory viewing in the Stuttaford household, and John Inman was the obvious star of the series. Some of my homosexual patients were initially rather cross because he exaggerated the stereotype of the camp gay, with languid hand movements and his obvious pleasure when taking inside-leg measurements.
His catchphrase "I'm free", with its obvious innuendo, became famous. Later, even most gay campaigners joined the other 22 million avid viewers as Inman's humour, so obviously in the pantomime tradition like that of his friend Danny La Rue, mitigated any charge that he was setting back the drive to banish discrimination. 
John Inman, 71, contracted hepatitis more than two years ago, after eating food contaminated with the virus. Hepatitis A is one of the three frequently confronted forms of hepatitis -hepatitis A, B and C -but there are other types that are more rare. They have been labelled hepatitis D (or delta hepatitis) and hepatitis E, F and G.
Hepatitis A is highly infectious and accounts for about 40 per cent of cases of hepatitis treated in this country. Many cases are so mild that the patient does not recognise its symptoms as being any more significant than some passing "tummy bug", but even if they have a sub-clinical infection they may still be infectious.
The usual cliched comment of doctors when consulted by a patient with hepatitis A is that although the patient feels like death to a greater extent than during the first stages of hepatitis B or C, death is a most unlikely outcome.
This standard reassurance is too simplistic and is based on the belief that hepatitis A, if uncomplicated by other problems, does not cause chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis. Although standard textbooks teach that chronic liver failure never follows hepatitis A, it is unwise in medicine ever to use the word never.
Conversely, hepatitis B and C are notorious for causing chronic low-grade hepatitis and eventually cirrhosis and liver failure, although this process often takes decades.
This is not to say that the initial symptoms of hepatitis A are not unpleasant; they are so disabling that one patient in five under the age of 40 is admitted to hospital. The usual pattern is that the attack starts with fever, headache and complete lack of appetite, then nausea and diarrhoea follow before the jaundice appears after about a week.
Hepatitis A is occasionally a cause of death (but not in more than one case in 1,000). This is most often the result of a fulminant hepatitis, a rare syndrome in which large numbers of liver cells die, the necrotic liver shrivels and the patient rapidly becomes severely jaundiced before dying of liver failure.
There are other complications caused by hepatitis A but in most cases these are short-lived and clear up without treatment, hence the textbook advice that the prognosis in hepatitis A is excellent. During the immediate convalescent phase some patients may get a recurrence of jaundice, and in others the initial jaundice may last for anything up to six months.
For several months after an attack of hepatitis A the patient feels weak, depressed and generally debilitated. This is known as the post-hepatitis syndrome.
A great advance in medicine over the past 25 years has been that both hepatitis A and B can be prevented by vaccination. In the case of hepatitis A, the initial dose is repeated six to 12 months later with a booster.
A form of the vaccination is available for children over the age of 12 months and it should become a routine injection for all those who spend their holidays abroad.
The mortality rate of hepatitis A increases with age - it is nearly two in 100 patients aged over 40, and among over-55-year-olds the mortality rate is 45 times greater than it is in adolescents.
Before this year's holiday in the sun, grandparents, parents and children should be queueing up for the first of their two hepatitis A injections.
Hepatitis A is transmitted by the faecal oral route, and so has a high prevalence in areas where standards of hygiene are low. The incubation period after eating food handled by grubby hands is two to six weeks.
Typically the contaminated foods include fresh fruits, salads, ice and shellfish.
In Britain the groups of people who are considered at maximum risk of catching it are those looking after children who are not yet potty trained, sewage workers and patients and staff in residential care homes for the mentally handicapped.
Epidemics have been common in military campaigns when inadequate attention has been given to the digging of latrines.
Hepatitis A may also be spread sexually, especially, for obvious reasons, in homosexual patients. Intravenous drug users, if they don't observe strict standards, are also at high risk.

19 February 2007_1.Author: by STEPHEN WILKIE
19 February 2007_1.chunks: A CALLOUS romeo was convicted yesterday of infecting his former girlfriend with HIV and Hepatitis C. Italian Giovanni Mola, 38, faces up to seven years in prison for condemning his young victim to an early death through unprotected sex. And last night, police appealed for any other women seduced by the rogue waiter to come forward. During his trial, two of Mola's former lovers approached authorities and revealed they had had sex with him but escaped infection. Mola's tragic victim, Miss X, who was a virgin when she met him, said he refused to wear condoms but did not reveal his infected status. The shock diagnosis turned her from a bubbly outgoing person to someone who lives a "much more isolated life". Mola was found guilty of culpably and recklessly failing to disclose he had the viruses. He repeatedly refused to wear a condom. The offence was committed between September 2003 and February 2004, at an address in Edinburgh, and elsewhere in the city. The jury of eight women and seven men took 80 minutes to return a majority-guilty verdict. Mola, who fled Scotland after he was charged and had to be extradited from Italy, showed no emotion as the verdict was read out. Judge Lord Hodge told him: "You have been convicted of a very serious sexual offence against Miss X. You have caused her lasting damage."

19 February 2007_1.Title: THE SECRET ASSASSIN
19 February 2007_1.Author: OLIVIA HOLCOMBE *TO BE ADVISED*
19 February 2007_1.chunks: LAST WEEK, BODY SHOP FOUNDER ANITA RODDICK REVEALED SHE'D CONTRACTED HEPATITIS C FROM TAINTED BLOOD. HERE, A DAUGHTER DESCRIBES THE TERRIBLE IMPACT OF A VIRUS THOUSANDS UNWITTINGLY CARRY FOR five years, Peter Nowak put up with the fatigue and flu-like feelings that occasionally plagued him. The advertising executive put his symptoms down to overdoing things. He'd developed a rather stoical approach to his health -- after all, it was nothing compared with the injuries he'd sustained in a car accident in 1979. Then, he'd undergone a blood transfusion in intensive care as the doctors battled to save his legs, which they feared would have to be amputated. Peter had spent three months recovering in hospital -- at the time, he'd considered himself lucky to have escaped with only painful skin grafts. Then, a few years after the odd symptoms first appeared, Peter's stomach started swelling up. Within two years it had grown to the size of a football, and his wife, Gaye, joked that he needed to go on a diet. Finally, in the spring of 2004, Peter went to see his GP, and was given a blood test. The results were unclear and the GP wrote to his local hospital asking for advice. But it wasn't until Peter developed an infection on his old leg injury nearly 18 months later that another blood test revealed Hepatitis C. It emerged that the strange symptoms of the past few decades were classic signs of the blood-borne virus. Within five months of his diagnosis, Peter Nowak was dead at the age of 53. Hepatitis C is a virus that can cause serious damage to the liver. It's estimated that one in four people with the virus gets rid of it naturally -- the others develop chronic Hepatitis C infection, which eventually causes cirrhosis (severe liver damage). There is a one in 20 chance the patient will develop liver cancer, or liver failure -- when a transplant is the only option. However, this merely buys time, as the infection eventually returns to re-infect the liver. It's thought there are up to 500,000 people with Hepatitis C in the UK -- yet only 70,000 know they have it. Symptoms can be vague, as in Peter's case, or even non-existent. Most people associate the disease with intravenous drug-taking, unprotected sex or infected tattoo or piercing equipment. But Peter fitted none of the stereotypes and couldn't understand how he'd contracted the illness. Then doctors asked whether he'd ever had a blood transfusion. As Peter remembered his car accident in 1979, the penny dropped. HIS daughter Kiri, 20, explains: 'Dad found out donated blood hadn't been screened for Hepatitis C before 1991, so thousands of people like him received infected transfusions.' Last week it was revealed that Body Shop founder Anita Roddick, like Peter, had contracted Hepatitis C from an infected blood transfusion. Although she'd had the transfusion 35 years ago, she was diagnosed only two years ago during routine blood tests. Experts say up to 100,000 people may have contracted Hepatitis C through blood transfusion, yet most do not know it. And the tragedy is that, like Peter, they will discover their condition too late. If Peter's illness had been caught early enough, he would have been able to undergo a year-long drug therapy of pegylated interferon and/or ribavirin. The drugs work by slowing down the reproduction and growth of the virus, and offer a 60 per cent chance of cure. However, when he was eventually diagnosed, Peter's liver was so damaged it couldn't filter out toxins and waste products, and he needed to have fluid drained from his stomach through a catheter every few weeks. Just before Christmas 2005, doctors at King's College Hospital, London, said his only hope was a liver transplant, and he was put on the national waiting list. Faced with a shocking diagnosis and an uncertain future, Peter did his best to stay positive for his anxious family. 'But he was going downhill in front of our eyes,' says Kiri. 'He started to look really pale and skinny -- almost not like Dad any more. 'We were upset things seemed so bad, but we hoped he'd soon receive a new liver.' But four days after Christmas, Peter woke up complaining of severe indigestion. Within hours, it had turned into agonising stomach pains and his wife Gaye, 51, decided to drive him to hospital. 'I came out to the car to say goodbye, but he was delirious,' says Kiri, a student. 'It was then I was gripped by a strange fear that I'd never see him again.' On the way, Peter passed out: he never recovered consciousness. Doctors said his damaged liver couldn't cope with a massive stomach infection. Not only did the Nowak family have to deal with the sudden loss of a beloved husband and father, but also with the knowledge that Peter's death could have been prevented if only he'd been tested for Hepatitis C earlier. According to Charles Gore, chief executive of the Hepatitis C Trust, increasing numbers of people are being diagnosed with the virus 20 or 30 years after contracting it. 'The tragedy is that most deaths from the virus are preventable,' he says. 'If sufferers are diagnosed before cirrhosis takes hold, 60 per cent of them can be cured. 'We estimate that up to 20 per cent of all sufferers will have contracted the virus from infected blood transfusions before screening started in 1991. 'Based on those figures, up to 100,000 people could have caught it from a transfusion.' While haemophiliacs who received blood products before 1991 are also at risk, most have been tested and have had treatment programmes in place for some time. But experts say government initiatives are inadequate for the thousands of other patients who could have contracted the disease through a transfusion. In 1995, the Department of Health initiated a 'look back' programme to trace recipients of blood that may have been infected with Hepatitis C. The programme focused on donors from before 1991 who had tested positive for Hepatitis C when they went to give blood again. The recipients of their pre-1991 blood were then tested for the disease. 'But this initiative relied on people donating blood more than once -- what about donors with Hepatitis C who never returned?' asks Charles Gore. 'Clearly, the "look back" missed a large proportion of potential sufferers.' To encourage more people to come forward for testing, the Department of Health launched a public awareness campaign, FaCe It, at the end of 2004. 'But the campaign can't have worked,' says Charles Gore. 'We need to be diagnosing at least 20,000 cases a year, not 8,000 as we are currently.' BY CONTRAST, the French health authorities are taking a much more proactive approach to finding their ' missing' cases, he says. 'In 1999, the French government set itself a phenomenally aggressive target of diagnosing 75 per cent of the total number of people with Hepatitis C within three years. This was four years before the British Government launched its campaign,' says Mr Gore. The good news is that there's 'a huge window of opportunity to spot the virus', says Graham Foster, Professor of Hepatology at Queen Mary School of Medicine, Barts and the London NHS Trust. 'The timescale from infection to developing cirrhosis is normally 30-40 years.' 'But take someone who was unwittingly infected by a transfusion in the 1980s, whose illness might be 25 years on. That's why we need to get the message across to middle-aged people who are most at risk. They can be tested by their GP, a sexual health clinic or at a hospital.' Early diagnosis also means people can make lifestyle changes to minimise chances of developing cirrhosis. Prof Foster stresses that stopping drinking and smoking, eating the right foods and getting proper medical care all help. Thoughts of what could have been done differently to save her beloved father still plague Kiri. 'It makes me so angry to think of all those years Dad was walking around with this deadly virus, but was oblivious,' she says. 'If more was done to trace people who had blood transfusions before 1991 and highlight this issue, he would have had a blood test sooner. And he'd probably be here today.' FOR more information, call the Hepatitis C Trust helpline on 0870 200 1200 or see www.hepctrust.org.uk ; FaCe It: www.hepc.nhs.uk THE JUICE DOCTOR FITNESS expert JANEY HOLLIDAY offers simple juice recipes to help tackle common ailments. 19 February 2007_1.Title: Victim's crusade to halt HIV sex monster
19 February 2007_1.Author: Annabelle Steggles
19 February 2007_1.chunks: Cop praise as ex convictedTHE brave victim of HIV fiend Giovanni Mola was last night praised for saving other women's lives with her fight to bring him to justice.The woman - known only as Miss X - may have even delayed vital treatment for the deadly Aids virus to ensure she was strong enough to send the beast to jail.Italian chef Mola, 38, was behind bars last night after being found guilty of infecting his ex-lover - a virgin till they met - with a death sentence of HIV and hepatitis C.VulnerableSpeaking after the verdict, Detective Chief Inspector Adrian Lowrie described how the brute had shown "absolutely no remorse".He said: "People were as massively impressed by the victim's quiet dignity and courage as they were horrified by the complete and utter disregard shown by Mola.He is despicable. "He took advantage of a vulnerable woman who trusted him and has given her a life sentence. This was her first relationship and she feels utterly betrayed. Now Miss X will never be a mother and has had to keep this knowledge from her friends, family and the whole community. "She will be on medication for the rest of her life. "DCI Lawrie added: "She took steps to make sure she was as well as possible to be able to give evidence. "That may have involved her delaying some aspects of her treatment. "Devastated Miss X has kept the disease a secret from her family, only telling her sister about the life-shattering diagnosis. Last night a source close to the case told how her bravery had saved other women from the same tragic fate.The source said: "Miss X is very brave to have stuck with it, even after Mola tried to evade justice by fleeing to Italy. "Had she not come forward, Mola might still be infecting other women. "What she has done has potentially saved other women from falling victim to Mola. "The source also revealed how Miss X had been pushed to the point of suicide after discovering her ex-lover had infected her. The insider added: "She feels her life is ruined. At one point she seriously considered suicide. "But she managed to pull herself back and found the strength to go ahead with the trial. "Mola, above, infected his victim during a fling in Edinburgh between September 2003 and February 2004.DamageHe chatted her up outside a supermarket in the city, then when she was reluctant to go on a date he sent her a text saying: "What's the harm in going out with a stranger? "He later boasted of having bedded 200 other women, but never told Miss X he had been diagnosed with the viruses in 2000. It took a jury at the High Court in Glasgow 80 minutes to find him guilty of culpably and recklessly infecting her.Mola, who fled Scotland after being charged and was extradited from Italy, showed no emotion as the verdict was read out. He will be sentenced next month.Judge Lord Hodge told him: "You have been convicted of a very serious sexual offence against Miss X. You have caused her lasting damage. "While you have been struck by tragedy in acquiring HIV and hepatitis C, it is deeply disturbing you should have been prepared to show such an indifference to the health and welfare of Miss X." Last night Mola's father Beniamino, pictured left, said: "I was hoping against hope he would be found not guilty but I had the sensation that would happen. "I still believe he is innocent and he has my full support. "My fear is they will now jail him for a very long time and the maximum sentence is life. "NHS Lothian yesterday said they were not aware of any other victims, but urged anyone with concerns to contact them.Mola's conviction is only the second of its kind in Scotland. Junkie Stephen Kelly, now 39, of Provanmill, Glasgow, was jailed in 2001 for knowingly infecting his ex Ann Craig, now 40, with HIV by having unprotected sex.annabellesteggles@the-sun.co.uk(C) The Sun, 2007

Vouchers seen as aid to kicking heroin habit
19 February 2007_1.Author: No author found
19 February 2007_1.chunks:
The Guardian - Final Edition

January 27, 2007 Saturday

Vouchers seen as aid to kicking heroin habit

BYLINE: Sarah Boseley, Health editor

SECTION: GUARDIAN HOME PAGES; Pg. 12

LENGTH: 276 words

Drug users on methadone for heroin addiction should be given shopping vouchers and other rewards as incentives to stay clean, according to draft guidance published for consultation. 
Voucher schemes have worked well in the US, according to the guidance from the National Institute for Clinical Excellence. Users should be given a prompt reward for a urine or blood sample that proves they are free of heroin or other illicit drugs, rising in value the longer they stay that way.
The guidance envisages that they might be given an initial voucher for a negative sample worth as little as £1.50, but the next might be £3 and the third £5.
If a sample proves positive for drugs, the value of the reward would drop back to the previous level. Other possible incentives are free parking spaces or meals within the clinic.
About 5,000 drug users, mostly in the US, have taken part in such schemes. According to Stephen Pilling, joint director of the National Collaborating Centre for Mental Health, which formulated the guidelines for Nice, they do not feel they are being patronised. "They felt very looked after," he added. "It is a move from an emphasis on monitoring and controlling people to one where you are taking a more positive and rewarding approach."
Extra rewards - perhaps £10 shopping vouchers - could be considered to encourage those at risk of additional health problems to have TB, HIV or hepatitis C tests.
Martin Barnes, chief executive of the charity DrugScope, said vouchers might help as part of a care plan which would give positive support and care, and preferably involve their other underlying needs, such as housing, training and employment.

19 February 2007_1.Title: Body Shop's Anita battles silent killer Hepatitis C
19 February 2007_1.Author: Jo Willey
19 February 2007_1.chunks: 'It's a bit of a bummer but you groan and move on'SHE has been a campaigning activist for ethical consumerism for more than three decades.But Dame Anita Roddick has taken on a new fight after a blood test revealed she has the killer virus Hepatitis C.The multi-millionaire Body Shop founder admitted yesterday that she has no idea how long she has left to live.In a candid statement on her website yesterday dubbed Hep C and Me, Dame Anita said: "I have Hepatitis C. It's a bit of a bummer but you groan and move on." Dame Anita, 64, contracted the disease from a blood transfusion while giving birth to her youngest daughter, Sam, in 1971. It went undetected until two years ago.She also has cirrhosis of the liver, one of the effects of the disease, known as the "the silent killer". "I didn't take it seriously when I knew that I had it. I just thought so what? I have had it for 30 years I will have it for another 30 years, " she said last night. "Now I have got to come to terms with mortality and knowing that I don't have very much time." Dame Anita has used her website to share her experience and raise awareness of the disease. "By the time I was diagnosed, I'd had Hep C for over 30 years.The virus actually works very slowly, over decades. "The word Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver, and that's what happens the liver is inflamed and scarred and you can get cirrhosis and liver cancer. "In fact I do have cirrhosis. I could still have a good few years even decades of life left but it's hard to say. I could be facing liver cancer tomorrow. What I can say is that having Hep C means that I live with a sharp sense of my own mortality, which in many ways makes life more vivid and immediate." Dame Anita spoke out just two months after the Health Protection Agency warned that Britain was facing a Hepatitis C timebomb over the next 10 years.It predicted that more than 10,090 people face liver failure or serious liver disease by 2015. Up to 2,540 of them will die if they do not receive a transplant.The HPA said 250,000 Britons carry the disease but the majority are unaware of it in 2005, it killed 160 people.Dame Anita has called for more public money to be spent on raising awareness because many people do not realise they are carrying the disease.She is now experiencing symptoms, although they were quite mild, she said but vowed to continue her campaign. "Well, I've always been a bit of a whistleblower and I'm not going to stop now. In a way, campaigning with The Hepatitis C Trust is business as usual for me. "I've always felt that activism is my rent for living on this planet and I've always wanted to celebrate and protect the human body. "In a way, speaking out about my Hep C is just carrying on what I helped to start at The Body Shop. Life has just taken a more interesting turn." Dame Anita began the 300strong chain of shops in 1976 with her husband Gordon. Almost 30 years later, she announced: "I don't want to die rich." She revealed plans to give away her 51million fortune and the sell-off started in 2005 with Body Shop shares worth 7.4million, which went to Amnesty International and Greenpeace.Away from the boardroom, Dame Anita has become a patron of the Hepatitis C Trust since her diagnosis.Trust chief executive Charles Gore, said: "We are delighted that someone so dynamic and with such a history of fighting passionately for important causes has agreed to support us. "Like many people with Hepatitis C, Anita is taking control of her health and speaking out about the urgent action needed to deal with this immediate public health challenge. "Anita is exactly the person we need to catapult Hepatitis C into the national consciousness and in doing so, we hope to help save thousands of lives." People infected with Hepatitis C often show no symptoms initially, but long-term effects can include liver damage and cancer.There is no vaccine to prevent Hepatitis C infection, but treatments are available which work in more than half of cases.A Department of Health spokesman said: "We do recognise Hepatitis C as an important public health issue. That is why we have set a clear national framework for action to tackle the virus."

19 February 2007_1.Title: People
19 February 2007_1.Author: No author in byline
19 February 2007_1.chunks: Every time you meet a fringed buckskin jacket on a chap of a certain age, you can be sure you're seeing a tragic victim of the classic television series Daniel Boone, watched by millions on the BBC in the late 1960s, in which the actor Fess Parker wrestled the Wild West to a fall and a submission every week for six years. The entire first series is about to be re-released on an eight-disc DVD box set. Meanwhile Parker, who also played Davy, Davy Crockett, King of the Wild Frontier in the Disney movie - still crinkle eyed and craggy jawed at 83 - is flourishing in his Californian vineyard: he has 20 acres of beachside land in Santa Barbara, and more than 700 acres of vines up in the hills, where he also owns a hotel and spa. Body Shop founder Dame Anita Roddick , pictured, revealed yesterday she is carrying the virus hepatitis C, and contracted it through a blood transfusion in 1971, at the birth of her youngest daughter Sam - now an entrepreneur in her own right, creator of the classy sex toys firm Coco de Mer. The silver lining is that her revelation is very good news for the Hepatitis C Trust, which often has difficulty publicising and fundraising for a condition that can be devastating in the long run, but is often symptom-less in the early years. Dame Anita has become a patron of the trust. She also revealed she now has cirrhosis of the liver, a common long term side effect: expect to hear lots from her, very loudly, and hopefully for many years to come. "It's a bit of a bummer, but you groan and move on," she said yesterday. At Christmas actor Ricky Tomlinson released a wildly successful single, available only as a video download: Christmas My Arse sold 53,000 downloads. Yesterday he released another single, available only as a 3 Mobile download, called - ah, you're there before me - Valentine's Day My Arse. You might like to have a nice foaming flagon of Alka Seltzer at hand before reading this one. Glasgow-based chef Domenico Crolla flew to Rome yesterday, to prepare a pizza for lawyer Maurizio Morelli, as a Valentine's gift for his wife Sabrina . Mr Morelli's was the highest bid, pounds 2,150, in an eBay charity auction. The pizza, named the Royale 007, was topped with - reach for that flagon now - Beluga caviar, Scottish wild smoked salmon, prosciutto with vintage balsamic vinegar, lobster marinated in vintage cognac, grilled venison, Aberdeen Angus beef, corn-fed chicken, white truffles, and shavings of real gold. It wallops the previous contender, Gordon Ramsay's white truffle pizza, which retails for a mere pounds 100 at his Maze restaurant in London. maev.kennedy@guardian.co.uk

19 February 2007_1.Title: Next stage is cancer..but I plan to be here for a good few years;Interview;Anita Roddick;Health
19 February 2007_1.Author: No author in byline
19 February 2007_1.chunks: Body Shop founder reveals her Hepatitis C to warn thousandsBODY Shop founder Dame Anita Roddick admitted yesterday that she is carrying the deadly hepatitis C virus.The Pounds 100million businesswoman caught the disease 35 years ago from a blood transfusion while giving birth to her elder daughter Sam.But in an interview with The Sun the 64-year-old tycoon reveals she had no idea she was ill until a routine blood test two years ago.Now she has decided to go public about her condition after being told that her liver is so badly damaged that she has cirrhosis.When you speak to Anita her youthful looks and boundless energy make it hard to believe she is seriously ill.But she says: "The next stage will be a tumour or cancer. I am being monitored very closely, every three months. "I don't need a liver yet, but it may come to that. There are no guarantees - there are very few livers. "Anita -who nevertheless describes herself as a "pathological optimist" -has genotype one hepatitis, the most aggressive and difficult form to treat. Treatment works in only 50 per cent of cases and there is a small risk of further liver damage.But she says: "I could still have a good few years -even decades -of life left, but it's hard to say. "Anita only discovered she had the virus when she had a medical for an insurance policy.She says: "Over the years I'd had hundreds and hundreds of medical checks but it was only recently, as the insurance got higher, I got older and I was doing so much travelling that they included the hepatitisC test. "They call it the silent killer, it's so anonymous. You don't have any symptoms. "In Britain 60,000 people have been diagnosed with hepatitis C, although health watchdog NICE believes 500,000 are infected. Some experts warn the real figure could be even higher.For a patient, the longer it goes undetected the worse the outlook. Three out of four chronic hepatitis C patients suffer liver damage and it in-creases the risk of liver cancer.For Anita, her husband Gordon and daughters Sam and Justine, her diagnosis has understandably come as a bombshell.Speaking exclusively to The Sun, Sam says: "It has really changed our relationship. You can't feel any more vulnerable in life than when your parent's health is at risk. "It makes you very aware of your own mortality, it makes you reflect on life and the things you love. "Anita, born in Sussex to Italian immigrant parents, launched The Body Shop in 1976 with just 15 products. She developed them in the garage of the family home. Last year she and Gordon sold their stake in the business to L'Oreal for Pounds 117million.Yet workaholic Anita still refuses to curb her hectic schedule. She has just become a patron of the Hepatitis C Trust and as we talk she fires questions at the charity's chief executive Charles Gore -"What about getting all the Cabinet tested?" "Prisons, what's happening in prisons? It must be a huge problem. "Then she tells me: "People have been saying I'm brave for speaking out but I don't get it. I couldn't imagine doing anything else. "I've always been a bit of a whistle-blower and I'm not going to stop now. "I am outraged that the Government has spent Pounds 40million on telling the public about the switchover to digital TV but only Pounds 3million on raising awareness of hepatitis C."The Sun has done a brilliant job getting the message out there but the Government's campaign has been a joke. "They can find Pounds 25billion for a Trident missile, billions to invade Iraq, so why can't they find the money to tackle this condition? "There are hundreds of thousands of people out there with undiagnosed hepatitis C."And what little money is being spent is not working. The latest figures show the Government's FaCe It awareness campaign is a flop.From July to September last year only 1,128 new cases were diagnosed -half the number of the previous quarter.Anita says: "It's the Government that needs to FaCe It -face the fact that people are dying needlessly. "* For more information, call the Hepatitis C Trust helpline on 0870 200 1 200 or visit the website hepctrust.org.uk.Learn more about hepatitis C at thesun.co.uk/news. * Case of Tracy De GietelinkLIKE Dame Anita, Tracy contracted the virus from an infected blood transfusion during pregnancy. She also only found out she was a carrier by chance when she donated blood.Tracy, 46, from Dover, says: "I got a letter from the blood service saying 'We have discovered you carry the hepatitis virus'. It was incredibly blunt. "At the time Tracy was working as a highly-paid PA in London. She says: "I was drinking, eating junk food, working long hours with lots of stress. I was doing all the wrong things but nobody warned me about the risks. "Two courses of treatment failed to clear the bug but Tracy says: "I'm lucky, I know I'm infected and I'm very, very careful. "She even insists her son Zac, nine, uses a separate sink to brush his teeth. * Case of Neil HudsonNEIL was given 164 units of blood after pneumonia led to septicaemia.One was contaminated with hepatitis C -but it was nine years before he knew. He says: "What's really frightening is that hundreds of thousands of people are walking around with it -and they don't know. "Neil, 36, a counsellor from South London, was diagnosed in 1999 when he was being treated for high blood pressure. He began treatment in 2001.He says: "I went clear but within three months the virus came back. After all the side-effects of the treatment, I was still ill."Neil had another year of treatment with pegylated interferon and has now been clear for two years.He says: "I think Anita Roddick is incredibly brave to speak out. "* Case of Kiri NowakKIRI's dad Peter died of a lack of information. He had no idea the blood transfusions that saved his life after a car crash in 1975 were infected. By the time he found out, it was too late.Peter, a designer, was 53 when he went into hospital with a leg infection just over a year ago.Routine tests revealed he had hepatitis C -and three months later he died.Student Kiri, 20, from Camberley in Surrey, says: "I'm angry the Government has done so little to raise awareness. "If they'd found it earlier he'd have had a better chance. It's great Anita Roddick is using her fame in such a positive way. By speaking out she will help so many. "* THE RISK FACTORSHEPATITIS C can be caught from the following: A blood transfusion carried out before 1991; medical or dental treatment abroad; a tattoo or piercing; unprotected sex; sharing a razor or a toothbrush; sharing drug equipment; exposure in the womb.

23 April 2008_1.Title: Killer transfusions will be investigated at last
23 April 2008_1.Author: Vic Rodrick
23 April 2008_1.chunks: A3MILLION inquiry into why thousands of people were infected with killer viruses in blood transfusions was announced by the Scottish Government yesterday.Health Secretary Nicola Sturgeon described the scandalas"oneofthe most tragic episodes" in the health service's history.The announcement fulfils a key SNP manifesto commitment and represents a milestone victory for sufferers who have campaigned tirelessly for an inquiry for more than 15 years.An independent team chaired by Lady Cosgrove, a former judge and sheriff, will investigate how blood and blood products tainted with hepatitis C and HIV infected patients.It will also probe the deaths of Reverend David Black, 66, and Eileen O'Hara, 72, following a High Court ruling in February that Scottish authorities had breached human rights laws by not holding fatal accident inquiries.They both died in 2003 after becoming infected with hepatitis C following NHS treatment.Solicitor Advocate Frank Maguire, of Thompsons Solicitors, who has campaigned on behalf of the families for three years, said they were "delighted" with the decision.Ms Sturgeon said:"This tragedy has blighted the lives of a number of people in Scotland and we are committed to a thorough inquiry to get to the bottom of what happened." Lady Cosgrove's remit is expected to include the sources of blood used by the NHS in Scotland at the time and whether heat treatment sterilisation should been introduced earlier.Philip Dolan, chairman of the Scottish Forum of the Haemophilia Society, said it was tragic that several of the victims had died during the fight for an investigation.He added: "This is a battle we have endeavoured to fight for years.We've had so many obstacles put in our way." Brian Adam, MSP for Aberdeen North, has campaigned on the issue since the parliament was created in 1999.Hesaid: "These answers are long overdue and it has taken two terms of parliament and finally a change of administration to see it happen." Mary Scanlon MSP, Tory health spokeswoman, welcomed the inquiry but urged Ms Sturgeon to revisit the question of compensation payments.She added: "Nothing can undo the pain and suffering to individuals and their families, but this is an important step."

February 2009_1.Title: Free needles for drug users 'good use of NHS money'
February 2009_1.Author: No author found
February 2009_1.chunks:
Guardian.com 

February 19, 2009

Free needles for drug users 'good use of NHS money' 

LENGTH: 485 words


HIGHLIGHT: Medicine watchdog advocates combining needle exchange schemes with treatment 

Providing free needles and syringes to people who inject heroin and cocaine is a cost-effective use of NHS money, the government's medicines watchdog said today.
The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (Nice) issued its first guidance on how harm reduction services for addicts should be run throughout England, suggesting combining non-judgmental needle exchange schemes with treatment to help users come off drugs. 
Prof Mike Kelly, director of the institute's public health division, said there are about 200,000 injecting drug users in Britain. He estimated about 25% of users share needles, putting themselves at a greatly increased risk of being infected with Hepatitis C or HIV.
Kelly said: "The cost to the NHS of caring for someone who injects drugs is around £35,000 over their lifetime. From a societal perspective, the average [lifetime] cost rises to an estimated £480,000 when you take into account the high cost of crime including criminal justice costs."
About 40% of drug users who inject are already infected with Hepatitis C and their risk of death is 10 times higher than among the population at large.
If needle exchange schemes are run well, they can provide an effective conduit for doctors, nurses and pharmacists to gain direct contact with hard-to-reach groups - the first step towards encouraging them to seek treatment.
Providing injecting drug users with extra years of healthy life was cost-effective for taxpayers, said Nice.
Kelly added: "Keeping in check the epidemic of Hepatitis and maintaining HIV at its relatively low levels is an important aim that this guidance will serve."
Needle and syringe exchange schemes have been provided throughout England for more than 20 years. They provide injecting drug users with sterile equipment, needle disposal bins and advice on safer injecting practices. Primary care trusts (PCTs) have had discretion on how to run services to meet local needs.
The Nice guidelines include advice on how PCTs should tailor the service to encourage injectors to seek treatment by offering more accessible opening times and locations.
Dr Mathew Hickman, chair of the Hepatitis C prevention working group at the Advisory Council for the Misuse of Drugs, said: "Needle and syringe programmes are a critical component of public health action to prevent Hepatitis C infections among injecting drug users.
"Evidence suggests that a combination of interventions is most effective. This means that staff need to use the opportunity they have with injectors actively to promote and refer people into treatment, such as opiate substitution programmes."
Dr David Sloan, vice-chair of the Public Health Interventions Advisory Committee, said: "Although HIV rates remain relatively low among injecting drug users in the UK, bad practice, such as the sharing of needles among multiple users, makes these individuals extremely vulnerable to any future outbreak."

March 2009_1.Title: INFECTED BLOOD VICTIMS 'DESERVE APOLOGY AND PROPER COMPENSATION'; SOPHIE GOODCHILD
March 2009_1.Author: No author in byline
March 2009_1.chunks: Thousands of victims of an NHS blunder involving contaminated blood today demanded an official apology from the Government.Treatment with imported blood that had not been properly screened exposed victims including children to viruses such as Aids and hepatitis C. The scandal which left more than 2,000 people dead and many terminally ill was described as a 'horrific human tragedy' by a long-awaited independent report published today.Lord Archer of Sandwell, who chaired the investigation, criticised ministers for failing to respond earlier to the disaster by halting imports of infected blood from countries including the US during the Seventies and Eighties. The former solicitor general said subsequent health crises such as variant CJD, the human form of mad cow disease, could have been avoided if officials had taken swift action.Lord Archer said at today's report publication: 'This matter is by no means closed. We are discovering viruses now that we didn't know existed. There could have been a system in place (if action had been taken earlier). And issues such as CJD might have been foreseen and even avoided. 'If you step on someone's foot on a crowded train then you may not yourself be to blame but you say 'sorry'. It (apologising) might help achieve closure. 'The Government is now under pressure to provide a new compensation deal for survivors.Evidence presented to the inquiry showed that widows and children have suffered as a result of inadequate financial settlements.One of the recommendations is that the existing settlement system is overhauled. No figure was given for possible new compensation levels, but Irish victims have already benefited by at least 100,000 from a similar scheme set up in their country.Lord Archer recommended that victims should also be entitled to health care not automatically available on the NHS such as counselling, home nursing and physiotherapy. They would gain access to this care through a special card-holder system.The report revealed that doctors and government officials knew as far back as the mid-Seventies that blood and blood products carried a danger of infection from viruses.But blood continued to be imported from countries such as the US where donors included paid prison inmates.The full scale of the contamination scandal only began to emerge at the height of Britain's Aids scare.Ministers have consistently refused funding for a formal public investigation and refused to provide any evidence to this inquiry.Campaigners said they welcomed the inquiry report and the 'tireless' work of the inquiry team.Chris James, chief executive of the Haemophilia Society, said: 'Successive governments have shamefully refused to fund a public inquiry and an independent inquiry held in public was the only way forward if the voices of those infected and the bereaved was ever to be heard. 'We are immensely grateful to Lord Archer and his inquiry team for their tireless endeavours to reveal the truth depth of this disaster.'

During the 1970s and 1980s, 4,670 haemophiliacs were given contaminated blood during routine treatment: 1,756 died. Some supplies were bought cheaply from American companies that used blood from prostitutes and prisoners, many with HIV and hepatitis C.Last Monday, a two-year privately funded independent inquiry, chaired by Lord Archer of Sandwell, demanded compensation for victims' families. "If you tread on somebody's foot on a crowded train, it may not be your fault, but at least you say sorry," said Archer, a former solicitor general. One woman told the inquiry she had been given a "death sentence", while others said they felt haemophiliacs were used as "guinea pigs".Some sufferers wanted more than an apology from ministers. Haydn Lewis, 52, who was infected during treatment, told BBC Radio 4: "An apology will not make any difference to me now. What I want from government is a reassurance that if I do not get through this liver transplant I have pending, my wife will be taken care of."

March 2009_1.Title: Blood scandal officials may be forced to testify
March 2009_1.Author: Severin Carrell Scotland correspondent
March 2009_1.chunks: Health officials involved in supplying blood products contaminated with hepatitis C and HIV could be compelled to give evidence in the first official inquiry into a scandal estimated to have so far cost 2,000 lives.Lord Penrose, a former high court judge appointed by Scottish ministers to head the inquiry, said yesterday he would use legal powers to force reluctant witnesses to appear and would formally investigate the conduct of UK ministers.The inquiry, expected to take three to four years, was set up by the Scottish Nationalist government in Edinburgh and given a pounds 3m budget after ministers in successive Tory and Labour governments refused a public or judicial inquiry.Nearly 4,700 people, chiefly haemophiliacs but also hospital patients given blood transfusions, became infected with Hepatitis C or both HIV and hepatitis C from the early 1970s. The Haemophilia Society said about 840 of the 1,200 people infected with both diseases had died, while about 1,200 infected solely with hepatitis C had since died. Another 63 wives and partners contracted HIV through secondary infections. Some of the contaminated blood had come from inmates in US prisons.Surviving victims have been able to claim pounds 20,000, and a further pounds 25,000 for the very seriously ill, in ex gratia payments under the government-backed Skipton fund set up in 2004. People infected with HIV have been given up to pounds 80,000 and monthly payments from another fund.Penrose said he and his team were aware their work "touches individuals and families who have suffered and continue to suffer, physically, mentally and emotionally [from] the consequences of treatment they were entitled to trust."

March 2009_1.Title: Compensation call for haemophiliacs
March 2009_1.Author: Andrew Jack
March 2009_1.chunks: The government should pay compensation and cover future health and insurance costs for the many hundreds of surviving haemophiliacs left infected by contaminated National Health Service blood products since the 1970s, an inquiry concluded .Ministers should also set up a committee to support haemophiliacs and manage their future treatment to the highest standards, says a privately funded report written under the chairmanship of Lord Archer of Sandwell, the former solicitor-general.The conclusions follow lengthy hearings demanded by haemophiliacs and convened unofficially two years ago after the government repeatedly refused to hold an official statutory inquiry into blood transfusions that led to HIV, hepatitis C and other viruses infecting nearly 5,000 people before tighter screening was introduced.Nearly 2,000 haemophiliacs have since died as a result of infection by blood bought from groups abroad at high risk of infection, including from inmates in US prisons. "Long after alarms had been sounded about the risks of obtaining paid-for blood donations . . . this practice continued," the report said. "It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that commercial interests took precedence over public health concerns. "The Department of Health said: "We have great sympathy for the patients and families affected by contaminated blood products in the 1970s and 1980s, and will study the findings of Lord Archer's report in detail. "The Scottish parliament has since established a statutory inquiry, while that covering England and Wales had no legal powers or official support.

20 May 2009_1.Title: Outcry at NHS blood transfusion payouts: No extra help for people infected with hepatitis C Inquiry had called for improved compensation
20 May 2009_1.Author: Sarah Boseley Health editor
20 May 2009_1.chunks: The government was accused yesterday of putting budget constraints ahead of victims of the worst treatment scandal in NHS history after deciding not to increase compensation for people infected with hepatitis C during routine blood transfusions.An independent inquiry into the scandal, chaired by Lord Archer of Sandwell, in February recommended larger payouts for nearly 3,000 people with haemophilia who had been infected with hepatitis C and HIV, as well as help for widows and dependants.Their hopes were dashed yesterday by a response from the Department of Health offering an increase for the minority who had been infected with HIV but nothing more than a review in five years' time for the rest.Archer said the response was a "faltering step that only compounds the anguish of the afflicted and bereaved". He said: "It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that humanitarian impulses have come a bad second to Treasury constraints. "Archer branded the new funding for patients with HIV "paltry", and said that the failure to increase help for those with hepatitis C and to offer payment to their dependants was "sadly lacking in understanding and in compassion".In the 1970s and 80s about 4,670 people with haemophilia were given blood contaminated with hepatitis C and 1,200 were unwittingly infected with HIV. The blood products came from commercial companies in the US, whose paid donors included drug addicts and prisoners.The health minister, Dawn Primarolo, publishing the government's response, said: "We deeply regret that these events occurred following NHS treatment. "In addition to pounds 150m already shared out in lump sums and discretionary payments, financial help for those with HIV would rise to pounds 12,800 per year, she announced. She gave a commitment to review financial relief for the others within five years and announced pounds 100,000 for the Haemophilia Society, which recently had its government funding cut by pounds 70,000.Chris James, chief executive of the Haemophilia Society, said: "The government claims to accept the moral case for action but then, by not implementing the recommendations in full, shows its contempt for the victims of what Lord Winston has described as the 'worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS'. "Lord Morris of Manchester, who was instrumental in getting the inquiry set up and who has raised the issues regularly in parliament, said: "This response will totally dismay the victims of an NHS treatment disaster that had already claimed the lives of 1,757 haemophiliac patients when I announced the setting up of the inquiry in February 2007. "Since then, he said, over 200 more patients had died.

20 May 2009_1.Title: BLOOD SUCKERS
20 May 2009_1.Author: GARY O'SHEA; GARY O'SHEA
20 May 2009_1.chunks: Ministers snub compo bid by NHS victimsMINISTERS yesterday snubbed a compensation bid by Brits who caught HIV and Hepatitis C from infected NHS blood.An inquiry this year had called for big lump sum payouts.Instead, HIV sufferers will get just 12,800 a year up from 6,400. Payments to Hep C victims currently up to 45,000 will not be reviewed for FIVE YEARS.Spouses of those who died will not get a penny.A total of 4,670 people with blood-clotting condition haemophilia caught Hep C from infected blood in the 1970s and 1980s. Of those, 1,243 also got HIV. So far 1,757 have died.The Sun revealed in 2006 how they were treated with blood bought from junkie convicts in the US.A two-year probe by Lord Archer of Sandwell called for payouts to match those in the Irish Republic where Hep C victims got 790,000 and HIV patients another 93,000.Health Minister Dawn Primarolo also snubbed calls to set up an advisory committee on haemophilia.Instead, those affected by the scandal can meet with the Government just twice a year. She offered victims the "greatest sympathy".Victim Bruce Norval, 43, of Inverness, said: "The Government gives billions to bankers but screws the little man every time.He added: "Any decent person would see that if you caused an accident you should pay what it costs to put it right. "It is a wholly inadequate solution an obscenity. "g.oshea@the-sun.co.uk

December 2009_1.Title: Hidden threat of hepatitis C; Q & A
December 2009_1.Author: No author in byline
December 2009_1.chunks: A friend in her late forties has developed liver trouble as a result of hepatitis C probably caught in her teens. She has been told that if it had been diagnosed earlier the damage might have been prevented. She is on the waiting list for a transplant. Should I ask my GP for a test?There are thought to be 200,000 people carrying the hepatitis C virus in the UK, many of whom will be unaware of it.Three out of four people who catch the blood-borne virus become long-term carriers, and one in five of them will develop life-threatening liver disease often 20 to 25 years later.The treatments that can eliminate the virus need to be used years before symptoms develop. The following groups should ask their GPs about a blood test to check for the infection:Anyone who had a blood transfusion before September 1991, or blood products (such as clotting factors) before 1986.Anyone who has ever shared equipment for injecting drugs, even if it was only once or twice.Anyone who has had unprotected sex with someone with the virus (or shared razors or toothbrushes that may have been contaminated with infected blood).Anyone who has had medical or dental treatment abroad, or had tattoos, piercings or acupuncture, where equipment may have been unsterile.Visit nhs.uk/hepatitisc for details.My seven-year-old son has just had his third attack of impetigo in as many weeks and it is now breaking out on his bottom as well as his face. He has had two courses of antibiotics, but it comes back within 48 hours of stopping them. Any ideas?Impetigo is an infection of the skin by the bacterium staphylococcus aureus.The classic weeping, crusty sores can appear anywhere on the body, but are particularly common on the face and buttocks though it can quickly spread elsewhere (and to others) from contaminated clothing and hands.Your son's story is not that unusual and I suspect he is harbouring the bacteria in his nose (many children do). Antibiotics will clear the infection from the skin but elimination from the nose often requires the use of a cream (eg, Naseptin), which is applied to the insides of both nostrils. If it's not cleared up, the cycle will start again if he simply picks his nose and then scratches his face.A telltale sign that he might be harbouring the bacterium in his nose is the presence of a sore crusty area just inside the top of either nostril. Your GP can do a swab to culture the bacteria and check that it is not resistant to commonly used antibiotics.In the meantime your son should use his own towel, and you should change it along with his pillow case, sheets and underwear daily.E-mail questions to drmark@thetimes.co.uk or write to times2, 1 Pennington Street, London E98 1TT

December 2009_1.Title: Patient's fear over hep-C lie
December 2009_1.Author: No author in byline
December 2009_1.chunks: AN osteopath wrongly told a patient she had a potentially deadly liver condition without carrying out tests, before "harassing" her at home, it was claimed yesterday.Swede Goran Stal, 48, saw the unnamed woman at his clinic in Forres, Morayshire, in May 2008.Yesterday a meeting of the General Osteopathic Council's professional conduct committee in London heard how she feared she would die after being told she had the hepatitis C virus.Stal allegedly warned her not to go to her GP, claiming blood tests would not detect the condition as it was "so deep inside her".And it was claimed he then made repeated telephone calls to her over a two-week period.The patient, who is in her mid-30s, said: "I asked what hepatitis C was and how one got it, and he could not answer me. In fact, he said, 'it's something to do with the skin'. I was thinking:'Am I going to die or something?'" Blood tests carried out by the patient's doctor proved conclusively that she did not have hepatitis C.Stal admits making a diagnosis not supported by valid tests and not referring her for further tests, but denies all other charges. The hearing continues.

December 2009_1.Title: Over-50s cases raise concern
December 2009_1.Author: Andrew Jack
December 2009_1.chunks: When Simon Rackstraw saw a 55-year-old man at his London clinic recently who was suffering from confusion and eye problems, the diagnosis was a troubling one that had eluded previous doctors: HIV contracted several years previously. "We are seeing a lot more older people, including those in their 60s and 70s, with very advanced stages of the disease," says Dr Rackstraw, medical director of Mildmay, a UK-based Aids charity that runs Europe's only neuro-cognitive impairment rehabilitation centre for those with HIV. "I have a new case every couple of weeks. "For two decades, most attention on both the prevention and treatment of HIV has focused on younger people. But two different groups are now emerging: people infected with HIV for the first time later in life; and those who have been in long-term HIV treatment but are suffering from a broad range of health problems. "HIV ages you anyway," says Dr Rackstraw, who describes an acceleration in relatively young patients of conditions including osteoporosis, cancer, dementia and cardiac conditions. He sees many such problems in people in their 40s, a decade or more before they would typically occur. They also have disproportionate infections of diseases such as Hepatitis B and C, resulting in liver damage.One glimmer of optimism is that Mildmay's own London clinic, originally a hospice for people with irreversible brain problems, found that HIV-related dementia had a different mechanism and could be successfully treated with anti-inflammatory drugs. "We have a lot of patients who five years ago would have been dead," he says.He says there is a need for greater research on the implications of different approaches to treatment for those with long-standing HIV, such as more individualised rather than standard dosages of medicines.Just as important are targeted policies to reduce risky behaviour in older people.But few studies have specifically studied the phenomenon. One rare analysis argued that 11 per cent of new cases of HIV in the US were in people over the age of 50; in Europe, an estimate placed it at 8 per cent. The trend is not limited to richer countries: a study in Brazil showed that between 1996 and 2006, new HIV infections in those aged over 50 jumped from 7.5 to 15.7 cases per 100,000 inhabitants.In a first attempt to study the issue and its implications, the UK's Terrence Higgins Trust, in conjunction with Age Concern and Help the Aged, is conducting the first national survey of people over 50 living with HIV in the UK, designed to improve services. (www.tht.org.uk/howyoucanhelpus/surveys/).It may be that older initial infection has long existed, but simply went undiagnosed in the past. However, some argue that the increasing use of erectile dysfunction drugs such as Viagra may have increased sexual activity and risk in later life.Whatever the reason, physiological changes in older people increase their risk of infection, and their weaker immune systems mean a more rapid progression of the disease than in younger sufferers.That highlights the need for increased awareness by doctors to ensure rapid diagnosis.It also suggests there should be more targeted programmes aimed at safer sex education for older people. In some countries where inter-generational sex is common, reducing risky behaviours among older people also helps protect younger ones too.

April 16, 2010 Friday

Court ruling may help contaminated blood victims win higher payouts

BYLINE: James Meikleguardian.co.uk

LENGTH: 879 words

ABSTRACT
Government faces pressure to give more compensation, but judge warns campaigners against 'false optimism' 

FULL TEXT
The government was under pressure today to make higher compensation payments to thousands of people with haemophilia who contracted hepatitis C after being given contaminated blood products in the 1970s and 1980s.
A classical music composer infected by HIV when he was nine, and later developed hepatitis, won a judicial review that challenged the basis of health ministers' decision last year not to increase the payments.
But the judge warned campaigners against "false optimism" over the outcome of the case and said the size of payouts, for what has been called the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS, remained a political matter. 
Andrew March, 36, sought to reverse the government's decision last year not to implement fully recommendations of an independent inquiry led by Lord Archer for a more substantial compensation package.
A total of 4,670 haemophiliacs in the UK were unwittingly given blood contaminated with hepatitis C and 1,200 were infected with HIV. The blood came from US sources, whose paid donors included drug users and prison inmates. About 2,000 of those infected are now dead.
Although the government last May announced increased compensation for those who contracted HIV, it only offered a review of payments to those given hepatitis in another five years. It refused to assess payments in the same way as Ireland. The Department of Health limited its response to the decision, saying it would "now consider the position".
, a campaign group for the infected haemophiliacs, said: "The government will now have to reconsider their original decision and remake it based on a lawful and factual basis. This time we would ask that they refrain from taking a cavalier attitude to such a crucial question. They may well arrive at the same decision ... however, this time, they must give sincere reasons which must withstand the scrutiny of public law. A little humility from the government would not go amiss."
It added: "We have effectively removed a major stumbling block in the process of working toward a full and final settlement."
The UK government's lawyer contesting March's case told the court that the basis for payments in Ireland was different. Phillipa Whipple said that while the Irish scheme was not "fault-based", there were findings of fault that gave a context to political decisions in Dublin over compensation in 1997. The UK government argued that it had funded various schemes that had, at May last year, paid out a total of £142m to those infected by NHS products.
Mr Justice Holman said the allocation of resources was entirely a matter for the government, but it had been faced with a specific recommendation, which it had rejected, of comparability or equivalence with Ireland, where "very much higher" payments were made to those infected and their dependents.
When the government was pressed as to why it rejected comparability, it had not merely repeated it could not afford it, but given a reason which, in his view, contained an error and did not withstand scrutiny. It continued to regard the Irish system as based on fault rather than on compensation.
He made "very, very clear" that he had merely quashed the existing decision in relation to the relevant Archer recommendation. "I have given no steer or indication whatsoever as to what the government may decide upon reconsideration, and it would be a grave abuse of my role if I were to do so. The campaign may now return to the political arena, but no one should leave this courtroom with a false optimism."
The judge refused permission to appeal, although leave can be sought directly from the court of appeal.
Outside court, March said: "Having the judgment go in our favour gives us no pleasure at all. The judge's decision proves the flawed basis on which the government made its decision not to implement the recommended compensation scheme. The judgment now compels the government to retake the decision lawfully and based on accurate information.
"We hope that the government will now consider the whole issue of compensating those so tragically affected by the contaminated blood disaster, instead of making token, derisory, ex-gratia payments."
Lord Morris, chairman of the , said: "A total of 1,974 have died in direct consequence of their NHS treatment in the worst ever treatment disaster in the history of the NHS, yet until today, the legal road to redress was blocked just as unbreakably as any prospect of securing justice by legislative means."
Morris, who was Britain's first minister for the disabled, added : "Now, with today's historic breakthrough, and the huge public backing for my contaminated blood bill, both the legal and legislative roads are opening. Our determination to ensure that right is done is totally vindicated and a just outcome is now in sight," he added.
Earlier, the judge had commended March, saying many other people interested in the cause owed him gratitude "for his tenacity or persistence".
Last month, the Guardian revealed  showing how government officials in the 1980s worried about controlling costs that might result from the developing scandal.

October 15, 2010 Friday

MPs debate compensation for those with blood tainted with HIV

BYLINE: Michael Whiteguardian.co.uk

LENGTH: 1135 words

ABSTRACT
Michael White: The problem came down to no one being quite sure exactly what an Irish-style compensation scheme for victims would cost 

FULL TEXT
In late morning yesterday the public gallery above the Commons chamber started filling up with people wearing red armbands with a yellow border. Stay with me for a moment on this one. It's a grim story.
Not having seen such armbands before I wondered if they represented a political movement. In a way they do: people seeking compensation for a fearful illness inflicted upon them through no fault of their own - and the protracted negligence of the state.
After listening to the day's agenda, Francis Maude setting fire to some quangos (with sceptical MPs pouring water on the blaze), David Davis, the born-again Tory libertarian, leapt to his feet to denounce what he saw as a government attempt to bully backbench MPs.
It was a trend throughout the 20th century and it has to be reversed, he said. So this debate was also about reasserting parliamentary power via one of these new "backbench business" day motions to which all frontbenches now pay lip service. 
What was it about? Here's where the armbands come in. Labour MP and Brownite ex-minister Geoffrey Robinson had tabled a backbench motion for debate - routine stuff - in which he urged the coalition to accept that haemophiliacs who got HIV-tainted blood transfusions in the 70s and 80s deserve a better compensation deal.
Specifically, the MP and his allies urged ministers - as they did Labour ministers under the last government - to embrace the findings of the independent Archer report (Lord Peter Archer is a former solicitor general) published in 2009 in which he reviewed the sad history - under both Labour and Tory regimes - of "killer blood", as the tabloids put it.
Stated simply, haemophiliacs used to die in their 20s until new methods of treating blood plasma opened up relief in the 1960s but also generated huge demand for plasma, which traditional blood donation in Britain could not meet.
David Owen, Labour's forceful health minister in 1974-76, struggled to promote self-sufficiency and failed. Pre-devolution Scotland moved faster to use heat-treated blood. Whitehall seemed both slow and careless.
The Tories proved no better after 1979 as it gradually dawned on people that imported blood from the US contained a high proportion of hepatitis C taint, common among poor people who sell blood in large quantities. Only in 1987 did another health minister, Tony Newton (always a good guy), announce a £10m ex-gratia fund to help victims. Only by 1991 was the screened blood supply secure again.
Twenty years on, £100m has been paid out by the MacFarlane (HIV) and Skipton (hepatitis C) trusts to 5,000 or so victims of infected blood transfusions. Some 1,200 have HIV, 4,670 hep C, 1,800 have died, so MPs were told yesterday. One MP reported a constituent being told he was HIV-positive at the age of nine.
Whitehall has staged at least two internal inquiries, although, as Lord Archer discovered, a lot of evidence was destroyed in "error". But no public inquiry was conceded; hence the £75,000 privately raised to fund Archer's two-year independent probe, instigated by Lord Morris, the ex-disability minister and president of the Haemophilia Society. He watched yesterday's skirmish from the press gallery.
Other countries have done better. In France two blood transfusion officials were jailed in 1993 ("scapegoats", said allies). Canada and, as long ago as 1991, Ireland, set up generous compensation schemes, the benchmark for yesterday's demands. Some Irish victims got (EURO)20,000 (£17,600), others up to (EURO)1m. I'll come back to that.
What angered Davis was that Robinson's motion had been subject to a government motion, tabled in the name of Andrew Lansley. The health secretary is a decent man and his amendment praised Labour's decision to raise annual payments to victims - some of whom have shattered lives - to £12,800 and promised to review those parts of Archer's report (the expensive bits) not yet implemented.
Actually, that's not much of a concession since the high court ordered ministers to conduct such a review in April. So much for the lip service.
The effect of the amendment was to delete all but three of Robinson's words ("that this house ... ") and insert Lansley's motion. Unacceptable, said Davis. There followed quite a spat.
Deputy speaker Dawn Primarolo explained that Speaker John Bercow had not accepted the amendment. Whereupon the deputy chief whip, Scots Lib Dem Alastair Carmichael, a large man, rose and protested that he could find no precedent for the chair - Bercow - refusing a government amendment.
Don't you dare challenge a ruling from the chair, matey, replied Primarolo. Or words to that effect. I'm not, said Carmichael, but ...
Red Dawn wasn't having it. She is new to the job but is a seasoned ex-minister who had to do a lot of the detailed coalface work for chancellor Gordon Brown. She knows her stuff. She was, incidentally, public health minister when Archer reported. .
So the debate proceeded. , starting near 1.05pm right at the bottom of the relevant page of Hansard. It is harrowing stuff, which may - or may not - be new to you.
I wish I could tell you it ended in a triumph for backbench power. Lansley was there, but slipped away early, having left the government's case (it's too expensive) to be made by the cerebral ex-health secretary Stephen Dorrell and by his own understrapper, Anne Milton, who is a tough guy.
Diane Abbott made her debut as Labour's public health spokeswoman and urged renewed efforts to sort out this lingering embarrassment.
Believe it or not, the problem came down to no one being quite sure what an Irish-style compensation scheme would cost. The Archer report appears to have suggested that it might be £3bn - not possible in a time of financial crisis, said Dorrell, though the Irish have stood by their deal made in the boom years by health minister Brian Cowen - now taoiseach in the bust years.
Yet Dr Phillip Lee, the new Tory MP for Bracknell and the only working GP now in the Commons, argued that there was a typo astray and the cost would not possibly be more than £1bn. Geoffrey Robinson leapt on the discrepancy, but Anne Milton stood her ground.
Tory MPs, who had been pretty slavish in supporting Francis Maude's "bonfire of the quangos", spoke in large numbers to support a better deal for their haemophiliac constituents - some of whom may have been wearing those red and yellow armbands in the gallery.
But when it came to the vote the result was 44 for Robinson's motion - almost all Labour so far as I can tell - and 285 (mostly Tory) for the government. All the same, I do not think the afternoon was wholly wasted. We shall see.

14 October 2010_1.Title: 2,000 DEAD AND STILL NO JUSTICE FOR THE VICTIMS OF BRITAIN'S BLOOD TRANSUSION SCANDAL; GOOD HEALTH VIEWPOINT
14 October 2010_1.Author: IAN BIRRELL
14 October 2010_1.chunks: A few months after his birth, Colin developed a bruise on his knee. It was seen by his aunt, whose son was haemophiliac, and she instantly knew what it meant the baby was also a sufferer from the blood disorder nicknamed the royal disease after it swept through Queen Victorias family.So began regular trips to hospital so that Colin could have infusions of the blood clotting agent Factor VIII, ensuring he could live a normal life. All went well until he was two years old and went in for an operation to have grommets put into his ears.The doctors used an old batch of the blood product, and the child was infected with HIV. Five years later, after months of terrible chest infections, raging fevers and debilitating diarrhoea, Colin died. He weighed just 13 pounds. After Colin was diagnosed with HIV, his parents were told to wear gloves when treating their son and to burn his mattress.Yet, even after his death, they received no explanation, no counselling, no apology. Their questions went unanswered their sons short life was shrouded in mystery. They were not even told for another three years that he had also been given highly-contagious hepatitis C, despite the huge risk to themselves and their other children.Colin was just one of thousands of people whose lives were destroyed in what Lord Winston called the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS.He was one of 4,670 British haemophiliacs left infected with Hepatitis C, of whom 1,243 were also infected with HIV. Almost 2,000 have since died as a result, with scores more needing organ transplants, and dialysis. Some victims inadvertently infected their partners.But what makes the saga so shameful is not just the short cuts, greed and incompetence that led to so many deaths. Its the cover-ups, the obfuscation and the heartlessness of successive governments that refused to admit to their failings and rejected pleas for help from suffering families.The combination of avarice, foolishness and poor regulation has echoes of the banking crisis. Both started in the poorest parts of the U.S. and left a trail of destruction worldwide.And last week, there was one more betrayal. In opposition, both the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats condemned the failure to deliver justice to the hundreds still afflicted by the contaminated blood scandal.But now in government, the Coalition has revealed little more compassion than its predecessors. Forced to respond to backbench pressure, ministers said compensation offered elsewhere was too costly to give to British people given the public spending crisis.It took nearly two decades for the horror of Colins story to emerge. The blood that killed him was discovered to have come from prisoners in Arkansas in the U.S.You would be hard-pressed to find many higher-risk blood donors. Under the governorship of Bill Clinton, who now tours the world promoting Aids prevention, the state prisons developed a multi-million dollar industry selling prisoners blood. The inmates were paid a small amount to give blood twice a week like little cows, said one Clinton aide later.This was not the only bad blood. One Canadian company was found to have extracted blood from Russian corpses, then re-labelled it as coming from donors in Sweden. The company also bought blood from Haitian slums and reportedly re-packaged out-of-date blood for sale in Europe.The result of this is that thousands of haemophiliacs in countries such as Britain, Canada, France, Ireland, Italy and Japan were infected with deadly viruses in the Seventies and Eighties.Haemophilia, a rare inherited disorder which means blood does not clot properly, leads to recurrent bleeding, usually into the joints, which may occur spontaneously or after injury.To prevent this, sufferers rely on injections of anti-coagulants made from blood plasma. Tragically, the product that helped give them a normal life led to their slaughter.Imagine the outcry if the numbers affected by tainted blood were killed in a one-off disaster. But, instead, these people have slipped away quietly one by one over the years, forgotten victims of a silent and avoidable holocaust.In Britain, taking blood from paid donors is deemed unsafe since it tends to attract the desperate in society.In the U.S., however, trade in prison blood was permitted until 1984. Then it was banned internally, but exports were allowed to continue. Incredibly, the British authorities continued to buy it, having delayed a drive towards self-sufficiency in blood products.Government papers leaked this year found that even as the resulting infections spread, officials displayed astonishing heartlessness. One Department of Health memo said: Of course, the maintenance of the life of a haemophiliac is itself expensive, and I am very much afraid that those who are already doomed will generate savings which more than cover the cost of testing blood donations. Vaccines that could have prevented deaths were ruled too expensive.No doubt such views explain why the results of an internal inquiry have never been published. Perhaps they also explain why, four years ago, Caroline Flint, then Public Health Minister, announced that key documents had been destroyed in error by a junior member of staff.Even when a privately-funded public inquiry was set up, the Government withheld vital papers allegedly on confidentiality grounds then refused to give evidence.The report of the two-year inquiry, released in February last year, condemned the horrific human tragedy. It concluded Britain was slow to react to the problems as they emerged and said commercial interests were put ahead of safety.But demands for all victims to be given decent compensation were brushed aside. There was a paltry increase in financial help for those with HIV, but nothing for those with hepatitis C beyond the promise of a review in five years time by which time many more will have died in penury.Theres also still no money for the widows of those who died before 2003 from hepatitis C.In Ireland, those infected with hepatitis C were awarded an average of 750,000 each after a public inquiry in 1991. But last week, ministers ruled out similar compensation, saying it would cost more than 3billion. The best they offered was a rapid, but limited, review into the cases of those infected with hepatitis C.As someone with a related, although less severe, blood disorder, I spent my childhood in the haematology departments of hospitals.Many of those children in beds beside me will now be dead, victims of this wretched chapter of greed. In France and Japan, people have been sent to jail for their role in the scandal. In Canada, the Red Cross was prosecuted for negligence.In Britain, this scandal has dragged on too long. There have been too many deaths, too much pain, too much grief and too many betrayals.The Government must admit its failures and accept that it let down people in the most tragic way possible if only to bring some peace at last to Colins family and thousands more like them.
