14 January 2015_1.Title: Cost of a cure
14 January 2015_1.Author: No author in byline
14 January 2015_1.chunks: Sir, Andrew Clarks article Money is the drug (Jan 19) does not take into account the real value of a cure. The cost of Sovaldi, a medicine that has a 90 per cent cure rate for patients with hepatitis C, can be viewed as high but when viewed against its value, it is low. Indeed, the assessment by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence has found Sovaldi to be extremely cost-effective, avoiding the need for liver transplants.Developing such medicines takes about 12 years and costs 1 billion. The value to the NHS is immense. Curing patients of illnesses frees up hospital beds and GP time, and means shorter waiting times and less need for community care. The value to society, in vastly reducing debilitating and life-threatening illnesses, is almost immeasurable. Medicines have a significantly higher value than their cost. We need to start thinking about medicines in this way, as more targeted, personalised medicines are being developed at even greater cost to the pharmaceutical industry.Stephen WhiteheadChief executive, the Association of the British Pharmaceutical Industry

14 January 2015_1.Title: Gilead and AbbVie take hepatitis C battle to Europe
14 January 2015_1.Author: No author in byline
14 January 2015_1.chunks: Europe is to become the next battleground between Gilead Sciences and AbbVie in their scramble to win share of the fast-growing market for hepatitis C drugs.The companies have been fighting a high-profile price war in the US over a new generation of blockbuster medicines that can cure most people with the virus within weeks.The pair are now preparing to open a new front across the Atlantic after European regulators gave AbbVie's hepatitis C treatment the green light on Friday.Competition will be welcomed by public-funded European health systems that have been rattled by the high cost of Gilead's Sovaldi medicine, which is priced at 34,983 for a 12-week course in the UK.Rick Gonzalez, AbbVie chief executive, said the company was "committed to working with local governments and healthcare systems to support broad access" to its treatment.According to the World Health Organisation there are about 15m people infected with hepatitis C in Europe - about one in 50 of the population. The disease leads to potentially life-threatening liver cirrhosis in about a third of cases.It was announced last week that NHS England would delay full-scale introduction of Sovaldi by four months until the end of July to give it more time to prepare. Patient groups saw this as a cost-saving measure.Charles Gore, chief executive of the UK-based Hepatitis C Trust, urged European governments and health providers to use the arrival of AbbVie's product as an opportunity to push for lower prices and wider access.He said: "Governments should say: 'give us a better price and we will guarantee higher volumes'. Here we have a life-threatening infectious disease which is suddenly curable in most cases. So let's find a way to give it to everyone. "The negotiating power of Europe's single-payer health systems has already secured discounts from Gilead of more than 36 per cent over the US price of Sovaldi and the entry of AbbVie could drive deeper cuts.AbbVie launched its product in the US last month at a price of $83,319 for a 12-week course - just below the price of Sovaldi and sharply less than the $94,500 charged by Gilead for a new Sovaldi-based combination treatment called Harvoni.This has triggered a discounting battle as the pair compete to sell their medicines to rival US health insurance plans.Both companies declined to comment on their European pricing strategy.AbbVie's treatment was approved on Friday by the European Medicines Agency for use in patients with the genotype 1 form of hepatitis C, which represent 60 per cent of cases.The market for hepatitis C drugs is forecast by Datamonitor Healthcare to increase from $2.9bn in 2013 to $19.2bn in 2016. Of this, the top five European markets - France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK - accounted for $872m in 2013, rising to a forecast $4bn next year.The medicines are replacing old interferon-based treatments that have much lower success rates and more unpleasant side effects.Gilead and AbbVie have sought to justify their high prices by arguing that curing the disease saves money in the long-run by avoiding the higher cost of liver transplants and other care.

14 January 2015_1.Title: German police to use anti-spitting hoods on suspects
14 January 2015_1.Author: Justin Huggler Berlin
14 January 2015_1.chunks: Prevalence of spitting by suspected criminals in Bremen has led to three officers being hospitalisedPolice in the northern German city of Bremen have been issued with a new weapon in their fight against crime: spit hoods, transparent cotton hoods that can be placed over detainees heads to prevent them spitting at officers.Apparently, being spat at has become such a common problem for police in Bremen that it is causing health concerns.The new hoods were issued after an incident in which three police officers had to be hospitalised for medical tests, after a drug addict infected with hepatitis C spat at them.The addict spat wildly around the police car in which he was detained, and his saliva landed on the mouth of a female officer, and in the faces of her two colleagues.But the new hoods are not without controversy: critics have compared them to the hoods worn by detainees at Gauntanamo Bay and US military prisons in Afghanistan.Those criticisms are rejected by the Bremen police union. You can see and hear through the hood, its chairman, Jochen Kopelke, told Spiegel magazine. Breathing is not difficult. In addition, the detainee will permanently supervised.Unlike the hoods used by the US military, the German police hoods are transparent and made of thin cotton.The police union has long called for the hoods to be issued, over fears police could be at risk of HIV infection if a detainee spits blood at them.There are situations in which attackers spit with everything they have in their mouths, Mr Kopelke said.The new hoods are carried in every police car, but officers are not allowed to use them pre-emptively: they can only be used on a suspect who has already spat at officers, or who is known to have a history of spitting.Despite the safeguards, other police forces in Germany have so far rejected the hoods as too draconian a measure. In Bremens neighbouring state of Lower Saxony, they are officially prohibited, while in other states they are only rarely used.

The Guardian

November 27, 2014 Thursday 12:05 AM GMT 

Doctors call for tougher laws on alcohol abuse to tackle liver disease crisis; 
The UK is the only country in western Europe except Finland where liver disease has increased over the past three decades

BYLINE: Sarah Boseley, heath editor

SECTION: POLITICS

LENGTH: 826 words

Senior doctors are calling for tougher government action on alcohol abuse, after warning that Britain is the only country in western Europe except Finland where liver disease has increased over the past three decades.
"There is a human, social, and financial imperative to act now if the UK's burden of liver disease and all its consequences are to be tackled and the NHS is not to be overwhelmed by the cost of treating advanced stage liver disease," said Professor Roger Williams, director of the Institute of Hepatology in London, lead author of a report from a new Lancet Commission.
Professor Jane Dacre, president of the Royal College of Physicians, agreed with the findings and called for the government to take a much stronger line with the food and drinks industries, introducing minimum unit pricing that makes the strongest alcoholic drinks the most expensive. 
The report is stark reading, she said. "Over the past 20-30 years, we have not been able to turn the tide of harmful drinking in the way we have been able to reduce the amount of smoking in the UK. At a national level we need the government to introduce national measures such as minimum unit pricing, and reduce the availability of alcohol, and restrict advertising and marketing."
The report points out that 70-90% of obese people are suffering from non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which - like alcohol - causes cirrhosis and can lead to early death.
"As a nation, we should stop pretending that voluntary agreements on alcohol and food will improve the situation - they don't, only legislation will do," said Dacre.
Jackie Ballard, chief executive of Alcohol Concern, warned that "the UK is in danger of losing the battle against liver disease, which goes against the trend in much of the rest of Europe where many of our neighbours are actually making progress.
"Figures show an alarming rise in hospital admissions from alcoholic liver disease over the past few years. For the first time we are seeing young people under 30 dying of alcoholic liver disease, the so-called 'alcopops generation', who have grown up in a society where alcohol is available at almost anytime, anywhere, at incredibly cheap prices and promoted non-stop."
The commission said the UK is the only country in western Europe except Finland where liver disease has increased over the past three decades. There have been vast improvements in health and life expectancy in other chronic diseases such as stroke, heart disease and many cancers. Liver disease "stands out as the one glaring exception". It is the third commonest cause of premature death in the UK. More than one million hospital admissions per year are for alcohol-related disorders. In England and Wales, 600,000 people have some form of liver disease, 60,000 of whom have cirrhosis. In 2012, there were nearly 11,000 deaths. "These figures represent increases of 62% in liver disease and 40% in cirrhosis in ten years," says the report.
Three-quarters of deaths from liver disease are the result of excessive drinking, but deaths as a result of obesity and also hepatitis C infection are also going up.
In western Europe, the opposite has happened, says the paper, citing France where liver deaths were 25 times higher than in the UK in 1960. "The French health services were prepared to deal with liver disease at every level," says the report. Controls on marketing were introduced, including bans on TV and cinema advertising and health warnings on bottles. Consumption of cheap strong wine dropped.
"The UK overtook France, Italy and Spain in terms of liver mortality in the 1990s and only Finland, where availability of alcohol has been liberalised as in the UK, has had a similar upward trend in liver mortality," says the report. In the UK, alcohol consumption has shifted substantially from moderate strength beer sold in pubs to strong lager, cider, wine and spirits sold by supermarkets for drinking at home. Taxation has not kept pace with rising incomes, making alcohol more affordable for heavy drinkers and young people. The report says: "As noted by the House of Commons health committee, 'The alcohol industry should not carry more weight in determining health policy than the Chief Medical Officer'."
Radical improvements are needed in services to spot people whose drinking is endangering their health and get them into treatment, says the report. Early detection by GPs is virtually non-existent. The problem is at its most severe in the most deprived areas of the country.
"The evidence outlined in the report, contributed by some of the UK's leading experts in the field, should leave nobody in any doubt about the present unacceptable levels of premature death and the overall poor standards of care being afforded to liver patients," said Professor Williams. Reforms would save the NHS money but must happen now. "The scale of the problem is too great for it to take second place to short-term political considerations," he said.

14 January 2015_1.Title: Governments must ask for fairer drug prices
14 January 2015_1.Author: No author in byline
14 January 2015_1.chunks: Sir, Researchers at the University of York are right to call for a reduction in the price pharmaceuticals companies are paid for their products ("Call to end care that goes against the greater good", February 19). It is not just cancer drugs that are unaffordable; the cost of fully vaccinating a child is now 68 times more expensive than it was in 2001.For too long, the pharmaceutical industry has been allowed to reap enormous profits while reinvesting just a fraction of its turnover into research and development of innovative new drugs. Meanwhile little has been done, for example, to improve treatments for tuberculosis in the last 50 years, leaving patients with ineffective treatment regimens with debilitating side effects. The pharmaceuticals industry also shrouds the prices it charges in secrecy. Currently, countries such as Morocco and Tunisia pay more for the pneumococcal vaccine than France does.Overstretched budgets are forcing health authorities in the UK and elsewhere to make impossible decisions. In Britain, hepatitis C patients now face delays in accessing NHS treatment because of the exorbitant price set by Gilead.Mdecins Sans Frontires/Doctors Without Borders (MSF) is calling for greater transparency about drug and vaccine research and development costs, as well as greater accountability, oversight and intervention from governments to ensure that pharmaceutical companies do not sell drugs and vaccines at any price they choose. We are urging GSK and Pfizer to reduce the pneumococcal vaccine price to $5 per child, inclusive of all three doses. Such a reduction is possible - the Indian manufacturer Serum Institute has announced that it plans to sell its version of the vaccine for $6. If patients are really our primary concern, then governments must ask for fairer and more transparent drug prices.Katy AthersuchMedical Access and Innovation Policy Advisor,Mdecins Sans Frontires/Doctors Without Borders (MSF)

25 March 2015_1.Title: Blood scandal report branded a 'whitewash'
25 March 2015_1.Author: CHARLIE COOPER
25 March 2015_1.chunks: NewsVictims of a contamination scandal in which thousands of people were given NHS blood products infected with hepatitis C or HIV have branded the official inquiry a "whitewash" after the findings were published yesterday.Every person in Scotland who had a blood transfusion before 1991 should be tested for hepatitis C, according to the sole recommendation of a six-year inquiry into one of the biggest treatment failures in NHS history.The Prime Minister issued an apology following the publication of the 1,800-page report by Lord Penrose. It concluded that little more could have been done by Scottish authorities to prevent the infections, which took place between 1970 and 1991, often caused by imported blood supplies and those collected in prisons.There was an angry response to the report from victims and relatives who had gathered at the National Museum in Edinburgh to see its publication, with shouts of "whitewash" after its conclusions were read out.The Haemophilia Society said it was "shocked and disappointed" with the findings.6The number of years it has taken for the inquiry to be completed - costing millions

25 March 2015_1.Title: HIV transfusion victims enraged by 'whitewash'
25 March 2015_1.Author: Alison Little
25 March 2015_1.chunks: CAMPAIGNERS reacted with fury yesterday to a "whitewash" report into a scandal in which thousands of people contracted HIV and Hepatitis C after being given contaminated blood by the NHS.Prime Minister David Cameron apologised to those whose lives have been ruined by the error and pledged an extra 25million towards compensation.Campaigners burned copies of the Penrose Inquiry and said they had not received a single answer to their questions.In the Seventies and Eighties, thousands of people - including hundreds of haemophiliacs - were infected with Hepatitis C or HIV during blood transfusions. Many have since died.The report for Scotland, the only part of the UK to hold an inquiry, said donors should have been screened more thoroughly and the collection of blood from prisoners should have stopped sooner.It said doctors' "patronising attitudes" meant patients were not adequately informed of risks - but "all that could reasonably be done was done".Its only recommendation was that anyone who had a transfusion in Scotland before 1991 should have a Hepatitis C test if they had not had one.Inquiry chairman and former High Court judge Lord Penrose was too ill to attend the presentation at Edinburgh's National Museum.Glenn Wilkinson from the Contaminated Blood Campaign said: "I feel devastated. I do not think we have had a single answer. "Mark Ward, who contracted Hepatitis C and HIV, said "anything could have been in that blood". He told the BBC: "I was treated as nothing more than a lump of meat to be experimented on. "Scottish Health Secretary Shona Robison accepted the recommendation to offer Hepatitis C tests and vowed to review and improve financial support schemes

25 March 2015_1.Title: Penrose report: Blood scandal inquiry branded a ‘whitewash’
25 March 2015_1.Author: Charlie Cooper
25 March 2015_1.chunks: Nearly 3,000 people in Scotland were infected with hepatitis C from infected bloodAll people in Scotland who had a blood transfusion before 1991 should be tested for hepatitis C, according to the sole recommendation of a six-year inquiry into one of the biggest treatment failures in NHS history.Victims of the blood contamination scandal, in which thousands of people were given blood products that were infected with hepatitis or HIV, received an apology from the Prime Minister, following the publication of a 1,800 page report by the Scottish judge Lord Penrose.However, some of the victims branded the inquiry a whitewash, after it concluded that little more could have been done by Scottish authorities to prevent the infections, which took place between 1970 and 1991, often caused by imported blood supplies and those collected in prisons.The report estimated that nearly 3,000 people in Scotland were infected with hepatitis C from infected blood and 60 people with HIV.It said more could have been done to screen for hepatitis C, and that blood donations from prisons, which were once common practice, should have been stopped sooner, because of the higher rates of hepatitis in prison populations.Health news: in picturesSpeaking in the House of Commons following its publication David Cameron said: It is difficult to imagine the feelings of unfairness that people must feel at being infected with something like hepatitis C or HIV as a result of a totally unrelated treatment within the NHS and to each and every one of those people I would like to say sorry on behalf of the government for something that should not have happened.He said the Government would improve the way that victims are paid compensation and pledged 25m next year for the scheme.Scotlands Health Secretary Shona Robison apologised on behalf of the Scottish NHS and government. Scotland is the only home nation to hold an inquiry into what was a UK-wide issue, and also affected other countries. The report said that Scottish safety measures compared well to other countries.Many of those infected were haemophiliacs, who require blood donations to help their blood to clot. Yesterday the Haemophilia Society said it was shocked and disappointed by the report.Had the UK become self-sufficient in blood products in the 1970s hepatitis C infections may not have had such prevalence in the bleeding disorders community together with a great reduction in HIV infection in the early 1980s, saving hundreds of lives, the group said in its early response to the report.The Haemophilia Society is therefore shocked and disappointed that Lord Penrose does not recognise from the evidence he has gathered that the UK government through its action and inaction caused the death and devastating long-term illness of so many of our community.Joe Peaty and Sue Threakall, co-chairs of the group Tainted Blood, which represents patients affected, said: After 30 40 years of suffering and loss of more than 2,000 lives, we expected more than a 30 second apology from the Prime Minister, and a in passing agreement from Labour leader Ed Miliband to follow what is already a half-hearted single recommendation from the Penrose report.

25 March 2015_1.Author: Michael Glackin
25 March 2015_1.chunks: An inquiry, chaired by Lord Penrose, into the use of contaminated blood from UK jails and borstals says the tragedy could not have been preventedIn the 1970s and 1980s, the National Health Service routinely used blood products from UK jails and borstals as well as American prisons.The practice contributed to a scandal that has been described as the worst treatment disaster in the history of the service. Hundreds died, many of them haemophiliac patients.But after six years and 12 million an inquiry, chaired by the judge Lord Penrose on behalf of the Scottish government, has concluded that there was nothing which could reasonably have been done at the time to prevent the tragedy.His report made one single recommendation: that anyone who had a blood transfusion in Scotland before 1991 should be offered a hepatitis C test if they had not had one before.Lord Penrose said that there were few aspects in which matters could or should have been handled differently and that the inquiry had to take into account the conditions at the time rather than to judge by todays standards.Despite this, and amid much criticism from victims at Lord Penroses failure to apportion blame, his report stated that more should have been done to screen blood and donors for hepatitis C in the early 1990s.Lord Penrose said that a recommendation by the advisory committee on the virological safety of blood for screening should have been made in May 1990 rather than in November of that year.The report said that the outbreak of the first Gulf war accounted for some delays in screening. 25 March 2015_1.Title: Trust must be won again
25 March 2015_1.Author: No author in byline
25 March 2015_1.chunks: After six years, it is time to act swiftly on Lord Penrose's conclusionsThe anger and frustration of those who have waited so long for Lord Penrose's report on the blood contamination that caused the deaths of hundreds of patients infected with HIV and hepatitis C is understandable. To learn, at the end of a sixyear process and a detailed investigation that produced a report running to more than 1,800 pages, that there is just one single recommendation at the end of it, must seem a baffling conclusion.No one is more apologetic for the length of time it has taken than Lord Penrose himself. He notes the frustration he and his team felt as they tracked down witnesses, combed through reports dating back over 20 years, then sent out release letters to those who had given evidence. And this is no dry and dusty report. Lord Penrose admits the discovery that blood, intended to heal and save, was the cause of disease and death, was "the stuff of nightmares," while those who administered the fatal transfusions were overcome by what he describes as "waves of hope, followed by waves of despair".That this report has been brought out at all is to the credit of the Scottish government. No similar investigation has been mounted elsewhere in the UK, and the SNP, which made a manifesto commitment that it would be completed, is to be congratulated on delivering on that promise. This has been described as the worst treatment disaster in NHS history, and to have left it unexplained and unexplored would have been a scandal.What has emerged will serve as an important lesson for those administering blood transfusions. With the benefit of hindsight it now seems the height of irresponsibility to have used blood from prisoners, many of whom were likely to have been drug users. The process should have been delayed until proper screening tests were available. And finally, far more care should have been taken to ensure that only properly screened blood was used on patients who so badly needed it.It is devastating now to learn that there was a fatal delay in following up on the recommendations of the Advisory Committee on the Virological Safety of Blood that more screening was needed. For seven vital months that advice was not acted on, and lives would have been saved if it had been. Those lessons have now been learnt but too late for those who suffered and died.The one recommendation Lord Penrose has made is being acted on, and it must be pursued as a matter of urgency: anyone who had a transfusion in Scotland before 1991 should be offered a hepatitis C test if they have not had one before.There has been one other change since that period in the Seventies and Eighties when contaminated blood was administered. That has to do with attitudes to the medical profession.Then, doctors were listened to with trust and respect they in turn tended to adopt a paternalistic attitude to their patients. That respect has been diluted over the years. Patients are far more likely to question the treatment they are given, to check it for themselves, to turn to the internet for research. That may cause the medical profession concern and, of course, it is an approach that can be overused and sometimes abused.But if that questioning attitude had been adopted 30 years ago, lives might have been saved. What is needed now is an immediate and open response to this report, close study of its conclusions, and the adoption of its recommendation, so that doctors can regain the trust that they have lost.

25 March 2015_1.Title: KILLER BLOOD 'WHITEWASH'
25 March 2015_1.Author: DEAN HERBERT
25 March 2015_1.chunks: Anger over HIV inquiry findingsA MAJOR inquiry into how thousands of patients were infected with deadly diseases from contaminated blood has been branded a whitewash by victims.More than 2,000 people from across the UK died, while thousands more have had their lives destroyed by HIV and Hepatitis C. The victims contracted the diseases after being given blood products taken from high-risk donors such as prostitutes and prisoners during treatment on the NHS.Some passed on diseases to partners and children, and others needed organs transplants.Scandal Yesterday Prime Minister David Cameron made a formal apology to the victims on behalf of the Government as a 1,800-page report into the scandal was published.Hundreds of those affected were in Scotland, the only part of the UK to hold an inquiry.The inquiry, chaired by Judge Lord Penrose, found that more should have been done to screen blood and donors for Hepatitis C in the early 1990s, and that the collection of blood from prisoners should have stopped earlier.But it said that once the risk of HIV and Aids emerged, "all that could reasonably be done was done".Lord Penrose is seriously ill in hospital and the statement was read out on his behalf by inquiry secretary Maria McCann. The report recommended that anyone who had a blood transfusion before September 1991 should be tested for Hep C.But families yelled: "Whitewash!" as soon as the inquiry statement was read out, while Bill Wright, from Haemophilia Scotland, insisted that "this is by no means the end of the story".Mr Wright, who got Hep C from a contaminated transfusion, added: "It's not about broken processes - it's about broken lives. We will never get the complete truth because too many people have died while waiting for the inquiry. "scotnews@dailystar.co.uk

25 March 2015_1.chunks:
The Times (London)

March 26, 2015 Thursday  
Edition 1; 
Scotland

'Nothing could have prevented tragedy'

BYLINE: Michael Glackin

SECTION: NEWS; Pg. 3

LENGTH: 636 words

In the 1970s and 1980s, the National Health Service routinely used blood products from UK jails and borstals as well as American prisons.
The practice contributed to a scandal that has been described as the worst treatment disaster in the history of the service. Hundreds of people in Scotland, and thousands across the rest of the UK, became infected with hepatitis C and HIV. Hundreds died, many of them haemophiliac patients.
But after six years and £12 million an inquiry, chaired by the judge Lord Penrose on behalf of the Scottish government, has concluded that there was "nothing which could reasonably have been done" at the time to prevent the tragedy. 
His report made one single recommendation: that anyone who had a blood transfusion in Scotland before 1991 should be offered a hepatitis C test if they had not had one before.
Lord Penrose said that there were "few aspects in which matters could or should have been handled differently" and that the inquiry had to take into account the conditions at the time rather than to judge by today's standards.
Despite this, and amid much criticism from victims at Lord Penrose's failure to apportion blame, his report stated that more should have been done to screen blood and donors for hepatitis C in the early 1990s.
Lord Penrose said that a recommendation by the advisory committee on the virological safety of blood for screening should have been made in May 1990 rather than in November of that year.
The report said that the outbreak of the first Gulf war accounted for some delays in screening. However, Lord Penrose also pointed to "unresolved issues in England and Wales as to how screening was to be funded". This, he said, meant that while some parts of Scotland were ready to begin screening in late 1990, the process was effectively delayed until well into 1991 owing to the need for "a uniform start date throughout the UK". The report also concluded that collecting blood from prisoners should have stopped sooner.
Lord Penrose said that the Home Office had favoured donations from those behind bars, as it offered them a chance "to make restitution to society". The report said that "with the benefit of hindsight" collection from prisoners was "inadvisable" and, owing, to the number with drug problems, should have been stopped sooner.
There was "clear evidence" at the time, it said, that many of these prisoners had been convicted of drugs offences and had admitted to having drug habits while in prison.
Lord Penrose also said that patients were not adequately informed of the risks of receiving blood products by medical staff because of the "paternalistic attitude" of doctors at the time. However, the inquiry concluded that nothing more could have been done to prevent the transmission of HIV, and that Scotland's practices at the time compared well to other countries.
Decades of disaster
1970s and 1980s: Thousands of patients, many haemophiliacs, were given blood contaminated with hepatitis C and HIV.
Mid-1980s: Blood begins to be heat-treated before use, to rid it of viruses.
1983: The first haemophiliac in the UK dies from Aids.
1986: Screening of blood for HIV starts after the identification of HIV and Aids.
1991: Testing for hepatitis C is introduced.
2004: Patients infected with hepatitis C from contaminated blood start to receive government compensation payments, based on the severity of their condition. ? 2006: A call from the health committee of the Scottish parliament for a public inquiry into contaminated blood is rejected. ? 2008: Nicola Sturgeon, the Scottish government health secretary, announces the Penrose inquiry. ? 2009: Lord Penrose opens his inquiry with a minute's silence. ? 2012: Closing submissions are given to the inquiry.
2015: Lord Penrose issues his report, which provokes anger from victims and their families.

25 March 2015_1.Title: Sturgeon pledges to deliver justice for blood victims
25 March 2015_1.Author: JANE CASSIDY
25 March 2015_1.chunks: NICOLA STURGEON pledged her 'absolute determination' to do everything she can to deliver justice and support to people affected by the contaminated blood scandal.The first minister added her own apology to NHS patients in Scotland who were given blood and blood products infected with hepatitis C and HIV in the 1970s and 1980s.During first minister's questions at Holyrood yesterday, Ms Sturgeon said: 'I want to say a very sincere and heartfelt sorry to everyone who has had to deal with the devastating impact of infected NHS blood and blood products. 'I can't begin to understand the difficulties and the many hardships that individuals and their families have had to contend with.' Many of the victims described the inquiry report as a 'whitewash' and called for greater support from politicians. Ms Sturgeon said the Scottish government will implement the inquiry's recommendation that anyone who had a blood transfusion before 1991 should be tested for hepatitis C. She said financial support for people affected will be looked at 'as a matter of urgency'. Pilot schemes will be set up with a view to establishing a national support service and there will be more funding for charities Haemophilia Scotland and the Scottish Infected Blood Forum.She added: 'I am absolutely determined we do everything we can to deliver justice and support to those who have suffered so much.'

25 March 2015_1.Title: Blood scandal was 'a tragedy'
25 March 2015_1.Author: Dean Herbert
25 March 2015_1.chunks: THE contaminated blood scandal amounts to "one of the greatest healthcare-related tragedies ever witnessed in this country", the Health Secretary has told the Scottish Parliament.Shona Robison's comments came as the victims demanded more compensation and the First Minister vowed to "deliver justice" for those affected.On Wednesday, the Penrose Inquiry, set up by the Scottish Government to find out how thousands of patients became infected with Hepatitis C and HIV in the 1970s and 80s, was published.But following a six-year probe costing 12million, the findings were branded a "whitewash" by victims after it concluded little could have been done to prevent the infections.The publication of the 1,800-page document prompted apologies from the Prime Minister and the Scottish Government but victims and their relatives said the report failed to provide any answers.Harm More than 2,000 people died in the UK after being given infected blood products and thousands of others had their lives damaged to a huge degree.Hundreds of those affected were from Scotland, which was the only part of the UK to hold an official inquiry.Ms Robison told MSPs: "We must keep the people who have been affected at the centre of our thoughts throughout this process. I can only express my deepest sympathy and regret to them. I am also very aware that for many the inquiry conclusions do not meet there expectations and the outcomes they would wish to see. "It is right to acknowledge that many patients and their families are of the view that the payments they receive are insufficient. "Bruce Norval, who contracted Hepatitis C after being given contaminated blood, insisted victims and their families were suffering "ongoing harm" and needed support as well as financial compensation.The 50-year-old, who lives in the Highlands, said he became ill when he was 15 after being diagnosed with haemophilia as a child and thought he was probably infected when he was three.He added: "This is ongoing harm that has been created by the lack of psychiatric and fiscal support for families who are left desperate in the wake of deaths from HIV and hepatitis. "Yes, the politicians should deal with it - there's no reason for them to compound a bad report with bad political decisions. "But if Penrose was to remain credible to victims, there should have been at least some acknowledgement of the colossal harm that has been caused by the secrecy around people's HIV and by the lack of anybody to talk to for families who are isolated, dying of diseases over periods of decades. "During First Minister's Questions at Holyrood yesterday, Nicola Sturgeon said: "As First Minister of Scotland and on behalf of the Government of Scotland and the NHS, I want to take this opportunity to say a very sincere and heartfelt sorry to everyone who has had to deal with the devastating impact of infected NHS blood and blood products. "I can't begin to understand the difficulties and the many hardships that individuals and their families have had to contend with. "Victims She said the Government will act to implement the inquiry's recommendation and review financial support as a "matter of urgency".Meanwhile at Westminster, health minister Jane Ellison, said that another inquiry into the contaminated blood scandal south of the Border would not be in the best interests of victims and their families. 'I can only express my deepest sympathy and regret to them' SHONA ROBISON

25 March 2015_1.Title: Robison in blood cash vow to victims
25 March 2015_1.Author: LINDSAY WATLING
25 March 2015_1.chunks: THE Scottish Government is to review the cash aid given to victims of the tainted blood scandal, Health Secretary Shona Robison said yesterday.Patients and families will be involved in the review process, she added. Responding to the Penrose Inquiry findings, Ms Robison said the scandal was among our "greatest healthcare tragedies".And she apologised to those who contracted HIV and hepatitis C after the NHS gave them infected blood and blood products in the 1970s and 1980s.Ms Robison told MSPs: "Many patients and their families believe their payments are insufficient. "We'll move ahead with reviewing these schemes. "Many victims called the inquiry a "whitewash".Ms Robison said: "I am very aware that for many the conclusions do not meet their expectations."

25 March 2015_1.Title: Contaminated blood payouts to be reviewed
25 March 2015_1.Author: Jeremy Watson
25 March 2015_1.chunks: Nicola Sturgeon apologises to those who contracted hepatitis C and HIV and pledges to do everything she can to support those affectedCompensation paid to Scottish victims of the blood-contamination scandal is to be reviewed to ensure that those affected have received justice for one of the greatest healthcare-related tragedies ever witnessed in this country.Nicola Sturgeon, the first minister, pledged her absolute determination yesterday to do everything she could to support those affected. She issued an unreserved apology to those who contracted hepatitis C and HIV from infected blood and blood products used by the NHS in the 1970s and 1980s.The Penrose inquiry, which was set up by the Scottish government and spent six years investigating the events, prompted angry criticism from victims groups after publishing its findings on Wednesday.Responding at first ministers questions at Holyrood, Mrs Sturgeon said: As first minister of Scotland, and on behalf of the government of Scotland and the NHS, I want to take this opportunity to say a very sincere and heartfelt sorry to everyone who has had to deal with the devastating impact of infected NHS blood and blood products.I cant begin to understand the difficulties and the many hardships that individuals and their families have had to contend with. We must do everything in our power to make sure that terrible events like these never, ever happen again.The inquiry found that more should have been done to screen blood and donors for hepatitis C in the early 1990s, and said the collection of blood from prisoners should have stopped earlier. Its single recommendation was that anyone who had a blood transfusion before 1991 should be tested for hepatitis C. Victims described the report as a whitewash and called for greater support from the government.I can understand the feelings, the frustration, even the disappointment of all of those affected by these dreadful events, Mrs Sturgeon said.We regard the publication of the report as the start of a process of further engagement with those affected, rather than an end to the investigations.She said the government would act to implement the inquirys recommendation and to review financial support for victims as a matter of urgency.We recognise that direct payments are only part of the support package for those affected. We will also, therefore, implement pilots to increase psychological and social work support, with a view to putting in place a national service.Shona Robison, the health secretary,called the scandal one of the greatest healthcare-related tragedies ever witnessed in this country, and said a focus group of patients and their families would be involved in the review.Speaking at Holyrood, she said: It is right to acknowledge that many patients and their families are of the view that the payments they receive are insufficient. We have committed to reviewing these schemes and we will now move ahead with that.

25 March 2015_1.chunks:
The Guardian

March 26, 2015 Thursday 4:54 PM GMT 

Scottish government tells contaminated blood victims: "We will do all we can to deliver justice and support"; 
As campaigners brand Penrose inquiry a whitewash, health minister sets out financial assistance review, families' advisory group and extra funding

BYLINE: Libby Brooks

SECTION: UK NEWS

LENGTH: 693 words

                     Nicola Sturgeon has pledged that the Scottish government will do "everything we can to deliver justice and support" to the victims of Scotland's contaminated blood scandal, after campaigners dismissed yesterday's Penrose inquiry report as a "whitewash".
On Thursday afternoon, Scottish health minister Shona Robison set out a series of measures, including: 

a review of financial assistance schemes for victims, to conclude by World Haemophilia Day in April 2016
establishing a patient and families reference group to help with the review of these schemes
pilots of increased psychological and social work support with a view to putting in place a national service
core funding for Haemophilia Scotland and the Scottish Infected Blood Forum for next three years
It estimated that nearly 3,000 people in Scotland were infected with hepatitis C and 78 people contracted HIV over 30 years ago after the authorities failed to screen blood supplies and blood products for the potentially fatal viruses. The charity Haemophilia Scotland estimates that 193 people have died as a result of the contamination. 
Victims and families reacted angrily to the findings of the five-year inquiry, headed by the former judge Lord Penrose, which offered only a single recommendation, for anyone who had a blood transfusion before 1991 to be tested for hepatitis C.
There were shouts of "whitewash" as the report was presented at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh on Wednesday morning, and several relatives burned a copy outside the building.
Describing the infected blood scandal as "the biggest tragedy that has faced our health service", Robison told the Holyrood chamber on Thursday afternoon:
 I realise there may be some criticism of the cost and length of time it has taken for the inquiry to reach its findings and I am very aware that for many the inquiry conclusions do not reach their expectations. 
She insisted that further action would be "driven by those affected", and stated that she was "open-minded" about whether to move forward on a UK-wide basis or act using devolved powers. (Because the contamination occurred more than three decades ago, early support schemes pre-date devolution.) But Robison insisted: "What I am clear about is that we will not stand back or stall on our moral duty to make sure those affected have the proper and adequate support."
Speaking earlier on Thursday at first minister's questions, Nicola Sturgeon said that she apologised "openly and without reservation" on behalf of the Scottish government and the NHS.
She stressed that the Scottish government regarded the publication of the report as only the beginning of engagement with those affected.
 As health secretary I set up the Penrose Inquiry. Now that I am first minister I am absolutely determined that we do everything we can to deliver justice and support to those who have suffered so much. 
                     Bill Wright of Haemophilia Scotland, himself in receipt of contaminated blood, welcomed both ministers' statements, saying:
 People are much more reflective today. The apology is what we've been looking for for many years, and it's clear there's a different approach in Scotland in terms of working with families. 
 After the initial fury yesterday, people will now start to look at the report in detail and at all of the evidence rather than the conclusions of one inquiry chairman. 
Wright added that the key issue now was one of pace. "There needs to be a balance between the immediate needs of those in poverty now and a longer-term settlement."
David Cameron yesterday likewise apologised and promised to release £25m in financial support for the victims immediately, and today under-secretary of state for health Jane Ellison told the Commons that she regretted that more could not be done in the present parliament.
 This is an interim response to a long and detailed report and all matters will need to be considered by the next government. I am very well aware of the high level of concern amongst sufferers with the way the current financial assistance schemes workand I certainly think they will need to be loooked at in more detail.

25 March 2015_1.chunks: THE PM yesterday apologised to people infected with HIV or Hepatitis C after receiving contaminated blood.David Cameron said it was difficult to imagine their "feelings of unfairness" after the NHS scandal of the 1970s and 80s. Thousands of Brits given blood transfusions before 1991 are now being urged to get checked.The Penrose Inquiry reported its findings into the scandal in Scotland yesterday. Scottish Health Secretary Shona Robison also apologised.

25 March 2015_1.Title: Cameron says sorry to thousands infected by HIV in NHS blood scandal
25 March 2015_1.Author: KAREN MORRISON
25 March 2015_1.chunks: DAVID Cameron has apologised on behalf of the British government to victims infected with HIV and hepatitis C through contaminated NHS blood. Thousands of haemophiliac patients contracted the deadly viruses in Scottish hospitals in the 1970s and 1980s through routine blood tests and transfusions.After an agonising six-year wait for the results of the Penrose inquiry, victims and their families were dealt another blow by being told that all that could reasonably be done was done".Some families shouted out whitewash" as soon as the statement ended.Campaigner Bill Wright, from Haemophilia Scotland, begged people to stay to listen to him, saying: This is by no means the end of the story. "One woman shouted: Weve shed enough tears. "Bill said, sobbing: I am one of you, I am infected. Its not about broken processes, its about broken lives. "More should have been done to screen blood and donors for hepatitis C in the early 1990s, the inquiry added, and the collection of blood from prisoners should have stopped earlier.But nothing could have been done to prevent the transmission of HIV, it said.A statement read on behalf of Lord Penrose, who led the inquiry, said: For people infected by HIV/Aids and/or hepatitis C, the impact on their lives and the lives of their loved ones has often been devastating. "The Prime Minister added in the Commons today: To each and every one of these people I would like to say sorry on behalf of the government for something that should not have happened. "People who had a blood transfusion in Scotland before 1991 should now be tested for hepatitis C, an inquiry published today has said.Warnings were released by medics as early as 1977 that blood products could transmit infections.More than 2,000 people affected by the scandal had died by 2012.

25 March 2015_1.Title: PM 'SORRY' FOR BLOOD SCANDAL
25 March 2015_1.Author: No author in byline
25 March 2015_1.chunks: CAMERON: I'M SORRYDAVID Cameron apologised to victims of the contaminated blood scandal as it emerged 3,000 Scots were given Hepatitis C or HIV by the NHS.A long-awaited public inquiry revealed thousands more patients than first thought were infected between 1970 and 1991.The PM told the Commons yesterday: "I would like to say sorry on behalf of the Government for Continued on Page Nine Continued from Page One something that should not have happened." In total, the inquiry identified 247 deaths due to tainted blood products in transfusions or as treatment for disorders such as haemophilia. An estimated 2,978 people were infected with Hep C and 78 with HIV.Among the victims were 21 children at Glasgow's Yorkhill hospital who contracted HIV.Amid anger at the report's findings, Lord Penrose urged Hep C tests on every Scot who had a blood transfusion before Robiin 1991. Health Secretary Shona Robison said: "On behalf of the NHS and Government in Scotland, I would like to say sorry to everyone affected. "First Minister Nicola Sturgeon, above, is due to repeat the apology during proceedings at Holyrood today.

25 March 2015_1.Title: Blood scandal victim left "totally and utterly disappointed"
25 March 2015_1.Author: RACHEL GUY
25 March 2015_1.chunks: A HAEMOPHILIAC who was given contaminated blood has spoken about the colossal harm" the scandal has caused as he demanded proper compensation" for those affected. Bruce Norval, who contracted hepatitis C, said he had been left totally and utterly disappointed" by the recent report into what happened.The Penrose Inquiry, which was set up by the Scottish Government, spent years probing events in the 1970s and 1980s when hundreds of people in Scotland were given contaminated blood by the NHS.Patients, many of whom had haemophilia, became infected with hepatitis C and HIV from the contaminated blood and products which should have helped to treat them.Prime Minister David Cameron and Scottish Health Secretary Shona Robison apologised to victims after yesterdays report found that more should have been done to screen blood and donors for hepatitis C in the early 1990s and said the collection of blood from prisoners should have stopped earlier.Mr Cameron confirmed 25 million of funding to improve financial support for the NHS patients who were infected with hepatitis C and HIV during the 1970s and 1980s.Mr Norval, who believes he was given infected blood when he was three years old, said more needed to be done.He insisted the victims and their families were suffering ongoing harm" and needed support as well as financial compensation.Mr Norval told BBC Radio Scotlands Good Morning Scotland programme: There are ongoing problems for victims families, even where the victim has died years earlier.This is ongoing harm that has been created by the lack of psychiatric and fiscal support for families who are left desperate in the wake of deaths from HIV and hepatitis. "He insisted: Yes, the politicians should deal with it - theres no reason for them to compound a bad report with bad political decisions.But... if Penrose was to remain credible to victims, there should have been at least some acknowledgement of the colossal harm that has been caused by the secrecy around peoples HIV and by the lack of anybody to talk to for families that are isolated, dying of diseases over periods of decades. "Mr Norval said he became sick with hepatitis C when he was 15, and was probably infected when I was three".He told how the disease has impacted on his health, saying: I have become unable to work, I feel nothing but pain, I have no sense of touch, I live with cancer checks every six months, I suffer from regular exhaustion, gastric upset.I dont go through a single day when I am not significantly unwell. "He said Nicola Sturgeon, who pressed for an inquiry while the SNP was in opposition had kept her word" by instigating the inquiry after the SNP came to power at Holyrood.But he added: I would like to see her now show the courage of her convictions and actually set forward to bring about proper compensation for victims in the way that she represented us in opposition. "He also stressed that victims needed more than financial compensation.Mr Norval said: Money would be good, but there is also the need for psychiatric support, theres the need to go out and find out what state some people are in.Some people, through the use of the HIV drugs and the hep C drugs, have become unwell just through those things. Weve got guys who are dependent on ageing and ailing families and who need to be assessed for care needs.We need to get out and stop people being punished beyond the obvious impacts of disease for being victims of this disaster."

25 March 2015_1.Title: Scottish ministers issue full apology to victims of contaminated blood scandal
25 March 2015_1.Author: Simon Johnson
25 March 2015_1.chunks: NICOLA STURGEON and her health minister yesterday issued unreserved apologies to thousands of people infected with deadly viruses in the 1970s and 1980s through contaminated NHS blood products.The First Minister emphasised her "absolute determination" to do everything she could to deliver justice and support to those affected, while Shona Robison said it was "one of the greatest health care-related tragedies ever witnessed in this country".The apologies came the day after the publication of the Penrose Inquiry report into the scandal, which was responsible for an estimated 2,000 deaths.Some of the survivors described it as a "whitewash" and burned copies at the launch in Edinburgh.Despite being six years in the making, costing 12million and its report running to 1,800 pages, the inquiry made only one recommendation: that the Scottish Government offer Hepatitis C tests to all those given blood transfusions before 1991.Ms Sturgeon said yesterday: "As First Minister of Scotland, and on behalf of the Government of Scotland and the NHS, I want to take this opportunity to say a very sincere and heartfelt sorry to everyone who has had to deal with the devastating impact of infected NHS blood and blood products. I can't begin to understand the difficulties and the many hardships that individuals and their families have had to contend with. It is important that we apologise to them openly and without reservation. "She said she could understand the feelings of those frustrated or disappointed by the report but she regarded it as the "start of a process of further engagement with those affected rather than an end to the investigations. "In a later statement to the Scottish Parliament, Ms Robison, the health minister, promised to review the schemes which provide financial aid to the victims and their families. A reference group of patients and families is to be set up to ensure they are involved in the review process, she said.The charities Haemophilia Scotland and the Scottish Infected Blood Forum will also receive public funding for the next three years.David Cameron has also apologised for the scandal and offered 25million for a new compensation fund, a sum some of the survivors have described as an insult.7 can't begin to understand the difficulties and many hardships that individuals have had to contend with. '

25 March 2015_1.Title: Penrose Inquiry into contaminated blood out today
25 March 2015_1.Author: Tony Bonnici
25 March 2015_1.chunks: An inquiry into how contaminated blood came to be used on patients who later developed hepatitis C and HIV is to be published today.The Penrose Inquiry examined the cases of hundreds of people in Scotland, many of whom were haemophiliac, from the 1970s and 1980s.The report is the most comprehensive investigation into how contaminated blood and blood products came to be used by the NHS.Many of those infected were children at the time and it is feared that hundreds have already died since receiving the contaminated products.Following demands from campaign groups, the independent public inquiry was set up by the Scottish government to investigate what went wrong and what lessons could be learnt.The inquiry, chaired by Lord Penrose, began six years ago and went on to hear evidence from 60 witnesses over 89 days.Its full findings, expected to run over a number of volumes, will be revealed at an event in Edinburgh today.Lord Penrose is unable to attend the launch because he is said to be seriously ill in hospital.Maria McCann, the secretary to the inquiry, will deliver a statement on his behalf.The Penrose Inquiry, which has cost millions of pounds, came to an end in March 2012. It had been due to report the following year but suffered delays along the way.The inquirys remit was to investigate how the NHS collected, treated and supplied blood.Lord Penrose also scrutinised what patients were told, how they were monitored and why patients became infected.The inquiry was further tasked with identifying any lessons and implications for the future, and making recommendations, but it does not deal with the issue of compensation.The inquiry is the most comprehensive ever conducted anywhere in the UK into what campaigners have dubbed the contaminated blood disaster.The charity Haemophilia Scotland estimates that more than 500 families in Scotland have either lost a loved one to the disaster or are living with the consequences of what happened.Bill Wright, its chairman, has compared the scale of the tragedy to any transport or football stadium disaster, saying he believes at least 5,000 people could have been infected across Britain.He said: In Scotland alone we estimate there are over 200 deaths. If you multiply that up to the UK then it gives you an idea of the scale of the catastrophe. There is a huge disaster right across Britain.Interested parties are expected to travel from all over Scotland, and further afield, for the launch event at the National Museum of Scotland.The UK government is expected to issue a response to the report following its publication.The Scottish government is also expected to respond today ahead of a ministerial statement on the Penrose Inquiry in the Scottish Parliament tomorrow.The campaign group TaintedBlood has said a large group of its members will be in Edinburgh for the launch.It will also have a group delivering flowers, in memory of the victims, to the UK Department of Health.The group said that although the Penrose Inquiry focuses on Scottish events and Scottish patients, the outcome is critically important for people south of the border, since all the events that Lord Penrose is investigating took place before devolution, under a Westminster government.When the publication date was previously announced, Shona Robison, Scotlands Health Secretary, said: The Scottish government instigated the Penrose Inquiry because we are determined to find out exactly what went wrong and what can be done in the future to ensure it can never happen again.Significant improvements have been made to NHS processes since these infections occurred.However, I await Lord Penroses final report with great interest.This is an extremely complex and detailed subject matter, and I am confident that Lord Penroses final recommendations will be invaluable to our health service as we continue to raise the standard of patient care in Scotland.

25 March 2015_1.Title: Blood patients in line for £3bn
25 March 2015_1.Author: No author in byline
25 March 2015_1.chunks: PATIENTS who contracted HIV and hepatitis C after being given contaminated blood products by the NHS could be in line for a 3.5billion payout.On Wednesday a public inquiry will publish its findings on the scandal that saw 5,000 Britons infected in the 1970s and 1980s.It is expected to confirm that, in some cases, doctors failed to tell patients they had contracted the life-threatening viruses.Last night, it was suggested that the Government faces a multibillion-pound bill, with those affected claiming they are entitled to at least 500,000 each.Most were haemophiliacs given a contaminated blood product from the US that was made up of blood from thousands of people, including prison inmates who were more likely to have HIV and hepatitis C.

25 March 2015_1.Author: No author found
25 March 2015_1.chunks:
The Times (London)

March 26, 2015 Thursday  
Edition 1; 
Scotland

Report into blood scandal 'is insult to the dead'; 
Victims feel the inquiry has wasted time, as well as money that could have helped them, writes Michael Glackin

BYLINE: Michael Glackin

SECTION: NEWS; Pg. 2,3

LENGTH: 684 words

Angry victims of the contaminated blood scandal yesterday burnt a copy of Lord Penrose's five-volume, 1,800-page report outside the National Museum, after it had been published.
David Fielding, from Bolton, Greater Manchester, who helped start the fire, said: "The report is an insult to the dead, and to the dying. Frankly I'm devastated; it's been a waste of time and money." Mr Fielding contracted hepatitis B and C following a blood transfusion he was given as part of his treatment for haemophilia in England.
His brother, who was also a haemophiliac and was similarly infected, died more than 20 years ago. 
Haemophilia sufferer Bruce Norval, from the Black Isle, near Inverness, dismissed the report as "too little, too late". The 50-year-old was contaminated with hepatitis C when he was just three years old, after receiving his first dose of blood product to treat haemophilia.
He said: "To say I'm appalled would be an understatement. It's a coat of varnish, an absolute farce. It doesn't take account of evidence from the patients. It does not match the evidence. I've watched friends die waiting for this."
He said the report failed to mention that patients were not told there was a risk of hepatitis from receiving products to help clot their blood.
He added: "Nobody bothered to tell us as individuals the cost of being clotted would be destruction of our livers." Gill Purnell, whose husband Bob died after being infected with contaminated blood, said the minute's silence for those who died, observed before the report was read out, was "a farce". Ms Purnell, who travelled up to Edinburgh from her home in Bristol with her son Edward, said: "It appears to have been a meaningless gesture, which is sadly how I feel about the entire report. It hasn't offered me any closure. My husband died needlessly and no one is responsible. It's adding insult to injury." She added: "My husband was a mild haemophiliac, less than 3 per cent, but he had so many illnesses from the hepatitis C by the time he died it was awful. "He had acute liver failure, they even amputated his leg. I came here for justice, but this is a whitewash. I'm not calling for prosecutions, but after 20 years of battling I do want the truth. My husband's medical records were destroyed."
Ms Purnell said she hoped the Scottish government would move swiftly to offer compensation to victims.
She said: "I think if the Scottish government acts now it will set a precedent for Westminster. I do welcome David Cameron's apology but I had hoped for greater accountability. Things have been covered up for too long."
Colette Wintle, a haemophiliac and former nurse, originally from Blanefield in Stirlingshire, became infected with hepatitis C in her teens after a routine operation to have her tonsils removed at the Glasgow Royal Infirmary. She said: "I'm disgusted. The entire report is a complete and utter whitewash. Penrose spent more of his statement expressing his support for the medical staff than he did for the victims. This has devastated my life."
She added: "The state has a moral responsibility to everyone who has been damaged or killed by what has happened. More than 2,000 people have been killed because of this and many more are dying from it. The government needs to pay hundreds of millions to compensate them all."
Ms Wintle said she now receives chemotherapy in a bid to combat the latter stages of liver disease caused by chronic hepatitis C. "Ultimately I haven't received justice today. My mother went to her grave weeping, blaming herself for all that had happened to me. She trusted the doctors, she had no idea they would give me commercial blood products from outside the UK."
David Tomkins, a haemophiliac from the west Midlands, was diagnosed with hepatitis C in 1989 but was told by his doctors only in 1991.
He said: "Words fail me. They would have been better off just giving the £12 million spent on this inquiry to the victims. Cameron's apology is good, but there is a need for greater transparency about why this happened, and for proper compensation to be paid. None of us asked to end up like this."
