25 March 2015_1.Title: PM's £25m for infected blood victims
25 March 2015_1.Author: No author in byline
25 March 2015_1.chunks: DAVID CAMERON today pledged 25 million to help compensate people infected with deadly diseases in the NHS contaminated blood scandal.The Prime Minister apologised in the Commons on behalf of the Government for the tragedy in the Seventies and Eighties which saw 7,500 victims contract HIV and hepatitis after receiving blood from high-risk donors.An inquiry today recommended anyone who had a transfusion before 1991 should be tested for hepatitis C. The money will support transitional arrangements to a better compensation system.

25 March 2015_1.Title: What is the Penrose Inquiry?
25 March 2015_1.Author: Jennifer Rigby
25 March 2015_1.chunks: Thousands of NHS patients were inadvertently infected with deadly diseases after being given contaminated blood in the 1970s and 1980s - now the Government is set to apologiseWhat is the Penrose Inquiry?Back in the 1970s and 1980s, thousands of National Health Service patients were inadvertently given contaminated blood products in one of the biggest treatment disasters ever.It is estimated that more than 2,000 people died as a result of the contaminated blood, which infected them with deadly diseases like HIV and Hepatitis C.Decades later, and after years of campaigning, the Scottish government announced that it would hold a public inquiry into what went wrong, and who was responsible, in 2008. Scottish judge Lord Penrose, chairman of the Court of Heriot-Watt University, led the inquiry, which has cost 11m. It will report its findings on Wednesday.What will the report include?After six years looking into the scandal, the Penrose Inquiry has produced an 1,800 page report into what happened.It will cover the scale of what took place at the time, as well as what has happened since. Around 7,500 people, many of them haemophiliacs, are known to have contracted HIV and hepatitis after being given blood products taken from high-risk donors such as prostitutes. Some then passed on their diseases to their partners or children, some needed organ transplants, and some died.Experts believe that the full scale of the tragedy is not yet known: the numbers who were infected by the failure but who have not yet been detected or contacted could be tens of thousands.Prime Minister David Cameron is expected to apologise in Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday after seeing the full report.Why has it taken so long?Many people believe that there was a cover-up around the scandal. Some patients report only getting letters about their contaminated blood seven years after treatment - by which time, they say, the chance for compensation was gone.There has been no public inquiry in England yet over the issue, decades on: i n 2009, Lord Archer led a privately-funded inquiry which recommended compensation for patients, but his recommendations were not implemented in full and, until now, there has been no official apology. Some support has been provided for victims and victims' families, but many have struggled and David Cameron has already promised to try and improve the situation for them - however, they say the situation is as bad as ever.Lord Archer accepted at the time that apportioning blame was difficult, suggesting that US suppliers of the contaminated blood products were largely at fault, but he also condemned the slow response of the Government then as well as the "shameful" failure of successive administrations to investigate the tragedy and help patients with the ongoing issues caused by it.The Penrose Inquiry only covers the Scottish NHS; but if David Cameron apologises as expected, those affected may be within their rights to expect wider implications. The Government is not likely to give its full response before the election, but it does intend to put aside extra money for victims.What do the victims of the scandal want?Many of the patients who received contaminated blood are expected to continue their fight for an overhaul of compensation payments following the Penrose report. They also want recognition of their suffering, and accountability from those in charge.One sufferer, Gill Fyffe, recently told The Telegraph : The Penrose Inquiry is about something more important than compensation. It is about accountability. To the thousands of people whose lives have been ruined by careless error, anything less is an insult.If Lord Penrose will demand accountability, and the courage which it costs, he will honour the courage my family have shown, alone and unsupported, for a quarter of a century.

25 March 2015_1.Title: PM's apology fails to quell infected blood victims' fury
25 March 2015_1.Author: JACK BLANCHARD
25 March 2015_1.chunks: DAVID Cameron apologised yesterday to more than 3,000 NHS patients given infected blood in the 1970s and 80s.In total 2,978 people contracted hepatitis C and 78 were infected with HIV in Scotland between 1970 and 1991.The Prime Minister, who announced 25million in support for the victims, said: "To each and every one of those people, I would like to say sorry on behalf of the Government for something that should not have happened. "A report following a six-year inquiry found more should have been done to screen blood for hepatitis C. But in relation to HIV it said that "all that could reasonably be done was done" . Victims dismissed the report as a "whitewash". Glenn Wilkinson, of the Contaminated Blood Campaign, said: "It's just a pile of ashes as far as I'm concerned. We certainly expected a lot more."

25 March 2015_1.Title: Contaminated blood victims deserve better
25 March 2015_1.Author: Shereen Nanjiani
25 March 2015_1.chunks: NO wonder the victims of the contaminated blood scandal feel betrayed.Despite a litany of failures which devastated the lives of more than 3,000 people, they're told nobody was to blame for their suffering.My heart went out to the victims and their families who gathered full of hope to hear the findings of the Penrose Inquiry. The grief and anger was etched on their faces.Some had waited 30 years for answers, many have endured endless pain after contracting Hepatitis C, HIV and AIDS from infected blood, others were there for relatives who didn't live to see this day. What they heard did nothing to alleviate their pain.The human cost of what's been called the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS has been truly devastating.Bruce Norvil was just three years old when he was infected with Hepatitis C.He had to retire at 30, can hardly walk, and is expected to live just another five years.Robert Mackie, who developed AIDS, saw two of his uncles, a cousin, and many friends die. He was left fearing he had passed the virus on to his wife and baby. Robert said: "I have been and am still going through hell. "There are many, many more who are going through hell.What shocked me was the number of people who described being kept in the dark about contracting infections, only discovering almost accidentally years later what was wrong with them. In that time some had passed the infection on to loved ones. How can no one be held to account for that? The report confirmed that although doctors realised patients had tested HIV-positive, they sometimes didn't tell them for up to SIX YEARS afterwards. Yet Lord Penrose, below, concludes they were not "in breach" of the ethics of the time.He said doctors were more "paternalistic" back then and not used to sharing information with their patients as they do today.Does that make them blameless? We've learned from other inquiries that the defence of "it was the culture at the time" no longer washes today.Blaming systemic failures feels like the usual cop out.It took six years to hear the evidence, yet out of 1800 pages the only recommendation was that everyone who had a blood transfusion before September 1991 should get Hepatitis C tests.Talk about stating the obvious.The only criticisms the report made: the practice of taking blood from drug-abusing prisoners went on too long, and more should have been done to screen blood for Hep C. Unanswered questions like why were medical records mysteriously destroyed have still not been addressed. It doesn't feel like justice.In the meantime, many victims are living in poverty because of the crippling cost of paying for their treatment. Their pain goes on but this mustn't be the end of the story. They need substantial financial compensation and they need it soon.It was left to the chairman of Haemophilia Scotland, Bill Wright himself infected with Hepatitis C to try to grasp at some positives: "We are hopeful that with the goodwill of politicians in Scotland we can sort this," he said, but he warned: "we will look dimly on any trying to score points with small amounts of cash".The victims and their families had to fight to get this inquiry, they've waited 30 years to even have their suffering acknowledged. The politicians owe it to them to sort this. It's already too late for many who have died, don't leave it too late for those who are still suffering.

25 March 2015_1.Title: TIME FOR THE GOVERNMENT TO ACT
25 March 2015_1.Author: DAVID WILKES
25 March 2015_1.chunks: IT WAS a remedy that became a killer at the centre of a huge public health scandal.Factor VIII was a clotting agent developed in the 1970s for haemophiliacs. Their condition means their blood fails to clot, and a minor cut can put sufferers at risk of bleeding to death.US companies made Factor VIII from blood from donors including drug addicts and vagrants infected with hepatitis C and HIV who had been paid cash. The unscreened products were imported because Britain did not supply enough 'home-grown' product.A quarter of a century ago, the Daily Mail campaigned to highlight the plight of haemophiliacs infected with contaminated blood products as part of their NHS treatment.The Mail's coverage included telling the story of Allen White, then 36, a haemophiliac who contracted Aids through a blood clotting agent, under the headline: 'A blindness to moral justice has abandoned this dying man. Surely his family deserves better. 'Mr White, a married father of two from Yorkshire, had to give up his job as a computer systems designer because of his deteriorating health. The article asked: 'Why doesn't the Government do the honourable thing about what the Haemophilia Society describes as "the biggest tragedy in NHS history"? 'After pressure on the Government to recognise the unique circumstances of the case, 1,200 haemophiliac Aids victims were promised 42million compensation in 1990. Regardless of whether they were taking legal action, those affected and their families got lump sums ranging from 21,000 to 60,500. Mr White said he would accept the offer to give him 'peace of mind' that his family would not be left penniless. But others said it was not enough, and accused the Government of 'buying off the embarrassment' of a court case.Scotland is the only part of the UK to hold an inquiry into the scandal. The Penrose Inquiry, which gave its findings yesterday, said 478 people acquired the hepatitis C virus from blood product therapy in Scotland and 2,500 acquired the virus from blood transfusion in Scotland between 1970 and 1991. Sixty patients acquired HIV from therapy with blood products and 18 from blood transfusion in Scotland.The Penrose Inquiry did not have the power to summon witnesses from outside Scotland - and has done little to abate the anger of many victims.Mark Ward, of Peacehaven, East Sussex, who contracted hepatitis C and HIV from contaminated blood he received as a child, said yesterday he had been treated as nothing more than a 'lump of meat to be experimented on'.He told BBC that the treatment was 'so dirty and filthy, and the places it was being sourced... anything could have been in that blood', adding: 'We were used as objects of research. 'Three men who contracted hepatitis C from blood transfusions have started a legal case to challenge the support available to them, and it is likely further legal action will follow. Daily Mail

25 March 2015_1.Title: Deadly toll is shocking
25 March 2015_1.Author: No author in byline
25 March 2015_1.chunks: HUMAN COST A SHOCKING death toll of children and adults infected with lethal diseases during NHS treatment was revealed.The inquiry found 478 people with haemophilia caught Hepatitis C between 1970 and 1991 before screening began.At least 193 are now dead.And of 60 haemophiliacs given HIV, 39 are known to have passed away.Another 18 blood transfusion patients were also given HIV and at least 15 of these are now dead.

25 March 2015_1.Title: Government to apologise for contaminated blood scandal
25 March 2015_1.Author: No author in byline
25 March 2015_1.chunks: The Government will apologise to thousands of NHS patients who were infected with deadly diseases by doctors using contaminated blood products.A formal statement of regret over the scandal that cost more than 2,000 lives will be given to the House of Commons later this week.It is understood the official apology, similar to those given in the wake of Bloody Sunday and the Hillsborough football disaster, follows the personal intervention of David Cameron.The statement will follow the publication on Wednesday of the Penrose Inquiry, a six-year report into the scandal.Nearly 8,000 people contracted HIV and hepatitis C in the Seventies and Eighties after being given imported blood from high-risk donors including prisoners and prostitutes. They were mainly haemophiliacs who were given a product to help their blood clot.Many patients died from the diseases after inadvertently infecting their partners and children, while others were left chronically ill and destitute.One Westminster source told the Mail on Sunday: "There's a feeling we need to right a historic wrong. This is a failure of even greater magnitude than Hillsborough." In the wake of the report, hundreds of patients are expected to launch fresh compensation claims against the UK and Scottish governments.

25 March 2015_1.Title: David Cameron apologises over Penrose Inquiry findings and creates new £25m fund for victims
25 March 2015_1.Author: Ben Riley-Smith and Auslan Cramb
25 March 2015_1.chunks: Prime Minister creates new funding to ensure victims can get funding from a single body rather than a variety of charitiesDavid Cameron has said sorry on behalf of the government to each and every one of the victims of the contaminated blood scandal and pledged a new 25 million fund to help them get compensation.The Prime Minister apologised in the Commons for the pain and suffering felt by those inadvertently infected by the NHS with deadly diseases during the 1970s and 1980s.Mr Cameron said it was right those who have suffered got an apology from the state after being asked about the scandal during his final Prime Ministers Questions before the election.The new money will help create a single body for victims of the scandal to get compensation. The current set-up, where victims can gain compensation from a number of different charities, had been criticised by campaigners for being over-complicated.It came alongside the publication of a 1,800-page report by the Penrose Inquiry, initiated by the Scottish Government, which has spent six years looking into the scandal.Around 7,500 people, many of them haemophiliacs, are known to have contracted HIV and hepatitis after being given blood products taken from high-risk donors such as prostitutes. Some 2,000 have Britons died.The 12 million investigation, chaired by Lord Penrose, contained just one recommendation that the Scottish Government should offer hepatitis C tests to all those given blood transfusions before 1991.It described the saga as the stuff of nightmares, but concluded that little could have been done differently at the time.The findings prompted a furious reaction in Edinburgh, with some sufferers setting fire to a copy of the five-volume report.However, Bill Wright, of Haemophilia Scotland, himself a sufferer, said that although he was disappointed by the report it had made the case for proper compensation for all those affected.He welcomed the politicians apologies, but described the 25 million interim offer from Mr Cameron towards a new compensation package, as an insult.In an emotional address, he assured those who said the inquiry was a cover-up that it was by no means the end of a cruel catastrophe.In Westminster, Mr Cameron told MPs: "To each and every one of those people I would like to say sorry on behalf of the Government for something that should not have happened. "He added: "While it will be for the next government to take account of these findings, it is right that we use this moment to recognise the pain and the suffering experienced by people as a result of this tragedy. "It is difficult to imagine the feelings of unfairness that people must feel at being infected with hepatitis C and HIV as a result of a totally unrelated treatment within the NHS. "Opposition leader Ed Miliband said Labour would act on the findings if the party wins on May 7, telling the Commons: "We undertake today to carry these recommendations forward as well. "Scotland Health Secretary Shona Robison also apologised on behalf of the NHS and the Government in Scotland.

25 March 2015_1.Title: It's too little, too late, says victim who was contaminated at just 3 years old
25 March 2015_1.Author: No author in byline
25 March 2015_1.chunks: FOR haemophilia sufferer Bruce Norval, the report is too little too late.The 50-year-old was contaminated with hepatitis C when he was just three years old after receiving his first dose of blood product to treat haemophilia.He said: 'To say I'm appalled would be an understatement. It's a coat of varnish, an absolute farce. 'It doesn't take account of evidence from the patients. It does not match the evidence. I've watched friends die waiting for this.' Mr Norval (pictured), who lives in the Black Isle near Inverness with his wife Christine, said the report fails to take into account the fact that patients were not told there was a risk of hepatitis from receiving products to help clot their blood.He said: 'We were not told there was a 100 per cent risk of hepatitis. Nobody bothered to tell us as individuals the cost of being clotted would be destruction of our livers. 'A few of us might have made different choices.'

25 March 2015_1.Title: Five patients of dentist test positive for hepatitis C
25 March 2015_1.Author: No author in byline
25 March 2015_1.chunks: FIVE patients of a dentist who was accused of breaching infection control measures have tested positive for hepatitis C.Everyone who had been treated by Desmond D'Mello, of Daybrook Dental Practice in Gedling, Notts, was offered tests after it emerged that they might have been put at risk of infection from blood-borne viruses.NHS England confirmed that 4,526 patients were tested, with five of these found to have hepatitis C. None were diagnosed with hepatitis B or HIV.Dr Vanessa MacGregor, a consultant in communicable disease control at Public Health England East Midlands, said that because blood-borne viruses are already present in the community, some positive test results were always expected. She added that, because there are multiple ways in which these infections can be transmitted, it was not possible to identify how those with hepatitis C caught it. "Effective treatments are available for all blood-borne viruses, which is why it is important to identify anyone who may have been at risk of infection, so treatment can be started if necessary," she saidMr D'Mello is being investigated by the General Dental Council and was given an interim suspension last August.Any of his former patients who have not yet been tested were urged to contact their GP if they were concerned.4,526 Number of patients of Desmond D'Mello who were tested for blood-borne viruses including hepatitis B and C and HIV

25 March 2015_1.Title: Victims of poisoned blood transfusions demand answers
25 March 2015_1.Author: Lucy Holden
25 March 2015_1.chunks: Victims of a blood scandal that infected hundreds of patients with HIV and hepatitis C have demanded a memorial to remember all those who died as a result of the treatment.The long-awaited findings of an inquiry by Lord Penrose are to be published today with victims and their families demanding answers to find out how hundreds of haemophiliacs and other patients were infected during the 1970s and 1980s.Campaigners also want compensation and a memorial to show that victims and their families are not being ignored.Bruce Norval, 50, has haemophilia and was contaminated with hepatitis C when he was three years old.He said: Our campaign is about getting proper compensation for victims and families. I want the legislation elements to be looked at. I want a memorial more than anything: 2,000 haemophiliacs have died so far. We need a memorial we need somewhere for our families to go and be able to know that the country is not ignoring what happened to us.Mr Norval said the benefits system that victims had to go through was a massive struggle and only compounds their feeling of worthlessness.Much of the infected blood given to haemophiliacs, as well as those having regular blood transfusions, came from Scottish and American prisons, where the rates of infection were high.It has been claimed that as many as 300 people died as a result of the scandal, with thousands of people given transfusions at the time. The contaminated transfusions stopped when blood was heat treated to eradicate viruses.Lord Penroses report is expected to outline for the first time how many people were infected and to shed light on their suffering.Mr Norval, who lives with his wife Christine on the Black Isle, near Inverness, can hardly walk. He said: My condition now means the only sensation my nerves pick up is pain it feels like bumblebees are trying to fly backwards through my fingers.I go through periods of stress and depression, but that depression has turned to anger. I want answers. I want an apology and I want proper compensation.He was first treated for haemophilia with blood transfusions as a boy. He said: Every treatment the doctor gave me, every needle I had put in my arm, was poisoning me with another dose of the virus.Little boys fall over a lot and so I was at one point seeing the doctor weekly. By the time I was 12, I was so sick that the doctors said my liver looked like I was drinking a bottle of whisky a day. It was that bad.Things only got worse. By the time he was 15, Mr Norval had lost a lot of weight and found that he could not concentrate in lessons at school. He was moved from the top sets to the bottom sets in every subject.He said: Then when I started work I struggled to hold down a job no matter how hard I tried. Id get sick and not be able to get out of bed and the harder I pushed myself to work, the worse I got.When Mr Norval was 30, he was forced to take early retirement on health grounds, which made him feel worthless, he said. I felt like I was no use to anyone. As a father and a husband I felt completely disempowered and I got angrier and angrier.His wife, Christine, 47, has just been told that she has breast cancer and said the results of the report cant come soon enough.She said: Bruce has been very, very ill and its had a huge impact on our family. For a long time we couldnt take a mortgage out because we didnt know whether he was going to live or die. It sounds awful, but it was an awful time.My daughter was so worried about him that she ended up in a mental health hospital she wouldnt come home from school because she was worried her daddy would be dead.

25 March 2015_1.Title: Agony of scandal's victims
25 March 2015_1.Author: Greg Christison
25 March 2015_1.chunks: THE Penrose Inquiry heard several victims deliver emotional accounts of how the scandal had devastated their lives.While most of those infected with Hepatitis C and HIV were haemophiliacs who were given contaminated blood products, that wasn't the case for all.A baby boy was infected with HIV after being given a blood transfusion when just minutes old.The inquiry heard from his mother - given the alias Amy to protect their identity - in June 2011.Two weeks past her due date, Amy was induced at Dundee's Ninewells Hospital, and following difficulties, she was given an emergency caesarean section.When she woke from her general anaesthetic, she was told her newborn was being treated in the special baby care unit, where he had been given a transfusion.He had become distressed during the complicated birth and had struggled to breathe, suffered renal failure and had fluid on the brain.He eventually made a good recovery, but six months later the family received a lifechanging knock at the door. Their GP revealed the tot had been infected with HIV. "To be told this was really devastating," Amy said.Throughout his childhood, the boy suffered various related illnesses, he bruised easily, lost weight and had a poor appetite.Despite this, Amy said he "sailed through school", before going on to sit a computer course at college.Now an adult, he stays in a flat with his brother, but does not have a job and struggles to lead a normal life.Although his mother revealed he is "happier in himself", she added: "He doesn't really do a lot at all. He is in the house quite a lot. "And he has never had a girlfriend. He just sort of keeps himself to himself. "I'm really bitter and angry about what has happened. "I feel it should never have happened."

25 March 2015_1.Title: Skeletons from the past revealed by Penrose report
25 March 2015_1.Author: Ben Borland
25 March 2015_1.chunks: THERE have been a number of public inquiries in recent years into scandals from the 1970s and 1980s. In fact, the steady emergence of skeletons from the national closet has been a recurring theme of David Cameron's first term as Prime Minister.The Bloody Sunday Inquiry set the tone in June 2010, reporting that British soldiers had in fact fired the first shots on that fateful afternoon in Londonderry in January 1972.Mr Cameron, then just a few weeks into his job, responded by offering a public apology in the House of Commons. "What happened, should never ever have happened," he said.Ever since then, the ghosts have continued to rise up and confound our cosy view of the past - Jimmy Savile and the fact he was aided and abetted by the BBC and the NHS; the Hillsborough Inquiry and the recent admission that police failures led to the deaths of 96 football fans; the still unfolding horrors of an Establishment paedophile ring operating with apparent immunity across the whole of the UK.For anybody who, like me, grew up during the 1970s and 1980s, it has been a shocking few years. The rose-tinted days of our youth now appear more like a rotten age of cover-ups, corruption and abuse.Yesterday, the Penrose Inquiry dragged yet another scandal from those disastrous decades into the public eye. Thousands of people were infected with Hepatitis C and HIV through NHS blood products, with hundreds dying.ONCE again, the Prime Minister found himself offering a public apology in the House of Commons. Echoing his words from five years ago, he said: "To each and every one of these people I would like to say sorry on behalf of the government for something that should not have happened. "Scottish Health Secretary Shona Robison also apologised, describing the events as a "terrible tragedy", and she will no doubt go even further when she makes a full statement to Holyrood at 2pm today.Already, tens of thousands of Scots who received a blood transfusion before 1991 have been given the terrifying news that they should get themselves checked for Hepatitis C or HIV without delay.Westminster's Department of Health is to provide a further 25million in compensation, while the next UK Government will be under severe pressure to set up a much larger fund.The victims themselves believe that a settlement in the region of 500,000 each is a "reasonable" and "conservative" estimate of what each infected person or their families deserve.If that were to be the case - and a similar inquiry in the Republic of Ireland resulted in average payments of 600,000 per person - then the overall bill is likely to run to billions.However, any compensation will have to be agreed at a future date as former High Court judge Lord Penrose did not make any recommendations in this area.Victims and their families could even have to resort to legal action to get a fair deal, adding further heartache, expense and delay to their already broken lives.However, the absence of compensation was not the reason why some furious campaigners shouted "whitewash" and burned copies of the Penrose Report on the streets of Edinburgh yesterday. They were expecting answers as to how this was allowed to happen; most of all, they were expecting doctors and health officials from the 1970s and 1980s to be named and shamed.After all, the six-year inquiry was delayed for many months so that warning letters could be sent to those who faced significant criticism in the report.In the event, Lord Penrose did not apportion any personal blame and indeed concluded there was "nothing which could have reasonably have been done" to prevent infections.He even said that health offi-cials in Scotland had fared relatively well when compared to other countries around the world. Ms Robison also stressed the "international" angle, and indeed she was correct; the contaminated blood products came from the USA, where donors were not properly vetted and infected people all over the world.HOWEVER, in particular, Penrose was set up to investigate the situation in Scotland - and the evidence heard by the inquiry raised disturbing questions.Why, for example, did doctors not tell patients they had contracted Hepatitis C or HIV, allowing them to infect their partners in some cases?Lord Penrose blamed a "paternalistic" attitude among the Scottish medical profession, yet surely this was something far more serious than simply an old-fashioned approach?Some campaigners believe patients were deliberately infected and used as "guinea pigs", an astonishing allegation which they are still determined to prove. Also, if nothing could have been done to prevent this tragedy, how did journalists working for ITV World In Action get hold of the story as long ago as 1975 - many years before the infected blood products were banned?The Penrose Report is a shocking indictment and yet, just like all those other scandals from the 1970s and 1980s, the suspicion remains that we have not heard the last of this particular issue. 'The evidence raised disturbing questions'

25 March 2015_1.Title: 'Dirty' dentist five get Hep C
25 March 2015_1.Author: No author in byline
25 March 2015_1.chunks: FIVE former patients of a dentist filmed breaking hygiene rules have tested positive for hepatitis C. Health chiefs urged all the 22,000 patients of Desmond D'Mello, 60, to get screened and 4,526 have been checked.There is no evidence the five caught hepatitis at Mr D'Mello's surgery in Daybrook, Notts, where he was filmed failing to wash his hands or change equipment between patients. However, the results are being passed to the General Dental Council which is investigating Mr D'Mello.

25 March 2015_1.Title: Way clear for new indyref
25 March 2015_1.Author: Jason Allardyce
25 March 2015_1.chunks: WESTMINSTER would not stand in the way of a second independence referendum despite concerns it could destabilise the economy, according to the UK government's legal adviser on Scotland.Former Lib Dem leader Lord Wallace, the advocate-general for Scotland, signalled that a future government would again agree to a referendum being underpinned by statute to give it legitimacy.Wallace piloted legislation through the Lords to give last year's referendum the legal standing and make the result binding as Holyrood does not have the power to hold its own legally binding vote on the issue.Asked whether Westminster would give legal basis to a second referendum, he told The Sunday Times: "Well, I think the precedent is there as to what happened and, as you well know, in the law precedent counts a lot. "However, he urged the SNP to stick to the suggestion made by previous leader Alex Salmond that another referendum would not be held for a generation. "To do otherwise is very destabilising, it's not healthy," said Wallace.SNP strategists, who are considering the possibility of another referendum within five Continued on page 2 uu Tainted blood uu Continued from page 1 who was infected with hepatitis C through his treatment for haemophilia in the 1980s, said: "The battle to get this inquiry was long. Those infected have been through years of pain and suffering while waiting for it. Too many have not survived while waiting. "The story doesn't stop with this inquiry. It is only a couple of chapters on the road to justice, when a new brighter volume can hopefully start. Lord Penrose's findings need to be followed by action. "A spokesman for the Scottish government said: "We will make a full response to the findings of the Penrose inquiry as soon as possible following publication, giving full consideration to any recommendations contained in the report. "Penrose is not expected to attend the launch of the report in Edinburgh as he is seriously ill. His recommendations will be read by Maria McCann, the inquiry secretary.

25 March 2015_1.Title: ‘Dirty’ dentist patients contract hepatitis C
25 March 2015_1.Author: ANDREW PARKER
25 March 2015_1.chunks: Hes accused of not sterilising equipmentFIVE patients of an alleged dirty" dentist have been diagnosed with hepatitis C, it emerged yesterday. Around 22,000 people treated by Desmond DMello were alerted in November after he was secretly filmed allegedly failing to change medical gloves between patients or properly sterilise equipment.More than 4,500 were given blood tests for HIV and other infections and the five were newly-diagnosed with hepatitis C a cause of major liver disease.It is still uncertain whether or not they contracted it at Mr DMellos Daybrook Dental Practice in Nottingham.Dr Doug Black, Medical Director for NHS England in Nottinghamshire, said: We had a duty to inform patients and offer the option for them to be tested.Were pleased these individuals have been identified and offered clinical support to aid their well-being. "Mr DMello, 60, is being investigated by the Care Quality Commission and the General Dental Council.Many former patients are taking legal action.His practice is under new ownership.

25 March 2015_1.Title: Infected haemophiliac has seen 3 family members die
25 March 2015_1.Author: Dean Herbert
25 March 2015_1.chunks: HAEMOPHILIAC Robert Mackie has endured the twin agonies of being infected with HIV and watching three members of his family die as a result of the contaminated blood scandal.The 64-year-old contracted HIV in 1984 but was not told about it until 1987.Mr Mackie, of Peebles, Peeblesshire, was infected along with three family members after all were given an infected batch of Factor VIII, a product that helps blood to clot.The father-of-two is one of only two people left alive out of 16 treated with the same batch at the Edinburgh Royal Infirmary. Mr Mackie, who also got Hepatitis C from the infusion, saw friends and family have their lives destroyed by Aids before it killed them.Luckily, he did not pass either disease on to his wife, Alice.In 1984, Mr Mackie got a throat infection which wouldn't clear up and was told he had a virus.In fact, it was his body reacting to the HIV virus.That December, Mr Mackie, his uncles, cousin and friends were told at a meeting at the hospital that some haemophiliacs in the area had developed HTLV3 - HIV's original name.Three years later, he was told he was one of those who had been infected with HIV.He learned he had contracted Hepatitis C 16 years later, and his illnesses have left him housebound.Before being infected, he hoped to work as a ghillie.Mr Mackie said: "As far as I'm concerned, these are criminal actions. ""It's unacceptable. I could have infected my wife, family, friends. "And, fortunately, I was not promiscuous. The risks were horrendous."

25 March 2015_1.Title: Prem star’s son expelled after 15 kids stabbed with needle
25 March 2015_1.Author: KATIE HODGE
25 March 2015_1.chunks: Footie lad kicked out as children tested for HIVA SCHOOL has expelled a top Premier League stars son and another pupil after 15 children were stabbed with a blood-testing needle.The 14-year-old was kicked out of the exclusive school in South East England along with the pal.They jabbed pupils with a diabetes pen, used by sufferers to test blood sugar levels.The children jabbed with the diabetes pen had to be tested for HIV, hepatitis and other blood-related infections.A source suggested that the footballers son pricked three pupils with the device.A school source said: Its been dreadful. The whole school is very upset about it.I should imagine the boy is absolutely distraught along with everyone else concerned. "It is thought the pen, which has a fine needle for testing the blood sugar levels of diabetes sufferers, belonged to a pupil.The two boys are said to have found it on a desk then jabbed it into others as a joke.Police were called over the episode at the school in South East England, which is a favourite with celebrities.Parents were urged to have their children blood tested. All the results came back negative.The source said: Its a fantastic school second to none. Its a sensitive situation.What they have done theyve probably done with a heavy heart but they think its the right course, not only for the boy but for the school and everybody else concerned. "The boys dad has played abroad but made his reputation in the Premier League.A source close to him claimed his son believed the diabetes device was an electric shock pen and that he was zapping students as a joke.A spokesman for the school, which educates kids from toddler age to sixth-form, said: We can confirm an incident took place last month involving a diabetic testing pen.The incident was extremely concerning and as soon as we became aware of it all parents of pupils involved were contacted and given advice from public health experts.We also spoke to the local police who, we understand, have now closed this incident. "Wise to be cautiousBy CAROL COOPER, Sun DoctorWITH a needle injury the main concerns are the blood-borne infections Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C and HIV.There are other illnesses that can potentially be transmitted through a needle injury such as glandular fever, malaria and some rare viruses.Of all these diseases, the most likely to be transmitted is Hepatitis B, followed by Hepatitis C and then HIV.You dont get symptoms for Hepatitis B for a long time and the incubation period is between 40 and 160 days which is why it would have been so important to look into this incident.If you think how many times people get injured at school and really nothing much happens, then hopefully this will be one of those incidents.

25 March 2015_1.Title: Prem star's son sparks HIV scare at school after 'stabbing 15 kids with used needle'
25 March 2015_1.Author: Tom Rawle
25 March 2015_1.chunks: A PREMIER League star's 14-year-old son has been kicked out of one of the UK's top schools after allegedly stabbing as many as 15 kids with a used blood test needle.The shocking incident sparked a serious health scare with pupils being forced to be tested for HIV and Hepatitis B and C.It is reported that two students one said to be the footballer's son found the sharp diabetes pen on a classroom desk at the exclusive school in South East of England.They then allegedly jabbed other students with the needle which is used to take blood to read sugar levels in what the boys thought was a harmless prank.Police were called to the scene after the incident last month and the school is said to have expelled the youngster and his friend, also 14.A school spokespersonA spokesman for the school told The Sun: "We can confirm an incident took place last month involving a diabetic testing pen. "The incident was extremely concerning and as soon as we became aware of it all parents of pupils involved were contacted and given advice from public health officials. "We also spoke to the local police who, we understand, have now closed this incident. "The results of the blood tests returned negative and the police have chosen not to take any further action.

25 March 2015_1.Title: WISE TO BE CAUTIOUS
25 March 2015_1.Author: CAROL COOPER
25 March 2015_1.chunks: WITH a needle injury the main concerns are the bloodborne infections Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C and HIV. There are other illnesses that can potentially be transmitted through a needle injury such as glandular fever, malaria and some rare viruses. Of all these diseases, the most likely to be transmitted is Hepatitis B, followed by Hepatitis C and then HIV. You don't get symptoms for Hepatitis B for a long time and the incubation period is between 40 and 160 days which is why it would have been so important to look into this incident. If you think how many times people get injured at school and really nothing much happens, then hopefully this will be one of those incidents.

25 March 2015_1.Title: HIV SCARE AT TOP SCHOOL AS BOYS JAB PUPILS WITH NEEDLE
25 March 2015_1.Author: CLAIRE DUFFIN AND SARAH HARRIS
25 March 2015_1.chunks: TWO boys of 14 have been expelled from a 15,000-a-year public school after pupils were stabbed with a needle.The 15 youngsters were given blood tests for HIV and hepatitis as a precaution following the classroom 'prank gone wrong'.It is understood the boys, from Claremont Fan Court School in Surrey, found a small device used by diabetics to prick the skin when checking blood sugar levels. They then reportedly jabbed their classmates.Once teachers became aware, they ordered emergency tests for a number of blood viruses as a precaution. All came back negative.Police were called following the incident last month but took no action.A spokesman for the school in Esher told The Sun: 'We can confirm that an incident took place last month involving a diabetic testing pen. 'It was extremely concerning and as soon as we became aware of it all parents of pupils involved were contacted immediately and given the advice received from public health experts. 'We also spoke to the local police who, we understand, have now closed this incident. 'While the risk of infection was low or negligible, children affected were advised to have blood tests, all of which proved negative. 'A Surrey police spokesman said officers had been notified of an incident at the school on February 5, adding: 'Following enquiries no further police action was required. 'Set in the historic landscaped grounds of the Claremont Estate, the school caters for 740 boys and girls, aged two to 18. Fees are up to 15,000 a year.It began life as two schools, one for girls and the other for boys. Both were established by teachers who were Christian Scientists. The girls' school, called Clear View, was set up in 1922 but outgrew its premises and moved to the Claremont Estate in 1931.The boys' school, called Fan Court, was established 11 years later and the two amalgamated as Claremont Fan Court School in 1978.On its website, it says it was 'founded on Christian values' but welcomes children 'from all faiths and none'.It adds: 'Our ethos recognises, cares for and values the potential of every child. 'With this recognition comes the expectation of high academic achievement and participation in sporting and cultural activities. 'Past pupils include television presenter Michaela Strachan and Joyce Grenfell, the actress and comedienne who died in 1979.The Claremont Estate was once home to Clive of India, who commissioned landscape architect Capability Brown to build him the present house and remodel the park.The school's headmaster, JonathanInsall-Reid, could not be reached for comment last night.c.duffin@dailymail.co.uk Daily Mail

25 March 2015_1.Title: Schoolboy, 8, tries to blow up balloon – turns out to be used CONDOM
25 March 2015_1.Author: Tom Rawle
25 March 2015_1.chunks: AN INNOCENT eight-year-old was told to quickly wash his hands and rinse his mouth out after he was found trying to blow up a USED condom.The boy had been playing with what he thought was a balloon when a teacher found it in his gob.Teachers chucked the condom away before it could be tested.And now there are fears the youngster could have contracted some form of sexually transmitted infection .The child's mum said: "When she took the 'balloon' out of his mouth, it was a used condom. "He's at risk for HIV, Hepatitis C, Herpes, Gonorrhea, Chlamydia. "The boy will now be subjected to ongoing tests throughout the year to make sure he is clear of disease.The child's mumDespite the incident happening on the grounds of Bennett Elementary School in Colorado, US, the institution has failed to take responsibility for the accident.School officials described the horrifying finding as "regrettable" but say they are not at fault for the matter.Superintendent Dennis Veal reacted to the situation, saying: "I guess I'd leave that up to the liability insurance as far as what coverage we have. "The boy's mum has argued that the authorities are not willing to pay for the treatment because it's taxpayers money.She argued: "I feel like I'm a taxpayer. 25 March 2015_1.Title: A betrayal to make you weep: That 1,800 Britons have been 'murdered' by tainted NHS blood is bad enough, but the grotesque way the victims have been denied justice is the scandal of our age
25 March 2015_1.Author: GUY ADAMS FOR THE DAILY MAIL
25 March 2015_1.chunks: * Mike Dorricott died from liver cancer after contracting deadly hepatitis C* 47-year-old one of hundreds to die having had contaminated NHS blood* Drug companies took blood from prostitutes, vagrants and drug addicts* Britain has provided only some of those given terminal illnesses by contaminated blood with payments, of between just 20,000 and 63,000Mike Dorricott died a week ago yesterday at the Freeman Hospital in Newcastle, in a room filled with those he loved most: his mum Jennifer, sister Jane, wife Ann and their grown-up daughters Sarah and Ellie.Aged just 47, he had spent his final days propped up in bed with tubes up his nose, drifting in and out of consciousness. His kidneys and liver were failing, his stomach and lungs were infected and he was in the terminal stages of liver cancer.When the end came, early that morning, it felt almost like a release. Mikes skin had long since turned yellow from liver failure, and he could no longer breathe unaided. A larger-than-life character known for his wicked smile and cheeky laugh, he had been reduced first to speaking in a whisper, then not speaking at all.Mike died peacefully, says a close friend, Sue Threakall. He was a wonderful man and they made sure he was told about all the people thinking of him and praying for him. He knew how much he was loved.It was, to all outward appearances, a dignified and peaceful farewell. Yet along with the sorrow there was also a real anger in that room, which continues to this day. For an appalling sense of injustice overshadowed Mr Dorricotts fate.It stretched back to 1996, when Mike, a successful businessman who lived in the Surrey commuter belt, had received life-changing news.A blood test, ordered by his doctor after he complained of fatigue, revealed that he had hepatitis C, an incurable virus which causes long-term damage to major organs.The condition, known as the silent killer because it can lie undetected for years, had already left him with severe cirrhosis, an irreversible scarring of the liver (often suffered by alcoholics). Without a transplant, Mike was likely to be dead in a few years. Even with one, his life would be seriously curtailed.The hepatitis wasnt just a case of simple bad luck. As Mike would soon discover, he had just become the latest blameless victim of perhaps the most egregious public scandal in modern British history.At its centre was contaminated blood or, more accurately, contaminated blood products.Between 1970 and 1991, against the recommendation of many experts, the NHS routinely imported such products from overseas.It would later emerge that many of them were supplied by drug companies that sourced blood by paying people in high-risk groups, such as prostitutes, vagrants and drug addicts, to donate it. The products were riddled with the blood-borne viruses hepatitis C and HIV.In a second terrible oversight, these highly dangerous products were then administered to British patients without being screened for the viruses, despite warnings from the World Health Organisation. Innocent patients were duly infected as a result. About 7,500 people, of whom roughly two-thirds were haemophiliacs, are now known to have been given hepatitis C during this period.Many are no longer with us, including Body Shop founder Dame Anita Roddick, who was infected by a blood transfusion after the birth of her daughter Sam in 1971. She died in 2007, aged 64, from a brain haemorrhage caused by the disease. According to an estimate by MPs, who debated the scandal in January, as many as 35,000 victims could have hepatitis C, which is often undetected for years, without yet being aware of it.Around 1,500 of the 7,500 confirmed hepatitis victims have also contracted HIV. Many then unwittingly passed it to their spouses. In the Eighties, when most of these transmissions occurred, Aids was a virtual death sentence. Three-quarters of them died.More than 1,800 people have so far lost their lives from contaminated NHS blood. Mike, a mild haemophiliac who was given a blood-clotting product called Factor VIII during a childhood hospital visit, is the most recent addition to their tragic ranks.By death toll alone, this makes it the biggest man-made disaster in postwar British history. Indeed, the leading medical scientist Lord Winston has called contaminated blood the worst treatment scandal in the history of the NHS.Numbers are only part of the terrible picture, however. For, as the Dorricott family and thousands like them will tell you, the most shameful aspect of this entirely preventable tragedy has been the appallingly shabby treatment of victims.Having been betrayed by the greed of drug companies that sold the blood which infected them, and the incompetence of public officials who purchased it, these innocent victims have faced years of cover-up and obfuscation by the very institutions that failed them.A culture of heartlessness and an abject refusal, across several tiers of government, to accept responsibility has resulted in thousands of childhoods ruined, families destroyed and careers derailed.Many of these blameless men and women, already facing terminal illness, have suffered the indignity of being forced into financial hardship by their condition, without being adequately compensated by the governments that caused it.Mike, formerly a high-flying executive with United Biscuits, is a case in point. In 2008, he found himself physically unable to work after having a second liver transplant.Then, at the age of just 40, having worked hard all his adult life, he was forced to forgo his comfortable salary for a relatively tiny pension that meant he was unable to service his mortgage. The family house in Farnham was sold and the Dorricotts moved to a smaller home in Yorkshire. The inheritance he had dreamt of leaving to his children disappeared.I wont be there for my wife and daughters, he said, shortly before his death. I wont get to walk them up the aisle. I wont be there to see our grandchildren. My wife will be on her own. The only thing that might mitigate this is a financial package, from the Government, that makes my family secure for the future.But no such package has ever been provided. Unlike in Ireland, where victims were individually assessed for losses and have received an estimated average of 275,000 each, Britain has provided only some of those given terminal illnesses by contaminated blood with payments, of between 20,000 and 63,000 provided strict conditions were fulfilled.To access funds, claimants must go through a humiliating and often baffling process of applying for grants or payments from one of five confusingly organised quangos and charitable trusts, in a system recently described by MPs as not fit for purpose.Unlike in France, Canada and Japan, not one bungling official has been prosecuted, held to account or named as being responsible. Successive governments have failed to apologise to the victims or offer adequate compensations.While other national tragedies, from Bloody Sunday to Hillsborough, have been the subject of hard-hitting and expensive official inquiries, successive health secretaries have refused to hold a proper investigation into contaminated blood. Only in Scotland has even the slightest effort been made to hold officials to account.There, a six-year investigation by Lord Penrose, a judge best known for conducting the public inquiry into the Equitable Life scandal, was published last month. It cost almost 12 million and ran to 1,800 pages, but was immediately dubbed a whitewash by campaigners, who walked out of its unveiling and promptly burnt a copy in front of TV crews.Penrose did not apportion any blame and made just one recommendation: that people who felt at risk should be tested for hepatitis. He said bungling officials should be judged by conditions that prevailed at the time rather than by todays standards.Take, in this context, the experience of Tony Farrugia, now a married father-of-three from Cambridgeshire, who lost his father Barry and two uncles, Victor and Dave who all suffered from haemophilia to viruses contracted from tainted blood-clotting product Factor VIII. Tony was 13 years old in 1984 when his dad learnt he had hepatitis C and 14 when his father was also declared HIV positive. Barry died of Aids the next year, aged just 37, when Tony was 15.Days later, social workers arrived at the family home and took Tony and his twin brother David (who were estranged from their natural mother) into care. The bereaved boys were then sent to separate homes, more than 100 miles apart. It would be a decade before they were reunited.It caused so much hurt and pain, says Tony. A family was split up because of this. Weve never had an apology, or any formal support from the government. Ive applied for help and been rejected every time. There has been no compensation for the years we lost. I was only given counselling last year. Its a betrayal.How does Tony feel at being told his experience was a natural by-product of conditions that prevailed at the time?Revolted, he says.Or consider the case of Sally Vickers, a 54-year-old former civil servant from Portsmouth, who was infected with hepatitis C during a blood transfusion in the early Eighties.She now has severe rheumatoid arthritis and cirrhosis of the liver from the condition, lives in acute pain and has been unable to work since the late Nineties. Once an independent career woman, today she lives on benefits in a one-bedroom council flat.I cant stand not working. Im not a lazy person, its just a terribly debilitating disease, she says. Ten years ago I was given eight years to live. Im 54 and already on borrowed time. Well, it just sucks.Hepatitis C, which struck in her 20s, prevented her from having children. She would love to travel in what remains of her life, but even if she could afford a holiday the condition has left her unable to get insurance. It has robbed me of so much, and Ive had nothing in return, she says.There are hundreds like Tony and Sally, and their tales are all heartbreaking. Speak to some of them, as I did this week, and you will be saddened and outraged in roughly equal measure.The scandal that sealed their fates stretches back to the early Seventies when health officials, faced with increased demand for blood products because of medical advances, decided to start importing them from the U.S. and Canada.This posed obvious dangers. Under UK law, blood donation was (and still is) required to be voluntary rather than paid-for, to prevent people from high-risk groups who are desperate for cash from signing up. Yet the NHSs new commercial suppliers were all paying for their product.Officials nonetheless chose to approve the imports. So, across the Atlantic, drug firms began sourcing blood from wherever they could find someone in need of a fast buck.Some of these new NHS suppliers created so-called skid row donor clinics, frequented by drug addicts, vagrants and prostitutes. Others set up shop in Haitian slums. One Canadian company even took blood extracted from Russian corpses and re-labelled it as having come from Scandinavian donors.In the U.S. state of Arkansas, then governed by Bill Clinton, who now tours the world promoting Aids prevention, prisons developed a multimillion-dollar industry by selling prisoners blood.Inmates were paid a small amount for giving blood twice a week. They were like little cows, one Clinton aide said later.It is hard to think of a more high-risk group. Yet their tainted blood flowed into Britain for years, despite apparent efforts to stem the trade.As early as 1975, Lord Owen, then Health Secretary, became concerned about imported blood and told the House of Commons that he wanted the NHS to be self-sufficient as soon as possible. But civil servants failed to act.By the late Seventies, NHS officials were slowly becoming aware of viruses in their donor pool. But they did little to ensure public safety. In May 1983, researchers warned the Department of Health that it should ban U.S. imports of blood-clotting agents. The warning was never followed up.In August that year, the first recorded haemophiliac died from Aids. Yet countless patients continued to be infected. Although the U.S. finally banned prison blood in 1984, exports were allowed to continue and, incredibly, the NHS continued to buy it.Even when safer, heat-treated products were introduced in the late Eighties, NHS doctors were allowed to choose whether they wanted to use them. Many decided to use up old, contaminated supplies first. Hundreds more people died as a result.Britain didnt start to screen blood properly until 1991. By then, at least 16 Western countries had already acted. Again, no apology or explanation for this oversight has ever been made.Equally appalling in the 25 years this scandal has been public knowledge has been the abject failure by all governments to try to put things right.Officials have also displayed appalling heartlessness.One Department of Health memo, leaked five years ago, showed civil servants attempting to work out how to spend the money the NHS might save from the deaths of hundreds of haemophiliacs (whom they appeared to regard as a drain on resources). Of course, the maintenance of the life of a haemophiliac is itself expensive, it began. Those who are already doomed will generate savings which more than cover the cost of testing blood donations.Vaccines that could have prevented deaths were ruled too expensive. Paperwork was lost. Repeated calls for public inquiries were rejected on cost grounds.Then, after victims set up a privately funded one in 2007, the Department of Health withheld vital papers, citing confidentiality, and refused to give evidence.A couple of years later, Caroline Flint, then Public Health Minister, caused further outrage by claiming that key documents detailing the scandal had been destroyed in error by a junior member of staff.Several victims who have tried to sue also found that crucial medical records had gone suspiciously missing.Joseph Peaty was one of 75 pupils at Lord Mayor Treloar College, an experimental boarding school in Hampshire for people with haemophilia, where all pupils were regularly given Factor VIII. He and almost all his peers contracted HIV, and 46 are now dead.A few years ago I discovered that they still had frozen blood samples from school, so I decided to get them tested to find out when exactly I contracted HIV, he says.At first I was told that it was too costly. Then, after I got the money together, they told me the samples had mysteriously vanished.It is symptomatic of the utter disrespect with which we have all been treated.For the past six years, many victims have clung to the hope that Lord Penroses report would give them what passes for closure, and lead to a formal government apology and a proper compensation package for them and their loved ones. Again, they have been cruelly disappointed.Mike Dorricott, like so many before him, took that disappointment to his grave. Two days before he died, he telephoned his friend Sue Threakall to ask about the reports long-awaited publication.Although Mike struggled to speak, it was clear that even at this stage all he wanted to know was whether the Government had finally agreed on proper compensation so that he could die with peace of mind, knowing his family would have the financial security that contaminated blood had taken away from them, she says.I couldnt tell my lovely, brave friend the truth that there was no compensation, no guarantee of security. Instead, I said simply that some money had been allocated pending a proper settlement. Whether he fully understood this I have no idea.And so, for thousands like Mike, the betrayal continues.

The Guardian

February 25, 2015 Wednesday 6:56 PM GMT 

Rough ride and a face like a wet weekend

SECTION: GLOBAL

LENGTH: 284 words

You quote Shashank Joshi of the Royal United Services Institute as saying "the decision to send trainers is shaped by the imperative to avoid escalation" ( The UK move in Ukraine is largely symbolic but raises a question - what happens next?, 25 February). So an escalation of the conflict is an attempt to avoid escalation? Will PodmoreLondon 
· Last week we were watching Wolf Hall. "Cor," I said to my husband, "you would think Mark Rylance would get tired of going round with a face like a wet weekend. If the wind changes it will get stuck like that." Then you publish a picture of him in Farinelli and the King ( Review, 24 February), and I see that it has! Margaret HarveyBridport, Dorset
· Once the Guardian has abolished the discriminatory "women and children" cliche ( Letters, 25 February), could it please act against "brutal murder" ( Lured by Isis: young girls who revel in brutality are offered cause, 21 February). There's no such thing as a nice, kind murder and calling a murder "brutal" is simply stating the obvious. Michael RankLondon
· The news that the 2022 Fifa World Cup is to be played in December ( Report, 25 February) is great news for England's top footballers. Now they will get the mid-season break they crave and be able to spend Christmas with their families. Gerard GordonWest Kirby, Wirral
· You inform us that a 31-year-old man caught hepatitis C from "a rougher-than-normal" sexual encounter ( Hunting the silent killer, 25 February). I'm sure I and other readers would be grateful to know how "rough" is "normal". Bob FrostDeal, Kent
